trendNotes.label: Group 14
trendNotes.essay: Descending from Carbon (C) to Silicon (Si) exhibits the classic inner-core shielding effect. The additional 3s²3p² shell increases the atomic radius significantly (+58%), causing valence electrons to experience a diminished effective nuclear charge (Z_eff). C–C bonds drastically outlast weaker Si–Si bonds. Silicon's network is an intrinsic semiconductor.

trendNotes.label: Group 17
trendNotes.essay: Fluorine to chlorine is the textbook halogen step: both want one electron, but fluorine is a much fiercer oxidizer because it is smaller and more electronegative. Chlorine still disinfects and forms a wide oxo-anion ladder (ClO⁻ to ClO₄⁻) that fluorine barely copies.

trendNotes.label: Group 1
trendNotes.essay: Lithium to sodium keeps the ns¹ pattern, but sodium’s extra shell makes the atom larger and easier to oxidize. Lithium’s small Li⁺ ion polarizes anions and dominates battery electrochemistry; sodium remains the everyday salt cation.

trendNotes.label: Group 18
trendNotes.essay: Neon and argon are both closed-shell gases, but argon is denser and far more abundant in air. Neither forms ordinary molecules; argon’s chemistry, like krypton’s, is a specialist topic, while neon is the lighting benchmark.

elements.name: Hydrogen

summary.beginner:
Hydrogen is the lightest element, and it is number 1 on the periodic table. You meet it in water, and it is the fuel that makes the Sun shine.

Its symbol is H. At room temperature hydrogen is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a nonmetal. It does not look or act like iron or copper. On the periodic table it is in row 1, column 1. In class those are called period 1 and group 1.

A hydrogen atom is the simplest atom there is: one proton in the center and one electron around it. When hydrogen joins oxygen it makes water, and stars shine by turning hydrogen into helium.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral hydrogen atom has 1 electron, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Hydrogen is a nonmetal gas in period 1 and group 1. Its atom is one proton and one electron, written 1s1.

The electron configuration is 1s1. Every electron is in the first shell: 1 electron. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

In water and in most acids the oxidation state is +1. A metal hydride is the exception, where hydrogen is the negative ion H-.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Hydrogen (Z = 1) has the ground-state configuration 1s1. The common nucleus is a single proton, so the Balmer series was the first spectrum a simple atomic model could explain.

Protium and deuterium are stable, and tritium is radioactive.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Hydrogen: say the name, write H, find Z=1 on the table, note the family (Nonmetal), and connect it to one real use — makes water and fuels stars.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Hydrogen: electron configuration 1s1, Typical oxidation states: +1. It sits in group 1. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. H–H single bond; proton is the nucleus.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Hydrogen: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Balmer lines; isotopes protium, deuterium, tritium If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated as inflammable air; later named hydrogen by Lavoisier.

elements.history:
In 1766 Henry Cavendish collected a gas from metals and acids and called it inflammable air. He showed that burning it produced water. Antoine Lavoisier later named it hydrogen, from the Greek for water-former, and listed it as an element.

The common isotope, protium, is a single proton. Deuterium was identified in 1931 and tritium in 1934. In 1913 the Balmer lines of hydrogen became the first spectrum explained by Bohr’s model of the atom.
elements.howDiscovered:
Henry Cavendish collected a gas by pouring acid onto iron, zinc, and tin and catching what bubbled off. The gas burned. In 1781 he exploded measured amounts of it with air and found that the product was water, and that the gas’s weight accounted for the water’s weight.

That closed the argument that the gas was a modification of ordinary air. Antoine Lavoisier repeated the combination, named the gas hydrogen, and put it on his list of elements. The discovery was a weighed reaction, not a new mineral.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Almost every hydrogen nucleus was made in the first few minutes of the Universe, once it had cooled enough for protons and neutrons to stick and before it cooled too far for them to fuse. The common isotope, protium, is that leftover proton. Deuterium was made in the same brief window. Stars destroy deuterium, so the deuterium still around is a fossil of those minutes.

Stars burn hydrogen into helium. They do not replace the cosmic supply. Tritium is a different, short-lived nucleus, knocked together by cosmic rays, and it is not part of the primordial stock.

trivia.title: Inflammable Air from Acids
trivia.summary: Henry Cavendish trapped the gas that metals give off in acid and found that it burned. What the flame left behind was the real surprise.
trivia.story: Henry Cavendish preferred a quiet bench and a balance to a crowd. When metals sat in acid, a gas bubbled off, and he caught it instead of letting it drift away. A flame set the gas alight, so he called it inflammable air and measured how it behaved. He then burned a weighed portion and collected the product, expecting some sharp or sooty residue. What he found was water. His account in 1766 made inflammable air a substance in its own right, years before a classroom name was attached to the letter H.

trivia.title: The Name Water-Former
trivia.summary: Antoine Lavoisier wanted chemical names to describe what substances actually did. A burning gas that produced water gave him a chance to prove the point.
trivia.story: Antoine Lavoisier was stripping old language out of chemistry and replacing it with names that reported facts. He knew the inflammable air from the English experiments, and he knew that burning it in oxygen produced water. He built the name hydrogen from Greek words meaning water-former. The name carried a claim: the gas was an element, and water was a compound, not an element itself. On the list of simple substances that he published, hydrogen had a place of its own. Students still write that choice every time they put an H at the start of a formula.

trivia.title: Fire at the Landing Field
trivia.summary: A famous passenger airship reached New Jersey in 1937 with a crowd waiting below. The landing turned into a fire before anyone could step safely away.
trivia.story: The Hindenburg had crossed the ocean and was easing toward its mast in New Jersey on a May evening in 1937. People on the field looked up at the huge silver shape. Then flame ran over the covering, and the ship fell in fire and wreckage while the landing crew scattered. For years afterward, investigators debated what made the first spark. They did not debate the lifting gas. The cells had been filled with hydrogen, which burns, because the helium that does not burn had not been made available for that ship.

trivia.title: Heavy Hydrogen in the Residue
trivia.summary: Harold Urey believed ordinary hydrogen hid a heavier twin in tiny amounts. Finding it meant staring at what was left after most of the sample was gone.
trivia.story: Nearly every hydrogen atom is the lightest atom there is, one proton and one electron. Harold Urey was convinced that a heavier stable twin existed and was simply scarce. In 1931 he took liquid hydrogen and let the bulk of it boil away, so that anything heavier would linger in the last fraction. He examined the light from that remainder. Extra lines sat where he had predicted a heavy isotope should announce itself. He named it deuterium, and hydrogen was no longer a single kind of atom but a small family.

trivia.title: A Balloon Ride on Hydrogen
trivia.summary: Soon after hot-air balloons left the ground, Jacques Charles prepared a silk balloon filled with a lighter gas. Paris was about to watch a different kind of flight.
trivia.story: Hot air was not the only way to rise. Jacques Charles filled a silk balloon with hydrogen, the light gas already known to catch fire, and in 1783 he stepped into the basket above Paris. The globe lifted because the gas inside weighed far less than the air it pushed aside. Crowds saw a man travel on a laboratory curiosity. Charles landed famous, and hydrogen had a public use at last. The same lightness that carried him remained a risk, since a flame and a torn bag could undo the triumph in a moment.

applications.title: Water
applications.body: Hydrogen is one of the two elements in water. Two hydrogen atoms join one oxygen atom to make the liquid in rain, rivers, and every drink.

applications.title: Stars
applications.body: The Sun is mostly hydrogen. Stars shine because hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium and release energy.

applications.title: Industry
applications.body: Factories combine hydrogen with nitrogen to make ammonia, the starting point for most fertilizer. Hydrogen is also added to oils, and it burns easily enough to be a fuel.

isotopes.note: Protium
Deuterium
Tritium

elements.astro: The Balmer series is the fingerprint of stellar atmospheres.

reaction.beginner: Hydrogen burns with oxygen to make water.
reaction.intermediate: A highly exothermic combustion used as a teaching reaction and a rocket reaction.
reaction.advanced: Illustration of a known reaction. ΔH is large and negative; it is not a lab result from this device.

sample.body: Pure hydrogen, sealed in glass. The gas has no color of its own, so the sample looks like a clear tube. This is the element by itself, not a compound.

elements.name: Helium

summary.beginner:
Helium is element 2, a gas that almost never joins with other elements. You meet it in party balloons and in the machines that keep scientific tools extremely cold.

Its symbol is He. At room temperature helium is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a noble gas. Left alone, it almost never joins other elements to make compounds. On the periodic table it is in row 1, column 18. In class those are called period 1 and group 18.

A helium atom has two electrons, and that pair fills its only shell. Because the shell is full, helium does not grab or share electrons the way oxygen or chlorine does.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral helium atom has 2 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Helium is a noble gas in period 1 and group 18. The 1s shell is full, which is why helium forms almost no compounds.

The electron configuration is 1s2. Every electron is in the first shell: 2 electrons. Oxidation states are not listed for this entry.

It has the lowest boiling point of any element. Below 2.17 K the common isotope becomes a superfluid, a liquid that flows with almost no friction.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Helium (Z = 2) has the ground-state configuration 1s2. Both electrons occupy 1s, so the first shell is closed and the ionization energy is the highest on the table.

Liquid helium is a quantum fluid, not an ordinary cold liquid.

Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Helium: say the name, write He, find Z=2 on the table, note the family (Noble gas), and connect it to one real use — party balloons and cryogenics.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Helium: electron configuration 1s2, Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. It sits in group 18. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. closed 1s² shell; almost no compounds.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Helium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; lowest boiling point; quantum fluid below 2.17 K If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: First seen as a solar emission line; later isolated on Earth by Ramsay.

elements.history:
During the 1868 solar eclipse, Pierre Janssen and Norman Lockyer saw a yellow line in the solar spectrum that matched no known element. Lockyer named it helium, from the Greek helios, the Sun. William Ramsay isolated the gas on Earth in 1895 from the uranium mineral cleveite.

Helium stayed a laboratory curiosity until natural-gas wells supplied it in quantity. Below 2.17 K the liquid becomes a superfluid, a discovery of the 1930s that made helium the benchmark quantum liquid.
elements.howDiscovered:
During the solar eclipse of 18 August 1868, Pierre Janssen passed the light of a solar prominence through a spectroscope and saw a yellow line close to, and not identical with, the sodium lines. Norman Lockyer found the same line in ordinary sunlight and argued it belonged to an element not yet found on Earth.

William Ramsay closed the search in 1895. He dissolved the uranium mineral cleveite in acid, collected the inert gas that came off, and sparked it. The yellow line matched the solar one. The element had been identified by a wavelength before anyone held a sample.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Most of the helium in the Universe was made in the first few minutes, about a quarter of ordinary matter by mass, while the cosmos was still hot enough for nuclei to fuse and then cooled below that point. Stars add a further share. Hydrogen fusion in their cores builds helium, and winds, planetary nebulae, and supernovae return some of it to space.

The helium in a party balloon has a separate biography. It is the alpha particles from uranium and thorium decaying in the crust, trapped in natural-gas wells. That gas is radiogenic. The helium in the Sun is the primordial and stellar kind.

trivia.title: A Yellow Line in Sunlight
trivia.summary: An eclipse gave astronomers a brief look at the Sun's outer glow. A yellow line in that light matched no element they could name.
trivia.story: The eclipse of 1868 briefly hid the bright disk of the Sun and let observers study the faint outer glow. Pierre Janssen, watching from India, saw a yellow line in the spectrum that was not the familiar line of sodium. Norman Lockyer found the same line and refused to force it onto an element already known. He argued that the Sun contained a new element, and he named it helium, from the Greek word for the Sun. The claim was bold, because no bottle of the gas existed on Earth. For years helium was a streak of light and a name, and nothing a chemist could weigh.

trivia.title: Helium Locked in Cleveite
trivia.summary: William Ramsay collected gas from a uranium mineral while hunting something else. The yellow line that appeared had already been seen, far from any bench.
trivia.story: Helium had been claimed in the Sun, and Earth still seemed to have none of it. William Ramsay turned to cleveite, a uranium mineral known to release a gas. In 1895 he collected that gas and sent an electric spark through a tube of it. The yellow line that shone was the solar line Lockyer had given to helium. The element named for the Sun had been sitting inside a rock. Ramsay's sample ended the search: what astronomers had only seen during an eclipse could now be held, carefully, as a gas on Earth.

trivia.title: The Lift That Would Not Burn
trivia.summary: Hydrogen could lift an airship, and it could also feed a fire. Engineers went looking for a gas that was almost as light and much less eager to burn.
trivia.story: A light gas is a gift to an airship and a worry to everyone aboard if the gas burns. After hydrogen ships were lost to fire, builders wanted lift without a flame they could not stop. Helium began to come out of certain natural-gas wells in amounts a factory could use, not only a few bubbles in a spectrum tube. It does not burn, and it almost never reacts. When designers could obtain it, they accepted a slightly heavier ship in exchange for a gas that would not feed a blaze. Helium had left the eclipse notebooks and become a material with a job.

trivia.title: The Liquid That Creeps Upward
trivia.summary: Cool helium far enough and it stops behaving like any liquid in a kitchen or a classroom beaker. The change forced physicists to describe a new kind of flow.
trivia.story: Helium is reluctant to become a solid, and even as a liquid it can shock a careful observer. Below 2.17 K the liquid is a superfluid. It pours with almost no friction, slips through cracks that would hold back ordinary liquid, and creeps as a thin film up and over the lip of a cup. Physicists in the 1930s had to accept that this was not a trick of dirty glassware. Helium, found first as a line in sunlight, had become the clearest everyday picture of quantum behavior in a bottle.

trivia.title: The Well That Would Not Light
trivia.summary: Drillers in Kansas struck gas and gathered a crowd for a celebration flame. The flame would not take, and the embarrassment sent samples to a university.
trivia.story: At Dexter, Kansas, early in the twentieth century, a new natural-gas well was reason for a public party. Someone tried to light the stream, and the fire died. The gas would not burn, which made the well look useless and the celebration foolish. Samples went to chemists at the University of Kansas, who separated the mixture and found a worthwhile amount of helium in it. A solar element was underground in quantity. The well that spoiled a lighting ceremony became a hint that helium could be mined, not only admired in an eclipse.

applications.title: Balloons
applications.body: Helium is lighter than air and, unlike hydrogen, it does not burn. That is why party balloons and some scientific balloons are filled with it.

applications.title: Keeping things cold
applications.body: Liquid helium is colder than any other liquid. MRI magnets and many physics experiments use it to stay near absolute zero.

applications.title: Shielding gas
applications.body: Welders sometimes use helium around a hot weld so oxygen in the air cannot spoil the metal. The gas does the job by refusing to react.

elements.name: Lithium

summary.beginner:
Lithium is element 3, a soft silver metal. The rechargeable battery in a phone or a laptop is the place most people meet it.

Its symbol is Li. At room temperature lithium is a solid. It is an alkali metal: soft, and quick to react with water. On the periodic table it is in row 2, column 1. In class those are called period 2 and group 1.

Lithium is light, and it reacts with water, so the pure metal is stored away from air. In a battery it is there because its atom gives up one electron very easily.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral lithium atom has 3 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Lithium is a solid alkali metal in period 2 and group 1. It is the lightest alkali metal, and the atom loses its one outer electron to form Li+.

The electron configuration is [He] 2s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

That outer electron is in 2s, beyond a filled 1s shell. The Li+ ion is small, which is why lithium behaves a little differently from sodium and potassium.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Lithium (Z = 3) has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s1. The low ionization energy of the 2s electron makes lithium a strong reducing agent.

Its small cation polarizes anions, which is the start of its distinctive organometallic chemistry.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Lithium: say the name, write Li, find Z=3 on the table, note the family (Alkali metal), and connect it to one real use — rechargeable-battery metal.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Lithium: electron configuration [He] 2s1, Typical oxidation states: +1. It sits in group 1. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. ns¹ alkali; very low ionization energy.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Lithium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; forms Li⁺ with a small, polarizing cation If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found in petalite; Davy isolated the metal soon after.

elements.history:
Johan August Arfwedson found a new alkali in the mineral petalite in 1817, working in Berzelius’s laboratory. Humphry Davy isolated a small amount of the metal by electrolysis soon afterward.

Berzelius named it lithium, from the Greek lithos, stone, because it turned up in rock rather than in plant ash like sodium and potassium. The metal stayed rare until the twentieth century, when its light ion became the working metal of rechargeable batteries.
elements.howDiscovered:
Johan August Arfwedson analyzed petalite from Utö in 1817 and, after removing silica and alumina, was left with a sulfate that was neither sodium nor potassium. The new alkali gave a different flame and different salts. Berzelius’s laboratory announced it that year.

Humphry Davy then passed a current through the moistened alkali and obtained a small amount of metal, enough to show that the earth could be reduced the way potash and soda had been. The discovery was the new alkali in the mineral. The metal came second, and in traces.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Lithium is fragile, and stars destroy it more readily than they make it. A little lithium-7 comes from the Big Bang. More of both lithium-6 and lithium-7 is chipped off carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen when cosmic rays strike interstellar gas. Novae and giant stars may add some lithium-7, which is then easy to burn away.

Old stars show less lithium-7 than the Big Bang calculation predicts. That shortage is still an open argument between the nuclear rates and the surfaces of the stars. The lithium in a battery is this scarce, mixed yield.

trivia.title: An Alkali Hidden in Petalite
trivia.summary: A pale mineral arrived in Berzelius's laboratory, and Johan August Arfwedson analyzed it as he would any new rock. The alkali he found matched neither soda nor potash.
trivia.story: Johan August Arfwedson was at work in Stockholm, in the laboratory of Jöns Jacob Berzelius, when he took up the mineral petalite. His analysis in 1817 showed an alkali with the habits of soda and potash and the identity of neither. The new material had come out of a stone, not out of the ash of plants. He could form its salts and study them. The metal itself stayed locked away, too reactive for the tools he was using. Even so, a third alkali metal had declared itself in a rock that did not look important at all.

trivia.title: Named for the Stone
trivia.summary: Sodium and potassium were known from plant ash, so a different origin deserved a different name. Berzelius looked at the mineral and chose a Greek word for stone.
trivia.story: The older alkali metals carried their biographies in their names, one linked to natron and one to potash. This new alkali had shown up in petalite and in other hard minerals. Berzelius named it lithium, from the Greek lithos, stone. The word told other chemists where to look, and where not to look. It was not another plant ash to be boiled out of a cooking pot. The name was a small map of the discovery: search the rocks, not the fireplace.

trivia.title: A Bead from the Current
trivia.summary: Salts of the new alkali were not the same thing as the metal. Humphry Davy turned an electric current on the melted compound and waited for a glint.
trivia.story: Arfwedson had proved that a new alkali was present, yet a white salt does not shine like a metal. Humphry Davy, fresh from freeing sodium and potassium with electricity, tried that method on lithium compounds. He passed a current through the molten material. A small amount of light, silvery metal separated, barely enough to see and far too little to manufacture. The bead was still decisive. Electrolysis had done what roasting and acids had not, and lithium could be pointed to as a metal, soft, light, and impatient to react.

trivia.title: A Salt Tried on Mania
trivia.summary: Lithium had been a mineral curiosity for more than a century when a psychiatrist tried its salts on a very different problem. The patients were not chemists.
trivia.story: Nobody mining petalite expected a medicine. The Australian psychiatrist John Cade turned to lithium salts while treating mania, the state in which mood and energy race and judgment frays. In 1949 he reported that patients in his care became calmer. Other doctors repeated the work and learned to watch the dose, because an amount that steadies can become a poison if it is too large. The element named for stone had entered the hospital as a salt, never as the wild metal. A jar of lithium metal would still be a fire hazard, not a pill.

trivia.title: Too Light, Too Eager
trivia.summary: A piece of lithium feels wrong in the hand if you expect every metal to be heavy. Water is where the quiet appearance breaks down.
trivia.story: Lithium metal is pale, soft enough to cut, and so light that a lump surprises anyone who has only handled iron or copper. On water it will not lie still. It skates, fizzes, and may catch fire, which is why a teaching sample stays under oil until the moment it is shown. That angry reaction is the hazard of the pure element. Years later the same atoms, trapped as ions inside a sealed battery, became the working core of rechargeable cells. The speck in the classroom and the battery in a pocket are one element, kept in very different cages.

applications.title: Batteries
applications.body: The rechargeable battery in a phone or a laptop moves lithium ions from one side to the other. That is the use most people meet, and the mining that supplies it is a real landscape.
applications.credit: NASA / METI / AIST / Japan Space Systems, public domain

applications.title: Medicine
applications.body: A few medicines are lithium salts, prescribed and dosed by a doctor. That is a compound in a pill, not a piece of the metal.

applications.title: Alloys
applications.body: Small amounts of lithium make some aluminum and magnesium alloys lighter and stiffer. The pure metal is stored away from air and water.

elements.name: Beryllium

summary.beginner:
Beryllium is element 4, a light gray metal that is stiff for its weight. It is mixed into special alloys for parts that must be light and strong.

Its symbol is Be. At room temperature beryllium is a solid. It is an alkaline-earth metal. These metals react, but less wildly than the alkali metals beside them. On the periodic table it is in row 2, column 2. In class those are called period 2 and group 2.

Beryllium dust is harmful to breathe, so it is not a metal for a classroom dish. The atom holds its two outer electrons more tightly than lithium holds its one.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral beryllium atom has 4 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Beryllium is a solid alkaline-earth metal in period 2 and group 2. Both outer electrons are in 2s, and the usual ion is Be2+.

The electron configuration is [He] 2s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

The Be2+ ion is tiny and polarizing, so many beryllium compounds are covalent rather than simple salts. The metal itself has an unusually high melting point for group 2.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Beryllium (Z = 4) has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s2. The diagonal relationship with aluminum shows up in the covalent chemistry of Be2+.

A filled 1s core and an empty 2p set leave the atom electron-deficient in many compounds.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Beryllium: say the name, write Be, find Z=4 on the table, note the family (Alk. earth), and connect it to one real use — light structural alloys.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Beryllium: electron configuration [He] 2s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It sits in group 2. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. ns² alkaline earth; +2 chemistry.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Beryllium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; high melting point for a group-2 metal If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from beryl as a sweet-tasting oxide, hence the name.

elements.history:
Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin recognized a new earth in beryl and emerald in 1798. The salts tasted sweet, so the element was first called glucinium. The name beryllium, from the mineral beryl, is the one that lasted. Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy isolated the metal independently in 1828.

Beryllium remained a specialist metal. Its stiffness and low density later made it a structural material in aerospace and in X-ray windows, always with care, because the dust is toxic.
elements.howDiscovered:
Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin dissolved beryl and emerald in acid, removed the silica, and precipitated a hydroxide that was not alumina. The salts of the new earth tasted sweet, which is why the first name was glucinium. In 1798 he showed that the earth from both gems was the same.

The metal waited thirty years. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy, working separately, heated the chloride with potassium and obtained a gray powder. The discovery of the element was the sweet earth. The isolation was the potassium reduction.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Beryllium is not a product of the Big Bang in any amount that survives, and it is not an ash of ordinary fusion. Stars burn it. Nearly all of it is made by cosmic rays splitting larger nuclei, carbon and oxygen above all, in the gas between the stars.

Beryllium-9 is the only stable isotope. Its scarcity in the crust is the scarcity of that chipping process. Geology can concentrate it into beryl. It cannot invent a supply the stars did not leave.

trivia.title: Sweet Salts from the Gem
trivia.summary: Emerald and beryl yielded a new earth to Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin, and the salts of that earth tasted sweet. The name suggested by the taste was not the one that survived.
trivia.story: Beryl and emerald were already famous as gemstones when chemists began to ask what earths they contained. In 1798 Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin separated a new earth from them. Salts made from it tasted sweet, and the element was first called glucinium, from a Greek word for sweet. Tasting an unknown salt was an old habit and a risky one, later abandoned. The sweet name hung on in some countries for years. The name that lasted was beryllium, taken not from the taste but from beryl, the mineral that had started the story.

trivia.title: Freed in the Same Year
trivia.summary: The new earth sat on the shelf for decades before it became a metal anyone could see. Two chemists, far apart, finished the job within the same year.
trivia.story: An earth in a bottle is a promise, not a metal. Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy each took up beryllium compounds, one in Germany and one in France, without a shared bench. In 1828 both reduced a beryllium salt with potassium and obtained the metal. The pieces were gray, light, and easy to overlook beside iron or copper. Neither chemist could fairly be erased from the story. Textbooks still name them together, which is a quiet way of admitting that the isolation was a tie.

trivia.title: Lamp Dust in the Lungs
trivia.summary: Early fluorescent lamps used beryllium compounds in their coatings, and the work looked modern and clean. The powder that drifted off those coatings did not stay harmless.
trivia.story: Beryllium is light and stiff, and industry was quick to find tasks for it. One of the first put beryllium compounds into the coatings of fluorescent lamps. Workers who mixed and applied the powders breathed dust too fine to notice. Some of them later developed berylliosis, a lung disease that scars breathing and does not politely go away. The lamps had been sold as a bright idea. The illness showed that a quiet silver metal can be dangerous as a dust even when a solid piece looks safe on a cloth.

trivia.title: Stiff, Light, and Transparent
trivia.summary: Glass stops too many X-rays, and many strong metals are far too heavy for the job designers had in mind. Beryllium offered a strange combination of talents.
trivia.story: After the dust danger was understood, beryllium could be reserved for work that needed its odd virtues. It weighs little and still resists bending, so aerospace builders later used it where a part must be stiff and cannot be heavy. It also lets X-rays through more readily than ordinary metals. Thin windows of beryllium became the way out for X-rays from a sealed tube. The element never turned into pots and pans. It remained a specialist metal, machined with ventilation and handled so that the powder did not become the next person's illness.

trivia.title: Glucinium Against Beryllium
trivia.summary: French chemists kept a name that honored a sweet taste, while others insisted on the gemstone. Journals and classrooms had to live with both until one of them faded.
trivia.story: A split name is a nuisance in a science that depends on shared words. Glucinium, recalling the sweet salts, remained the favorite in France, and the symbol Gl showed up in print. Elsewhere the element was beryllium, recalling beryl and emerald. Students translating a paper had to stop and ask which metal was meant, though there was only one. Over time the mineral name won and glucinium slipped into old books. A taste had been a striking clue in 1798, and a bad thing to immortalize once chemists admitted that the tongue is not a testing instrument.

applications.title: Light alloys
applications.body: Beryllium is stiff and very light, so it goes into parts for spacecraft and into special alloys that must not sag.

applications.title: X-ray windows
applications.body: A thin beryllium window lets X-rays out of a tube while holding the vacuum in. The metal is transparent to those rays in a way glass is not.

applications.title: A hazard to respect
applications.body: Beryllium dust and fumes can scar the lungs. The useful alloys are made in controlled shops, not sanded on a workbench at home.

elements.name: Boron

summary.beginner:
Boron is element 5, a hard brittle element that is not quite a metal. You meet it in heat-proof glass and in some laundry powders.

Its symbol is B. At room temperature boron is a solid. It is a metalloid, between the metals and the nonmetals in the way it behaves. On the periodic table it is in row 2, column 13. In class those are called period 2 and group 13.

Boron does not look like a typical metal, and it does not conduct electricity the way iron does. Its atoms often share electrons in a way that leaves them short of a full set.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral boron atom has 5 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Boron is a solid metalloid in period 2 and group 13. The configuration is 2s2 2p1, and boron is electron-deficient in many of its compounds.

The electron configuration is [He] 2s2 2p1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 3. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

Boranes share pairs of electrons across more than two atoms. In glass, boron oxide is part of the network that keeps the material from cracking when it is heated.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Boron (Z = 5) has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s2 2p1. Planar BX3 compounds contrast with tetrahedral borates.

The empty p orbital on boron accepts a pair of electrons, which is the Lewis-acid side of its chemistry.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Boron: say the name, write B, find Z=5 on the table, note the family (Metalloid), and connect it to one real use — borosilicate glass and detergents.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Boron: electron configuration [He] 2s2 2p1, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 13. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. electron-deficient bonds; allotropes.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Boron: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; planar BX₃ vs tetrahedral borates If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from borates; Davy independently reduced boron compounds.

elements.history:
Borax was known in antiquity as a flux. In 1808 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard, and Humphry Davy working separately, reduced boron compounds and obtained an impure element. Henri Moissan prepared a much purer sample later in the century.

The name comes from borax, itself from the Arabic buraq. Boron’s electron-deficient bonding, and the contrast between boric acid and the boranes, became a set piece of inorganic chemistry.
elements.howDiscovered:
Borax and boric acid were already industrial chemicals. In 1808 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard heated boric oxide with potassium metal and obtained a dark, impure solid. Humphry Davy, in the same year, electrolyzed moistened boric acid and got a similar material.

Both products were badly contaminated, and critics said so. The evidence that a new element was present was chemical: the oxide could be reduced to something that was not carbon, silicon, or a known metal, and it regenerated boric acid. Henri Moissan’s later reductions gave a much cleaner sample. The 1808 work is the discovery because both camps produced the same new substance.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Boron sits with lithium and beryllium. Quiet fusion does not leave it behind. Cosmic rays knocking pieces off carbon and oxygen supply most of it. A second channel matters for boron-11: neutrinos pouring out of a collapsing stellar core can knock a fragment off carbon-12.

Boron-10 is mainly the cosmic-ray product. The two isotopes therefore record different mixes of the two channels, which is why their ratio is a clue to what happened in the gas before the Sun formed.

trivia.title: Carried Under the Name Buraq
trivia.summary: Long before boron was called an element, workshops bought a white salt that helped metals flow. The salt's old name never really left the element.
trivia.story: Borax moved along trade routes when no chemist was hunting elements. Goldsmiths used the white crystals as a flux, so that hot metal would flow and join, and glassworkers knew the same salt. Much of it came from dry lake beds, packed and sold as a tool rather than a mystery. Arabic speakers called it buraq, and European tongues turned that into borax. When an element was finally pulled from borax compounds, it inherited the salt's name. Boron is the workshop word, shortened and kept.

trivia.title: Dark Lumps and a Quarrel
trivia.summary: Paris and London both attacked boron compounds in 1808, and both produced something dark and imperfect. Each laboratory wanted credit for an element still mixed with leftovers.
trivia.story: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard were reducing boron compounds in Paris while Humphry Davy worked apart in London. In 1808 both efforts produced a dark material, mostly a new element and still badly impure. Davy used an electric current, while the French pair used potassium to drag boron out of its oxide. Each camp announced a discovery, and critics answered that the lumps were mixtures. The quarrel was fair, because the samples really were poor. Boron clings so tightly to other atoms that a clean piece waited for later chemists, Henri Moissan among them, who finally showed the element with far less contamination.

trivia.title: Innocent-Looking White Powders
trivia.summary: Borax left the workshop and turned up in washrooms and medicine chests. The familiar white grains made it easy to forget that a chemical can still do harm.
trivia.story: Cheap boron compounds soon drifted from foundries and glass shops into ordinary cupboards. Borax softened wash water, and boric acid was sold as a gentle antiseptic that people dusted onto skin and, carelessly, near food. Those powders looked as mild as salt or sugar, which encouraged a careless habit. The mild look was a trap. Swallowed in any serious amount they are poisonous, and muddled medicine chests and household mistakes caused real illnesses. The element that began as a goldsmith's flux had to be learned a second time, as a chemical a family may store and must not taste.

trivia.title: Glass That Survives a Flame
trivia.summary: A beaker heated in one spot and cold in another can crack without warning. Boron compounds in the glass made that sudden failure much less common.
trivia.story: Most familiar glass is a network of silica, and a sharp change of temperature can tear it. Borosilicate glass weaves boron oxide into that network, so the solid expands and shrinks less when it is heated. A flask can meet a burner, and a dish can leave a hot oven, with a much smaller chance of a crack shooting through the wall. Brand names made the glass ordinary in the twentieth century. The idea itself was chemical, not magical. Boron, once only a flux in the shop, had become part of the container that survived the experiment.

trivia.title: Bonds the Old Rules Missed
trivia.summary: Compounds of boron and hydrogen refused to match the tidy bonding pictures that worked for carbon. The mismatch became a famous puzzle, and some samples were risky to keep.
trivia.story: Chemists who had learned carbon's neat electron pairs expected boron to behave in a cousinly way. The boranes, made of boron and hydrogen, did not. Their formulas looked short of electrons, and their shapes pushed theorists into new pictures of the chemical bond that filled lectures for decades. Several of the simpler boranes also catch fire in air, so a sample could destroy itself while a researcher was still drawing the structure. Special vacuum equipment became part of the craft. Borax had suggested a tame element, and the boranes proved that boron had another, much less polite chemistry.

applications.title: Heat-proof glass
applications.body: Borosilicate glass, the kind used in lab beakers and some bakeware, contains boron. It expands less when it is heated, so it is less likely to crack.

applications.title: Detergents
applications.body: A boron compound called borax has been used in laundry powders and cleaning mixes. It is a salt of boron, not the hard element itself.

applications.title: Plant nutrient
applications.body: Plants need a trace of boron. Too little shows up in the crop, and too much is harmful, so fertilizer formulas measure it carefully.

elements.name: Carbon

summary.beginner:
Carbon is element 6, and living things are built from it. The same element is charcoal, the graphite in a pencil, and diamond.

Its symbol is C. At room temperature carbon is a solid. It is a nonmetal. It does not look or act like iron or copper. On the periodic table it is in row 2, column 14. In class those are called period 2 and group 14.

Carbon atoms join to each other in long chains and rings, which is why so many different molecules can be made from it. Diamond is hard because every atom is tied tightly to four neighbors. Graphite is soft because the atoms form sheets that slide.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral carbon atom has 6 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Carbon is a solid nonmetal in period 2 and group 14. Carbon's chemistry is catenation: atoms linking to one another in chains, rings, and networks.

The electron configuration is [He] 2s2 2p2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 4. Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +2, --4. The one courses meet most often is +4.

Diamond is a 3D network of single bonds. Graphite is sheets of atoms with delocalized electrons, which is why it conducts electricity along a sheet and marks a page.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Carbon (Z = 6) has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s2 2p2. The contrast is sp3 in diamond against sp2 in graphite, graphene, and most organic molecules.

A C-C single bond is much stronger than the Si-Si bond below it, which is why carbon, not silicon, is the backbone of life.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +2, --4. The one courses meet most often is +4. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Carbon: say the name, write C, find Z=6 on the table, note the family (Nonmetal), and connect it to one real use — backbone of living molecules.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Carbon: electron configuration [He] 2s2 2p2, Typical oxidation states: +4, +2, -4. It sits in group 14. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. catenation; diamond vs graphite.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Carbon: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; sp² vs sp³; C–C bond energy dwarfs Si–Si If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Known as charcoal, soot, and diamond long before it was an element.

elements.history:
Charcoal, soot, and diamond were known long before anyone called them one element. In 1772 Lavoisier burned a diamond in oxygen and obtained the same gas as from burning charcoal, which tied the forms together. The name carbon is from the Latin carbo, coal.

The nineteenth century sorted the allotropes. Graphite, diamond, and later fullerenes and graphene are the same element in different networks, and organic chemistry is the chemistry of its chains.
elements.howDiscovered:
Charcoal, soot, and diamond were familiar long before anyone treated them as one element. The experiment that tied them together was combustion. In 1772 Antoine Lavoisier burned a diamond in a closed vessel with a burning glass and collected the same fixed air that burning charcoal produced.

He weighed the vessel. The gas accounted for the diamond. Graphite later joined them. Carbon was discovered by showing that three very different solids were the same simple substance, because each of them became carbon dioxide and nothing else.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Carbon is built in the cores of stars that are burning helium. Three helium nuclei meet and make carbon-12, the triple-alpha step. A little of that carbon captures one more helium nucleus and becomes oxygen, so the amount of carbon a star returns depends on how the race between those two captures goes.

Red giants and massive stars both run the reaction. Winds and supernovae put the carbon into space. The carbon in coal, diamond, and living tissue is that stellar ash, gathered into the cloud that became the solar system.

trivia.title: The Diamond and the Charcoal
trivia.summary: A diamond and a lump of charcoal did not look like relatives. Antoine Lavoisier burned the jewel to see whether the difference survived the fire.
trivia.story: Diamond, charcoal, and soot had lived in different trades for centuries, and almost nobody treated them as one substance. In 1772 Antoine Lavoisier used a powerful burning lens to heat a diamond in oxygen until the stone was gone. He collected the gas that formed. It was the same gas he obtained when charcoal burned. The glittering mineral and the black fuel had been carbon in two disguises. The experiment did not make diamonds cheap, but it ended the idea that a jewel was a private kind of matter with no link to the hearth.

trivia.title: A Name Taken from Coal
trivia.summary: Once diamond and charcoal were the same element, the element needed a word. Latin already had a plain name for coal, and chemistry borrowed it.
trivia.story: Lavoisier's burning diamond showed a kinship, and the kinship needed a label that miners and jewelers could share. The word chosen was carbon, from the Latin carbo, coal. It pointed at the familiar black fuel rather than at the rare crystal. That was a deliberate plainness. Coal, charcoal, and later graphite could all sit under one name even when they looked nothing alike. The name also marked a boundary: carbon was an element, and the endless compounds of life and industry would be built from it rather than confused with it.

trivia.title: Sixty Atoms in a Ball
trivia.summary: Soot from a hot carbon experiment was supposed to be ordinary mess. In 1985 a few researchers found a molecule in it with a shape nobody had planned.
trivia.story: Graphite and diamond were the famous forms, and then a third shape turned up in the soot. In 1985 Harold Kroto, Richard Smalley, and Robert Curl vaporized graphite and found molecules made of sixty carbon atoms. The atoms closed into a hollow ball, a pattern of hexagons and pentagons like a football. They called the molecules buckminsterfullerene, soon nicknamed buckyballs, after the domes of Buckminster Fuller. Carbon, the element of coal and diamonds, could also curl into a cage. The discovery opened a family of forms that older textbooks had no page for.

trivia.title: A Gas with No Warning Smell
trivia.summary: Charcoal and coal have warmed rooms for centuries. The danger in a closed space is not always the flame you can see.
trivia.story: Carbon is the fuel in charcoal and in coal, and a bright fire looks like the whole story. Carbon monoxide, a gas with no color and no useful smell, can come from a fire that does not burn cleanly. People who slept near poorly vented stoves have been poisoned by it. The gas grips the blood in place of oxygen, so a sleeper grows drowsy and may never wake. The hazard is old and ordinary, which is why it keeps returning in winter rooms and in garages. Carbon's cheerful fire and this invisible gas are closer neighbors than the flames suggest.

trivia.title: The Pencil That Was Not Lead
trivia.summary: Writers called the dark core of a pencil lead, and the mineral itself was once sold under a name that meant the same. The mark on the page was never that metal.
trivia.story: A pencil line looks like soft metal rubbed onto paper, and for a long time people said lead because that is what the darkness resembled. The mineral in the stick was graphite, a form of carbon, nicknamed black lead or plumbago. Clay mixed with the graphite made the core harder or softer, which is why pencils come in grades. No lead was required for the mark. The confusion lasted in ordinary speech even after chemists had separated the element from the metal it imitates. Every homework sentence written in pencil is a small deposit of carbon.

applications.title: Living things
applications.body: Proteins, fats, DNA, and sugars are built on chains and rings of carbon. No other element forms that variety of stable molecules.

applications.title: Diamond and graphite
applications.body: Diamond is a hard form of carbon used to cut and to sparkle. Graphite is the soft form in pencil lead and in some lubricants.

applications.title: Fuel and steel
applications.body: Coal, charcoal, and the carbon in oil are fuels and, in a blast furnace, the ingredient that pulls oxygen away from iron ore.

reaction.intermediate: Complete combustion of carbon. Incomplete combustion yields CO.

elements.name: Nitrogen

summary.beginner:
Nitrogen is element 7, the gas that makes up most of the air. Plants need it in a usable form, which is why it is a big part of fertilizer.

Its symbol is N. At room temperature nitrogen is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a nonmetal. It does not look or act like iron or copper. On the periodic table it is in row 2, column 15. In class those are called period 2 and group 15.

The nitrogen in air is paired up as N2, and that pair is hard to break. Lightning, special bacteria, and factories can break it so plants can use the atoms.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Nitrogen is a nonmetal gas in period 2 and group 15. The N2 molecule has a triple bond, so it is surprisingly unreactive at room temperature.

The electron configuration is [He] 2s2 2p3. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 5. Oxidation states in this dossier are --3, +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is --3.

Once that bond is broken, nitrogen shows oxidation states from -3, as in ammonia, up to +5, as in nitric acid. The Haber-Bosch process makes ammonia from N2 and hydrogen.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Nitrogen (Z = 7) has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s2 2p3. The triple bond dissociation energy is why atmospheric nitrogen is a reservoir, not a reagent, until a catalyst or an organism fixes it.

In biology the important forms are ammonia, nitrate, and the nitrogen of amino acids.

Oxidation states in this dossier are --3, +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is --3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Nitrogen: say the name, write N, find Z=7 on the table, note the family (Nonmetal), and connect it to one real use — 78% of dry air; amino acids.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Nitrogen: electron configuration [He] 2s2 2p3, Typical oxidation states: -3, +3, +5. It sits in group 15. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. triple bond in N₂; inert at room T.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Nitrogen: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Haber–Bosch; oxidation states −3 to +5 If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated as the gas left after oxygen and carbon dioxide were removed from air.

elements.history:
Daniel Rutherford isolated a gas in 1772 by removing oxygen and carbon dioxide from air and found that what remained would not support life or flame. He called it noxious air. Jean-Antoine Chaptal named it nitrogen in 1790. The French name azote, from Greek for lifeless, is still the root of nitride and azo.

Nitrogen’s triple bond kept the atmosphere’s main gas inert until the Haber–Bosch process, industrialized in the 1910s, fixed it as ammonia. That single reaction remade fertilizer and explosives.
elements.howDiscovered:
Daniel Rutherford let a mouse breathe in a closed volume of air, then absorbed the fixed air with alkali. What remained would not support a flame or another animal. He called it noxious air and published the experiment in 1772. Cavendish and Scheele reached a similar residue by other routes.

The residue was still mixed with the argon that no one yet knew about, so the gas was not pure nitrogen. It was pure enough to show that most of the air was a distinct substance, neither oxygen nor carbon dioxide. Jean-Antoine Chaptal named it. The discovery was what was left when the active part of air had been removed.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Nitrogen is made in stars that already contain carbon and oxygen. In the CNO cycle, protons are added until the nucleus spends most of its time as nitrogen-14, the slow step of the cycle, and some of that nitrogen is later mixed out to the surface.

Intermediate-mass stars and giants do most of this returning. A star that makes its own carbon first, then runs the cycle, can make nitrogen even from gas that started with little carbon. The nitrogen in air and in protein is that processed stellar gas.

trivia.title: The Air That Smothered Flame
trivia.summary: Daniel Rutherford removed the gases he already understood from a sample of air. What remained could not keep a candle lit or a mouse alive.
trivia.story: Air was not one thing, and Daniel Rutherford set out to see what was left when the lively part was gone. In 1772 he removed oxygen and carbon dioxide from a sample and studied the residue, and a flame sank and went out. An animal could not live in it. He called the leftover noxious air, a name for a gas that seemed only to spoil the room. He had isolated the main gas of the atmosphere without yet knowing how large its share was. The dull remainder would turn out to be most of every breath.

trivia.title: Lifeless, Then Given a Name
trivia.summary: The gas that smothered flames needed a better name than a complaint. A French chemist chose one word, and Greek offered another that still hides in the vocabulary.
trivia.story: Noxious air was a description of a disappointment, not a name that could last. In 1790 Jean-Antoine Chaptal named the gas nitrogen. French chemists also kept azote, from Greek words meaning no life, because the gas would not support a flame or a breath. That older idea never fully left the language, and nitride and azo still carry the root. The element that Rutherford had found by subtraction now had a positive identity, even though its most obvious talent was refusing to do what oxygen did. Most of the air had been hiding under a name that meant lifeless.

trivia.title: Ammonia from the Open Air
trivia.summary: Crops needed nitrogen, and the air was full of it, yet plants could not use the gas directly. Early in the twentieth century that lock began to open.
trivia.story: Farmers already knew that nitrogen compounds made fields greener, and they also knew that the nitrogen overhead was stubborn. The triple bond in the gas kept it aloof from soil and from most chemistry. Fritz Haber found a laboratory route from that gas to ammonia, and Carl Bosch turned the route into a factory process in the 1910s. Fertilizer could then be made from the air rather than dug from distant deposits. The same ammonia later supplied explosives factories as well as farms. One industrial reaction changed what the world could grow, and what it could fight with.

trivia.title: Bubbles on the Way Up
trivia.summary: A diver working deep is fine while the pressure stays high. The danger waits in the ascent, inside blood that has been breathing ordinary air.
trivia.story: Nitrogen is most of the air a diver carries, and under pressure more of it dissolves in the blood and tissues. Stay down, and the dissolved gas is quiet. Rise too fast, and the pressure falls before the body can unload it calmly. Bubbles form, and the illness called the bends can twist joints, confuse the mind, and threaten life. Divers learned to ascend on a schedule, or to switch gases, because the element that seems so idle in a classroom jar is not idle in a bloodstream. The hazard is a change of pressure, not a poison in the tank.

trivia.title: Four Fifths of Every Breath
trivia.summary: Oxygen gets the credit for keeping a flame and a body alive. The larger part of the air has a different job, and it is easy to forget it is there.
trivia.story: A breath feels like oxygen, because oxygen is the part the body spends. Most of the inhale is nitrogen, passing in and out with little chemical fuss, and that bulk is not a waste. It dilutes oxygen so that fires and lungs meet a moderated gas rather than a pure one, and it is the reservoir industry later learned to tap. Food packers use it to push oxygen away from snacks that would otherwise go stale. The element Rutherford found as a lifeless leftover is the main ingredient of the sky. Its quietness is the reason a room full of air does not burn like a torch.

applications.title: The air
applications.body: About four fifths of dry air is nitrogen. You breathe it in and out all day, and it does not burn.

applications.title: Fertilizer
applications.body: Plants need nitrogen in a form they can use. Factories turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia and then into fertilizer.

applications.title: Proteins
applications.body: Every protein contains nitrogen, in the amino acids the protein is built from. That nitrogen started, ultimately, as gas in the air.

elements.name: Oxygen

summary.beginner:
Oxygen is element 8, the gas in air that lets a fire burn and lets you breathe. It is also part of water.

Its symbol is O. At room temperature oxygen is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a nonmetal. It does not look or act like iron or copper. On the periodic table it is in row 2, column 16. In class those are called period 2 and group 16.

Most of the oxygen you meet is O2, two atoms joined together. A third form, ozone, is a sharp-smelling gas high in the atmosphere that blocks some of the Sun's ultraviolet light.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral oxygen atom has 8 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Oxygen is a nonmetal gas in period 2 and group 16. Ordinary oxygen is the diradical O2, which is why it supports combustion.

The electron configuration is [He] 2s2 2p4. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 6. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --2.

In water and in most oxides the oxidation state is -2. Peroxides are the -1 case, and ozone is a separate allotrope with its own chemistry.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Oxygen (Z = 8) has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s2 2p4. The two unpaired electrons in O2 explain both its paramagnetism and its role as the terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration.

Oxides, peroxides, and ozone are three different oxidation stories, not one.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Oxygen: say the name, write O, find Z=8 on the table, note the family (Nonmetal), and connect it to one real use — you breathe it; water’s oxygen.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Oxygen: electron configuration [He] 2s2 2p4, Typical oxidation states: -2. It sits in group 16. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. diradical O₂; supports combustion.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Oxygen: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; oxides, peroxides, ozone photochemistry If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Prepared from mercuric oxide; Scheele found it independently.

elements.history:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele prepared oxygen around 1772, and Joseph Priestley published the same gas in 1774 after heating mercuric oxide. Lavoisier overthrew the phlogiston story with it and named it oxygen, meaning acid-former, because he wrongly thought every acid contained it.

The name stuck even after that theory did not. Oxygen became the reference for combustion, respiration, and the oxide minerals that make up most of the crust.
elements.howDiscovered:
Joseph Priestley focused sunlight on mercuric oxide, which he called mercurius calcinatus per se, and collected a gas in which a candle burned violently and a mouse lived longer than in ordinary air. He published this in 1774. Carl Wilhelm Scheele had prepared the same gas from several oxides and from nitre, probably earlier, and his book appeared in 1777.

Priestley interpreted the gas as air with its phlogiston removed. Lavoisier reversed the explanation: the gas was an element, and metals gained it when they calcined. The laboratory fact was the same in both camps. Heating a red powder, or treating an oxide with acid, released a gas that was a large fraction of the air and the supporter of combustion.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Oxygen is the main metal a massive star returns. During helium burning, carbon-12 captures a helium nucleus to make oxygen-16. Neon burning later frees still more oxygen. The star’s explosion, a core-collapse supernova, throws it out.

Oxygen-16 is an especially tightly bound, even nucleus, which is why oxygen is more abundant in the Sun and in the crust than its neighbors. Water, silicates, and the oxygen of the air are this supernova product.

trivia.title: Two Paths to the Same Gas
trivia.summary: Carl Wilhelm Scheele prepared a lively gas and was slow to publish. Joseph Priestley, working another way, told the world first and gave the gas a theory Scheele did not share.
trivia.story: Oxygen was found twice, by men who did not share a bench. Carl Wilhelm Scheele prepared it around 1772 by heating compounds that release it, and he described a gas in which a flame burned fiercely. His account sat unpublished while Joseph Priestley, in 1774, heated mercuric oxide, collected the same gas, and printed the news. Priestley called it dephlogisticated air, fitting it to the theory he trusted. Scheele had the earlier preparation and the later book. The element entered science as a quarrel about priority and about what a brighter candle was supposed to mean.

trivia.title: Phlogiston on Trial
trivia.summary: A popular theory said that burning objects gave off a mysterious substance. Antoine Lavoisier followed the new gas through the fire and argued the opposite.
trivia.story: Phlogiston was the name of a fluid that burning things were supposed to lose. It explained flames in words that many chemists liked and that weights refused to support. Lavoisier weighed what happened when substances burned in the new gas and when animals breathed it. The gas was taken up, not a mystery fluid given off. He threw the old theory out and rebuilt combustion as a combining with this element, and Priestley never accepted the defeat. The argument was polite in print and stubborn in person, and it decided the language of fire for the next century.

trivia.title: Named for Acids by Mistake
trivia.summary: Lavoisier thought every acid had to contain the new gas, and he named the gas for that belief. The belief failed, and the name stayed anyway.
trivia.story: Lavoisier did more than attack phlogiston. He named the gas oxygen, from Greek words meaning acid-former, because he was sure that every acid contained it. The idea organized his system and then slowly fell apart as chemists met acids with no oxygen in them at all, and hydrochloric acid was an early embarrassment to the theory. The name, though, had already settled onto the element. It is a monument to a wrong explanation that happened to be attached to a right substance. Students learn the word long before they learn that the man who coined it was mistaken about acids.

trivia.title: The Breath and the Furnace
trivia.summary: Once oxygen had a name, it explained more than a brighter candle. Bodies, ores, and furnaces were all doing versions of the same taking-up.
trivia.story: Lavoisier showed that a breathing animal and a burning candle both consumed oxygen and both produced the same kind of fixed air. The comparison was shocking in its plainness. Life was not exempt from the chemistry of the flame. Industry later used the same gas on purpose, blowing it into furnaces so that iron could be refined faster, and sending it into hospitals so that struggling lungs could meet a richer air. The element Priestley had bottled over mercury became the reference for burning, breathing, and the oxides that make up so much of the crust. A laboratory gas had been the hidden partner of ordinary air all along.

trivia.title: Fire in a Sealed Cabin
trivia.summary: A ground test of a new spacecraft in 1967 was supposed to be a rehearsal on the pad. The cabin air was not the mixture the crew breathed on an ordinary day.
trivia.story: Apollo 1 sat on the ground in 1967 for a test, with Virgil Grissom, Edward White, and Roger Chaffee sealed inside. The cabin atmosphere was oxygen-rich, a choice meant to simplify the machine. A fire started during the test. In that air the flames grew with a speed the crew could not outrun, and all three men died. Later spacecraft flew with a less dangerous mix once they had left the pad. The element that keeps every person alive had shown, in a closed metal room, how quickly it takes the side of a fire.

applications.title: Breathing
applications.body: The oxygen in air is what your cells use when they release energy from food. A fire uses the same gas when it burns.

applications.title: Water
applications.body: Water is hydrogen joined to oxygen. Most of the oxygen atoms on the surface of the Earth are locked in water and in rock, not free in the air.

applications.title: Steelmaking
applications.body: A blast furnace uses oxygen-rich air to burn carbon and to help turn iron ore into iron. Hospitals also pipe pure oxygen to patients who need it.

elements.name: Fluorine

summary.beginner:
Fluorine is element 9, a pale gas that is extremely eager to join other elements. A calmer form of it, fluoride, is what you meet in toothpaste.

Its symbol is F. At room temperature fluorine is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a halogen, a reactive nonmetal in the column next to the noble gases. On the periodic table it is in row 2, column 17. In class those are called period 2 and group 17.

Fluorine atoms pull electrons toward themselves more strongly than any other element. That is useful in toothpaste and dangerous in the pure gas, which is not a classroom chemical.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral fluorine atom has 9 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Fluorine is a halogen gas in period 2 and group 17. Fluorine has the highest electronegativity, and in compounds it is almost always oxidation state -1.

The electron configuration is [He] 2s2 2p5. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 7. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1.

The F-F bond is actually weak, which is one reason the element is so reactive. Hydrogen fluoride is special because of strong hydrogen bonds between molecules.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Fluorine (Z = 9) has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s2 2p5. There is no positive oxidation state in ordinary chemistry: fluorine is the oxidant, not the oxidized.

The small size of fluoride also gives HF its hydrogen-bond network and its ability to etch glass.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Fluorine: say the name, write F, find Z=9 on the table, note the family (Halogen), and connect it to one real use — toothpaste fluoride; strongest oxidizer.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Fluorine: electron configuration [He] 2s2 2p5, Typical oxidation states: -1. It sits in group 17. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. highest electronegativity.
