discovery.text: Isolated by electrolysis of potassium hydrogen fluoride.

elements.history:
Fluorspar was used as a flux for centuries, and the name fluorine comes from the Latin fluere, to flow. Chemists suspected an element in hydrofluoric acid long before anyone could isolate it. Several were poisoned in the attempt. Henri Moissan succeeded in 1886 by electrolyzing potassium hydrogen fluoride in a platinum cell.

Fluorine is the most electronegative element, and for decades it had almost no compounds except fluorides. The xenon fluorides of the 1960s were the surprise that opened noble-gas chemistry.
elements.howDiscovered:
Fluorspar and hydrofluoric acid were known, and the acid attacked glass and poisoned the chemists who worked with it. Several attempts to isolate the element inside it ended in injury. Henri Moissan succeeded on 26 June 1886 by electrolyzing a solution of potassium hydrogen fluoride in anhydrous hydrogen fluoride, in a platinum-iridium cell cooled below zero.

A yellow-green gas appeared at the anode and set silicon and carbon on fire. That violence was the evidence. Nothing else known would do it, and the gas could not be decomposed further. The discovery was an electrolysis cold enough, and a cell resistant enough, that the product survived long enough to be seen.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Fluorine is easy for a star to destroy and hard for one to keep. The leading account of fluorine-19 is the neutrino process: neutrinos from a collapsing core strike neon-20 and chip it down to fluorine, which the explosion then ejects before the star can burn the fluorine away.

Aging giant stars can make a smaller share and dredge it into their winds. Either way the yield is small. Fluorine’s rarity, in minerals and in the cosmic mix, is the rarity of a nucleus that barely escapes the star that made it.

trivia.title: The Spar That Helped Metals Flow
trivia.summary: Metalworkers used a colorful mineral for centuries without isolating anything from it. The mineral's Latin name already said what it was good for.
trivia.story: Fluorspar sat in the workshop long before it sat in the periodic table. Heat it with an ore, and the melt flowed more easily, which is what a flux is for. The name fluorine comes from the Latin fluere, to flow, a tribute to that old job rather than to the gas nobody had yet freed. Chemists could make fierce acids from the spar and could guess that an element was hiding in them. Guessing was not isolating. The mineral was tame enough to ship in barrels, and the element inside it was not tame at all.

trivia.title: A Gas That Injured Its Hunters
trivia.summary: Hydrofluoric acid clearly held a missing element, and several chemists tried to pull that element free. The attempts hurt the people who made them.
trivia.story: Fluorine's compounds were known, and the element itself kept attacking the chemists who chased it. The Knox brothers were badly injured in their attempts and had to abandon the work. Paulin Louyet continued the hunt and died from the effects, and Jérôme Nicklès died as well. Those injuries and deaths were the cost of the hunt, and the element remained unbottled. Other researchers saw the pattern and still felt the element had to exist. The isolation had become a wager against a substance that punished curiosity.

trivia.title: Moissan's Platinum Cell
trivia.summary: By 1886 the missing halogen was a famous unsolved problem. Henri Moissan built an apparatus that could survive the gas, and the gas did not spare him.
trivia.story: Henri Moissan approached fluorine as a problem of containment as much as of chemistry. In 1886 he isolated the gas by electrolysis in a platinum apparatus that could withstand it. A pale yellow gas appeared, and it was the element, and the victory was real and immediately unpleasant. Moissan was sickened by the gas he had isolated, the same substance that had injured the Knox brothers and killed Louyet and Nicklès. He had ended the search without making fluorine gentle. The most reactive element on the table had finally been seen, and it had bitten the man who saw it.

trivia.title: Fluoride and a Public Argument
trivia.summary: A tiny amount of fluoride can harden tooth enamel, and cities began to put it in drinking water. Not everyone agreed that a public supply should carry it.
trivia.story: Fluorine's fame in ordinary life is not the pale gas, which almost nobody meets. It is fluoride, the ion, in toothpaste and in some drinking water, and dentists noticed that a little of it helped teeth resist decay. Towns that added fluoride to the water supply saw fewer cavities, and they also saw protests. Opponents called the addition a medicine forced on everyone, and supporters called it a simple protection. The argument was about trust and dose, not about whether the element existed. Fluorine had traveled from a deadly isolation to a dispute at the kitchen tap.

trivia.title: The Noble Gas Gave Way
trivia.summary: Textbooks had called the noble gases unwilling to form compounds. Fluorine, in the 1960s, forced one of them to break that rule.
trivia.story: For decades fluorine seemed to have a short list of partners, mostly as ordinary fluorides, and the noble gases were said to have none. The claim was neat enough to teach and wrong enough to collapse. In the 1960s chemists prepared compounds in which xenon bonded to fluorine. A gas that had been a symbol of refusal had been persuaded by the most aggressive element on the table. The surprise opened noble-gas chemistry and made older chapters look overconfident. Fluorine's story of injuries and a platinum cell ended, in a way, with a lesson: the element that was so hard to free was also hard for other atoms to ignore.

applications.title: Toothpaste
applications.body: Fluoride in toothpaste is a compound of fluorine, not the pure gas. It helps tooth enamel resist acid.

applications.title: A fierce reactant
applications.body: Fluorine gas reacts with almost everything, which is why it is used in industry to make non-stick coatings and special plastics, under strict controls.

applications.title: Not a home chemical
applications.body: The pure element burns tissue and is not a demonstration reagent. The fluoride in a toothpaste tube is a different, much calmer substance.

elements.name: Neon

summary.beginner:
Neon is element 10, a gas that does not form ordinary compounds. When electricity passes through it, it glows the orange-red of a classic neon sign.

Its symbol is Ne. At room temperature neon is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a noble gas. Left alone, it almost never joins other elements to make compounds. On the periodic table it is in row 2, column 18. In class those are called period 2 and group 18.

Neon's outer shell is full, eight electrons in the second shell, so it has no reason to react. The glow is the atom giving light back after the electric current bumps its electrons.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral neon atom has 10 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Neon is a noble gas in period 2 and group 18. A closed 2s2 2p6 shell is why neon has no stable molecules.

The electron configuration is [He] 2s2 2p6. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8. Oxidation states are not listed for this entry.

The familiar orange-red is a mix of many visible emission lines, not a single wavelength. Liquid neon is also used as a cold, inert refrigerant.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Neon (Z = 10) has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s2 2p6. The emission spectrum is dense in the red and orange, which is why a pure neon discharge does not look white.

Compounds are a specialist topic. The closed shell is the classroom fact.

Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Neon: say the name, write Ne, find Z=10 on the table, note the family (Noble gas), and connect it to one real use — orange-red discharge tubes.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Neon: electron configuration [He] 2s2 2p6, Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. It sits in group 18. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. closed p⁶ shell; no stable molecules.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Neon: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; many visible emission lines; sonified as THz/10¹² If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from liquefied air after argon and krypton.

elements.history:
William Ramsay and Morris Travers isolated neon in 1898 by fractional distillation of liquid air, after they had already found argon, krypton, and xenon. A new crimson glow in a discharge tube told them the fraction was a new gas. They named it neon, from the Greek neos, new.

Georges Claude turned that glow into commercial lighting in the 1910s. Neon signs made the element a public word, even when later tubes used other gases for other colors.
elements.howDiscovered:
William Ramsay and Morris Travers liquefied air and distilled it in fractions. After argon had been removed, a light fraction sparked in a discharge tube with a crimson glow that matched no known gas. They collected it in 1898 and named it from the newness of the line.

The amount in air is small, about 18 parts per million, which is why the gas waited until liquid air could be taken apart carefully. The discovery was a boiling point and a spectrum. There was no mineral and no chemical reaction, only a fraction that glowed a color argon did not.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Neon-20, the common isotope, is built by carbon burning in massive stars. Two carbon nuclei fuse, and one frequent result is neon plus a helium nucleus. The supernova that ends the star returns that neon to space.

Neon-22 has a second path. Helium burning on nitrogen-14 builds it in massive stars and in giants, and that neon-22 also releases neutrons those stars use for slow capture of heavier elements. The neon in air is mostly the neon-20 from massive stars.

trivia.title: A Crimson Glow in Cold Air
trivia.summary: William Ramsay and Morris Travers were separating the gases dissolved in liquid air. One fraction, sparked in a tube, shone a color they had not already assigned.
trivia.story: Argon was already known when William Ramsay and Morris Travers started distilling liquid air in earnest. In 1898 they collected fraction after fraction, looking for anything that was not oxygen, nitrogen, or the gases they had already named. A discharge tube was their witness. One fraction glowed a brilliant crimson that matched no familiar fill. The color was the announcement. They had a new element in the cold residue of ordinary air, present in a trace and impossible to see until the rest of the air had been peeled away.

trivia.title: The Gas Named New
trivia.summary: The crimson fraction needed a name that would not pretend the gas had been familiar. Greek supplied a short word for exactly that situation.
trivia.story: Ramsay and Travers did not reach for a mineral or a homeland when they named the new gas. They chose neon, from the Greek neos, meaning new. The word recorded the experience of the experiment: a fraction that had not been on yesterday's list. It was a modest name beside helium's Sun and argon's idleness, and it fit a gas found in scraps. Neon is scarce in air, which is why it had waited until liquid air could be taken apart carefully. The name says discovery, not origin in a mountain or a myth.

trivia.title: Letters Hired the Glow
trivia.summary: The crimson discharge that identified neon was too striking to leave in a physics tube. An inventor turned it into writing that a street could read.
trivia.story: A glow in a laboratory tube is a result. Georges Claude looked at the same glow and saw a sign. In the 1910s he bent glass tubes into letters and filled them so that neon's red-orange light could spell a shop or a product above a sidewalk. The tubes drew current, the gas shone, and advertising acquired a night color of its own. Cities changed after dark. An element isolated by patient distillation became one of the few that ordinary people could point at and name, even if they never learned how small its share of the air is.

trivia.title: When the Sign Is Another Gas
trivia.summary: Nighttime letters in blue, green, or white are often still called neon. The word survived a change that the gas itself did not make.
trivia.story: Claude's first successful signs used neon, and the red light taught the public the element's name. Later tubes needed other colors, and other gases and coatings supplied them. A blue letter might contain a different fill entirely, yet the whole craft kept the name neon. The mismatch is a small public confusion with a real history behind it. Neon remains the classic red-orange, and the word on the street became larger than the element. Ramsay's new gas had donated its name to a kind of light, including lights that no longer needed it.

trivia.title: Almost Lost in the Distillate
trivia.summary: Liquid air holds only a trace of the new gas, and a clumsy fraction would have thrown it away. The crimson tube was what stopped the chemists from moving on.
trivia.story: Neon does not announce itself in a room. There is too little of it in each breath, and it does nothing colorful until electricity is passed through a concentrated sample. Ramsay and Travers could easily have filed the faint fraction with leftovers and gone on to the next boiling point, and the discharge tube made the miss harder. Crimson light is a poor thing to ignore, and they did not ignore it, and the episode is not an accident with a victim. It is a near-miss in a cold laboratory, rescued by a color. The element named new was almost an unnamed residue.

applications.title: Signs
applications.body: A classic neon sign is a glass tube of neon with a current through it. The gas glows orange-red.

applications.title: Other colors
applications.body: Many signs that people call neon are actually other gases or tinted glass. Pure neon is the orange-red one.

applications.title: A cold liquid
applications.body: Liquid neon is an inert refrigerant, colder than liquid nitrogen and less expensive than liquid helium for some jobs.

elements.name: Sodium

summary.beginner:
Sodium is element 11, a soft metal that reacts hard with water. You meet it every day as part of table salt, not as the pure metal.

Its symbol is Na. At room temperature sodium is a solid. It is an alkali metal: soft, and quick to react with water. On the periodic table it is in row 3, column 1. In class those are called period 3 and group 1.

In salt, sodium has given its outer electron to chlorine. The pure metal is stored under oil because air and water attack it.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Sodium is a solid alkali metal in period 3 and group 1. The single 3s electron is lost to give Na+, the ion in table salt and in body fluids.

The electron configuration is [Ne] 3s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

Sodium floats on water and the reaction produces hydrogen gas and a hot alkaline solution. That is a demonstration with real hazards, not a home experiment.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Sodium (Z = 11) has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s1. Na+ is the main cation outside animal cells.

The metal's low ionization energy and the solubility of its salts are the same fact seen in the lab and in physiology.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Sodium: say the name, write Na, find Z=11 on the table, note the family (Alkali metal), and connect it to one real use — table salt’s metal.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Sodium: electron configuration [Ne] 3s1, Typical oxidation states: +1. It sits in group 1. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. soft alkali; vigorous with water.

discovery.text: Isolated by electrolysis of molten caustic soda.

elements.history:
Soda and salt are ancient. Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1807 by electrolyzing molten caustic soda, a few days after he had isolated potassium. The symbol Na is from the Latin natrium, itself from natron, the mineral soda of Egypt. The English name sodium was proposed by Ludwig Wilhelm Gilbert.

Sodium stayed a laboratory metal because it reacts violently with water. Its ion, not the metal, is the everyday substance: table salt, soaps, and the main cation outside living cells.
elements.howDiscovered:
Humphry Davy had isolated potassium from molten potash with a voltaic pile. A few days later, in October 1807, he applied the same current to molten caustic soda. Globules of metal appeared at the cathode, burned in air, and skated on water the way potassium did, with a different flame.

Soda and salt were ancient. The element was the metal inside them, and it had never been seen because any chemical reducing agent strong enough to free it was not yet in use. The current was the tool. The violent reaction with water was the proof that the globules were a new alkali metal and not a by-product of the potash experiment.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Sodium has a single stable isotope, sodium-23. It is made in massive stars during carbon burning, and again when neon burns explosively in the supernova. A cycle of proton captures on neon, the neon-sodium cycle, adds a further share in stars hot enough to run it.

Sodium is odd-numbered, with an unpaired proton, so it is less abundant than magnesium or neon on either side. The salt in the ocean is still that stellar sodium, dissolved out of rock that formed from the same gas.

trivia.title: A Current Through Caustic Soda
trivia.summary: Humphry Davy had just pulled a metal from potash when he turned the same current on melted caustic soda. Another silvery substance was about to appear.
trivia.story: Soda and salt were ancient, and the metal inside them was not. A few days after he isolated potassium, Humphry Davy electrolyzed molten caustic soda. The current tore a soft, shiny metal out of the melt. It was 1807, and the metal was far too reactive to leave on an open bench. Davy had shown that the alkali in soda was not a compound of something already known but the oxide of a new element, and the globules were small and the claim was large. Ordinary washing soda had been hiding a metal that water would immediately attack.

trivia.title: Natron, Soda, and a Symbol
trivia.summary: Egypt's old mineral soda already had a name, and Latin had kept it. The English name of the new metal came from a different word, proposed by a different man.
trivia.story: The symbol Na does not match the English word sodium, and the mismatch is historical. Na comes from natrium, and natrium comes from natron, the mineral soda of Egypt, used for cleaning and for preparing the dead. The metal Davy isolated was the metal of that ancient alkali. Ludwig Wilhelm Gilbert proposed the English name sodium, built from soda rather than from natron. Two languages kept two memories of the same substance. A chemist writing NaCl is quietly using the older, Egyptian path, while the word on the jar says sodium.

trivia.title: Fire on a Bowl of Water
trivia.summary: The new metal looked calm for a moment after it was cut. Water was the test that showed why it could not be stored like iron.
trivia.story: Davy's sodium was soft enough to dent with a knife and shiny only until the air dulled it, and placed on water, it did not sink and sit. It rushed about, hissed, and often caught fire, throwing the calm of the bowl into a small violent scene. The metal was tearing hydrogen out of the water and heating itself as it went. That behavior is why teaching samples live under oil and why a flood of water is the wrong picture of safety for a sodium fire. The element of table salt is gentle only as the ion. As the metal, it is a standing argument with moisture.

trivia.title: The Ion in the Saltcellar
trivia.summary: Pure sodium metal never reached the dinner table, and it was never meant to. The ion, paired with chlorine, became one of the oldest seasonings people know.
trivia.story: What kitchens call salt is not the metal Davy saw skating on water. It is sodium chloride, a crystal that has seasoned food and preserved meat for thousands of years, and soaps were boiled with sodium alkalis. Living bodies keep sodium ions outside their cells as part of the traffic of nerves and fluids. The violent metal and the quiet crystal are the same element in different bonds. Industry learned to make the metal when it needed a fierce reagent, then locked it away from damp air. Everyday sodium remained the ion in the shaker, not the lump in the jar.

trivia.title: Days After the Other Alkali
trivia.summary: Potassium came first, and sodium followed within days on the same kind of apparatus. The speed of the second discovery made the first one look like a method, not a lucky melt.
trivia.story: Davy's potassium had been a sensation, a metal from plant ash that burned on water, and he did not pause to polish the fame. Within days he ran the same style of electrolysis on caustic soda and watched a second metal appear. The pair proved that the alkali earths of the workshop were not elements themselves. They were compounds, and electricity could undress them. The week in 1807 changed the map of the light metals. Sodium might have stayed an unnamed ingredient of salt for longer if potassium had not shown Davy exactly where to put the current next.

applications.title: Table salt
applications.body: Table salt is sodium chloride. The sodium in it has already reacted and is part of a calm crystal, not the soft metal.

applications.title: Street lights and nerves
applications.body: Older yellow street lamps were sodium vapor. In the body, sodium ions help nerve cells send signals.

applications.title: Industry
applications.body: Sodium hydroxide, made from salt, is used to make soap, paper, and many other chemicals. The pure metal is a starting point in some of those plants.

elements.name: Magnesium

summary.beginner:
Magnesium is element 12, a light metal that burns with a brilliant white flame. It is in lightweight alloys, and a magnesium atom sits at the center of the green molecule in leaves.

Its symbol is Mg. At room temperature magnesium is a solid. It is an alkaline-earth metal. These metals react, but less wildly than the alkali metals beside them. On the periodic table it is in row 3, column 2. In class those are called period 3 and group 2.

The pure metal is protected by a thin coat that forms in air, so a bar of it can look calm until it is heated. Plants use it inside chlorophyll, the molecule that catches sunlight.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral magnesium atom has 12 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Magnesium is a solid alkaline-earth metal in period 3 and group 2. Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+, and the metal burns with an intense white flame.

The electron configuration is [Ne] 3s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

It is less reactive than calcium, which sits below it, but it still reacts with acids. Grignard reagents, RMgX, are a major use of that reactivity in organic chemistry.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Magnesium (Z = 12) has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s2. The Mg2+ ion is smaller and more polarizing than Ca2+, so its compounds are a step more covalent.

Chlorophyll is a coordination complex of magnesium, not a lump of the metal.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Magnesium: say the name, write Mg, find Z=12 on the table, note the family (Alk. earth), and connect it to one real use — chlorophyll’s metal; light alloys.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Magnesium: electron configuration [Ne] 3s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It sits in group 2. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. +2 chemistry; burns with a bright flame.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Magnesium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Grignard reagents; less reactive than calcium If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated by electrolysis of magnesia.

elements.history:
Magnesia, a white earth from Magnesia in Greece, was long confused with lime. Joseph Black distinguished magnesia alba in 1755. Humphry Davy isolated a small amount of the metal in 1808 and named it magnesium. Antoine Bussy prepared it in bulk in 1831.

The bright white flame of burning magnesium became a nineteenth-century light source for photography and signaling. The ion later turned up at the center of chlorophyll.
elements.howDiscovered:
Joseph Black had already shown that magnesia alba was not lime. Humphry Davy tried to electrolyze the earth directly and got little. In 1808 he mixed moistened magnesia with mercuric oxide, passed the current, and distilled the mercury out of the amalgam that formed. A small amount of metal remained.

Antoine Bussy prepared it in quantity in 1831 by heating magnesium chloride with potassium. The discovery of the metal is Davy’s amalgam. The discovery of the earth is Black’s distinction of magnesia from lime, without which the electrolysis would have been a repetition of the calcium experiment.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Magnesium-24 is built from helium nuclei by carbon burning and by neon burning in massive stars, and supernovae return it. It is one of the products astronomers call alpha elements, alongside oxygen, silicon, calcium, and titanium.

Magnesium-25 and magnesium-26 need extra neutrons, captured during helium and carbon burning. A radioactive cousin, aluminum-26, decays into magnesium-26. Its gamma rays are how telescopes map stars that made this part of the table in the last million years. The magnesium in an alloy is the stable mix.

trivia.title: A White Earth from Magnesia
trivia.summary: A district in Greece gave its name to a white earth that physicians and chemists kept confusing with lime. Joseph Black insisted the two earths were not the same.
trivia.story: Magnesia, a region in Greece, lent its name to a white earth used as a medicine and a puzzlement. For a long time the powder was tangled with lime, because both were white, both were alkaline, and both turned up in the same kinds of bottles. In 1755 Joseph Black separated magnesia alba from lime and showed that the chemistry did not match. The earth had its own identity decades before anyone held the metal. When a metal was finally freed, it kept the geographic name. Magnesium is a place-name that became an element, after a careful argument about two white powders.

trivia.title: A Speck, Then a Quantity
trivia.summary: Humphry Davy recognized the metal and coaxed out only a little of it. A generation later another chemist prepared enough that the element could be studied in bulk.
trivia.story: Black had distinguished the earth, and the earth was still not a metal. In 1808 Humphry Davy isolated a small amount of magnesium by electrolysis and gave the element its name, and the sample proved the point and did not stock a shelf. Antoine Bussy, in 1831, prepared the metal in bulk, so that other chemists could see a real quantity rather than a trace on an electrode. The gap between those dates is the story of a stubborn oxide. Magnesium prefers its compounds, and tearing it free took a better preparation than Davy's first speck. Once the bulk metal existed, its bright burning became impossible to overlook.

trivia.title: Bitter Water at Epsom
trivia.summary: A spring in England tasted bitter and drew visitors who hoped the water would heal them. The dissolved salt was a magnesium compound, not a mystery of the well.
trivia.story: Long before the metal was isolated, people drank and soaked in the water of a spring at Epsom. The water was bitter, and the crystals that formed from it became a famous medicine, Epsom salt. Chemists later showed that the salt is magnesium sulfate. Invalids traveled for a cure that was really a soluble compound of an element still unnamed as a metal. The fashion faded, and the salt stayed in pharmacies as a familiar remedy. Magnesium had a public life as a bitter crystal centuries before it had a public life as a silvery ribbon, and the spring was the element's first widespread introduction.

trivia.title: A Flash for the Camera
trivia.summary: Burning magnesium throws a white light strong enough to freeze a face in a dark room. Photographers and signalers adopted the flame before factories thought about weapons.
trivia.story: Set magnesium alight and the flame is blinding, white, and hard to look at directly. Nineteenth-century photographers used that burst to light a portrait when the sun would not cooperate. Signalers used the same brilliance to send a flash across a distance. The metal that Davy had held only as a speck had become a portable source of day. The light is the friendly chapter of a fierce reaction. Anyone who has seen a ribbon burn in a classroom remembers the smoke and the glare, and how ordinary the gray metal looked the moment before the match.

trivia.title: Incendiaries in the Record
trivia.summary: The same white flame that lit a photograph could be turned to destruction. Wartime records include magnesium as an incendiary metal, a fact of history rather than a set of instructions.
trivia.story: A metal that burns with intense white heat will eventually be noticed by armies. In the wars of the twentieth century, magnesium was used in incendiary weapons because the flame is ferocious and the metal is light enough to carry. That wartime use sits in the record beside the camera flash. Cities learned what a magnesium fire looks like, and firefighters learned that it is not an ordinary wood fire. The classroom ribbon and the wartime weapon are the same chemistry at two scales, and one is a demonstration. The other is a record of harm.

applications.title: Light metal
applications.body: Magnesium alloys are light and strong enough for luggage, car parts, and some aircraft pieces.

applications.title: Green leaves
applications.body: A magnesium atom sits at the center of chlorophyll, the molecule that makes leaves green and catches sunlight.

applications.title: Flares
applications.body: Burning magnesium gives an intense white light, which is why it was used in flares and in old camera flash powder.

elements.name: Aluminium

summary.beginner:
Aluminium is element 13, a light metal used for cans, foil, and airplane parts. A thin clear coat forms on its surface and keeps it from rusting the way iron does.

Its symbol is Al. At room temperature aluminium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 3, column 13. In class those are called period 3 and group 13.

Aluminium looks dull only because of that coat of oxide. Underneath, the metal is shiny, and it carries electricity well enough to be used in power lines.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral aluminium atom has 13 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Aluminium is a solid post-transition in period 3 and group 13. The metal is protected by a tightly held layer of Al2O3, and the ion in compounds is Al3+.

The electron configuration is [Ne] 3s2 3p1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 3. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

Aluminium oxide is amphoteric: it reacts with both strong acids and strong bases. The metal's low density and that oxide film are why aircraft use it.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Aluminium (Z = 13) has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p1. The oxide film is only a few nanometers thick and self-healing in air, which is passivation rather than a lack of reactivity.

Al3+ is small and highly charged, so anhydrous aluminum chloride behaves as a covalent Lewis acid.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Aluminium: say the name, write Al, find Z=13 on the table, note the family (Post-transition), and connect it to one real use — aircraft metal; foil and cans.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Aluminium: electron configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p1, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 13. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. amphoteric oxide; FCC metal.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Aluminium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; protected by Al₂O₃; 3+ chemistry If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Prepared the metal from alumina; Wöhler improved the method.

elements.history:
Alum was used as a mordant in the ancient world. Hans Christian Ørsted prepared impure aluminium metal in 1825, and Friedrich Wöhler improved the isolation in 1827. Henri Sainte-Claire Deville’s process of the 1850s made small bars that were still as costly as silver.

The name comes from alum, from the Latin alumen. Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult independently invented the electrolytic process in 1886, and aluminium went from a court curiosity to a structural metal.
elements.howDiscovered:
Hans Christian Ørsted heated aluminium chloride with potassium amalgam in 1825 and, after distilling off the mercury, found a lump of metal that resembled tin. Friedrich Wöhler repeated the reduction with potassium metal in 1827 and obtained a powder he could melt into a purer button.

Alum itself was ancient, and the oxide alumina was already distinguished from silica and from other earths. The discovery of the element was the reduction of the chloride. The samples were small and impure. Henri Sainte-Claire Deville’s later process, and then the Hall–Héroult electrolysis, made the metal in bulk. They did not discover it.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Aluminum-27, the only stable isotope, is made in massive stars, in carbon and neon burning and in the explosion. Proton captures and the rearrangement of nuclei near silicon both feed it. It comes out with the other products of the supernova.

Aluminum-26 is a radioactive neighbor with a half-life near 700,000 years. Massive stars make it, and satellites see its decay gamma ray across the Milky Way. The aluminum in the crust is the stable isotope. The radioactive one is a tracer of recent stellar deaths, not a mineral.

trivia.title: From Alum to a Difficult Metal
trivia.summary: Alum had been a dyer's chemical since antiquity, and the metal inside it stayed hidden. Two nineteenth-century chemists, a few years apart, finally produced a sample.
trivia.story: Dyers used alum as a mordant, a helper that fixed color to cloth, long before anyone called the base of it an element. The name aluminium comes from alum, and alum comes from the Latin alumen. Hans Christian Ørsted prepared an impure metal in 1825. Friedrich Wöhler improved the isolation in 1827 and produced a sample that other chemists could trust more easily. The metal was light, and it was expensive to make, and naming it was the easy half. Getting a lump that was truly aluminium, and not a mixture wearing a new label, took those two successive efforts.

trivia.title: The Dinner Story People Tell
trivia.summary: By the 1850s small bars of aluminium existed, and they cost as much as a precious metal. A famous table is often dragged into the tale.
trivia.story: Henri Sainte-Claire Deville's process in the 1850s made aluminium in small bars that still sold like silver. People still tell a story about Napoleon III's table: the most honored guests, the tale says, were given aluminium utensils, and lesser guests made do with gold. Whether that seating chart is solid history or a good anecdote, the price behind it is real. The new metal was a court curiosity, shown off because almost nobody could have it. Deville could not yet flood a market. Aluminium's early fame was the fame of scarcity, a light metal dressed up as a luxury.

trivia.title: A Cap on the Monument
trivia.summary: The Washington Monument needed a tip, and the builders chose a metal most visitors had never owned. In 1884 that choice was still a boast.
trivia.story: Stone rises, and the very top of the Washington Monument was finished with a small pyramid of aluminium. The cap was set in place in 1884, when the metal was still costly and still a novelty in any sizable piece. Visitors who would later think of aluminium as the stuff of cans were, in that year, looking at a rare material chosen for a national landmark. The cap did a practical job and a symbolic one. It said that the difficult metal from alum had become something a country could put on display. Cheap aluminium, from a process not yet in charge of the industry, was still two years away.

trivia.title: The Same Discovery Twice
trivia.summary: In 1886 a young man in Ohio and a young man in France solved the same costly problem. Neither needed the other's notebook.
trivia.story: Aluminium stayed a luxury until electricity became the factory. In 1886 Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Héroult in France, working independently, found how to draw the metal from molten ore with a strong current, and the processes matched closely enough that the industry still speaks both names. Hall was barely out of college, and Héroult was just as young. Each had to defend his claim in a world quick to suspect copying, and the evidence pointed to a true tie. Once the current ran at industrial scale, the court metal became foil, aircraft, and window frames. Scarcity had been a problem of method, and the method had arrived twice.

trivia.title: Aluminium or Aluminum
trivia.summary: Humphry Davy tried more than one spelling before the metal was even isolated. Britain and America later picked different survivors, and the table had to choose.
trivia.story: Davy suggested a name from alum before a pure metal existed, and he did not freeze the spelling. Alumium, aluminum, and aluminium all appeared as the word settled. British usage kept aluminium, with the extra syllable that matches other element names. American usage settled on aluminum, shorter and already printed on company signs. The split is harmless in a shop and annoying in a textbook that crosses a border, and international chemistry chose aluminium. The metal from the monument cap and from Hall's cell is one element with two public spellings, a naming quarrel that outlived every quarrel about who isolated it.

applications.title: Airplanes and cans
applications.body: Aluminum is light, and a clear oxide coat keeps it from rusting through. Aircraft skin, drink cans, and foil are the everyday forms.

applications.title: Power lines
applications.body: Aluminum conducts electricity well and is much lighter than copper, so many overhead power lines are aluminum.

applications.title: The oxide coat
applications.body: The dull surface of a can is a thin, tight layer of aluminum oxide. That layer is why the metal survives rain.

elements.name: Silicon

summary.beginner:
Silicon is element 14, the element computer chips are made from. You also meet it in sand and glass, joined with oxygen.

Its symbol is Si. At room temperature silicon is a solid. It is a metalloid, between the metals and the nonmetals in the way it behaves. On the periodic table it is in row 3, column 14. In class those are called period 3 and group 14.

Pure silicon is a shiny gray solid that conducts electricity only a little, which is exactly what a chip needs. Sand is silicon dioxide, a network of silicon and oxygen, not the pure element.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral silicon atom has 14 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Silicon is a solid metalloid in period 3 and group 14. Elemental silicon is a semiconductor with the same diamond-like network that carbon uses in diamond.

The electron configuration is [Ne] 3s2 3p2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 4. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4.

The band gap is about 1.1 eV, small enough for electronics and large enough that the pure solid is not a metal. Silicon-silicon bonds are weaker than carbon-carbon bonds, so silicon does not form the long chains life is built from.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Silicon (Z = 14) has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p2. Doping with group 13 or group 15 atoms turns that modest conductivity into the n-type and p-type silicon of a transistor.

Silica, SiO2, is a covalent network, which is why quartz and glass do not behave like a pile of small molecules.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Silicon: say the name, write Si, find Z=14 on the table, note the family (Metalloid), and connect it to one real use — chips and glass.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Silicon: electron configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p2, Typical oxidation states: +4. It sits in group 14. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. diamond-cubic semiconductor.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Silicon: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; band gap ~1.1 eV; weaker catenation than carbon If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from silica after earlier work by Gay-Lussac and Thenard.

elements.history:
Silica, as flint, quartz, and glass, is ancient. In 1824 Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated reasonably pure silicon by reducing potassium fluorosilicate. The name, which he gave, is from the Latin silex, flint. Gay-Lussac and Thénard had prepared an impure form earlier.

Silicon was a chemical footnote until the twentieth century. Zone refining and the transistor turned the element into the semiconductor of electronics, while silica remained the network of glass and rock.
elements.howDiscovered:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius heated potassium metal with potassium fluorosilicate in 1824, washed the mass with water until the soluble salts were gone, and was left with a brown amorphous powder. The powder burned to silica. Gay-Lussac and Thénard had seen a similar impure material earlier and had not established it.

Silica, as flint and quartz, was ancient. The element was the powder that could be burned back to silica and that was not carbon. Berzelius’s washing step is what made the claim convincing: the potassium and the fluoride were gone, and the residue was still there.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Silicon-28 is the principal ash of oxygen burning in massive stars. Oxygen nuclei fuse, and the burning tends toward silicon, the most tightly bound nucleus the star can stockpile before the final collapse. Silicon burning then consumes part of that stock on the way to iron.

What survives is the silicon the explosion freezes before the conversion can finish. Silicon-29 and silicon-30 take a share of neutrons during the same burning. Sand, glass, and the rocky planets are largely this frozen supernova ash.

trivia.title: Named for a Piece of Flint
trivia.summary: Flint, quartz, and glass were ancient crafts before anyone isolated the element in them. The Latin word for flint became the element's name.
trivia.story: People knapped flint into tools, melted sand into glass, and set quartz in jewelry without a theory of elements, and the common ingredient was silica. When Jöns Jacob Berzelius finally had a sample of the element itself, he named it from the Latin silex, flint. Silicon is a scholar's word for a substance the Stone Age had already used. The name points at the rock, not at the gray powder in his dish. Glassmakers did not change their furnaces because a chemist had chosen a Latin root. They had been handling silicon's oxide all along, under shop names that never needed a periodic table.

trivia.title: Berzelius and the Gray Element
trivia.summary: An impure form of silicon already existed when Berzelius tried again. He wanted a sample clean enough to deserve the name he was about to publish.
trivia.story: Gay-Lussac and Thénard had prepared an impure silicon earlier, a hint rather than a settled element. In 1824 Jöns Jacob Berzelius reduced potassium fluorosilicate and obtained silicon that was reasonably pure. The product was not a gem and not a metal in the everyday sense. It was a gray, brittle element that chemistry could finally point to. Berzelius gave it the name from flint and put it on a firmer footing than the earlier dirty samples. Isolation, for silicon, meant separating it from the oxygen it loves, and the rocks had never given it up willingly.

trivia.title: The Earlier Dirty Sample
trivia.summary: Before Berzelius, two French chemists had already forced a silicon compound to yield something new. Their product was real enough to matter and too impure to settle the question.
trivia.story: Discovery is sometimes a second attempt that gets the credit because the first attempt was muddy. Gay-Lussac and Thénard reduced a silicon compound and obtained a substance that later knowledge recognizes as impure silicon. They did not yet have the clean element or the lasting account. The work sat in the background while Berzelius, in 1824, made the case that persuades a textbook. The earlier pair were not imagining things, and they were early. Silicon's history has this near-miss built into it: a dark, contaminated sample that pointed the right way and could not, by itself, finish the proof.

trivia.title: From Sand to the Chip
trivia.summary: For a century silicon was a chemical footnote beside its famous oxide, sand. Then electronics needed an element that could conduct a little, and not too much.
trivia.story: Silica remained the main way people met silicon: glass, stone, and mortar. The element itself was a poor conductor compared with copper and a poor insulator compared with glass, which looked like a useless middle, and twentieth-century electronics needed exactly that middle. Zone refining made silicon extraordinarily pure, and the transistor age, after an early start with another element, settled on silicon chips. A grain of purified sand, rearranged, became the engine of a calculator and then of almost every device in a pocket. The flint of the old name had become a wafer. The change was purity and design, not a new discovery of the element.

trivia.title: Dust That Scars the Lungs
trivia.summary: The oxide of silicon is ordinary in rock and in a workshop floor. Breathed as fine dust, year after year, it is not ordinary at all.
trivia.story: Quarry workers, miners, and stone cutters have always lived in dust, and not all dust is the same. Fine silica, the oxide that glass and flint are made of, can scar the lungs when it is inhaled for long enough. The disease is silicosis, a stiffening of the breath that no cough clears. It is not a sudden accident with a single bang. It is a slow injury from a substance that looks as harmless as sand on a beach, and silicon the element became the chip. Silica the dust remained a reason for masks, water sprays, and laws about the air in a cutting shed.

applications.title: Computer chips
applications.body: Nearly every computer chip is a slice of silicon, altered in tiny regions so it can switch electrical signals.

applications.title: Sand and glass
applications.body: Sand is mostly silicon dioxide, silicon joined to oxygen. Melted with other ingredients, that sand becomes the glass in windows and bottles.

applications.title: Solar cells
applications.body: A solar panel is also silicon, made so that sunlight knocks electrons loose and produces a current.

elements.name: Phosphorus

summary.beginner:
Phosphorus is element 15, and your body uses it in bones and in DNA. Farmers meet it in fertilizer.

Its symbol is P. At room temperature phosphorus is a solid. It is a nonmetal. It does not look or act like iron or copper. On the periodic table it is in row 3, column 15. In class those are called period 3 and group 15.

There is a white form that must be kept under water because it catches fire in air, and a red form that is much calmer. The phosphorus in bones and in DNA is joined to oxygen, not stored as the pure element.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral phosphorus atom has 15 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Phosphorus is a solid nonmetal in period 3 and group 15. White phosphorus and red phosphorus are allotropes, and biology uses phosphorus almost entirely as phosphate, oxidation state +5.

The electron configuration is [Ne] 3s2 3p3. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 5. Oxidation states in this dossier are --3, +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is --3.

White phosphorus is P4 tetrahedra and is dangerously reactive. Red phosphorus is a network and is the form in matches. Fertilizers supply phosphate, not the element.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Phosphorus (Z = 15) has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p3. The P-O bonds of phosphate are the currency of ATP and the backbone links of DNA.

Oxidation states from -3 to +5 exist, but +5 dominates anything a cell or a farm actually uses.

Oxidation states in this dossier are --3, +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is --3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Prepared from urine; the first element discovered in recorded experiment.

elements.history:
In 1669 Hennig Brand, searching for the philosopher’s stone, distilled a waxy solid from urine that glowed in the dark. It was the first element with a recorded laboratory discovery. The name phosphorus, light-bearer, describes that glow.

Brand’s white phosphorus is dangerously reactive. The red allotrope and the phosphate minerals came later. Phosphate esters became the backbone of DNA and the currency of cell energy.
elements.howDiscovered:
In 1669 Hennig Brand evaporated a large volume of urine to a paste, mixed the residue with sand, and heated it hard in a retort. A waxy substance distilled over, glowed in the dark, and caught fire in air. He had been looking for a way to make gold.

The glow and the fire were the evidence that the distillate was not a known wax or a salt. It was the first element isolated by a recorded laboratory procedure, and the procedure was a distillation. Later chemists made the same substance from bones and from phosphate rock, which showed that the urine had been a source of phosphate, not a unique one.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Phosphorus-31 is the only stable isotope, and the odd proton number makes it a side product rather than a main ash. It forms in massive stars during neon and oxygen burning, and in the explosive burning of the supernova, where neutron captures on silicon also feed it.

The yield is small next to silicon and sulfur. That scarcity is cosmic, not only geological. The phosphate in DNA and in fertilizer rock is a minor channel of the same massive-star explosions that supplied the silicon around it.

trivia.title: A Glow from the Alchemist's Shed
trivia.summary: Hennig Brand was looking for the philosopher's stone, the dream that turns cheap matter into gold. He ended with a wax that shone in the dark.
trivia.story: In 1669 Hennig Brand boiled down a great quantity of urine, not as a doctor but as an alchemist, and he was hunting the philosopher's stone. The residue he heated gave him a waxy solid that glowed in the dark and caught fire more readily than any honest candle. It was phosphorus, the first element with a recorded laboratory discovery, and it was not gold. Brand had failed at the quest and succeeded at something he had no name for yet. The glow was beautiful and treacherous. He had isolated an element by chasing a fable, and the element was more dangerous than the gold would have been.

trivia.title: The Name Light-Bearer
trivia.summary: The waxy solid from Brand's furnace announced itself without a label. Its glow suggested the Greek word that became the element's name.
trivia.story: Brand's substance needed a name that a visitor could understand in a dark room. Phosphorus, from Greek words meaning light-bearer, described the pale glow and ignored the urine, the failed gold, and the fire risk. The name is poetic, and the substance was commercial almost at once. Brand and later makers showed the glow to paying audiences, and a discovered element had become a spectacle. The word still sounds gentle, like a morning star, which is a poor guide to the white form's temper, and the name records the wonder. The handling rules record everything the wonder left out.

trivia.title: The Match Workers' Jaw
trivia.summary: White phosphorus made matches that struck anywhere, and factories hired workers to handle it all day. The illness that followed had a bitter nickname.
trivia.story: Strike-anywhere matches were a convenience built on white phosphorus. In the factories, workers breathed fumes from the white phosphorus they handled day after day, and toothache came first. Then the bone of the jaw could die, the face swelled, and the pain lasted, and the illness was called phossy jaw, and it could kill. The description is ugly enough without the surgical details that filled medical reports. Public anger and later bans pushed white phosphorus out of matches in many countries. The glow that had delighted an alchemist's guests had become an occupational disease with a name of its own.

trivia.title: A Redder and Calmer Form
trivia.summary: White phosphorus was not the only way the element could be arranged. A red form, much less eager to catch fire, changed what a match factory could use.
trivia.story: The element that glowed in Brand's dish is the white allotrope, waxy, poisonous, and ready to ignite. A red form was later prepared, darker and much less eager to catch fire. Match makers learned to use that calmer form so white phosphorus could leave the factories. The change did not make phosphorus harmless in every compound, and it did remove the worst of the match-trade fumes. An element can be the same element and a different practical danger, depending on how the atoms are stacked. The red powder is the version that let the match survive the scandal.

trivia.title: From a Failed Search for Gold
trivia.summary: Brand never produced the stone that was supposed to enrich him. The waxy element he did produce became, much later, part of bones, fields, and the chemistry of cells.
trivia.story: The philosopher's stone was a promise of wealth, and Brand's glow did not pay that promise in his lifetime. Phosphorus remained a curiosity and a hazard until chemists learned the quieter chemistry of phosphates, and bones and teeth hold phosphate, and fertilizers made from phosphate rock fed fields. Inside cells, phosphate links store and spend energy, and they form the backbone of DNA. None of that was visible in the alchemist's shed. The episode is a failed search that stumbled into an element, then a long wait before anyone knew the element was already inside the searcher. Brand was looking for gold in urine and found a piece of his own body's chemistry.

applications.title: Bones and DNA
applications.body: Bones contain calcium phosphate, and the backbone of DNA uses phosphate links. Both are phosphorus joined to oxygen.

applications.title: Fertilizer
applications.body: Crops remove phosphorus from the soil, and fertilizer puts it back. The form plants use is phosphate, not the white element that catches fire.

applications.title: Matches
applications.body: The striking surface of a safety match uses red phosphorus. White phosphorus, a different form, is dangerous and is not a household material.

elements.name: Sulfur

summary.beginner:
Sulfur is element 16, a yellow solid once called brimstone. It is in some proteins in your body, and industry uses it to make sulfuric acid.

Its symbol is S. At room temperature sulfur is a solid. It is a nonmetal. It does not look or act like iron or copper. On the periodic table it is in row 3, column 16. In class those are called period 3 and group 16.

The yellow chunks are rings of eight sulfur atoms. When proteins are built, a little sulfur helps some of them hold their shape.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral sulfur atom has 16 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Sulfur is a solid nonmetal in period 3 and group 16. The common allotrope is S8 rings, and sulfuric acid is the industrial destination of most mined sulfur.

The electron configuration is [Ne] 3s2 3p4. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 6. Oxidation states in this dossier are --2, +4, +6. The one courses meet most often is --2.

Oxidation states run from -2, as in hydrogen sulfide, to +6 in sulfate and sulfuric acid. The smell of rotten eggs is the -2 form, not the yellow solid.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Sulfur (Z = 16) has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p4. Sulfur's many allotropes and its wide oxidation range, -2 through +6, are why it appears in proteins, in sulfide ores, and in the contact process for H2SO4.

Acid rain chemistry is the oxidation of SO2 toward sulfate.

Oxidation states in this dossier are --2, +4, +6. The one courses meet most often is --2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Sulfur: say the name, write S, find Z=16 on the table, note the family (Nonmetal), and connect it to one real use — proteins (cysteine) and sulfuric acid.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Sulfur: electron configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p4, Typical oxidation states: -2, +4, +6. It sits in group 16. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. S₈ rings; many allotropes.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Sulfur: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; oxidation −2 to +6; acid rain chemistry If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Known as brimstone in ores and volcanic deposits.

elements.history:
Sulfur, called brimstone, was known from volcanic deposits and from metal ores long before it was classed as an element. Lavoisier placed it among the elements in 1789. The name is from the Latin sulfur, of uncertain older origin.

The contact process for sulfuric acid, industrialized in the nineteenth century, made sulfur the starting point of the heavy chemical industry. The same element sits in the amino acids cysteine and methionine.
elements.howDiscovered:
Sulfur was gathered from volcanic ground and from the roasting of sulfide ores long before it had a place in a list of elements. Alchemists burned it, sublimed it, and combined it with metals. What they could not do was split it into simpler bodies.

Antoine Lavoisier put it among the elements in 1789 for that reason: it survived every attempt at decomposition and entered into compounds of definite weight. The discovery, for an ancient substance, was the decision that brimstone was already simple.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Sulfur-32 is built with silicon when massive stars burn oxygen, and the supernova returns both. Sulfur is abundant in the Sun for the same reason oxygen, silicon, and calcium are: the burning favors these even, tightly bound nuclei.

Heavier sulfur isotopes, especially sulfur-36, need additional neutrons and record a contribution from neutron capture. The sulfur in ore, and in the amino acids cysteine and methionine, is still the oxygen-burning product.

trivia.title: Brimstone from the Volcano
trivia.summary: Yellow crystals around volcanic vents were a familiar trade good long before chemistry had a list of elements. People already had a stern name for them.
trivia.story: Sulfur did not wait for a discoverer. It crusted the ground near volcanoes and turned up in metal ores, a yellow solid that burned with a sharp blue flame and a choking smell, and preachers called it brimstone and used it as an image of punishment. Merchants sold it as a practical substance for bleaches, medicines, and workshops. Nobody isolated it from a hidden compound in a famous year, because the element was already sitting in the open. Lavoisier, in 1789, did the quieter job of placing brimstone among the elements. The yellow rock had been known for ages, and the classification was the new part.

trivia.title: Written onto the Element List
trivia.summary: Ancient familiarity is not the same as a place in a chemical system. Lavoisier had to decide whether brimstone was simple or merely a mixture with a strong smell.
trivia.story: A substance can be famous and still lack a scientific rank. Sulfur had been burned in rituals and in workshops for centuries when Antoine Lavoisier set out his list of elements in 1789. He put sulfur on that list as a simple body, not as a compound waiting to be split. The decision matched the failure of every attempt to break it into simpler pieces. The name he and others used came from the Latin sulfur, an old word of uncertain deeper origin, and brimstone remained the popular name. The list gave the yellow element a formal seat beside carbon and phosphorus, the other solids that had been known by their fires.

trivia.title: Sulfur Pumped from the Deep
trivia.summary: Some sulfur beds lie too far down for a miner with a shovel. Herman Frasch bet that the element could be brought up as a liquid rather than as a chunk of ore.
trivia.story: Sicily's volcanic sulfur had supplied the world, and American beds were buried too deep for the same kind of digging. Herman Frasch proposed to melt the underground sulfur in place and pump it to the surface, and hot water went down the wells. Molten sulfur came up, and then cooled into the familiar yellow solid. The Frasch process, late in the nineteenth century, turned a geological inconvenience into a supply. Workers watched a yellow stream arrive from a hole in the ground, which is as strange a harvest as chemistry offers.

trivia.title: Rubber Meets Sulfur
trivia.summary: Natural rubber was sticky in the heat and brittle in the cold, and Charles Goodyear spent years trying to cure that temper. The change he needed involved sulfur.
trivia.story: Raw rubber frustrated everyone who tried to make it into a reliable object, and heat made it gummy, and cold made it crack. Charles Goodyear kept mixing and heating samples through years of failure and debt. In 1839 he heated rubber with sulfur, and the mass became tough, springy, and far less sensitive to the weather, and he called the change vulcanization. People still tell the moment as an accident on a hot stove. The documented core is the heating with sulfur and the year. A gummy plant resin had become a material for tires and seals, and sulfur was the ingredient that tamed it.

trivia.title: The Sharp Smell of Industry
trivia.summary: Sulfur's largest modern role is easy to miss, because the element is converted into an acid and sent onward. Coal smoke made the same smell a public nuisance.
trivia.story: Burn sulfur and the sharp gas that forms is sulfur dioxide, a choke in the throat and a cause of truly foul air. Coal that carried sulfur made that gas part of city fogs when factories and hearths were busiest. The same element, carefully burned and converted, became sulfuric acid, the heavy liquid at the center of industrial chemistry, and fertilizers, dyes, and countless other products started from that acid. The contact process scaled the conversion up in the nineteenth century. Sulfur's hazard and sulfur's usefulness share a smell, and one is the uncontrolled fume. The other is the acid plant that learned to catch the fume and put it to work.

applications.title: Sulfuric acid
applications.body: Most sulfur mined or recovered from fuels is burned and turned into sulfuric acid, one of the chemicals industry uses in the largest amounts.

applications.title: Proteins
applications.body: Some amino acids contain sulfur, and a link between two sulfur atoms helps many proteins hold their shape.

applications.title: Rubber and matches
applications.body: Vulcanized rubber is heated with sulfur so it is tough rather than sticky. Sulfur is also part of the chemistry of matches and of black gunpowder.

elements.name: Chlorine

summary.beginner:
Chlorine is element 17, a green-yellow gas with a sharp smell. A tiny controlled amount disinfects drinking water, and chlorine is also part of table salt.

Its symbol is Cl. At room temperature chlorine is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a halogen, a reactive nonmetal in the column next to the noble gases. On the periodic table it is in row 3, column 17. In class those are called period 3 and group 17.

In salt, chlorine has taken an electron and become part of a calm crystal. The pure gas is a different thing: it attacks tissue, and it is not something to make or smell on purpose.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Chlorine is a halogen gas in period 3 and group 17. Elemental chlorine is Cl2, a strong oxidizer, while chloride ion is the calm form in salt.

The electron configuration is [Ne] 3s2 3p5. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 7. Oxidation states in this dossier are --1, +1, +5, +7. The one courses meet most often is --1.

Oxidation states go beyond -1. Chlorate and perchlorate are the higher, more oxidizing oxyanions. PVC is a polymer built from a chlorine-containing monomer.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Chlorine (Z = 17) has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p5. Disinfection uses the oxidizing power of chlorine compounds, not a jar of the gas in a kitchen.

The jump from Cl- to ClO- to ClO3- to ClO4- is the oxyanion ladder courses compare with fluorine, which barely copies it.

Oxidation states in this dossier are --1, +1, +5, +7. The one courses meet most often is --1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Chlorine: say the name, write Cl, find Z=17 on the table, note the family (Halogen), and connect it to one real use — disinfectant and PVC.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Chlorine: electron configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p5, Typical oxidation states: -1, +1, +5, +7. It sits in group 17. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. diatomic gas; strong oxidizer.

discovery.text: Released from hydrochloric acid and pyrolusite.

elements.history:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele released a greenish gas from hydrochloric acid and pyrolusite in 1774 and thought it was an oxygen compound of muriatic acid. Humphry Davy showed in 1810 that the gas was itself an element and named it chlorine, from the Greek chloros, greenish yellow.

Chlorine’s first large use was bleaching. Drinking-water disinfection in the early twentieth century, and later PVC, made the element industrial. The chloride ion is also the main anion of seawater.
elements.howDiscovered:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele warmed hydrochloric acid with pyrolusite, manganese dioxide, and collected a dense greenish gas. It bleached litmus and attacked metals. He published the preparation in 1774 and took the gas to be muriatic acid with oxygen stuck to it, which was the going theory.

Humphry Davy tested that theory in 1810. He could get no oxygen out of the gas, charcoal would not reduce it, and its compounds with phosphorus and with metals behaved as if the gas itself were the simple body. The laboratory preparation is Scheele’s. The recognition that the green gas was an element, and not a compound of oxygen, is Davy’s.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Chlorine is odd-numbered, so it is not one of the main ashes. Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 form in the explosive oxygen and silicon burning of supernovae, as side products of the same zones that make sulfur and argon.

The two isotopes are not made in the same ratio in every zone, and measurements in stars and in meteorites use that ratio as a tracer. The chloride of seawater is this supernova chlorine, later dissolved from rock.

trivia.title: Scheele's Greenish Yellow Gas
trivia.summary: Carl Wilhelm Scheele let an acid meet a black ore and caught the gas that boiled off. He filed it as a compound, which left the real argument for later.
trivia.story: In his laboratory in 1774, Carl Wilhelm Scheele treated hydrochloric acid, then called muriatic acid, with the mineral pyrolusite. A greenish yellow gas came off, denser than air, and sharp enough to hurt the lungs, and it bleached colors and made animals suffer. Scheele believed he had made an oxygen compound of the acid, because that is what the chemistry of his moment encouraged him to see. He named nothing we would call an element. The gas was real, dangerous, and misfiled. Chlorine entered the record as a misunderstanding with a smell.

trivia.title: Davy Calls It an Element
trivia.summary: For decades the green gas was treated as a compound that still hid oxygen. Humphry Davy tested that belief until it broke, and then he named what was left.
trivia.story: Scheele's gas spent years on the wrong shelf. Chemists who still liked oxygen in every acid tried to find oxygen in it and kept failing in suggestive ways. In 1810 Humphry Davy argued that the gas was not a compound at all. It was a simple substance, an element, and the acid made from it contained hydrogen and this gas, not oxygen, and he named it chlorine, from the Greek chloros, greenish yellow. The name describes the look of the gas in a jar, and the argument describes a break with Lavoisier's acid theory. A color became a name only after a theory lost.

trivia.title: Bleach First, Then the Tap
trivia.summary: Cloth mills wanted a faster way to whiten fabric than sunlight on a field. The green gas did the job, and much later a diluted use of it reached city water.
trivia.story: Chlorine's first large market was bleaching. Cloth that once sat for weeks in the sun could be whitened with chlorine water, and mills adopted the speed, and the work was harsh on the people who stood over the vats. Early in the twentieth century a quieter use spread: cities began adding small amounts of chlorine compounds to drinking water to kill germs that spread disease. The taste in a swimming pool is a cousin of that decision. A gas that Scheele could barely stand to breathe had become, in tiny controlled dose, a public-health tool. The dose is the whole difference between the mill and the tap.

trivia.title: A Cloud at Ypres
trivia.summary: By 1915 chlorine was an industrial gas moved in heavy containers. At the Second Battle of Ypres it was turned on soldiers, and the memory is still grim.
trivia.story: Chlorine had been a bleach and a chemical feedstock. In 1915, at the Second Battle of Ypres, it was released as a weapon, and a greenish yellow cloud drifted into the lines. Soldiers who met the dense gas choked, and many were injured or killed. The episode is remembered as an early poison-gas attack of that war, and the suffering is the story. A gas first caught over a laboratory bench had been scaled up until it could be aimed at people. Later rules of war tried to put that use outside the boundary of allowed weapons.

trivia.title: The Main Salt of the Sea
trivia.summary: The fierce gas is not the form of chlorine that covers most of the planet. Seawater's familiar salt is where the element spends its quiet abundance.
trivia.story: A jar of chlorine gas is a small, angry sample of an element that is mostly dissolved. In the sea, chlorine has already done its reacting and sits as chloride ions, paired largely with sodium. Evaporate a pan of seawater and the white crystals are the same salt that seasons food. The element Davy named for its green color is, in that form, colorless and essential, and living bodies use chloride as well. The war cloud and the ocean salt are a harsh contrast, and both are chlorine. The ion is the one a swimmer actually meets, even when a pool smells of the gas's sharper chemistry.

applications.title: Drinking water
applications.body: A carefully controlled dose of chlorine, or of a chlorine compound, kills germs in drinking water and in swimming pools.

applications.title: Table salt
applications.body: The chlorine in table salt is the chloride ion, paired with sodium. It is not the green gas.

applications.title: Plastics
applications.body: PVC, the plastic in some pipes and window frames, is made from a chlorine-containing building block. The pure gas is an industrial hazard, not a craft supply.
