elements.name: Argon

summary.beginner:
Argon is element 18, a gas in the air that almost never reacts. Welders use it as a shield so hot metal does not burn in oxygen.

Its symbol is Ar. At room temperature argon is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a noble gas. Left alone, it almost never joins other elements to make compounds. On the periodic table it is in row 3, column 18. In class those are called period 3 and group 18.

About one percent of air is argon, left behind when oxygen and nitrogen are taken out. Its outer shell is full, which is why it sits with helium and neon.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral argon atom has 18 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Argon is a noble gas in period 3 and group 18. Argon was the first noble gas isolated from air, and its closed shell is why it is the shielding gas in welding.

The electron configuration is [Ne] 3s2 3p6. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 8. Oxidation states are not listed for this entry.

It is denser and far more abundant than neon. A few compounds exist under special conditions, but ordinary chemistry treats argon as inert. Geologists also use the decay of potassium-40 to argon to date rocks.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Argon (Z = 18) has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p6. K-Ar and Ar-Ar dating work because 40K decays to 40Ar and the argon stays trapped in a mineral until the rock is heated.

Chemically, the closed shell still means no ordinary molecules.

Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Argon: say the name, write Ar, find Z=18 on the table, note the family (Noble gas), and connect it to one real use — inert welding atmosphere.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Argon: electron configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p6, Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. It sits in group 18. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. closed shell; first noble gas isolated from air.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Argon: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; used in K-Ar dating of rocks If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found as a denser leftover when oxygen and nitrogen were removed from air.

elements.history:
Lord Rayleigh found that nitrogen prepared from air was slightly denser than nitrogen prepared from ammonia. With William Ramsay, in 1894, he removed oxygen and nitrogen from air and was left with a new gas that would not react. They named it argon, from the Greek argos, idle.

Argon was the first noble gas isolated from air and the clue that a whole group was missing from the table. It is now the inert atmosphere of welding and of many laboratory gloveboxes, and the daughter product used in potassium–argon dating.
elements.howDiscovered:
Lord Rayleigh weighed nitrogen prepared from ammonia and nitrogen left after oxygen was removed from air. The atmospheric gas was heavier, by about half a percent, more than his errors allowed. William Ramsay removed oxygen with hot copper and then nitrogen with hot magnesium, and a residual gas remained, about one percent of the air.

The residue had no chemical reactions they could find, and its spectrum was new. They announced it in 1894. The discovery was a discrepancy in a density, followed by a subtraction: take out everything that could be taken out, and weigh what refused to leave.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
The argon in the Sun is mostly argon-36, built by oxygen burning in massive stars, with argon-38 beside it. That is the argon the Galaxy makes as a gas and returns in supernovae.

The argon in Earth’s air is a different isotope. Almost all of it is argon-40, the decay product of potassium-40 in rocks, accumulated in the atmosphere over geologic time. A cylinder of welding argon and a sample of solar argon are the same element and two different histories.

trivia.title: Nitrogen That Weighed Too Much
trivia.summary: Lord Rayleigh prepared nitrogen in two ways and trusted his balance. The samples should have matched, and the one from air was stubbornly heavier.
trivia.story: Lord Rayleigh measured the density of nitrogen with the patience of a man who trusts a third decimal place. Nitrogen made from ammonia had one weight, and nitrogen taken from air, after he removed everything he thought air contained, was slightly heavier. The difference was small and repeatable, which made it worse than a sloppy error he could shrug off. A careful experiment that disagrees with itself is a clue, and Rayleigh could not blame the balance forever. Something invisible in the air was riding along with the nitrogen and adding mass. The something had no smell, no color, and no desire to react.

trivia.title: The Gas That Would Not Work
trivia.summary: William Ramsay joined the hunt for whatever was hiding in atmospheric nitrogen. When the busy gases were gone, a remainder sat in the tube and refused every chemical chore.
trivia.story: Rayleigh's heavy nitrogen needed a chemist willing to strip air still further. William Ramsay worked with him, and in 1894 they removed oxygen and nitrogen from the air until a small fraction remained. The gas would not burn, would not support burning, and would not form the compounds they offered it. They named it argon, from the Greek argos, idle, and the insult was accurate. Argon is about one percent of the air, abundant and almost unemployed. The idle fraction had been the extra weight in Rayleigh's flask, and a density error had been a new element.

trivia.title: Keeping the Filament Alive
trivia.summary: A hot lamp filament burns away if ordinary air reaches it. An idle gas turned out to be exactly the roommate a glowing wire needed.
trivia.story: Argon's refusal to react looked like a dead end and became a product. Early electric lamps used a vacuum so the carbon or metal filament would not burn. A little argon, sometimes mixed with another quiet gas, let the bulb run with the filament protected and with less of the metal boiling away. Welders later used the same idleness, flooding a hot joint with argon so oxygen could not reach the molten metal. The gas named for doing nothing had a career in standing between hot metal and the air. Rayleigh's nuisance weight became the atmosphere inside a light bulb.

trivia.title: A Column the Table Lacked
trivia.summary: One idle gas could have been a freak. Argon instead suggested that a whole family was missing from the periodic table, with empty seats still to fill.
trivia.story: Mendeleev's table had no comfortable room for a gas that formed no compounds. Argon was the first noble gas isolated from air, and it was a clue rather than a finished group. If one inert element hid in nitrogen's weight, others might hide in the same air, at different boiling points. Ramsay's later work found them. The table gained a column that nobody had predicted with argon's clarity. The tense part of the story is the first refusal: many chemists wanted the heavy nitrogen to be an experimental mistake, because a new group is a lot to accept from a tiny difference on a balance, and the balance won.

trivia.title: A Clock Left in the Rock
trivia.summary: Argon does almost nothing in a chemical sense, which makes it a strange partner for telling time. In certain minerals it accumulates anyway, and geologists learned to read it.
trivia.story: Potassium in a mineral slowly changes, and one of its radioactive forms becomes argon. The argon, having no chemistry to carry it off, can stay trapped in the crystal. Measure the potassium still there and the argon stored beside it, and the pair behaves like a clock for the age of the rock. A gas named idle is idle enough to be a reliable accumulation. Rayleigh had found it as a nuisance in a density experiment, and geologists found it as a record. The element that would not react became evidence of how long a stone had been a stone.

applications.title: Welding
applications.body: Argon is blown around a weld so the hot metal meets an inert gas instead of oxygen. The weld stays clean.

applications.title: Light bulbs
applications.body: Some bulbs are filled with argon so the hot filament lasts longer than it would in air.

applications.title: Dating rocks
applications.body: A little of the potassium in a mineral slowly becomes argon. Measuring that argon tells geologists how long the rock has been solid.

sample.body: Pure argon, sealed in glass. The gas has no color of its own, so the sample looks like a clear tube. This is the element by itself, not a compound.

elements.name: Potassium

summary.beginner:
Potassium is element 19, a soft metal that reacts even more eagerly than sodium. In food and in your nerves you meet it dissolved in water, not as the pure metal.

Its symbol is K. At room temperature potassium is a solid. It is an alkali metal: soft, and quick to react with water. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 1. In class those are called period 4 and group 1.

Bananas are famous for it, but the potassium there is a charged form mixed into the food, not a lump of metal. Your nerves use that charged form, together with sodium, to send signals.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral potassium atom has 19 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Potassium is a solid alkali metal in period 4 and group 1. The outer electron is in 4s and is lost to give K+, the ion inside living cells.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 4s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 8, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

Potassium is larger than sodium, so K+ and Na+ do different jobs across a cell membrane. The metal itself reacts violently with water and is kept under oil.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Potassium (Z = 19) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 4s1. The Na+/K+ pump spends metabolic energy to keep K+ inside cells and Na+ outside.

The very low ionization energy of the 4s electron is why the pure metal is never the form in food.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Potassium: say the name, write K, find Z=19 on the table, note the family (Alkali metal), and connect it to one real use — bananas and nerve signals.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Potassium: electron configuration [Ar] 4s1, Typical oxidation states: +1. It sits in group 1. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. largest common alkali ion in cells.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Potassium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; K⁺ Na⁺ pump; very low ionization energy If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated by electrolysis of molten potash.

elements.history:
Potash, the ash of burned plants, was an old industrial alkali. Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1807 by electrolyzing molten potash, the experiment that opened his series of alkali and alkaline-earth metals. The symbol K is from the Latin kalium, from alkali. The English name potassium is from potash.

The metal is too reactive for ordinary handling. The ion carries nerve signals and is the partner of sodium in the membrane pump of animal cells.
elements.howDiscovered:
In October 1807 Humphry Davy touched the poles of a voltaic pile to a piece of moist potash, which the current melted. Metallic globules formed at the negative pole, burst into flame in air, and decomposed water. He had been trying to decompose the fixed alkalis, which Lavoisier had suspected were compounds and which nobody had split.

Potash itself was the ash of plants, an old industrial alkali. The element was the metal that appeared only when the current was strong enough to tear it out of the melt. Sodium followed within days on the same apparatus. The method, not a new ore, was the discovery.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Potassium is odd-numbered and less abundant than calcium or argon. Potassium-39, the common isotope, is made in the explosive burning of massive stars, in the oxygen- and silicon-burning shells the supernova shocks. Slow neutron capture in giant stars adds a share.

Potassium-40 is long-lived, with a half-life of about 1.25 billion years. Stars made it, the solar system inherited some, and its decay still heats the Earth’s interior and supplies the argon-40 of the air. The potassium in minerals is mostly the stable 39, with a trace of that clock.

trivia.title: Metal from a Pot of Ash
trivia.summary: Potash was a workshop alkali made from burned plants. Humphry Davy melted it and applied a current, hoping the ash still hid a metal.
trivia.story: Burn a plant, leach the ash, and boil the liquor down, and the white residue is potash, an old industrial alkali. In 1807 Humphry Davy melted that potash and passed an electric current through it. Globules of a silvery metal appeared at the electrode, and they did not behave like any metal already on his shelf. This was the experiment that opened his run of alkali and alkaline-earth metals, and the sample was small and frantic. Davy had turned a soap-maker's chemical into an element. Potassium existed before anyone could hold it, inside every pot of ash, disguised as a compound.

trivia.title: Potash, Kalium, and the Letter K
trivia.summary: The English name remembers the pot of ash. The symbol remembers a Latin word for alkali, which is why K and potassium do not match.
trivia.story: Davy's metal needed a name that ordinary English could say. Potassium comes from potash, and potash comes from the pot in which plant ash was boiled. The symbol is K, from the Latin kalium, itself drawn from alkali. Two histories are packed into one box on the table. A student who looks for a P and finds nothing is meeting that double origin, not a misprint, and the name points at a kitchen and a field. The symbol points at the older chemical word for the bitter salts, and both are honest, and they simply refuse to start with the same letter.

trivia.title: A Faint Activity in the Body
trivia.summary: Most potassium atoms are stable, and the body is full of them. A tiny share is not stable, and it has always been part of being alive.
trivia.story: Potassium ions help nerves fire, and bananas get joked about for holding the element, and almost all of that potassium is quiet. A small fraction is potassium-40, a natural radioactive isotope that has been in rocks, in plants, and in people for as long as there have been people. It decays slowly and contributes to the background radiation a body already lives with, and no accident put it there. It is part of the element's natural mixture. The metal Davy isolated is a fierce laboratory specimen. The isotope in a living cell is a whisper, present in everyone and easy to forget.

trivia.title: Ash That Farmers Sought
trivia.summary: Before anyone isolated the metal, potash was bought, sold, and spread. Fields and soap kettles were the element's early career.
trivia.story: Potassium's first economy had no electrolysis in it. Settlers and farmers burned wood, saved the ash, and sold potash to soap makers and to glassworks. Some of it went back onto fields as a fertilizer, replacing what crops had pulled from the soil, and the trade was messy, smoky, and older than Davy's battery. When mines of potassium salts were later opened, they continued the same job more cleanly: feed the ion to plants. The pure metal remained a specialist reagent, stored away from water. The element that matters in a furrow is the ion the ash already contained, centuries before it had a letter K.

trivia.title: A Lilac Flame on Water
trivia.summary: Davy's new metal could not be left on a damp bench. The moment it met water, the experiment stopped being a quiet separation.
trivia.story: Potassium is softer than sodium and even less willing to coexist with water. A small piece dropped on a bowl races, melts from its own heat, and burns with a lilac flame. Davy saw that violence immediately and understood he had not made a tame silver. The flame is pretty in a demonstration and unforgiving in a spill, and teachers keep the metal under oil and use a speck. The hazard is the element wanting its compounds back, especially the hydroxide it forms with water. That violence is why potassium metal never became a household object, while its ion became a necessity.

applications.title: Nerves and food
applications.body: Potassium ions inside your cells help nerves and muscles work. Fruits and vegetables are the ordinary way people meet it.

applications.title: Fertilizer
applications.body: Potash fertilizer supplies potassium that crops take out of the soil. It is a potassium salt, not the metal.

applications.title: The metal itself
applications.body: Pure potassium reacts violently with water and is kept under oil. It is a laboratory and industrial chemical, not a supplement.

elements.name: Calcium

summary.beginner:
Calcium is element 20, the metal locked inside your bones and teeth as compounds. Lime, chalk, and cement are calcium compounds too.

Its symbol is Ca. At room temperature calcium is a solid. It is an alkaline-earth metal. These metals react, but less wildly than the alkali metals beside them. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 2. In class those are called period 4 and group 2.

You do not meet shiny calcium metal in a kitchen. You meet calcium carbonate in chalk and limestone, and calcium ions doing jobs in muscles and in hard water.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral calcium atom has 20 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Calcium is a solid alkaline-earth metal in period 4 and group 2. Calcium chemistry is the +2 ion, Ca2+, in bones, limestone, and hard water.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

Heating limestone drives off carbon dioxide and leaves lime, CaO. Hard water is mostly dissolved calcium and magnesium salts.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Calcium (Z = 20) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 4s2. Ca2+ is both a structural ion in apatite and a signaling ion in cells.

Carbonate rocks are a calcium reservoir, not a source of the free metal.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Calcium: say the name, write Ca, find Z=20 on the table, note the family (Alk. earth), and connect it to one real use — bones, lime, cement.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Calcium: electron configuration [Ar] 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It sits in group 2. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. hard water; +2 ion.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Calcium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Ca²⁺ signaling; carbonate rocks If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from lime by electrolysis.

elements.history:
Lime, from burning limestone, was a Roman building material. Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808 by electrolysis, with help from Berzelius, and named it calcium from the Latin calx, lime. The metal itself was a nineteenth-century curiosity.

The ion is the one that matters: limestone and marble, bones and teeth, cement, and the hardness of water. Calcium carbonate is the mineral record of shells and reefs.
elements.howDiscovered:
Lime was an ancient product of burned limestone. Humphry Davy failed to electrolyze it directly. In 1808, with a suggestion from Berzelius, he mixed moist lime with mercuric oxide, electrolyzed the paste, and distilled the mercury away from the amalgam. A silver-white metal remained, in small amount.

The metal burned back to lime. That cycle was the proof: the earth had been reduced, and the product regenerated the earth. Calcium was discovered as a metal only after the alkaline earths were accepted as oxides waiting for a strong enough reduction, which the pile and the mercury cathode provided.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Calcium-40 is a doubly magic nucleus, built by oxygen burning and silicon burning in massive stars and ejected in the supernova. It dominates the calcium of the Sun and of limestone.

The neutron-richer isotopes, up to calcium-48, are not made by that even chain of helium nuclei. They need a neutron-rich environment, and calcium-48 in particular is still argued over. Bone, chalk, and cement are the common isotope, the massive-star product.

trivia.title: Lime Older Than the Metal
trivia.summary: Romans burned limestone to make lime for mortar long before anyone thought of lime as the oxide of a metal. The building trade had the compound, not the element.
trivia.story: Heat limestone in a kiln and it becomes quicklime, a caustic white solid that builders have slaked and mixed into mortar for thousands of years, and Roman structures still show that craft. The word calcium comes from the Latin calx, lime, so the element's name bows to the kiln rather than to a laboratory dish. Nobody in ancient Rome isolated the metal, and nobody needed to. Lime, limestone, and marble were the useful forms. When a chemist finally pulled a metal out of the compounds, he named it for the ash the builders already trusted. Calcium is a modern word nailed onto an ancient material.

trivia.title: Davy Pulls a Metal from Lime
trivia.summary: The alkali metals had fallen to electrolysis, and lime was a harder target. Humphry Davy, with help from Berzelius, forced calcium out in 1808.
trivia.story: Lime resisted the methods that had worked quickly on potash and soda. In 1808 Humphry Davy, aided by advice and materials from Berzelius, electrolyzed a moistened mixture and obtained a small amount of calcium metal, and the sample was a curiosity, not a structural material. It proved that lime was the oxide of an element and not an element itself. Builders did not switch from limestone to the metal, which would have been a useless expense. The nineteenth century kept calcium metal as a chemical specimen. The ion and the carbonate went on holding up walls, the same job they had before Davy's current ever ran.

trivia.title: Shells, Bones, and Reefs
trivia.summary: Limestone is often a cemetery of shells. Animals have been depositing calcium compounds for ages, and human skeletons do a version of the same storage.
trivia.story: A chalk cliff is a crowd of tiny shells, pressed into stone, and each shell was built from calcium carbonate by a living creature. Coral reefs are the same idea at the scale of a coastline. Bones and teeth store calcium in a different mineral, hard enough to carry a body and to chew, and the metal itself never appears in these structures. The ion does, arranged by biology into shapes that last. When the animal dies, the shell can become the limestone a later kiln will burn. Calcium's famous uses are mostly these compounds, passing from reef to rock to mortar without anyone needing the pure element.

trivia.title: The Kiln's Caustic Product
trivia.summary: Quicklime looks like a harmless white powder until it meets water, including the water in skin. Lime burners learned that lesson long before the metal was known.
trivia.story: The hazard in the calcium story is usually not the soft metal, which few people handle, and it is quicklime, the product of the kiln. When quicklime meets water it slakes, heating strongly and forming a caustic slurry, and on skin, that reaction burns. Workers in old lime kilns treated the powder with a respect that the pretty white color does not suggest. Even the slaked lime used in mortar can irritate until it has set. The element's everyday danger is a building material, not a rare laboratory fire. Calcium metal can be reactive too, and still the injuries that fill the historical record belong to the lime.

trivia.title: Cement in the Growing City
trivia.summary: Mortar was old, and a stronger binder was wanted for bridges, pipes, and apartment blocks. Cement took lime's ancient chemistry and fired it into a new setting habit.
trivia.story: Lime mortar served for centuries and then met the nineteenth century's appetite for bigger work. Cement, made by firing limestone with clay and grinding the result, sets even under water and hardens into a stone of its own, and calcium compounds are the heart of that setting. Cities poured it into foundations, and engineers reinforced it with steel. The pure metal Davy isolated remained almost irrelevant to the skyline. What rose over streets was the same element the Romans had burned in kilns, now proportioned and fired with a control they did not have. A soft laboratory metal and a concrete pier share an element and almost nothing else.

applications.title: Bones and teeth
applications.body: Bone and tooth mineral are calcium compounds. Dairy foods and many greens are the usual sources in a diet.

applications.title: Cement and lime
applications.body: Cement, mortar, and agricultural lime are calcium compounds made from limestone. They are among the most-used materials on Earth.

applications.title: Hard water
applications.body: The scale in a kettle is mostly calcium carbonate left behind when hard water boils. A water softener trades those calcium ions for sodium.

elements.name: Scandium

summary.beginner:
Scandium is element 21, the first metal of the middle block of the table. It is uncommon, and small amounts go into special aluminum alloys.

Its symbol is Sc. At room temperature scandium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 3. In class those are called period 4 and group 3.

Scandium is not a metal you find in a hardware store. Its atom is the start of a new pattern: electrons begin to fill a set of d orbitals.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral scandium atom has 21 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Scandium is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 3. The configuration is 3d1 4s2, and the ion you meet in compounds is almost always Sc3+.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d1 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

Losing those three electrons leaves a noble-gas core. Scandium's size and +3 charge make it resemble the heavy rare earths more than iron or copper.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Scandium (Z = 21) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d1 4s2. After the lanthanide contraction, yttrium is close to scandium in size, which is why the two travel together in ores.

There is no important +2 chemistry.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Scandium: say the name, write Sc, find Z=21 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — first transition metal.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Scandium: electron configuration [Ar] 3d1 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 3. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. 3d¹ 4s²; almost always +3.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Scandium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; similar to yttrium in size after the lanthanide contraction If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from euxenite and gadolinite earths.

elements.history:
Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap under boron and predicted an element he called ekaboron. Lars Fredrik Nilson separated that element from the rare earths euxenite and gadolinite in 1879 and named it scandium for Scandinavia. Per Teodor Cleve soon showed that it matched Mendeleev’s prediction.

Scandium stayed scarce. It is the first of the transition metals, almost always in the +3 state, and a light alloying addition rather than a bulk metal.
elements.howDiscovered:
Lars Fredrik Nilson was separating the rare earths of euxenite and gadolinite. In 1879 a fraction of the ytterbia gave an oxide whose atomic weight and salts matched none of the known earths. The spectrum showed lines that belonged to the fraction and not to ytterbium.

Per Teodor Cleve examined the same earth and pointed out that its properties were the ones Mendeleev had published for ekaboron, the gap under boron. The discovery was a fractional crystallization that refused to stay a single earth, confirmed by a spectrum and by a predicted atomic weight. The metal itself was isolated later.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Scandium has one stable isotope, scandium-45, and the odd proton number keeps it rare. It is made mainly in supernovae, as a side product of explosive oxygen and silicon burning. Slow neutron capture in giant stars adds a further share.

There is no abundant path of helium captures that stops on scandium, which is why it sits in a valley between calcium and titanium on the cosmic abundance curve. The scandium in a light alloy is that minor channel, concentrated later by geology.

trivia.title: The Gap Mendeleev Left
trivia.summary: Dmitri Mendeleev's table had a blank space under boron, and he refused to pretend the blank was a mistake. He described an element he had never held.
trivia.story: When Mendeleev arranged the elements by their patterns, one seat under boron stayed empty, and he did not hide the gap. He predicted an element he called ekaboron and sketched the properties it ought to have, including a low density for a metal and an oxide of a certain kind, and the prediction was a risk. If nothing ever appeared, the table looked like a guessing game. If something appeared and matched, the table looked like a map. For years ekaboron was only a word in a Russian chemist's notebook. The rocks that actually held it had not yet been read carefully enough.

trivia.title: Nilson Separates the Earth
trivia.summary: Rare minerals from Scandinavia were a tangle of similar earths. Lars Fredrik Nilson, working through that tangle in 1879, found one that the tangle had been hiding.
trivia.story: Euxenite and gadolinite are dark, unhelpful-looking minerals, full of the rare earths that resemble one another. Lars Fredrik Nilson separated those earths with the tedious chemistry the job required. In 1879 he reached an earth that was not yttrium and not the neighbors he already knew, and he had a new element. The sample was small, as scandium samples tend to be, and it was real. Nilson was not chasing Mendeleev's nickname when he started the separation, and he was cleaning up a mineral. The match to ekaboron came as a consequence, once someone compared the new earth with the old prediction.

trivia.title: Named for Scandinavia
trivia.summary: The new earth had been pulled from Scandinavian minerals, and the name recorded the place. A predicted ghost had acquired a homeland.
trivia.story: Nilson named the element scandium, for Scandinavia, the region whose minerals had surrendered it. The name is geographic, like magnesium's, and it says nothing about color or reactivity because those were not the drama. The drama was that it existed at all, in a group of earths that had fooled analysts before. Scandium is the first of the transition metals, almost always in the +3 state, and it is scattered rather than piled into rich ores, and the name sounds local. The element is not especially local. It took Scandinavian minerals, and a chemist willing to separate them, to make the local name possible.

trivia.title: Cleve Checks the Prediction
trivia.summary: A new earth is not automatically the element a theorist ordered. Per Teodor Cleve set Nilson's scandium beside Mendeleev's ekaboron and looked for a mismatch.
trivia.story: Predictions are cheap until someone measures. Per Teodor Cleve took the element Nilson had separated and compared it with what Mendeleev had written down for ekaboron. The atomic weight, the character of the oxide, and the general behavior lined up, and Cleve said so plainly. The gap under boron had been a real seat, not a decorative hole. For Mendeleev the confirmation was a public victory, one of the moments when the periodic table stopped being a filing system and became evidence, and Nilson had found the element. Cleve had shown that the finding was the one the table had been waiting for.

trivia.title: Scattered, and Still Useful
trivia.summary: Scandium is not vanishingly rare in the crust, yet it almost never forms a mine of its own. That awkward distribution kept it a specialist metal.
trivia.story: After the triumph of the prediction, scandium refused to become common in the marketplace. It is spread thinly through many rocks and concentrated in few of them, so a lump of the metal stayed costly, and alloys were the practical answer. A small addition of scandium to aluminium lightens and strengthens pieces used in aircraft and in sporting equipment, where a little performance is worth the price. The metal never supplied a famous accident. The tense episode was the empty square. Ekaboron had been imagined as a missing pillar, and scandium arrived as a pinch in someone else's alloy.

applications.title: Aluminum alloys
applications.body: A little scandium makes some aluminum alloys stronger without making them much heavier. Aerospace and sports equipment have used those alloys.

applications.title: Lighting
applications.body: Scandium iodide in some metal-halide lamps helps the light look more like daylight.

applications.title: Not a hardware-store metal
applications.body: Scandium is uncommon and is sold to alloy makers, not as a bar for a workshop. The interesting chemistry is the steady +3 ion.

elements.name: Titanium

summary.beginner:
Titanium is element 22, a strong metal that is light for its strength. Airplanes use it, and a white compound of it colors a lot of white paint.

Its symbol is Ti. At room temperature titanium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 4. In class those are called period 4 and group 4.

The metal resists corrosion because a tough oxide coat forms on the surface. The white in paint is not the metal. It is titanium dioxide, a powder.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral titanium atom has 22 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Titanium is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 4. Titanium is light, strong, and protected by a passivating oxide, and the usual oxidation state is +4.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d2 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 10, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +4.

TiO2 is the white pigment. Lower oxidation states exist, but +4 dominates ores and products. The metal's strength-to-weight ratio is why aerospace uses it.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Titanium (Z = 22) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d2 4s2. The passivating TiO2 film is why the metal survives seawater and the body.

In compounds the +4 state is d0, which is also why the pigment is white rather than colored.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +4. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Titanium: electron configuration [Ar] 3d2 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +4, +3, +2. It sits in group 4. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. light, strong, corrosion-resistant.

discovery.text: Found in Cornish ilmenite; Klaproth named it after the Titans.

elements.history:
William Gregor, a Cornish clergyman, found a new metal oxide in the black sand menachanite in 1791. Martin Heinrich Klaproth rediscovered it in a Hungarian ore in 1795 and named it titanium, for the Titans. Matthew Hunter isolated a pure ductile metal only in 1910.

The Kroll process of the 1940s made titanium a structural metal. Its oxide, already used as a white pigment, is still the form most people meet.
elements.howDiscovered:
William Gregor, in Cornwall, separated the black sand menachanite from the stream with a magnet, dissolved it in acid, and removed the iron. A white oxide remained. In 1791 he reported that the oxide was not a known earth. He did not obtain the metal.

Martin Heinrich Klaproth independently found the same oxide in Hungarian rutile in 1795 and gave the element its name. A ductile metal came only in 1910, when Matthew Hunter heated the chloride with sodium in a sealed bomb. The discovery was the white oxide that survived after the iron had been taken out of a magnetic sand.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Stable titanium, mostly titanium-48, is a product of explosive silicon burning. The supernova assembles a radioactive parent, chromium-48, which decays through vanadium-48 down to titanium-48. The hot, expanding debris, called alpha-rich freeze-out, contributes more.

A radioactive cousin, titanium-44, is made in the same explosions and decays onward to calcium. Its gamma rays are still seen in the remnant Cassiopeia A. The titanium in an airframe is the stable isotope, frozen out of blasts of that kind before the Sun formed.

trivia.title: Black Sand in a Cornish Stream
trivia.summary: William Gregor was a clergyman who studied minerals in his spare hours. A black sand in his parish did not match the ores he knew.
trivia.story: In Cornwall, a black sand called menachanite collected in streams, heavy and easy to overlook. William Gregor, a clergyman with a chemist's habits, analyzed it in 1791 and found a new metal oxide mixed with iron. He suggested a new metal, sometimes remembered under a name drawn from the local valley. The report did not make him famous, and the oxide did not give up a useful lump of metal. Gregor had still seen the element first. Titanium's discovery begins with a parish curiosity and a careful amateur, not with a grand laboratory and a finished ingot.

trivia.title: Klaproth Names the Titans
trivia.summary: A few years after Gregor's sand, Martin Heinrich Klaproth met the same oxide in a different ore. He gave the metal a name large enough to stick.
trivia.story: Martin Heinrich Klaproth, working in 1795 on a Hungarian ore, rediscovered the oxide Gregor had found in Cornwall. He did not keep the local nickname. He named the metal titanium, for the Titans, the giant family of Greek myth. The name promised strength, which was optimistic, because nobody could yet isolate a clean, workable metal. Klaproth's authority as an analyst made the element real to other chemists in a way Gregor's parish paper had not, and two men had found one oxide. The mythological name won, and the Cornish sand became a footnote to a Titan.

trivia.title: A Century to a Workable Metal
trivia.summary: Knowing titanium's oxide was not the same as holding a bar that could be bent. The element stayed tangled with oxygen and nitrogen long after its name was settled.
trivia.story: Titanium's compounds were common enough, and the pure metal was exasperating. It soaks up oxygen and nitrogen when it is hot, so ordinary smelting produced a brittle mess rather than a ductile bar. Matthew Hunter finally isolated a pure, workable metal in 1910, more than a century after Gregor's sand, and the delay was the story, and chemists had not been lazy. The element had been difficult. Hunter's sample showed that titanium could be a metal in the practical sense, light and strong, once a workable sample finally existed. The Titans of the name had stayed stuck in their oxides for a century.

trivia.title: White Paint in the Can
trivia.summary: Most people never meet titanium metal. They meet the oxide, a fierce white pigment that replaced older whites with a dangerous reputation.
trivia.story: Titanium dioxide is brilliantly white, stable, and widespread in paint, plastic, and paper. For much of the twentieth century it pushed aside lead white, a pigment that had poisoned painters and residents for generations. The new white did the visual job without that particular metal's toxicity, and sunscreen and toothpaste later used the same oxide. A person can live among titanium compounds and never see the gray metal. Gregor's black sand and a bright kitchen wall are the same element, once as an ore and once as a pigment milled fine. The famous use is the color, not the structural bar.

trivia.title: The Kroll Process Arrives
trivia.summary: Hunter had proved that workable titanium existed. Industry still needed a route to tons of it, and that route came much later, in the middle of the twentieth century.
trivia.story: A laboratory ingot is a proof, and a factory is a different problem. In the 1940s William Kroll's process made titanium metal in industrial amounts rather than in pinches. Aircraft designers could order a light, corrosion-resistant metal instead of only admiring a laboratory lump. Titanium stopped being an oxide with a mythic name and became a structural metal beside aluminium and steel. The black sand Gregor found in Cornwall had taken about a hundred and fifty years to reach a factory floor.

applications.title: Aircraft
applications.body: Titanium is as strong as many steels and much lighter, and it resists seawater. Airframes and engine parts use it.

applications.title: White paint
applications.body: The white in a lot of paint, plastic, and toothpaste is titanium dioxide, a powder, not the metal.

applications.title: Implants
applications.body: Hip joints and bone screws are sometimes titanium because the body tolerates the metal and the oxide on its surface.

elements.name: Vanadium

summary.beginner:
Vanadium is element 23, a metal added to steel to make it tougher. You rarely see the pure metal, but the alloy is in tools and engine parts.

Its symbol is V. At room temperature vanadium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 5. In class those are called period 4 and group 5.

Vanadium can show several colors in its compounds, because it can lose different numbers of electrons. That variety is also why it helps some industrial reactions along.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral vanadium atom has 23 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Vanadium is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 5. Vanadium uses several oxidation states, from +2 up to +5, and V2O5 is the catalyst in the contact process for sulfuric acid.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d3 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 11, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +5, +4, +3. The one courses meet most often is +5.

The metal itself is added to steel in small amounts. The colorful ions are a teaching example of how d electrons change color.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Vanadium (Z = 23) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d3 4s2. V2O5 works in the contact process by cycling oxidation state as it transfers oxygen to SO2.

The spread from +2 to +5 is typical early-transition-metal chemistry.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +5, +4, +3. The one courses meet most often is +5. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Vanadium: say the name, write V, find Z=23 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — steel strengthener; catalysts.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Vanadium: electron configuration [Ar] 3d3 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +5, +4, +3. It sits in group 5. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. many oxidation states +2 to +5.

discovery.text: Found in Mexican ore; later confirmed by Sefström, who named vanadium.

elements.history:
Andrés Manuel del Río found a new metal in Mexican lead ore in 1801 and called it erythronium, then withdrew the claim when it was mistaken for chromium. Nils Gabriel Sefström rediscovered it in Swedish iron ore in 1830 and named it vanadium, for Vanadis, a name of the goddess Freyja. Henry Roscoe isolated the metal in 1867.

Vanadium’s many oxidation states, and the colored ions that come with them, made it a teaching example of transition-metal chemistry. A small addition hardens steel.
elements.howDiscovered:
Andrés Manuel del Río, in Mexico City, worked on a brown lead ore from Zimapán. In 1801 he extracted a substance whose salts were red in acid and whose behavior was not that of chromium, which he knew. He named it erythronium. A later opinion from Paris, that the ore was only chromate, led him to withdraw.

Nils Gabriel Sefström found the same element in 1830 while examining the brittleness of iron from the Taberg mine. He dissolved the iron, separated a new acid, and showed it was neither chromic nor uranic. Friedrich Wöhler then connected Sefström’s acid with del Río’s ore. The discovery was made twice, by wet analysis of a lead ore and of an iron, and the first finder was talked out of it.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Vanadium-51 is almost the whole of natural vanadium, and it is a decay product. Supernovae make manganese-51 and chromium-51 in explosive silicon burning, and those nuclei decay to vanadium-51. The odd proton number is why the element is scarce beside chromium and titanium.

Core-collapse supernovae and the white-dwarf explosions called Type Ia both contribute. The vanadium added to steel began as those short-lived parents in the iron-peak debris, not as a nucleus the star stored as vanadium.

trivia.title: Erythronium, Then a Retreat
trivia.summary: Andrés Manuel del Río found a new metal in a Mexican ore and named it for its red salts. A discouraging report from Europe made him take the claim back.
trivia.story: In 1801 Andrés Manuel del Río, working in Mexico, examined a brown lead ore and extracted a metal whose salts turned a striking red. He called it erythronium, from the Greek for red. Then a report reached him that the sample was only chromium, already known and already famous for colored salts, and del Río withdrew. The retreat was understandable and, as it turned out, wrong, and his ore really did hold a new element. The episode is a discoverer talked out of his own discovery by a plausible mistake, and chromium was the decoy. The red salts had been trying to say something else.

trivia.title: Named for the Goddess Vanadis
trivia.summary: Thirty years after del Río stepped back, a Swedish chemist met the same element in iron ore. He gave it a new name, and this time the name stayed.
trivia.story: Nils Gabriel Sefström found an unusual element in Swedish iron ore in 1830. The salts were richly colored, which made him think of a goddess associated with beauty, and he named the element vanadium, for Vanadis, another name of the Norse goddess Freyja. He did not set out to rescue del Río's withdrawn claim, yet the chemistry matched. Erythronium and vanadium were the same metal, and the later name is the one that stuck. A Mexican discovery had been lost to a false identification, then found again in a Swedish furnace sample. The goddess won the naming, and the first discoverer won the story only in hindsight.

trivia.title: Roscoe Holds the Metal
trivia.summary: Colored salts proved that vanadium existed, and they were not the metal. Henry Roscoe kept going until he had the element itself.
trivia.story: Sefström's vanadium was known through its compounds, the way many elements spend their early years, and isolating a clean metal took another generation. In 1867 Henry Roscoe reduced a vanadium chloride and obtained the metal, settling what the colored solutions had only implied. The sample was not a household object, and it was proof. Vanadium prefers to share its electrons in several different ways, which is why the salts that started the story are so many colors. Roscoe's metal closed the sequence that del Río had opened and abandoned. An element mistaken for chromium was, at last, a lump of itself.

trivia.title: A Row of Colored Bottles
trivia.summary: Vanadium's compounds change color as the element's oxidation state changes. Teachers still line the bottles up, because the sequence is hard to forget.
trivia.story: A single element that can look yellow, blue, green, or violet, depending on its compounds, is a gift to a classroom and a puzzle to a new student, and vanadium supplies that row. The colors are not dyes poured in from outside. They come from the way vanadium's electrons sit in each oxidation state. Del Río had noticed the reds and been punished for the observation. Sefström had been charmed by the same talent, and the bottles are the element's personality. Steelmakers care about a different consequence of those many states, but a student usually meets vanadium first as a spectrum on a shelf, each solution a different mood of one metal.

trivia.title: A Pinch Inside the Steel
trivia.summary: Vanadium metal is not poured into bridges by the ton. A small addition changes how steel behaves, which is why the element joined the industrial list.
trivia.story: The colored bottles are the teaching story, and the steel mill is the tonnage. A small amount of vanadium dissolved into steel makes the alloy tougher and more resistant to shock. Tools, axles, and springs took the addition once metallurgists trusted it. The element that had been withdrawn, renamed, and finally isolated became an invisible ingredient in objects that look like ordinary steel, and nothing on the surface says Vanadis, and the name stays in the analysis. Del Río's red salts and a hard spring are far apart in appearance and close in the table. The famous use is a pinch, not a plank.

applications.title: Tough steel
applications.body: A small amount of vanadium in steel makes the steel finer-grained and tougher. Tools and springs use that alloy.

applications.title: Sulfuric acid plants
applications.body: Vanadium pentoxide is the catalyst that helps turn sulfur dioxide into sulfur trioxide on the way to sulfuric acid.

applications.title: Colorful ions
applications.body: Vanadium compounds can be purple, green, blue, or yellow depending on the oxidation state. That is a teaching exhibit more than a product.

elements.name: Chromium

summary.beginner:
Chromium is element 24, the metal that helps stainless steel resist rust. A thin coat of it is the shiny chrome on taps and trim.

Its symbol is Cr. At room temperature chromium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 6. In class those are called period 4 and group 6.

The name comes from the Greek word for color, because chromium compounds can be yellow, orange, or green. The metal itself is silvery. Some of those colored compounds, especially the +6 ones, are toxic.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral chromium atom has 24 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Chromium is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 6. Chromium's ground configuration is the exception 3d5 4s1, and stainless steel uses a thin oxide of the metal to resist rust.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d5 4s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 13, 1. Oxidation states in this dossier are +6, +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +6.

Cr3+ is the common ion in ordinary salts. Cr6+, as in chromates, is a strong oxidizer and a serious toxin, which is why school labs have moved away from it.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Chromium (Z = 24) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d5 4s1. The half-filled 3d5 set is why chromium is 4s1 3d5 rather than 4s2 3d4.

Corrosion resistance is a Cr2O3 film, not a property of the shiny metal alone. Cr(VI) and Cr(III) should never be treated as the same hazard.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +6, +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +6. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Chromium: say the name, write Cr, find Z=24 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — stainless steel and chrome plate.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Chromium: electron configuration [Ar] 3d5 4s1, Typical oxidation states: +6, +3, +2. It sits in group 6. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. half-filled 3d⁵ 4s¹ exception.

discovery.text: Isolated from Siberian red lead ore (crocoite).

elements.history:
Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin analyzed Siberian red lead ore, crocoite, in 1797 and isolated a new metal from it. The salts were brightly colored, so he named the element chromium, from the Greek chroma, color. The metal itself is silvery and corrosion resistant once a thin oxide film forms.

Chrome plating and stainless steel made chromium a household word in the twentieth century. The same element’s +6 compounds are toxic, which is why the chemistry of chromate is taught with a warning.
elements.howDiscovered:
The mineral was crocoite, lead chromate, from the Berezov mine in Siberia. Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin boiled the powdered ore with potassium carbonate. Lead carbonate dropped out, and a yellow solution remained. Acid turned the solution orange. Evaporating and treating the residue gave a new acid.

He heated that oxide with charcoal in a crucible and obtained a gray metal. The colored salts were the clue that the acid was not molybdic acid or a known one. The metal that burned back to the green oxide was the proof. The whole discovery is one sequence: dissolve the red ore, remove the lead, and reduce what is left.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Chromium sits in the iron peak. The common isotope, chromium-52, is largely the daughter of radioactive iron-52, made when silicon burns explosively in a supernova and the debris freezes out near nuclear statistical equilibrium. Iron-52 decays through manganese-52 to chromium-52.

Core-collapse supernovae and Type Ia supernovae both contribute. A star that is quietly fusing does not stockpile chromium. Past the iron peak, fusion consumes energy, and chromium is reached in the explosion.

trivia.title: Red Crystals from Siberia
trivia.summary: A bright orange-red mineral from Siberia arrived in a Paris laboratory. Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin treated it as a puzzle, not as a dye.
trivia.story: Crocoite is a lead mineral so red that it looks like a pigment already, and specimens from Siberia were collector's pieces. In 1797 Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin analyzed the crystals and worked the chromium out of them as a separate metal. The ore's color had been a signal, not a stain rubbed on from outside. He isolated the new element from a mineral that painters might have wanted to grind up and use directly, and the metal he obtained was not red. That contrast became the element's first surprise: a silvery substance hiding in a mineral that looked like sealing wax. The Siberian crystals had been the advertisement.

trivia.title: A Name Taken from Color
trivia.summary: The metal from crocoite was gray, and its compounds were not. Vauquelin named the element for the colors, which is what people would actually see.
trivia.story: Vauquelin could have named his metal for Siberia or for the red ore. He named it chromium, from the Greek chroma, color, because the compounds spread across a painter's range of yellows, oranges, and greens, and the name predicts the laboratory shelf rather than the ingot. Chrome yellow and related pigments later put that decision into pictures and wallpapers. The metal itself stays silvery, protected by a thin oxide film that makes it resist corrosion. Color is the public face, and the film is the industrial one. Both were sitting in the red crystals, waiting for a chemist who looked past the obvious pigment.

trivia.title: Shine, Then Stainless Kitchens
trivia.summary: Chromium's oxide film is invisible and useful. Plating and steel alloys turned that film into a household word.
trivia.story: A thin coat of chromium on a cheaper metal made bumpers, taps, and furniture gleam, and the gleam became the word chrome. Stainless steel took the same element into the bulk of the alloy, where a transparent oxide skin keeps ordinary rust from getting started, and twentieth-century kitchens filled with both uses. The metal Vauquelin isolated from a rare red ore had become ordinary on purpose. People who never learned the Greek root still said chrome when they meant bright and hard to stain. The name from color survived, even though the surface a hand touches is silver. The color stayed in the compounds, and the shine stayed on the steel.

trivia.title: Wells at Hinkley
trivia.summary: Hexavalent chromium is a useful industrial form and a dangerous one in drinking water. In Hinkley, California, residents discovered it had reached their wells.
trivia.story: Chromium in stainless steel is one thing. Chromium in the +6 state, in waste from industrial plating and cooling, is another. At Hinkley, California, wastewater carrying hexavalent chromium seeped into the groundwater. Families who had trusted their wells learned that the water was contaminated, and a long fight followed over what the company owed the town. An element can be a bright kitchen tap and, in another compound, a poison in the aquifer under the same kind of town, and Hinkley made that difference famous.

trivia.title: Bright Salts, Quiet Metal
trivia.summary: Students who know chromium only from colored bottles are surprised by the metal. The ingot looks calm, and the calm is a surface.
trivia.story: Open a jar of a chromium salt and the color is the first fact. Hold the metal, and the color is gone, replaced by a cool shine. The oxide film on the surface is too thin to see and thick enough to change the chemistry, which is why the metal shrugs off weather that would redden iron. Vauquelin saw both faces at the start: loud compounds, quiet metal. The Hinkley wells involved yet a third face, the hexavalent compounds that dissolve and travel, and one element, three reputations, and the classroom should keep them apart. Color is not always a warning, and a silver surface is not always the whole story of what the compounds can do.

applications.title: Stainless steel
applications.body: Stainless steel stays bright because a little chromium forms a thin, tight oxide that keeps rust from starting.

applications.title: Chrome plate
applications.body: A thin coat of chromium on another metal is the shiny finish on some taps and trim. The coat is hard and resists tarnish.

applications.title: Colored compounds
applications.body: Chromium pigments have been yellow, orange, and green. The ones that contain chromium in the +6 state are toxic, which is why many have been phased out.

elements.name: Manganese

summary.beginner:
Manganese is element 25, a hard metal that steelmakers add to iron. A common battery also uses a compound of it.

Its symbol is Mn. At room temperature manganese is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 7. In class those are called period 4 and group 7.

You are more likely to meet manganese inside steel, or as a black powder in a battery, than as a bar of the pure metal. One famous compound is deep purple when it is dissolved.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral manganese atom has 25 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Manganese is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 7. Manganese has many oxidation states, and the purple permanganate ion is the +7 state teachers use as an oxidizer.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d5 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 13, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +7, +4, +2. The one courses meet most often is +7.

In steel, manganese is added for strength and to control sulfur. In a dry cell, manganese dioxide is the material that accepts electrons.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Manganese (Z = 25) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d5 4s2. MnO4- is intensely colored because of charge-transfer transitions, and it is a strong oxidizer in acid.

The metal's own structural use in steel is a separate, much more ordinary story.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +7, +4, +2. The one courses meet most often is +7. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Manganese: say the name, write Mn, find Z=25 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — steel and dry-cell batteries.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Manganese: electron configuration [Ar] 3d5 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +7, +4, +2. It sits in group 7. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. many oxidation states, +2 and +7 common in teaching.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Manganese: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; MnO₄⁻ is a strong, purple oxidizer If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Reduced from pyrolusite; Scheele had studied the ore.

elements.history:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele recognized a new earth in pyrolusite, and Johan Gottlieb Gahn reduced that ore to the metal in 1774. The name manganese is a corruption of magnesia, because pyrolusite was long confused with magnetic iron ores called magnes.

Manganese became the scavenger added to steel to remove sulfur and oxygen. In the laboratory, the purple permanganate ion is the familiar strong oxidizer of titration.
elements.howDiscovered:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele treated pyrolusite with acid and recognized that the black ore was the oxide of a new metal, not an ore of iron or of the magnet. Johan Gottlieb Gahn, in 1774, ground the oxide with charcoal and oil, heated the paste hard, and found a button of metal in the crucible.

The button was brittle and gray, and it regenerated the black oxide when burned. Scheele supplied the identification of the earth. Gahn supplied the reduction. Pyrolusite had been a glassmaker’s reagent for years. The discovery was showing that the reagent was the ore of a metal nobody had isolated.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Manganese-55 is the only stable isotope, and it is the daughter of cobalt-55 made in supernovae. The yield is higher, relative to iron, in Type Ia explosions, the disruption of a white dwarf, than in the collapse of a massive star. The manganese-to-iron ratio in a star is one clue to which kind of blast enriched it.

The odd proton number keeps manganese below chromium and iron on the abundance curve. The manganese added to steel, and the manganese in the purple permanganate ion, began as that cobalt parent in a thermonuclear explosion.

trivia.title: The Ore That Cleared the Glass
trivia.summary: Glassmakers had a black mineral that could take a green tint out of a melt. They used it for the effect long before they knew which element was responsible.
trivia.story: Old glass often leans green because iron hides in the sand. Pyrolusite, a black manganese ore, was the glassmaker's correction. Add a little to the melt and the green fades, which made the ore valuable long before it was called an element. Craftsmen did not need a theory, and they needed a clear window. The same mineral was later the source from which the metal was isolated, so the workshop had been handling manganese compounds for a practical reason while chemists were still sorting what the black powder was, and a decolorizer sounds like a removal of color. It was really a second element, balancing the first.

trivia.title: Gahn Reduces the Black Ore
trivia.summary: Carl Wilhelm Scheele recognized a new earth in pyrolusite. Johan Gottlieb Gahn took the next step and pulled out a metal.
trivia.story: Scheele studied pyrolusite and concluded that it held a new earth, distinct from the ores it resembled. In 1774 Johan Gottlieb Gahn reduced that ore and isolated manganese metal. The product was brittle and unimpressive beside copper or iron, which is why the compounds had been the useful part, and Gahn's reduction still mattered. It turned a glassmaker's additive into an element with its own place. Scheele supplied the recognition, and Gahn supplied the metal. The black powder that had been clearing green glass could now be connected to a lump that was neither iron nor the magnesia people had confused it with.

trivia.title: A Name Tangled with Magnesia
trivia.summary: Pyrolusite looked enough like other black ores to inherit a confused name. Manganese is what happens when a word for magnesia wears down.
trivia.story: The name manganese does not celebrate a discoverer or a country. It is a worn-down form of magnesia, because pyrolusite was long mixed up with magnetic black ores that carried that older word, and the confusion is preserved in the spelling. Chemists eventually separated manganese from magnesium, two elements that share a linguistic ancestor and almost nothing else in behavior, and one is the light metal of flashes and alloys. The other is the brittle metal from the glassmaker's ore. The names still trip students, and the trip is historical. Two different earths once lived under overlapping words, and only one of them kept a version of the original label.

trivia.title: Purple in the Burette
trivia.summary: A deep purple solution of permanganate is a classroom classic. A few drops can announce the end of a titration by refusing to disappear.
trivia.story: Manganese in the +7 state forms the permanganate ion, and the color is an intense purple that a drop will tint a whole beaker, and in a titration, that color is the signal. As long as the other reagent remains, the purple vanishes as the permanganate is consumed. When the purple stays, the reaction has run out of partner, and students remember the moment the flask flushes pink. The metal Gahn isolated is not purple, and the glassmaker's ore is not purple, and the ion is. Manganese became, in the teaching laboratory, the element you can watch arrive. The strong oxidizing habit behind the color is also why the solution is handled with care and kept off skin and clothing.

trivia.title: Illness from the Ore Dust
trivia.summary: Manganese is added to steel for good reasons, and miners and smelter workers have breathed its dust for bad ones. The illness builds slowly.
trivia.story: Steelmakers add manganese to pull sulfur and oxygen out of a melt and to toughen the finished metal. That usefulness put people into mines and furnaces where the dust and fume were part of the air, and breathed for long enough, manganese can damage the nervous system. The illness, called manganism, brings trouble with movement and mood that a short cough does not explain. It is an occupational disease, documented among workers, not a legend attached to a single dramatic day. The purple titration and the steel additive are the friendly chapters. The dust is the chapter that required ventilation, masks, and a willingness to treat a useful element as a chronic hazard.

applications.title: Steel
applications.body: Manganese is added to almost all steel, to make it tougher and to keep sulfur from making the metal brittle.

applications.title: Batteries
applications.body: The black paste in an ordinary dry-cell battery is manganese dioxide. It accepts electrons as the battery runs.

applications.title: A purple oxidizer
applications.body: Dissolved potassium permanganate is an intense purple solution used as an oxidizer in labs and, carefully, in water treatment.
