elements.name: Iron

summary.beginner:
Iron is element 26, the metal of steel, bridges, and the red in your blood. It is also a huge part of Earth's core.

Its symbol is Fe. At room temperature iron is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 8. In class those are called period 4 and group 8.

Iron left in the rain turns to rust, a flaky oxide that does not protect the metal underneath. A little iron in hemoglobin is what lets red blood cells carry oxygen.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral iron atom has 26 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Iron is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 8. Iron is ferromagnetic, it rusts in moist air, and biology uses the Fe2+ and Fe3+ switch.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d6 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 14, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +3.

Steel is iron with a controlled amount of carbon and, often, other metals. Rust is not a tight protective film, which is why paint and galvanizing exist.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Iron (Z = 26) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d6 4s2. The Fe2+/Fe3+ couple is the redox pair in hemoglobin, in cytochromes, and in the blast furnace running the other way.

Ferromagnetism comes from unpaired d electrons aligned across the crystal.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Iron: say the name, write Fe, find Z=26 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — steel, blood’s heme, Earth’s core.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Iron: electron configuration [Ar] 3d6 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +3, +2. It sits in group 8. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. ferromagnetism; rusts in moist air.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Iron: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ redox in biology and industry If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Worked as metal from meteorites and bog ores for millennia.

elements.history:
Iron is prehistoric. Meteoritic iron and bog ore were worked before smelting from common oxides became widespread, and the Iron Age is named for that shift. The symbol Fe is from the Latin ferrum. No one person discovered it.

Blast furnaces, steel, and the magnetic behavior of iron shaped industry. In biology the same element sits in heme and carries oxygen. Most of Earth’s core is an iron–nickel alloy.
elements.howDiscovered:
Iron was worked before any chemical notion of an element existed. Meteoritic iron could be hammered as it was found. Bog ore and then common oxides were smelted with charcoal, which both heated the charge and reduced it.

There is no discoverer and no year. What later counted as the demonstration that iron is an element was the failure of every attempt to decompose the metal, and Lavoisier’s placement of it among the simple bodies. The practical discovery is the smelt: an ore, a fire, and charcoal, giving a metal that could be forged.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Iron is where fusion stops paying. Silicon burning in a massive star, and the explosive burning after collapse, build nuclei up to the iron peak, and the most favored product of the explosion is nickel-56. Nickel-56 decays to cobalt-56 and then to iron-56, the common isotope. Type Ia supernovae make a large share of that nickel-56 as well.

Further fusion would absorb energy, so a living star does not climb past this peak. The iron in the Earth’s core, in hematite, and in heme is supernova ash. Slow neutron capture adds a trace beside the explosive yield.

trivia.title: Iron That Fell from the Sky
trivia.summary: Before furnaces could smelt ordinary ore, people sometimes found iron already metallic, lying where a meteorite had fallen. A few famous objects were made from that gift.
trivia.story: Most iron on the ground is locked in oxides and has to be won with fire and carbon, and meteorites are different. Some arrive as metal, an iron-nickel alloy that a patient worker can hammer. Early people used that sky-iron for rare blades and tools when smelting was still unknown or out of reach. A dagger buried with Tutankhamun was later shown by chemical tests to be meteoric iron, not metal from an earthly furnace. The object is a king's treasure and a mineral specimen at once, and no one discovered iron in a laboratory. Some of the first iron anyone shaped had already been refined in space.

trivia.title: Ferrum, with No Discoverer
trivia.summary: Every other light metal in the early table has a person attached to it. Iron has a Latin name, a symbol, and a prehistory instead of a discoverer.
trivia.story: The symbol Fe comes from the Latin ferrum, a word the Romans used for a metal they did not think of as new, and iron was already old when Rome was new. Bog ore, meteorites, and eventually smelted oxides fed a trade that named an age. No Cavendish or Davy stands at the head of the chapter, because the chapter opened before chapters existed. Textbooks that list a discoverer for iron are guessing at a continent and a millennium. The honest line is that the element was known from antiquity. The scientific work came later: understanding the allotropes, the magnetism, and the reasons a little carbon turns iron into steel.

trivia.title: The Age Named for Tools
trivia.summary: Bronze had been the metal of status and weapons. When ironworking spread, the everyday tool changed, and historians borrowed the metal's name for the era.
trivia.story: A metal becomes an age when many people can obtain it, not when a king owns one dagger. Iron ores are widespread, and once smelting from common oxides spread, farmers and soldiers could have hard tools without depending on scarce tin, and the Iron Age is the name historians use for that shift. It was not a single Tuesday and not a single country. It was a slow replacement of one working metal by another. The element that had fallen rarely from the sky became the element of plows, nails, and blades, and fame, for iron, is this abundance. The laboratory metals nearby on the table never equipped a whole era.

trivia.title: The Red in the Blood
trivia.summary: A blade uses iron for hardness. A living body uses a few grams of it for a different job, and the color of blood is part of that chemistry.
trivia.story: Hemoglobin carries oxygen in red blood, and at the center of its heme sits iron. The metal that makes a nail also makes a breath possible, in an amount that would not fill a large tool. Deficiency leaves a person tired, which is the quiet medical face of the element. The red color of blood is not a dye added to plasma, and it is the iron complex doing its work. Meteoric iron and a blood cell are an absurd pair until the table puts them together. Ancient smiths did not know they were hammering the same element their veins were using, and chemistry is what made the connection visible.

trivia.title: A Pillar That Barely Rusts
trivia.summary: Iron's usual fate in the rain is a red flake that eats the surface. One famous pillar has stood in the open for many centuries and refused that fate.
trivia.story: Leave an iron nail in the weather and oxygen and water will return it toward the ore it came from, and rust is the element's slow, ordinary accident. In Delhi, a massive iron pillar has stood outdoors for many centuries with remarkably little rust, a fact that has invited both careful metallurgy and a lot of legend. The metal is not magic and not stainless chromium steel. Its purity, its surface, and the climate it lived in combined to protect it. The pillar is a surprise, not an explosion and not a miracle. It shows that iron's reputation for rotting is a tendency, not an instant law, and that ancient smiths sometimes made better metal than the rust on a modern fence suggests.

applications.title: Steel and structures
applications.body: Iron, turned into steel, is the metal of bridges, rails, reinforcing bars, and car bodies. The ore is mined in huge amounts.

applications.title: Blood
applications.body: Hemoglobin uses a little iron to carry oxygen in red blood cells. That is a trace of iron in a protein, not a piece of metal.

applications.title: Magnets
applications.body: Iron is the familiar magnetic metal. Motors, transformers, and refrigerator magnets depend on that property, often as an alloy.

elements.name: Cobalt

summary.beginner:
Cobalt is element 27, a metal used in strong magnets and in blue glass. A tiny amount is also in vitamin B12, which your body needs.

Its symbol is Co. At room temperature cobalt is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 9. In class those are called period 4 and group 9.

The blue of some old glass and pottery comes from cobalt compounds. The pure metal is silvery and can be magnetized, like iron and nickel.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral cobalt atom has 27 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Cobalt is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 9. Cobalt is ferromagnetic, and its important oxidation states in simple compounds are +2 and +3.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d7 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 15, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +3.

Vitamin B12 holds one cobalt atom at the center of a large organic ring. That is a trace nutrient, not a reason to handle the metal.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Cobalt (Z = 27) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d7 4s2. In cobalamin the cobalt cycles oxidation state to carry out rearrangements a cell cannot do with carbon alone.

The metal's ferromagnetism is the same d-electron physics as iron, in a different lattice.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Cobalt: say the name, write Co, find Z=27 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — magnets, blue glass, vitamin B₁₂.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Cobalt: electron configuration [Ar] 3d7 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +3, +2. It sits in group 9. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. ferromagnetic; +2/+3.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Cobalt: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; central atom in cobalamin If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Shown to be a distinct metal in Swedish cobalt ores, not bismuth.

elements.history:
Miners called certain ores kobold, German for a goblin, because they looked like copper ore and gave arsenic fumes instead of copper. Georg Brandt showed in 1735 that the blue color of smalt came from a distinct metal, the first metal discovered with a recorded scientific claim. The name cobalt kept the goblin.

Cobalt blue glass and pigments came first. The metal’s ferromagnetism and its place at the center of vitamin B12 came much later.
elements.howDiscovered:
Certain ores colored glass blue and gave off arsenical fumes when heated, which is why miners distrusted them. Georg Brandt, at the Swedish Board of Mines, took the blue pigment smalt, dissolved it, and in 1735 obtained a regulus that was not copper, iron, bismuth, or arsenic.

He showed that the blue of the glass followed this metal and disappeared when the metal was removed. That is the discovery: a controlled separation, and a color that tracked the new metal rather than a known one. It is the first metal with a recorded laboratory claim of that kind.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Cobalt-59, the only stable isotope, is mostly the daughter of nickel-59 made alongside the iron peak in supernovae. A further share is added by slow neutron capture in massive stars and in giants, past the point where fusion helps.

Cobalt is scarce next to iron because it is a side product of the blasts that make iron, plus a neutron-capture tail. The cobalt in a magnet, and the cobalt at the center of vitamin B12, is that combined yield.

trivia.title: Miners Blame a Kobold
trivia.summary: Some ores looked like copper and then misbehaved in the fire. German miners had a name for the mischief, and the name was a goblin.
trivia.story: A miner who expects copper and gets a foul furnace instead feels cheated by the rock. Certain ores in the German mountains looked promising and then gave off arsenical fumes, poisonous and useless for the copper they had seemed to promise. The miners blamed a kobold, a goblin of the underground, and the nickname stuck to the ore. It was a way of talking about repeated disappointment and about sickness that followed the smoke. The goblin was not a discovery, and it was a complaint. Chemistry later walked into that complaint and found a metal the miners had been naming without knowing it.

trivia.title: Brandt Finds the Blue Metal
trivia.summary: Blue glass owed its color to something miners had been throwing aside. Around 1735 Georg Brandt showed that the color came from a metal of its own.
trivia.story: Smalt, a blue glass ground up for pigment, was already a trade item. Georg Brandt studied it and, in 1735, showed that the blue came from a distinct metal, not from copper and not from a purified arsenic trick. He had isolated cobalt, the first metal with a recorded scientific claim to discovery, and the goblin name stayed, and cobalt is the kobold, translated into a permanent element. Brandt's work turned a superstition into a substance that could be weighed. The fumes the miners hated were real, and so was the metal hiding behind them. A color in glass had been the clue that the ore was not a failed copper after all.

trivia.title: Blue Glass and Painters' Color
trivia.summary: Once cobalt was known as a metal, its old job in blue glass made more sense. Painters and potters kept using the color that had exposed the element.
trivia.story: Cobalt's first fame was a pigment. Smalt and later cobalt blue gave glass, porcelain, and paintings a blue that resisted the fading that ruined dyes from plants. The color sits in the compound, a reliable stain at kiln temperatures that would destroy a flower extract. Artists used it without needing to see the gray metal Brandt had isolated, and the element entered culture as a hue. Only much later did the metal itself become interesting for magnets and for alloys that must stay strong when they are hot. The goblin's ore had a beauty that the miners, coughing in arsenical smoke, were in no position to admire.

trivia.title: The Metal Inside the Vitamin
trivia.summary: Cobalt's industrial uses were not its last surprise. A vitamin required for healthy blood turned out to hold a single atom of the old goblin metal.
trivia.story: Vitamin B12 is needed in tiny amounts, and the lack of it causes a serious anemia. When chemists worked out the structure, they found cobalt sitting at the center of a complicated ring. A metal discovered in a blue pigment and a miner's curse was part of human nutrition, and the amount in a body is small, and the absence is not. Cobalt had traveled from a furnace that disappointed copper seekers to a molecule that cells require. Nobody tasting the vitamin would think of smalt or of arsenical ore, and the connection is invisible without analysis. It is one of the element's best surprises, and it came long after Brandt.

trivia.title: Fumes Instead of Copper
trivia.summary: The kobold story sounds like folklore until the smoke is taken seriously. The ore that refused to yield copper was giving off arsenic, and miners were the ones in the way.
trivia.story: The hazard attached to cobalt's discovery is not a fire in a modern plant, and it is the arsenical fume from the ore itself. Miners heated rocks that looked like copper ore, and instead of a clean metal they got smoke that poisoned them. Headaches, illness, and a ruined batch of metal were the practical result, and Brandt's identification did not make the ore kind. It explained why the copper never appeared and why the smoke was more than a goblin story, and arsenic was along for the ride in those minerals. Cobalt's early history is a workplace illness misunderstood as mischief, then redescribed as chemistry. The blue pigment came out of the same unhappy rock.

applications.title: Magnets and alloys
applications.body: Cobalt goes into strong permanent magnets and into alloys that stay hard when they are hot, including some cutting tools.

applications.title: Blue glass
applications.body: A little cobalt compound gives glass and glaze a deep blue. The color has been used for centuries.

applications.title: Vitamin B12
applications.body: Vitamin B12 holds one cobalt atom in a large molecule. People need a trace of that vitamin, which is not the same as needing the metal.

elements.name: Nickel

summary.beginner:
Nickel is element 28, a tough metal mixed into stainless steel and coins. It resists corrosion, so it stays bright where iron would rust.

Its symbol is Ni. At room temperature nickel is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 10. In class those are called period 4 and group 10.

A nickel coin is not pure nickel, but the element gives its name to the coin. Small amounts in steel, and a coating on some metals, are the everyday uses.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral nickel atom has 28 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Nickel is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 10. Nickel's common oxidation state is +2, and the metal is valued for corrosion resistance.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d8 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 16, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

Finely divided nickel is a hydrogenation catalyst. Stainless steels pair nickel with chromium so the alloy stays tough and rust-resistant.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Nickel (Z = 28) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d8 4s2. Raney nickel is a high-surface-area catalyst, not a special isotope.

The +2 aqueous ion is green, a d8 color, and organonickel chemistry goes well beyond that school ion.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Nickel: say the name, write Ni, find Z=28 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — stainless steel and coins.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Nickel: electron configuration [Ar] 3d8 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It sits in group 10. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. corrosion resistance; +2.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Nickel: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Raney nickel hydrogenation catalyst If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from niccolite; named after the German Kupfernicht, or false copper.

elements.history:
Axel Fredrik Cronstedt isolated a metal from the ore Kupfernickel, devil’s copper, in 1751, and named it nickel. Like cobalt ores, niccolite had frustrated miners who expected copper. Cronstedt showed the metal was neither copper nor cobalt.

Nickel stayed a minor metal until electroplating and stainless alloys. It is also the catalyst of fat hydrogenation and a major constituent of many meteorites.
elements.howDiscovered:
Axel Fredrik Cronstedt took the ore the German miners called Kupfernickel, devil’s copper, because it looked like a copper ore and yielded none. In 1751 he dissolved it, precipitated the arsenic, and was left with a green solution from which he reduced a white metal. The metal was magnetic, hard, and not copper, cobalt, or iron.

The green salts were the signature he could follow through the separations. The discovery was the refusal of the ore to be the metal it resembled, followed by a reduction of what the separations had concentrated.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Nickel is an iron-peak element in its own right. Nickel-58, the common isotope, can be assembled directly when the explosion reaches nuclear statistical equilibrium. Nickel-60 comes from the decay of zinc-60 and of iron-60 in the alpha-rich freeze-out of the same debris.

Both kinds of supernova contribute, and nickel rides with iron into planetary cores. The nickel in stainless steel and in iron meteorites is this peak. It is not a later rarity built only by neutron capture.

trivia.title: Old Nick's Disappointing Copper
trivia.summary: German miners had a second treacherous ore after the kobold. They called this one Kupfernickel, because it looked like copper ore and refused to produce copper.
trivia.story: Kupfernickel means something close to Old Nick's copper, Nick being a name for the devil. The ore was reddish and promising, and the furnaces would not give the miners the metal they were paid to find. Like the cobalt ores, it felt like a trick. The nickname put the blame on a spirit when the blame belonged to a misidentification, and the rock was not failed copper. It was a different metal's ore, often mixed with arsenic, and it was never going to yield a copper ingot no matter how skillful the smelter. The devil's name stuck hard enough to become, eventually, a word in every textbook.

trivia.title: Cronstedt Names the Metal
trivia.summary: Axel Fredrik Cronstedt took the ore that miners had given up on and treated it as an unknown rather than as a bad batch of copper. In 1751 he had a white metal.
trivia.story: Cronstedt was not content to repeat the miners' disappointment. He worked the Kupfernickel through a careful reduction and, in 1751, isolated a white metal that was not copper, not cobalt, and not a mixture of the two. He named it nickel, shortening the ore's insult into the element's name. The proof mattered because the two goblin ores were easy to confuse with each other and with copper, and Cronstedt separated them, and a devil's nickname became a respectable metal. The miners had been right that the ore was treacherous and wrong about what treachery meant. It meant a new element, sitting where copper was supposed to be.

trivia.title: A Bright Coat on Cheaper Metal
trivia.summary: Nickel stayed a minor metal until a thin layer of it could make another surface look expensive. Electroplating gave the old devil's copper a domestic job.
trivia.story: A lump of nickel is useful, and a coating of nickel is how most households first met it. Electroplating laid a bright, corrosion-resistant skin on steel and brass, so that a cheap object could look finished. Bathroom fittings, instruments, and machine parts took the coat. Stainless alloys later put nickel into the metal itself, beside chromium, so the element miners could not turn into copper became a way to protect other metals. Cronstedt's white specimen had been a curiosity, and the plated tap is that curiosity domesticated, often as a shine thinner than a millimeter.

trivia.title: Neither Copper nor Cobalt
trivia.summary: The obvious objection to Cronstedt's metal was that he had simply made an impure sample of something known. He spent the claim on showing what the metal was not.
trivia.story: A new metal in the eighteenth century had to survive the accusation of being an old metal badly prepared. Cronstedt's critics could say nickel was copper dirtied with arsenic, or cobalt under another name. The ores encouraged that suspicion, because arsenic, cobalt, and nickel keep one another's company in the ground. Cronstedt's experiments answered by difference: the metal's color, its solutions, and its refusal to behave like the neighbors. The dispute was the tense episode, a laboratory argument rather than a battlefield, and isolating nickel was only half the work. The other half was persuading other chemists that Old Nick's copper had been real and distinct all along.

trivia.title: Coins, Alloys, and an Itch
trivia.summary: Nickel went into coins and everyday alloys, and then into jewelry that some skin would not tolerate. The rash was common enough to become part of the element's public reputation.
trivia.story: The five-cent piece that Americans call a nickel is only partly the element, and the nickname shows how familiar the metal became. Alloys for coins, for kitchenware, and for industrial parts multiplied its uses, and then came the itch. A fair number of people develop a contact allergy to nickel, a rash where a button, a watch, or a cheap earring touches skin. The hazard is not a fume from the eighteenth-century ore, and it is an immune argument with a modern alloy. Manufacturers learned to coat the metal or limit it in items worn against the body. Cronstedt's white metal had found a way to annoy miners first and jewelry wearers later, by two entirely different routes.

applications.title: Stainless steel and coins
applications.body: Nickel toughens stainless steel and has given its name to a coin. The coin is an alloy, not pure nickel.

applications.title: Batteries
applications.body: Nickel appears in several rechargeable batteries, paired with other metals. The electrode is a compound or an alloy, not a bare lump.

applications.title: A catalyst
applications.body: Finely divided nickel helps add hydrogen to oils, the step that makes some margarines and industrial chemicals. The powder is a factory material.

elements.name: Copper

summary.beginner:
Copper is element 29, the red-brown metal of electrical wires and old coins. It carries electricity better than almost any other element.

Its symbol is Cu. At room temperature copper is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 11. In class those are called period 4 and group 11.

Copper roofs turn green over the years as a coat forms in the weather. That coat protects the metal, which is why old copper roofs last. Brass and bronze are copper mixed with other metals.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral copper atom has 29 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Copper is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 11. Copper is an excellent conductor, and its compounds are often colored, especially the blue of aqueous Cu2+.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 1. Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +1. The one courses meet most often is +2.

Brass is copper with zinc, and bronze is copper with tin. The metal resists corrosion better than iron, which is why it was useful long before anyone explained electrons.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Copper (Z = 29) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s1. The configuration is 3d10 4s1, another half-step exception like chromium.

Cu2+ is d9 and blue in water. Cu+ is d10 and typically colorless, which is why the two ions do not look like the same element.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +1. The one courses meet most often is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Copper: say the name, write Cu, find Z=29 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — wires, coins, enzymes.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Copper: electron configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s1, Typical oxidation states: +2, +1. It sits in group 11. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. excellent conductor; colored ions.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Copper: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Cu²⁺ aqueous blue; bronze and brass If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Native metal of tools, coinage, and wiring long before atomic theory.

elements.history:
Copper was worked in the Near East before 5000 BCE, first as native metal and then smelted from ore. The Bronze Age is the age of its alloy with tin. The name copper and the symbol Cu come from Cyprus, Latin cuprum, the island that supplied Roman ore.

It remained the metal of coinage, roofing, and later of electrical wire, because among common metals only silver conducts better. The blue of its aqueous ion is one of the first colors a chemistry student learns.
elements.howDiscovered:
Native copper can be picked out of rock and hammered cold, and that is how the oldest copper objects were made. Smelting came later: heat a carbonate or sulfide ore with charcoal and the metal runs. The alloy with tin is bronze, harder than either metal, and that discovery is prehistoric and was made more than once.

No person is credited. The element was recognized as simple because the metal survived cupellation and could be dissolved and precipitated back as the same red metal. Cyprus gave the Latin name. The original finding was a native metal in the ground.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Copper lies just past the iron peak, where fusion no longer releases energy. Copper-63 and copper-65 are made by the weak s-process: neutrons released during helium and carbon burning in massive stars are captured slowly onto iron-peak seeds. Explosive burning in the supernova adds more, in the alpha-rich freeze-out.

The main slow process of giant stars, which matters for strontium, barium, and lead, contributes less of the copper. The copper of ores is this massive-star product, later concentrated by hot water in the crust.

trivia.title: The Island in the Name
trivia.summary: Copper was worked for thousands of years before Rome, and Rome still left its mark on the name. The island that supplied the empire became the word.
trivia.story: Copper does not have a discoverer, because people in the Near East were hammering native metal and smelting ore before 5000 BCE, and the name arrived much later, through Rome. Cyprus was a famous source of copper ore, and the Latin cuprum, metal of Cyprus, gave the element its English name and its symbol Cu. A place became a word, and the word outlived the Roman trade routes. When a student writes Cu, the island is still in the abbreviation. The metal itself was older than that empire and older than the alphabet that recorded it. Cyprus named a fame that the eastern Mediterranean had already been using for millennia.

trivia.title: The Age Made with Tin
trivia.summary: Soft copper tools bend, and tin is not a great blade by itself. Together they made bronze, and the alloy was important enough to name an age.
trivia.story: Native copper can be hammered into a bead or a simple blade, and the blade dulls and bends. Add tin, and the alloy called bronze is harder than either metal alone. That discovery, made more than once in the ancient world, changed tools, weapons, and status. The Bronze Age is the period when this alloy organized trade, because tin and copper are not always found in the same hills, and ships and caravans moved one toward the other. Copper's early fame is not the wire in a wall. It is the partnership with tin that let cities arm and equip themselves before ironworking was widespread, and the element was ancient, and the alloy made it historical.

trivia.title: Paris Green on the Walls
trivia.summary: A brilliant green pigment made from copper and arsenic looked like a triumph of color. People who made it, and people who lived with it, became ill.
trivia.story: Nineteenth-century rooms loved a strong green, and Paris green supplied it, and the pigment is a copper arsenite, vivid and poisonous. Workers who ground and brushed it were exposed to arsenic, and households who lived among painted or papered walls were exposed as well, especially where damp let the chemistry wander, and illness followed the color. The pigment was also spread on crops as an insecticide, which carried the same element combination into fields. That vivid green was a warning: a copper compound can carry a second element that does the harm. The green that looked like a leaf was not a leaf. It was a hazard with good taste in decoration.

trivia.title: The Wire That Carried Current
trivia.summary: Silver conducts electricity a little better than copper, and silver is the wrong price for a city's cables. Copper became the metal inside the walls.
trivia.story: When electric lighting and motors spread, engineers needed a conductor that was good enough and common enough, and silver wins on conductivity and loses on cost. Copper is next among ordinary metals, ductile, and able to be drawn into wire by the mile. Roofs had already used the metal, and coins had used it, but the cable was a new scale. A modern room hides kilograms of copper in circuits that earlier centuries would have reserved for a pot or a statue, and the island metal became an infrastructure. Aluminium later took some long-distance lines, and copper stayed the usual choice inside buildings. The Bronze Age alloy had found a job that tin does not share.

trivia.title: Nuggets Before the Furnace
trivia.summary: Smelting came after people had already met copper as metal, not only as ore. Some deposits offered nuggets ready for the hammer.
trivia.story: Not every early copper object began in a furnace. Native copper occurs as metal in certain rocks, and communities who found it could anneal and hammer it without first learning to reduce an ore. That stage sits at the front of the metal's history, before the Bronze Age and before Cyprus gave Rome a word. The nuggets were rare compared with ore, and they mattered because they taught what the metal looked like, and later smelters knew what they were trying to produce. A student who sees only wire and pennies misses this beginning. Copper introduced itself as a find, a red lump in a stone, before anyone built the heat to pull it out of a green mineral.

applications.title: Wires
applications.body: Copper is the usual metal in electrical wiring because it conducts so well and can be drawn into wire.

applications.title: Plumbing and roofs
applications.body: Copper pipe carries water, and copper roofs last for decades under a green coat that protects the metal.

applications.title: Alloys
applications.body: Brass is copper with zinc, and bronze is copper with tin. Both were useful long before anyone explained why copper conducts.

elements.name: Zinc

summary.beginner:
Zinc is element 30, a metal coated onto steel to keep it from rusting. That coat is called galvanizing, and you can see it on some nails and roofing.

Its symbol is Zn. At room temperature zinc is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 12. In class those are called period 4 and group 12.

The zinc corrodes first, on purpose, and the steel underneath lasts longer. Your body also uses a little zinc in enzymes, in amounts far smaller than a nail.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral zinc atom has 30 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Zinc is a solid transition metal in period 4 and group 12. Zinc's d shell is full, so the only common oxidation state is +2, and the metal is used as a sacrificial anode.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

The oxide is amphoteric. Galvanizing works because zinc is more reactive than iron and is consumed instead of the steel.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Zinc (Z = 30) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2. A filled 3d10 shell is why Zn2+ is colorless, unlike the transition ions just before it.

Sacrificial protection is an electrochemical fact: the zinc is the anode and the iron is spared.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Zinc: say the name, write Zn, find Z=30 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — galvanizing and enzymes.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Zinc: electron configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It sits in group 12. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. full 3d¹⁰; always +2 in compounds.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Zinc: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; amphoteric oxide; sacrificial anode If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from calamine; known in alloys much earlier.

elements.history:
Brass, the alloy of copper and zinc, is ancient, but isolating the element was harder because the metal boils out of its ore. India smelted zinc by distillation centuries before Europe. Andreas Sigismund Marggraf isolated it in 1746 and described it clearly enough that he is credited with the discovery. The name may come from the German Zinke, meaning prong or tooth.

Galvanizing, the zinc coating on steel, is the modern bulk use. The ion is also essential in enzymes, including carbonic anhydrase.
elements.howDiscovered:
Zinc boils out of a hot ore, so an ordinary open smelt loses it as smoke. At Zawar in Rajasthan, medieval furnaces condensed that vapor on purpose, in a retort, and collected the metal. European craftsmen meanwhile made brass by heating copper with zinc ore, without ever holding a lump of zinc.

Andreas Sigismund Marggraf made the European isolation explicit in 1746. He heated calamine, a zinc carbonate, with charcoal in a closed vessel and scraped the metal off the cooler wall. The discovery, as a published demonstration, is that condensation. The metal had already been made wherever someone thought to cool the smoke.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Zinc is made just beyond iron. Alpha-rich freeze-out in supernovae is a major channel, and the weak s-process in massive stars is the other. Zinc-64 is the most abundant of the five stable isotopes.

The heavier zinc isotopes take a larger share of neutron capture. Zinc is common enough, among iron-peak neighbors, that the metal in brass and in galvanizing is ordinary supernova debris.

trivia.title: Furnaces at Medieval Zawar
trivia.summary: Brass was ancient, and the zinc inside it usually vanished as a vapor if a smelter tried to win the metal alone. At Zawar, in India, metallurgists caught that vapor.
trivia.story: Zinc boils away at a temperature ordinary smelting reaches, so the metal can leave an ore as fumes and never collect as an ingot. For a long time Europe used brass, the alloy of copper and zinc, without treating zinc as a separate metal on the shelf. At Zawar, in medieval India, workers distilled the vapor and condensed zinc on purpose. The furnaces there produced the element centuries before European textbooks had a clear account of it, and the achievement was practical metallurgy, not a published discovery paper. Zinc's story starts with a success that later credit sometimes skipped. The metal was known to the people who made it, whether or not a distant academy had agreed.

trivia.title: Marggraf Describes the Metal
trivia.summary: Europe had seen zinc-like metal and still argued about it. Andreas Sigismund Marggraf's work in 1746 was clear enough that he received the credit for identifying the element.
trivia.story: Samples of metal from the East, and a few European distillations, had already hinted that a new substance was involved in brass, and the hints were muddy. In 1746 Andreas Sigismund Marggraf isolated zinc and described it with the clarity other chemists could repeat and believe. He is the discoverer in the European record for that reason, not because no one had ever held the metal. The credit is a little unfair to Zawar and a little faithful to the rule that a discovery includes a public, testable account, and Marggraf supplied the account. The tense part of the story is the gap between making a metal and being believed to have named an element. Zinc fell into that gap for centuries.

trivia.title: A Name That May Mean Tooth
trivia.summary: Zinc's name is less settled than its chemistry. A German word for a prong or tooth is the leading explanation, and it may be the right one.
trivia.story: Some element names come from a place, and some from a property everyone agrees on, and zinc is less tidy. The word may come from the German Zinke, a prong or tooth, because the metal can form pointed crystals as it condenses. The explanation fits the way the metal shows up in a cooler part of a furnace, jagged rather than in a neat puddle, and it is still a may, not a carved inscription. Other origins have been suggested, and none deserves a louder claim than the evidence, and the uncertain name matches the uncertain recognition. An element that escaped as vapor also escaped a single obvious etymology. Students can learn the metal without pretending the word is more certain than it is.

trivia.title: Brass Older Than Its Metal
trivia.summary: People alloyed zinc with copper before they agreed that zinc was an element. The golden metal of instruments and fittings is older than the isolated name.
trivia.story: Brass looks like a metal of its own, yellow and workable, and for a long time that appearance was enough. Copper smelted with certain ores picked up zinc without a smelter writing the second element down. Ornaments, coins, and later scientific instruments used the alloy while arguments about the vapor in the furnace continued, and the use preceded the identification, and Marggraf's description did not invent brass. It explained a color and a behavior that workshops already trusted. Zinc is unusual in this way: its famous early use is an alloy that hid it. The pure metal, silvery and less admired, came into view later than the golden mixture.

trivia.title: Coating Steel, Irritating Lungs
trivia.summary: A thin layer of zinc keeps steel from rusting as fast, which made galvanizing a bulk industry. Heating that coating, or the metal itself, can make workers briefly ill.
trivia.story: Steel rusts, and a coat of zinc sacrifices itself first, which is why galvanized sheet and pipe cover so much of a modern town. The coating is the element's main bulk use. Welders and brass founders meet a different side of the same metal. When zinc is heated hard enough to fume, the oxide can cause metal fume fever, a flu-like illness with chills and aches that usually passes and is still a real injury. The illness usually passes, and it is still a real injury from an otherwise protective coating. Zinc from Zawar, described by Marggraf, now spends much of its life as a gray skin on steel, quiet until someone burns through it.

applications.title: Galvanizing
applications.body: A coat of zinc on a steel nail or a roof sheet rusts first, on purpose, and the steel underneath lasts much longer.

applications.title: Brass
applications.body: Brass is zinc mixed with copper. Door hardware, instruments, and fittings use it because it is harder than copper and resists corrosion.

applications.title: The body
applications.body: A number of enzymes need a zinc ion to work. The amount in food is tiny compared with the zinc on a galvanized bucket.

elements.name: Gallium

summary.beginner:
Gallium is element 31, a soft metal that can melt from the warmth of your hand. It is used in some electronics, not as a household metal.

Its symbol is Ga. At room temperature gallium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 13. In class those are called period 4 and group 13.

Gallium looks a bit like aluminum, but it is far less common and it melts just above room temperature. Do not try a melting trick with an unknown sample. The pure metal is not a toy.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral gallium atom has 31 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Gallium is a solid post-transition in period 4 and group 13. Gallium melts just above room temperature, and its chemistry is mainly the +3 oxidation state.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 3. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

Gallium arsenide and gallium nitride are semiconductor materials in LEDs and fast electronics. The low melting point is a metal property, not a sign that the element is a liquid like mercury.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Gallium (Z = 31) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p1. The melting point is 303 K, so a warm day can liquefy the metal while it is still a normal crystalline solid at a cool room temperature.

The +3 ion resembles aluminum. The lower +1 state is a minor path.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Gallium: say the name, write Ga, find Z=31 on the table, note the family (Post-transition), and connect it to one real use — semiconductors and low-melting alloys.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Gallium: electron configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p1, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 13. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. melts in your hand on a warm day.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Gallium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; liquid near room temperature; +3 If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found spectroscopically in zinc blende, then isolated.

elements.history:
Mendeleev predicted eka-aluminium in 1871, including a low melting point and a density near 6 g/cm³. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found the element spectroscopically in a zinc blende in 1875 and isolated it the same year. He named it gallium, for Gallia, France. The match to Mendeleev’s numbers was one of the periodic table’s public victories.

Gallium melts just above room temperature, which is why a warm hand liquifies a lump. It is now a semiconductor metal, mostly as gallium arsenide and gallium nitride.
elements.howDiscovered:
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran dissolved a zinc blende from the Pyrenees and placed the solution in the spark of a spectrometer. In 1875 he saw a pair of violet lines that belonged to no known element. He concentrated the hydroxide, dissolved it in potassium hydroxide, and electrolyzed it. Metal deposited on the platinum cathode.

The first bead was small. It melted in a warm hand, and its density and spectrum matched the lines that had started the search. Mendeleev’s predicted eka-aluminium sat close to the measured properties. The discovery tool was the spectroscope. The confirmation was a current that plated out a metal with those lines.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Gallium-69 and gallium-71 are fed by both neutron-capture channels. The slow process in aging giant stars, the asymptotic giant branch, builds a large share: a neutron at a time, with time for a nucleus to decay between captures. The rapid process, in a neutron-rich blast, supplies the rest.

Gallium is odd-numbered and scarce. The gallium in a semiconductor is that neutron-capture product. Fusion in a stellar core never reaches it. The iron peak is as far as energy-releasing fusion goes.

trivia.title: A Name for France
trivia.summary: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran picked a patriotic name for his new metal, and a later rumor claimed he had signed it with his own surname.
trivia.story: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran did not reach for a planet or a mineral when he named element 31. He chose gallium, from Gallia, an old name for France. The choice was patriotic and plain enough for a scientific paper. Later readers noticed that his surname, Lecoq, means the rooster, and that the Latin word for rooster is gallus. A rumor grew that he had hidden a private joke inside the public name. He rejected that reading, and the name that remains is the one he stated in public: a French metal, found in a zinc ore, for a French chemist.

trivia.title: Lines in a Zinc Ore
trivia.summary: A spectrum from a zinc blende showed lines that matched no known metal, and Boisbaudran spent 1875 turning that clue into a sample he could weigh.
trivia.story: Boisbaudran was hunting elements with a spectroscope, the instrument that turns a hot sample into a set of colored lines. In a zinc blende he saw lines that belonged to no metal on his charts. That optical clue started a chemical chase through the ore. By the end of 1875 he had separated a small sample of the element itself, not merely a hint of it. The spectrum had promised a metal, and the flask delivered one. Gallium entered the table as a laboratory substance, isolated in the same year it was first seen as light.

trivia.title: The Predicted Soft Metal
trivia.summary: Dmitri Mendeleev had already described eka-aluminium, including a low melting point, and gallium became a public test of whether the table could forecast matter.
trivia.story: Four years before gallium was found, Dmitri Mendeleev left a blank under aluminium and called the missing element eka-aluminium. He forecast a soft metal with a density near six grams per cubic centimeter and a melting point that would be unusually low. When Boisbaudran published his first density, the number sat well below that forecast. Mendeleev did not abandon the table. He pressed the discoverer to measure again. A fresh determination landed near six, close to the prediction, and the periodic table won a public argument that classrooms still repeat.

trivia.title: A Spoon in the Hand
trivia.summary: Gallium looks like an ordinary solid on the bench, yet a warm palm is enough to begin a demonstration that chemistry teachers still pass around the room.
trivia.story: Gallium is a silver-white metal that feels ordinary until a hand or a warm room gets hold of it. It melts at about 30 °C, just above a cool day and just below body temperature. A teacher can pass a gallium spoon around a class and watch the bowl soften into a puddle in a palm. Nothing has burned, and nothing has exploded. The trick is only the melting point, sitting awkwardly close to the temperature of skin. That is why the spoon is a demonstration rather than a disaster, and why students remember the metal long after the puddle is cooled back into a lump.

trivia.title: Chips and Blue Lamps
trivia.summary: Beyond the melting trick, gallium became a semiconductor metal, built into compounds that power fast electronics and bright blue and white lights.
trivia.story: The hand-melting stunt is how most students meet gallium, but factories meet it as a semiconductor. Joined with arsenic, it becomes gallium arsenide, a material used in fast electronics and in some solar cells. Joined with nitrogen, it becomes gallium nitride, the compound that made bright blue and white LEDs practical. Those solids are hard, useful, and far from the puddle on a teacher’s tray. The same element that fails as a teaspoon succeeds as a light and as a chip. Gallium’s modern life is in phones, lasers, and lamps, which is a serious career for a metal that cannot keep its shape in a warm hand.

applications.title: LEDs and chips
applications.body: Gallium nitride and gallium arsenide are the materials in many LEDs and in some fast electronics. The pure metal is not what you see glowing.

applications.title: A metal that melts easily
applications.body: Gallium melts just above room temperature, so a warm hand can liquefy a piece. That is a real property and a poor party trick with an unlabelled sample.

applications.title: Thermometers
applications.body: Some high-temperature thermometers have used a gallium alloy instead of mercury. The alloy is chosen to be liquid, and it is still not a toy.

elements.name: Germanium

summary.beginner:
Germanium is element 32, a shiny gray element used in fiber optics and in some electronics. It behaves a little like silicon, which sits above it.

Its symbol is Ge. At room temperature germanium is a solid. It is a metalloid, between the metals and the nonmetals in the way it behaves. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 14. In class those are called period 4 and group 14.

Germanium was predicted before it was found, because an empty space on the table said an element like silicon should exist. Today a little of it helps carry light signals down a fiber.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral germanium atom has 32 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Germanium is a solid metalloid in period 4 and group 14. Germanium is the ekasilicon Mendeleev predicted, a semiconductor between silicon and tin.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 4. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4.

The element has the diamond structure. It was an early transistor material and is still used where its optical properties beat silicon.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Germanium (Z = 32) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p2. The prediction of ekasilicon is a historic success of the periodic law: atomic weight, density, and oxide formula were forecast before the element was isolated.

The band gap sits between silicon and the metallic behavior of tin.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Germanium: say the name, write Ge, find Z=32 on the table, note the family (Metalloid), and connect it to one real use — fiber optics and semiconductors.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Germanium: electron configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p2, Typical oxidation states: +4. It sits in group 14. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. ekasilicon; diamond-like structure.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Germanium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; semiconductor between Si and Sn If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from argyrodite; Mendeleev had predicted ekasilicon.

elements.history:
Mendeleev’s ekasilicon was an even sharper prediction: atomic weight, density, and the character of the oxide. Clemens Winkler isolated the element from the mineral argyrodite in 1886 and named it germanium, for his country. The properties landed close to the prediction.

Germanium was the semiconductor of the first transistors in the 1940s, before silicon took that role. It remains the material of some infrared optics and fiber systems.
elements.howDiscovered:
Clemens Winkler received the new silver mineral argyrodite from the Himmelsfürst mine at Freiberg and analyzed it in 1886. Silver and sulfur did not add up to 100 percent. About 7 percent was missing. He precipitated a sulfide from the missing fraction, converted it to an oxide, and reduced the oxide to a gray metal.

The metal’s atomic weight and the density of its oxide landed on Mendeleev’s ekasilicon. The discovery was a bad analysis that refused to balance, followed by a reduction of the residue. The spectroscope was not required. The balance was.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Germanium’s isotopes do not share one origin. The lighter ones are largely the weak s-process in massive stars, the same neutron source that feeds zinc. The heavier ones take more from the main slow process in giant stars and from the rapid process.

Germanium-70, 72, 73, and 74 are the common mix in the metal. A bar of germanium is a blend of massive-star neutrons, giant-star neutrons, and the rapid blasts. The semiconductor use came long after that mix was already fixed in the solar cloud.

trivia.title: Named After a False Start
trivia.summary: Clemens Winkler isolated a gray metal from a silver mineral and nearly gave it a name that a false discovery had already claimed.
trivia.story: Clemens Winkler, working at Freiberg, met a new silver mineral called argyrodite that refused to add up. The known elements in it did not account for the whole sample. He worked the missing fraction out of the ore and found a gray metal. Naming it was its own small problem. He nearly chose neptunium, but that word had already been attached to a claimed element that did not hold up. Germanium, for his country, was the name he published in 1886; the mineral had been a puzzle, and the name that survived made the answer sound like a national event.

trivia.title: Eka-Silicon Comes Close
trivia.summary: Mendeleev’s sketch of eka-silicon was unusually detailed, and chemists watched to see whether Winkler’s metal would land on those predicted numbers.
trivia.story: Mendeleev had left a more detailed blank than usual under silicon. He predicted an atomic weight, a density, and the kind of oxide the missing element should show. When Winkler’s germanium appeared, its measured character sat close to that sketch. The agreement felt uncanny to people who still doubted that a table could forecast a substance. Gallium had already been one public victory for the same method. Germanium made the method look repeatable, as if the empty squares were waiting rooms for real elements; Winkler had found a metal, and the table looked as if it had been expecting that metal by name.

trivia.title: The First Transistor Metal
trivia.summary: A piece of germanium carried the first working transistor at Bell Laboratories, years before silicon became the familiar face of electronics.
trivia.story: In December 1947, at Bell Telephone Laboratories, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built a point-contact transistor on a piece of germanium. William Shockley, the third physicist in the work, soon developed the idea into a sturdier design. The device could amplify a signal, which is the trick underneath modern electronics. Germanium was the semiconductor they could purify well enough at the time. Silicon later took the main role because it behaves better when hot and because it is far more common. The first success still belonged to Winkler’s metal; every later chip is a descendant of that small germanium experiment.

trivia.title: Tonics and Injured Kidneys
trivia.summary: Germanium left the electronics bench and appeared in shops as a health powder, which physicians then connected with harm that had nothing to do with transistors.
trivia.story: Germanium is not a famous poison, and the metal inside a transistor is not a snack. Even so, powders and elixirs containing germanium compounds were sold in the late twentieth century as health tonics. People swallowed them for benefits the sellers could not really promise. Physicians then reported patients with injured kidneys after long use of those products. The element had no business as a supplement. Its respectable work stayed in crystals and in optical parts, not in a medicine bottle; a metal that helped start the electronics age acquired a quieter, uglier chapter when it was packaged as a cure.

trivia.title: Windows for Heat Light
trivia.summary: Ordinary glass is blind to some infrared colors, so instrument makers turned to germanium when they needed a lens that could pass heat rays.
trivia.story: Silicon took the transistor, but germanium did not leave the workshop. It is transparent to a band of infrared light that ordinary glass blocks. Cameras that see heat, and some fiber and night-vision systems, use germanium lenses and windows. The metal is brittle and costly, so it appears as a carefully cut part rather than as a beam in a building. Winkler, working in the 1880s, could not have pictured a heat camera. He would still have recognized the gray element in the lens; the ore that would not add up became a window for colors the human eye never sees.

applications.title: Fiber optics
applications.body: A little germanium in the glass of a fiber changes how the fiber bends light, which helps carry a signal.

applications.title: Electronics
applications.body: Germanium was an early transistor material and is still used in some infrared optics and detectors.

applications.title: A predicted element
applications.body: Mendeleev left a gap under silicon and described the missing element before it was found. Germanium filled that gap.

elements.name: Arsenic

summary.beginner:
Arsenic is element 33, a brittle gray element, and many of its compounds are poisonous. Tiny controlled amounts appear in some electronics, not in food.

Its symbol is As. At room temperature arsenic is a solid. It is a metalloid, between the metals and the nonmetals in the way it behaves. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 15. In class those are called period 4 and group 15.

Arsenic has a long and grim history in pigments and poisons. That history is why it is a bad example to treat casually. The element itself is a metalloid, not a typical metal you could bend.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral arsenic atom has 33 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Arsenic is a solid metalloid in period 4 and group 15. Arsenic is a metalloid with common oxidation states +3 and +5, and many of its compounds are toxic.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p3. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 5. Oxidation states in this dossier are --3, +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is --3.

Gallium arsenide is a semiconductor, which is a modern use under industrial controls. Old green pigments that contained arsenic are a warning, not a craft project.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Arsenic (Z = 33) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p3. The +3 and +5 states parallel phosphorus, but arsenic's compounds are far more toxic and less central to life.

Semiconductor uses do not make the element safe to handle.

Oxidation states in this dossier are --3, +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is --3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Arsenic: say the name, write As, find Z=33 on the table, note the family (Metalloid), and connect it to one real use — semiconductors; toxic in some forms.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Arsenic: electron configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p3, Typical oxidation states: -3, +3, +5. It sits in group 15. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. metalloid; +3 and +5.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Arsenic: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; GaAs analog; historical pigments If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Described as a distinct substance; isolation methods came later.

elements.history:
Arsenic compounds, especially the sulfides orpiment and realgar, were ancient pigments and medicines. Albertus Magnus is often credited with describing the free element in the thirteenth century. The name comes from the Greek arsenikon, itself from a Persian word for the yellow pigment.

The element’s reputation is its toxicity. It is also a metalloid used to dope semiconductors, and a reminder that a substance known for centuries was an element only once the idea of an element was clear.
elements.howDiscovered:
The yellow and red sulfides, orpiment and realgar, were ancient pigments. Heating them with a reducing agent drives off the sulfur and leaves a brittle gray solid that sublimes. Albertus Magnus, in the thirteenth century, is the writer usually credited with describing that reduction, using soap as the reducing agent.

The metal was still easy to confuse with antimony. What established arsenic as its own element was the repetition of the reduction on different ores, always giving the same sublimate, with the same poisonous oxide and the same refusal to split further. The discovery is a roast and a sublimation, done on a pigment.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Arsenic-75 is the only stable isotope. It sits where the slow capture of giant stars and the rapid capture of neutron-rich blasts both contribute, and solar abundances ask for both.

Arsenic is odd-numbered, which is why it is rarer than germanium or selenium. The arsenic of ores is that mixed neutron-capture yield, gathered into sulfide minerals long after the stars that made it had died.

trivia.title: Yellow Pigment, Old Name
trivia.summary: Long before anyone called arsenic an element, its yellow and red sulfides were already pigments, and the Greek name for them came from Persian.
trivia.story: Orpiment and realgar, the yellow and red sulfides of arsenic, were paints and medicines in the ancient world. People ground them, traded them, and feared them without sorting a pure element out of the compound. The Greek name arsenikon came from a Persian word for the yellow pigment, and English arsenic grew from that chain. For centuries the color and the danger were familiar, while the idea of a chemical element was not yet available to name what the pigment contained. Arsenic is a reminder that a substance can be ancient and still wait for a definition. The pigment came first, and the element was a later way of understanding it.

trivia.title: Often Credited, Thin Record
trivia.summary: Medieval tradition points to Albertus Magnus when a discoverer is wanted for arsenic, and careful histories keep the words often credited beside his name.
trivia.story: Albertus Magnus, a thirteenth-century scholar, is the name most often attached to early descriptions of arsenic. He is often credited with describing the free element in that century, not merely its colorful ores. The record is thin, because medieval notes and later legends have blurred together. No laboratory notebook survives that would satisfy a modern historian of chemistry. The metal was certainly known in the medieval centuries, long before periodic tables and spectroscopic lines. Classrooms can pass the credit on only with those two words, often credited; that caution is part of the story, not a footnote someone forgot to delete.

trivia.title: Green Rooms That Sickened
trivia.summary: A fashionable green pigment put an arsenic compound on parlor walls, and damp houses turned that color into a quiet household danger.
trivia.story: Carl Wilhelm Scheele’s green, a copper arsenite pigment, became a favorite color for wallpaper and cloth in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Rooms looked bright, fresh, and modern. In damp houses the pigment could give off poisonous arsenic compounds into air and dust. People living among those green walls grew ill, and doctors slowly connected the sickness with the decoration. The fashion was a real poisoning hazard, widespread and ordinary rather than rare. Once the cause was understood, getting the paper off the wall mattered more than any single famous anecdote; the color was beautiful, and the element inside it was not a decoration.

trivia.title: A Mark the Jury Could See
trivia.summary: James Marsh had watched a poisoning case fail for lack of lasting evidence, and he answered with a courtroom test that left something visible.
trivia.story: In 1836 James Marsh, a British chemist, published a test that could reveal tiny amounts of arsenic and leave a visible mark for a jury to examine. A few years earlier he had worked on a poisoning case, and the sample he produced did not last long enough to persuade the court. The accused person went free, which stung the chemist as well as the science. Marsh wanted a result that would still be there when the testimony was given. His test became a standard tool of forensic chemistry and made hidden arsenic much harder to deny. The story is about evidence that survives a trial, not about how to use the poison.

trivia.title: A Trace Inside the Chip
trivia.summary: The old poison also has a precise job in electronics, where a tiny controlled amount of arsenic changes the way silicon conducts electricity.
trivia.story: Arsenic’s reputation is toxicity, and that reputation is earned. Compounds of the element have poisoned people in homes, in workplaces, and in crimes. The same element, in tiny controlled amounts, is added to silicon chips so the crystal conducts electricity in a chosen way. Semiconductor factories treat it as a hazard to be contained, which fits everything else in its history. A substance known for centuries became an element, in the modern sense, only when chemists could separate it and name what they had. The chip and the green wallpaper are one metalloid living in two worlds; both worlds require the danger to be taken seriously.

applications.title: Semiconductors
applications.body: Gallium arsenide, used in some LEDs and high-speed electronics, contains arsenic. The work is done in sealed industrial processes.

applications.title: Old pigments, a warning
applications.body: Some historical greens contained arsenic compounds and were poisonous. They are a reason to treat old paint with care, not a recipe.

applications.title: Wood treatment, now restricted
applications.body: Arsenic compounds once preserved outdoor wood. Many countries have limited that use because the element is toxic.
