elements.name: Selenium

summary.beginner:
Selenium is element 34, a gray element that conducts electricity better in the light. A trace of it is a nutrient, and too much is harmful.

Its symbol is Se. At room temperature selenium is a solid. It is a nonmetal. It does not look or act like iron or copper. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 16. In class those are called period 4 and group 16.

Selenium sits under sulfur and can sometimes stand in for it, which is why a tiny amount matters in the body. The gray form was used in old photocopiers because light changed how well it carried electricity.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral selenium atom has 34 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Selenium is a solid nonmetal in period 4 and group 16. Selenium is a photoconductor and the next-door neighbor of sulfur, with a common oxidation state of -2 in selenides.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p4. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 6. Oxidation states in this dossier are --2, +4, +6. The one courses meet most often is --2.

Several allotropes exist, from a red powder to a gray metallic form. In biochemistry a few enzymes use selenocysteine, which is not a reason to take extra selenium.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Selenium (Z = 34) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p4. The gray allotrope's photoconductivity made it an early light sensor.

Biologically, selenium is essential at trace levels and toxic above them, a narrow window typical of many heavy nonmetals.

Oxidation states in this dossier are --2, +4, +6. The one courses meet most often is --2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Selenium: say the name, write Se, find Z=34 on the table, note the family (Nonmetal), and connect it to one real use — photocopiers and dietary trace.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Selenium: electron configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p4, Typical oxidation states: -2, +4, +6. It sits in group 16. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. photoconductor; −2 analog of sulfur.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Selenium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; allotropes; glutathione peroxidase If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found in the residue of sulfuric acid from Fahlun pyrite.

elements.history:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius found a red residue in the slime of a sulfuric-acid plant at Falun in 1817. He first thought it was tellurium, then showed it was a new element and named it selenium, from the Greek selene, the Moon, because tellurium had been named for the Earth.

Selenium’s conductivity rises in the light, which made it the photoconductor of early meters and copiers. It is also a trace element in the enzyme glutathione peroxidase.
elements.howDiscovered:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius was following an impurity in the sulfuric acid made at Gripsholm from Falun pyrite. In 1817 the red mud in the lead chambers, which he first took for tellurium, gave a precipitate that smelled of radish when burned and showed a spectrum and a chemistry tellurium did not have.

He reduced the oxide with potassium and obtained a gray form, and he also prepared the red form. The discovery is that mud. The acid plant had concentrated a trace out of the pyrite, and the smell, the color, and the failure to match tellurium were the evidence.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Selenium has six stable isotopes, and they split among channels. Several are fed by the slow process in giant stars. The neutron-richer ones take a large share from the rapid process. Selenium-74 is proton-rich. It belongs to the gamma process, in which a supernova’s light knocks neutrons off heavier seed nuclei.

The selenium in a photoconductor is therefore a blend. Past the iron peak, a single kind of star is rarely the whole story of an element.

trivia.title: The Red Residue at Falun
trivia.summary: A red slime from a sulfuric acid works looked like tellurium at first, and Jöns Jacob Berzelius refused to stop when that identification failed.
trivia.story: Jöns Jacob Berzelius spent 1817 puzzling over a red residue from the slime of a sulfuric acid plant at Falun, in Sweden. Tellurium was the obvious suspect, because the residue behaved a little like that rare metalloid. He tested the guess with more care, and the guess failed. The substance was new. He had almost walked past it by giving it an older name that the tests would not support. Selenium exists as an element because a careful chemist was willing to admit that the first identification was wrong; the acid plant had produced a waste, and the waste turned out to be a discovery.

trivia.title: Named for the Moon
trivia.summary: Tellurium had already been named for the Earth, so Berzelius looked upward and chose the Moon for the element he had just separated from it.
trivia.story: Once Berzelius was sure the red residue was not tellurium, he needed a name that would remember the mix-up. Tellurium came from tellus, the Latin word for Earth. He chose selenium from selene, the Greek word for the Moon. The pair of names is a small poem: Earth and its satellite, two elements that chemists had confused with each other. The Moon name stuck even though selenium is more common in the crust than its partner. Every time a student translates the word, the old mistake is still visible inside it; a wrong identification became the most memorable thing about the name.

trivia.title: The Smell That Warns
trivia.summary: Heat selenium, or handle certain compounds of it, and an odor arrives before any instrument does, sharp enough that chemists treat it as a warning.
trivia.story: Selenium has a smell that students remember longer than its atomic number. When the element is heated, or when certain compounds of it are handled, the odor is sharp and unpleasant, often compared with garlic or rotten radish. It is a real property of the chemistry, not a story added for color. The smell is also a warning, because selenium is toxic in excess even though a trace of it is essential in the body. Berzelius’s workplace at Falun would have carried that odor while he argued with the residue. An element named for the Moon announces itself with a very earthly smell; the nose, in this case, is part of the science.

trivia.title: Drums That Held a Page
trivia.summary: Selenium conducts electricity better in the light, and that odd habit let early photocopiers hold an image long enough to print it.
trivia.story: Shine light on selenium and it conducts electricity better than it does in the dark. That photoconductivity looked like a curiosity in the nineteenth century, useful mainly in a few light meters. In the twentieth century it became the heart of early photocopiers. A drum coated with selenium could hold an electric charge in the dark and lose charge where light struck, so toner stuck in the shape of a page. Offices around the world were running on a residue from a Swedish acid plant. Silicon and organic coatings later replaced many of those drums; Selenium had already taught machines how to see a document.

trivia.title: Too Little in the Soil
trivia.summary: Parts of China saw a heart illness linked to selenium-poor soils, which showed that an element famous for being toxic can also be missing.
trivia.story: Selenium’s hazard is real. Too much of it sickens people and animals, and the margin between enough and too much is narrow. The opposite problem showed up in parts of China as Keshan disease, a heart illness linked to soils poor in selenium. Where the element was scarce in food, the disease was more common, and adding selenium to the diet was part of the public response. Scientists still treat the illness as more than a single missing nutrient. Even so, the episode put selenium on the map as a trace the body needs, not only as a smelly poison; the copier drum and the dinner plate turned out to share one element.

applications.title: Glass and photocopiers
applications.body: Selenium colors some glass red, and the gray form was used in early photocopiers because light changed how well it conducted.

applications.title: A trace nutrient
applications.body: A few enzymes in the body use selenium. The useful amount is tiny, and extra selenium is harmful.

applications.title: Alloys
applications.body: A little selenium improves the machining of some steels and brasses. It is added at the mill, not in a home shop.

elements.name: Bromine

summary.beginner:
Bromine is element 35, one of the only elements that is a liquid at room temperature. It is a red-brown halogen used in some flame retardants and in water treatment.

Its symbol is Br. At room temperature bromine is a liquid, which is unusual for an element. It is a halogen, a reactive nonmetal in the column next to the noble gases. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 17. In class those are called period 4 and group 17.

The liquid gives off a choking brown vapor, so it is not something to pour or sniff. In the sea it is present as a dissolved form, not as the pure liquid.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral bromine atom has 35 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Bromine is a liquid halogen in period 4 and group 17. Bromine is a diatomic liquid, Br2, and a weaker oxidizer than chlorine.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p5. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 7. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1.

The red-brown vapor is the same Br2 escaping the liquid. Organobromine compounds include flame retardants and a few historically important sedatives.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Bromine (Z = 35) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p5. Being liquid at room temperature is a consequence of Br2's polarizability, not of a metallic bond.

Oxidation state -1 is the bromide ion. Higher states appear in bromates.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Bromine: say the name, write Br, find Z=35 on the table, note the family (Halogen), and connect it to one real use — the liquid halogen; sanitizer.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Bromine: electron configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p5, Typical oxidation states: -1. It sits in group 17. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. diatomic liquid; red-brown vapor.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Bromine: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; organobromine fire retardants If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from Montpellier brines as a brown liquid.

elements.history:
Antoine Jérôme Balard isolated a dark red liquid from Montpellier salt brines in 1826, after treating them with chlorine. Justus von Liebig had set the same substance aside as a chloride of iodine. Balard named it bromine, from the Greek bromos, stench.

Bromine is the only nonmetal element that is liquid at room temperature. Its salts became photographic silver bromide and, later, flame retardants and drilling fluids.
elements.howDiscovered:
Antoine Jérôme Balard worked with the bitter liquor left after salt had been crystallized from Montpellier seawater. In 1826 he passed chlorine into it. The liquor turned orange. He extracted the color into ether, treated the extract with potash, and regenerated a dense red liquid by acid and manganese dioxide.

Justus von Liebig had set a similar liquid aside as iodine chloride. Balard’s regeneration showed a substance that was driven out by chlorine, the way iodine and chlorine displace each other, and that was liquid at room temperature. The discovery was a displacement reaction in a waste brine.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Bromine-79 and bromine-81 are each a mixture of the slow process in giant stars and the rapid process in neutron-rich blasts. Bromine is odd-numbered, so the yields stay small beside selenium and krypton.

Merging neutron stars are the leading site of the rapid process, and some rare supernovae are still discussed. The bromine in a brine was made in those events and in giants, then inherited by the cloud that became the Sun.

trivia.title: A Dark Liquid from Brine
trivia.summary: Antoine Jérôme Balard was working the salt brines at Montpellier when a dark red liquid appeared and refused to match any element he knew.
trivia.story: Antoine Jérôme Balard isolated a dark red liquid from the salt brines of Montpellier in 1826. A chlorine treatment of those leftover waters produced a liquid that matched no known element and was certainly not a dye. Its vapor stung, and its color was hard to ignore once it had separated. Balard studied it until he was sure it stood beside chlorine and iodine as its own substance. Publication made the discovery his in the eyes of other chemists. The red liquid was the first clear sight of an element that is already a liquid on the shelf, with no need for anyone to melt it; Bromine looks calm in the bottle only until the stopper moves.

trivia.title: The Bottle Set Aside
trivia.summary: Justus von Liebig had already seen the same red liquid, filed it as a familiar compound, and only understood the miss after someone else published.
trivia.story: Justus von Liebig had met bromine before Balard’s paper and had set the sample aside. He thought it was a chloride of iodine, a reasonable label for a dark, sharp liquid in that part of the shelf. When Balard’s report arrived, the bottle became an embarrassment rather than a discovery. Carl Löwig, then a student in Germany, had also prepared the element around the same time, but his account reached print later. Priority went to the chemist who published a clear claim. Bromine’s birth is shared in the laboratory and single on the page; missing an element can be as simple as trusting the wrong label on a bottle you already own.

trivia.title: Named for the Stench
trivia.summary: The red liquid smelled so bad that Balard took its name from a Greek word for stench, and the word still fits the closed bottle.
trivia.story: Balard named the element bromine, from the Greek bromos, meaning stench, and the name was honest. Open a bottle carelessly and the vapor announces itself before anyone reads the label. The smell is sharp and irritating, nothing like a clean sea breeze, even though the element is won from brines. Chlorine already had a choking reputation among chemists who worked with the halogens. Bromine joined that family as the one you can see as a liquid and regret smelling. The name on the bottle is a warning written in Greek; beauty of color and nastiness of odor arrived in the same sample, and the odor won the naming.

trivia.title: Burns on the Chemists
trivia.summary: Bromine is the only nonmetal that stays liquid in an ordinary room, and that liquid burned the skin and lungs of people who studied it.
trivia.story: Bromine is the only nonmetal element that is liquid at ordinary room temperature, which makes it look almost tame in a glass bottle. The look is misleading. The liquid and its vapor burn skin, eyes, and breathing passages. Early investigators, proud of the samples they had isolated, were hurt by the very liquid that made their reputations. Those injuries were chemical burns, and they taught laboratories to seal the bottle and respect it. The hazard is the element itself, spilled on skin or breathed as vapor, and anyone who has met it understands why the name means stench and why the burns were remembered.

trivia.title: Film, Flame, and Wells
trivia.summary: Silver bromide helped photography happen, and later bromine compounds moved into flame retardants and into the dense fluids used around oil wells.
trivia.story: Silver bromide, a salt of the new element, darkens when light hits it. That reaction helped make photographic film, alongside the other silver halides that turned cameras into everyday tools. Much later, bromine compounds were mixed into plastics as flame retardants and into dense fluids used during drilling. Each use traded on the element’s chemistry, and each brought arguments about pollution and safety that Balard never faced. The red liquid in a Montpellier dish had become an industrial ingredient. Its story runs from a salt marsh to a strip of film and then to a factory rule book; a stench in 1826 grew into products that whole industries then had to control.

applications.title: Flame retardants
applications.body: Some plastics contain bromine compounds that slow a fire. The use is industrial, and several of those compounds have been restricted.

applications.title: Water treatment
applications.body: Bromine compounds disinfect some pools and industrial water. The red liquid element itself is not poured into a pool.

applications.title: The liquid halogen
applications.body: Bromine is one of the only elements that is liquid in a normal room, and the vapor is choking. It is a fume-hood chemical.

elements.name: Krypton

summary.beginner:
Krypton is element 36, a rare gas in the air. Bright lamps use it, and it almost never forms compounds.

Its symbol is Kr. At room temperature krypton is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a noble gas. Left alone, it almost never joins other elements to make compounds. On the periodic table it is in row 4, column 18. In class those are called period 4 and group 18.

Krypton is heavier than argon and much less common. When it is trapped in a tube and given an electric current, it contributes to a bright white light.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral krypton atom has 36 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Krypton is a noble gas in period 4 and group 18. Krypton is a heavier noble gas, and it does form a few fluorides under forcing conditions.

The electron configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p6. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 8. Oxidation states are not listed for this entry.

Ordinary chemistry still treats it as inert. KrF2 is a real compound and a powerful oxidizer, not a material anyone keeps on a shelf.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Krypton (Z = 36) has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p6. KrF2 shows that a closed shell is a high barrier, not an absolute ban, once the oxidizer is fluorine and the conditions are harsh.

Lighting uses the emission spectrum, not the fluoride.

Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Krypton: say the name, write Kr, find Z=36 on the table, note the family (Noble gas), and connect it to one real use — bright white lamps and excimer lasers.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Krypton: electron configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p6, Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. It sits in group 18. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. heavier noble gas; a few fluorides.

discovery.text: Isolated from liquefied air by fractional distillation.

elements.history:
Ramsay and Travers found krypton in 1898 in the residue left after liquid air had given up its lighter gases. They named it from the Greek kryptos, hidden. A brilliant line spectrum confirmed it was a new element, not an impurity of argon.

Krypton was the last of the classic noble gases from air to seem completely inert. Krypton difluoride, prepared in 1963, showed that the heavier members of the group do form compounds.
elements.howDiscovered:
After Ramsay and Travers had boiled the lighter noble gases out of liquid air, a small residue remained. In 1898 a discharge through that residue showed a bright yellow-green line and a pale violet glow that were not argon’s. They measured a new density and a new spectrum on a few cubic centimeters of gas.

The method was fractional distillation pushed one step further than neon. Krypton hides in the least volatile fraction. The discovery is a line in a discharge tube and a density that did not match any gas already named.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Krypton’s stable isotopes are a blend of slow neutron capture in giant stars and rapid neutron capture in mergers and related blasts. Krypton is chemically inert, so once it is made it stays a gas until a new star and its planets trap it.

The krypton in air is that trapped gas. It was not made in the Earth. It was made in earlier generations of stars and in neutron-rich events, and it rode into the solar system already as krypton.

trivia.title: Hidden in Leftover Air
trivia.summary: After lighter gases boiled out of liquid air, William Ramsay and Morris Travers found brilliant spectral lines that argon could not explain.
trivia.story: William Ramsay and Morris Travers were working through liquid air in 1898, letting the lighter gases boil away and examining what remained. Argon was already known, and a lazy explanation would have called any new glow an impurity of argon. The residue refused that label. Its spectrum showed brilliant lines of its own, the signature of a separate element. They had not mined a rock or burned a plant. They had found a gas that had been mixed into every breath, present and unseen, until the air itself was taken apart; Krypton was the hidden one in the last fraction, waiting for someone to distill the sky with enough patience.

trivia.title: A Word That Means Hidden
trivia.summary: Ramsay and Travers chose a Greek word meaning hidden, which described both the gas in the air and the chemistry it refused to show.
trivia.story: Ramsay and Travers named the gas krypton, from the Greek kryptos, hidden. The word fitted a substance that had sat inside ordinary air until a careful distillation uncovered it. It also fitted the mood of the noble gases, a family that barely answered the usual chemical questions. Krypton would not combine in the ways a student of 1898 expected from a newly found element. Hidden described the discovery and, for a long time, the chemistry as well. The name stayed accurate to the history even after the gas was later persuaded into a few compounds; a label chosen for secrecy still tells the truth about how the element was found.

trivia.title: The Meter’s Orange Line
trivia.summary: From 1960 until 1983 the world’s meter was tied to the wavelength of an orange-red line in the light of krypton-86.
trivia.story: Length used to mean a metal bar kept carefully in a vault. By 1960 that bar was no longer a good enough definition of the meter. The new definition used a set number of wavelengths of the orange-red light from a lamp of krypton-86. A gas Ramsay and Travers had found in leftover air had become the ruler of the metric system. The arrangement lasted until 1983, when the meter was tied instead to the speed of light. Krypton lost the official job, but it had held the world’s unit of length for more than twenty years; a hidden gas spent a generation as the standard of distance.

trivia.title: The Inert Label Cracks
trivia.summary: Krypton was filed as a gas that would never bond, until a fluoride made in 1963 showed that the heavier noble gases could form compounds.
trivia.story: For decades after 1898, krypton was filed under the word inert. Textbooks said the noble gases formed no compounds, and krypton obeyed that lesson in ordinary laboratories. In 1963 chemists prepared krypton difluoride, a real compound, difficult and reactive, and still genuine. The old word inert had already been wounded the year before by a xenon compound, and krypton confirmed that the heavier noble gases were not forever aloof. The gas remains calm in the air people breathe. It is no longer a promise that chemistry owns a family which can never bond; hidden was a good name, and inert turned out to be only a long pause.

trivia.title: Lamps and Quiet Windows
trivia.summary: After the meter moved on, krypton kept smaller jobs in intense lamps and in window gaps that need a better insulator than plain air.
trivia.story: Krypton did not retire when the definition of the meter changed. It fills some high-intensity lamps and flashes, where a discharge through the gas makes a hard white light. It is also sealed between panes of glass as an insulating fill, slower to carry heat than ordinary air. Both uses depend on a gas that is scarce, so the element stays expensive and is saved for places where air is not good enough. Nobody distills krypton for amusement. They do it because the hidden gas, in the right socket or the right window, earns its cost; a residue of liquid air became a product with a price.

applications.title: Bright lamps
applications.body: Krypton fills some high-performance lamps and flashes. The light is bright and white compared with neon's orange-red.

applications.title: Windows
applications.body: Double glazing is sometimes filled with krypton because the heavy gas slows heat leaking through the window.

applications.title: A rare gas
applications.body: Krypton is a tiny fraction of air. Pulling it out is a job for an air-separation plant, not a classroom.

sample.body: Pure krypton, sealed in glass. The gas has no color of its own, so the sample looks like a clear tube. This is the element by itself, not a compound.

elements.name: Rubidium

summary.beginner:
Rubidium is element 37, a very soft metal that reacts violently with water. It turns up in research labs and special light sensors, not as a household metal.

Its symbol is Rb. At room temperature rubidium is a solid. It is an alkali metal: soft, and quick to react with water. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 1. In class those are called period 5 and group 1.

Rubidium looks a little like potassium and behaves even more eagerly. There is no reason to seek out the pure metal. Its interesting uses are in instruments, not in products you hold.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral rubidium atom has 37 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Rubidium is a solid alkali metal in period 5 and group 1. Rubidium is a heavier alkali metal, with a single 5s electron and a very low ionization energy.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 5s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 8, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

It melts on a warm day, like cesium. Rubidium atomic clocks and photocells use the atom's easily moved outer electron.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Rubidium (Z = 37) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 5s1. The 5s electron is so weakly held that rubidium is one of the species cooled into Bose-Einstein condensates.

Bulk chemistry is the familiar alkali story: M+ salts and a metal that must be kept from air and water.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Rubidium: say the name, write Rb, find Z=37 on the table, note the family (Alkali metal), and connect it to one real use — research alkali; photocells.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Rubidium: electron configuration [Kr] 5s1, Typical oxidation states: +1. It sits in group 1. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. softer and more reactive than potassium.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Rubidium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; lowest density after lithium among solids here If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Detected by its deep-red spectral lines in lepidolite.

elements.history:
Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, using the spectroscope they had just developed, saw deep red lines in the mineral lepidolite in 1861. They named the element rubidium, from the Latin rubidus, deep red. Bunsen isolated the metal the same decade.

Rubidium is an alkali metal more reactive than potassium. It has little bulk use. Its atomic-clock transition and its photocells are the modern reasons to separate it.
elements.howDiscovered:
Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff examined the mineral lepidolite with the spectroscope they had just built. In 1861 two dark red lines appeared that were not potassium’s and not lithium’s. Bunsen then processed about 150 kilograms of the mineral, precipitating the chloroplatinates and crystallizing them again and again until the new alkali was concentrated.

The spectrum found the element when the sample was still a mixture. The crystallization produced a salt pure enough to name and to put back into the flame, where the same red lines returned. The metal was prepared soon after by reduction. The discovery instrument was the prism.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Rubidium-85 is largely a product of the slow process in giant stars. Rubidium-87 is long-lived, with a half-life near 50 billion years, and it receives both the slow process and the rapid process. Its slow decay to strontium-87 is the clock used in rubidium-strontium dating of rock.

The element is an alkali metal and stays scarce. The rubidium in a mineral is mostly the giant-star isotope, with a trace of the radioactive one that the dating method reads.

trivia.title: Red Lines in Lepidolite
trivia.summary: Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff aimed their new spectroscope at lepidolite and saw deep red lines that none of their charts could claim.
trivia.story: Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff had just built a spectroscope that sorted the light of a flame into lines. In 1861 they turned it on the mineral lepidolite and saw deep red lines that matched nothing they already knew. A new element was announcing itself as a color. They still had to pull a sample out of the rock, and Bunsen isolated the metal later in the same decade. The discovery began as light rather than as a lump in the hand. Rubidium is one of the elements that spectroscopy found before a chemist could hold it; the red lines were the whole invitation, and the mineral was only the envelope.

trivia.title: Named for Deep Red
trivia.summary: The Latin word rubidus, meaning deep red, became the element’s name because the spectrum showed that color before anyone saw the metal.
trivia.story: Bunsen and Kirchhoff named the element rubidium, from the Latin rubidus, deep red. They were naming a line in a spectrum. The metal itself, once isolated, is a soft silver alkali metal, not a red crystal on a shelf. The color lives in the light it emits when excited, which was the clue that gave it away in lepidolite. That gap between the name and the appearance confuses students who expect a red solid. The name is a memory of the experiment; without those red lines, the mineral would have kept its secret, and the soft metal would have stayed mixed into other alkalis for longer.

trivia.title: A Metal That Will Not Wait
trivia.summary: Rubidium sits below potassium among the alkali metals, and moist air or a drop of water is enough to show why it is stored with care.
trivia.story: Rubidium is an alkali metal, more reactive than potassium, which is already a metal teachers handle with tongs and keep under oil. Left in moist air, rubidium loses its shine at once. Meet water, and it reacts violently, so violently that the hydrogen given off can catch fire. That is why the pure metal is a laboratory curiosity rather than a material for construction. Bunsen’s sample was a triumph of isolation and a nuisance to store. The red lines were beautiful, and the metal they revealed wanted to burn its way back into compounds; the hazard is the element’s impatience, visible as soon as the container fails.

trivia.title: Clocks Smaller Than Caesium
trivia.summary: Rubidium has almost no bulk industry, yet a microwave transition in its atoms runs compact atomic clocks and certain light-sensitive cells.
trivia.story: Rubidium never became a metal of bridges or electrical cables, because it is scattered in minerals and eager to react. The reasons to separate it today are quieter than a steel mill. A microwave transition in its atoms runs compact atomic clocks, useful in laboratories and in navigation gear when a full caesium clock is more than the job needs. Rubidium photocells turn light into an electrical signal. The element that announced itself as red lines now helps measure seconds and watches photons. Its fame is precise, which suits a metal that almost nobody sees; spectroscopy found it, and spectroscopy, in a way, is still what people use it for.

trivia.title: From a Flash to a Lump
trivia.summary: Isolating rubidium proved that the red lines belonged to a real metal, and the metal then set about attacking whatever tried to hold it.
trivia.story: Seeing a spectral line is not the same work as holding a metal. Bunsen took on that second job and isolated rubidium during the 1860s, working its compounds down until a soft, silvery metal appeared. The sample had to be kept away from air and water or it would vanish back into salts. Spectroscopy had been the easy clue, and classical chemistry was the hard labor. Kirchhoff’s optics and Bunsen’s flasks were a partnership: one found the lines, and the other fought the metal. Rubidium’s early history is that handoff, from a red flash in a mineral to a dangerous little lump; both halves of the partnership were required.

applications.title: Atomic clocks and sensors
applications.body: Rubidium atoms are used in some compact atomic clocks and in light sensors. The device uses the atom's outer electron, not a lump of metal.

applications.title: Research
applications.body: Physicists cool rubidium atoms when they study matter at extremely low temperatures. The metal is sealed because it reacts violently with water.

applications.title: Not a household metal
applications.body: There is no rubidium pan and no rubidium supplement worth taking. The pure metal is a specialty chemical.

elements.name: Strontium

summary.beginner:
Strontium is element 38, a metal similar to calcium. Its compounds give fireworks a crimson color.

Its symbol is Sr. At room temperature strontium is a solid. It is an alkaline-earth metal. These metals react, but less wildly than the alkali metals beside them. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 2. In class those are called period 5 and group 2.

Your bones are calcium compounds, and strontium can sometimes stand in for calcium, which is not always a good thing. One radioactive form, made in nuclear reactions, is dangerous for that reason. The red in fireworks is the everyday public use.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral strontium atom has 38 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Strontium is a solid alkaline-earth metal in period 5 and group 2. Strontium is an alkaline-earth metal and forms Sr2+, and its flame test is a strong crimson.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 5s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

The metal reacts with water, though less famously than sodium. Strontium-90 is a fission product that the body can mistake for calcium.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Strontium (Z = 38) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 5s2. The flame color is an atomic emission of strontium, not a property of the Sr2+ ion in water.

Sr-90's hazard is biological mimicry of calcium plus beta decay, a nuclear fact rather than a chemical flame test.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Strontium: say the name, write Sr, find Z=38 on the table, note the family (Alk. earth), and connect it to one real use — fireworks crimson; bones analog.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Strontium: electron configuration [Kr] 5s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It sits in group 2. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. like calcium but larger.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Strontium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; ⁹⁰Sr is a fission-product bone seeker If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Recognized in strontianite from Strontian, Scotland.

elements.history:
In 1790 Adair Crawford recognized that a mineral from the Scottish village of Strontian was not barium ore. Thomas Charles Hope confirmed a new earth, and Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808. The name strontium kept the village.

The crimson flame of strontium salts became a firework color. The fission product strontium-90, which follows calcium into bone, made the element a public word again in the nuclear age.
elements.howDiscovered:
Adair Crawford compared a mineral from the lead mines at Strontian with witherite, the barium carbonate. In 1790 the chloride from the Strontian mineral was more soluble, and the earth was lighter, than barium’s. Thomas Charles Hope confirmed a distinct earth and showed that its salts burned crimson, not the green of barium.

Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808 by the mercury-cathode electrolysis he was using on the other alkaline earths, then distilled off the mercury. The discovery of the earth was a solubility and a flame color. The discovery of the metal was the current.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Strontium sits on the first peak of the slow process. A closed shell of 50 neutrons makes these nuclei reluctant to capture another neutron, so material piles up. Aging giant stars make most of strontium-88, the common isotope.

The rapid process adds a share, especially to the neutron-richer isotopes. Strontium lines in stars are one way to watch the slow process turn on as the Galaxy ages. The strontium in a crimson firework is that giant-star pile-up.

trivia.title: A Village Kept on the Table
trivia.summary: A heavy mineral from Strontian in Scotland refused to behave like barium ore, and the village stayed in the element’s name after the metal was proved.
trivia.story: In 1790 Adair Crawford studied a mineral from Strontian, a village in the Scottish Highlands, and decided it was not the barium ore everyone expected. The earth inside it behaved differently in the flame and in its salts. That was the beginning of a new element, even though Crawford had a new earth rather than a shiny metal in a bottle. The name strontium kept the village when later chemists finished the work. A place most students never visit is spoken every time the element is named. Strontian’s rock became a word in chemistry classrooms around the world; the mineral, later called strontianite, had been misfiled, and the misfiling was the discovery.

trivia.title: Hope Confirms, Davy Isolates
trivia.summary: Thomas Charles Hope showed that the Strontian earth was truly separate, and Humphry Davy then pulled strontium metal out of its compounds.
trivia.story: Crawford’s claim of a new earth needed allies before a metal could appear. Thomas Charles Hope, in Edinburgh, studied the Strontian material and confirmed that it was distinct from baryta, the earth of barium. The metal was still locked inside its compounds. Humphry Davy, who was isolating the alkali and alkaline earth metals with electricity, produced strontium metal in 1808. The village had supplied the name, Hope had supplied the confirmation, and Davy supplied the element in metallic form. Strontium’s discovery is a chain of people rather than a single afternoon; the insight of 1790 and the metal of 1808 are both part of the credit, and neither one replaces the other.

trivia.title: Crimson Over the Crowd
trivia.summary: Strontium salts turn a flame crimson, and firework makers took that color as the standard red of public celebrations.
trivia.story: Hold a strontium salt in a flame and the fire turns crimson, a fact that firework makers seized at once. Reds in a public display are very often strontium compounds, chosen because the color is strong and easy to recognize against the night. The pure metal is not what flies into the sky. A compound of the element is what glows when the burst heats it. Crawford’s strange earth from a Highland village became a color people cheer for on holidays. The pleasure in the sky rests on a Scottish mineral that once confused hunters of barium; a laboratory flame test grew into a celebration that whole cities can see.

trivia.title: Teeth That Held Fallout
trivia.summary: Strontium-90 from atmospheric bomb tests followed calcium into bone, and a survey of shed baby teeth made that path visible to the public.
trivia.story: Strontium sits just below calcium on the table, and the body can mistake one for the other in the way it builds bone. The fission product strontium-90, scattered by atmospheric nuclear tests, followed calcium into milk, into growing bone, and into children’s teeth. During those years the Baby Tooth Survey in the United States collected shed teeth and found the radioisotope in them. The result was a public fact, not a private laboratory note. It made fallout personal, a metal from weapons tests lodging where skeletons form. Strontium, the firework color, became a word parents heard in warnings; the hazard was the isotope that followed calcium into bone.

trivia.title: A Heavy Coat on the Tube
trivia.summary: Older television tubes needed glass that could stop stray X-rays, and strontium compounds were mixed into the screen for that quiet job.
trivia.story: The crimson flame is strontium’s showy use, but the element also did a quiet job inside older television sets. Color picture tubes produced X-rays as a side effect of their operation, and the glass of the screen had to absorb them. Strontium compounds went into that glass because the element is heavy enough to help stop the rays and was available in quantity. When flat screens replaced tubes, that particular market faded. The element did not vanish from industry. It remains a specialist metal, a firework color, and the parent of a nuclear isotope that nobody wants in bone; a Highland earth ended up between a viewer and a tube.

applications.title: Red fireworks
applications.body: Strontium compounds give fireworks and flares a crimson color. The color is the public use of an otherwise quiet metal.

applications.title: Magnets and glass
applications.body: Strontium ferrite is a common permanent-magnet material, and strontium compounds are used in some picture-tube and ceramic glass.

applications.title: A caution about one isotope
applications.body: Strontium-90, made in nuclear fission, can be taken up by bone because it resembles calcium. That isotope is a hazard, not a firework ingredient.

elements.name: Yttrium

summary.beginner:
Yttrium is element 39, a silvery metal used in materials that glow in screens and in some lasers. It is grouped with the rare earths in many lessons even though it sits above them.

Its symbol is Y. At room temperature yttrium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 3. In class those are called period 5 and group 3.

Yttrium is not rare in the way the name sounds, but it is hard to separate from its neighbors. A little of it in a crystal can help make a laser.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral yttrium atom has 39 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Yttrium is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 3. Yttrium is almost always Y3+, and chemically it behaves like the heavy lanthanides.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d1 5s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

YAG, yttrium aluminum garnet, is a host crystal for lasers. The metal is also used in phosphors and in some specialty alloys.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Yttrium (Z = 39) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d1 5s2. Y3+ is a closed-shell ion with no d or f electrons, so color and magnetism in yttrium materials come from the dopant, not from yttrium itself.

Its radius matches the later lanthanides because of the lanthanide contraction.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Yttrium: say the name, write Y, find Z=39 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — phosphors and alloys.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Yttrium: electron configuration [Kr] 4d1 5s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 3. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. chemically close to heavy lanthanides.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Yttrium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; often +3; YAG lasers If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from ytterbite; the metal came later.

elements.history:
Johan Gadolin examined a black mineral from Ytterby, Sweden, in 1794 and separated a new earth, yttria. The metal yttrium was isolated much later. The village of Ytterby went on to lend its name to ytterbium, terbium, and erbium as well.

Yttrium behaves like a heavy lanthanide even though it sits above them in group 3. Yttrium aluminum garnet became a laser host, and yttrium barium copper oxide was the first superconductor to work above the boiling point of nitrogen.
elements.howDiscovered:
Johan Gadolin dissolved a black mineral from the Ytterby quarry, later called gadolinite, in acid. In 1794, after removing silica and beryllia, he precipitated an earth that was not lime, not magnesia, and not the other earths then known. He reported it as a new earth, yttria.

The earth was a mixture, which the next century spent peeling apart, but the first separation was real: a fraction with its own reactions and its own weight. The metal was isolated much later by reduction of the chloride. Yttrium was discovered as an earth that would not match the list.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Yttrium-89 is the only stable isotope, and it is mainly a slow-process product of giant stars, sitting with strontium and zirconium on the light peak. The closed neutron shell that stalls capture is the reason those three elements are richer than their neighbors.

A smaller rapid-process share is allowed by the models and is not the bulk. The yttrium in a laser crystal is the ash of neutrons added slowly inside red giants that died before the Sun formed.

trivia.title: A Black Stone from Ytterby
trivia.summary: Johan Gadolin took apart a heavy black mineral from a Swedish quarry in 1794 and separated an earth the village would make famous.
trivia.story: Johan Gadolin, working in 1794, examined a black mineral that had come from the quarry at Ytterby, near Stockholm. Inside it he separated a new earth, which was named yttria. He did not isolate the pure metal, and the tools of the 1790s were not ready for that harder job. What he did prove was that the rock held something unknown. Yttria became a prize that later chemists kept splitting, because the earth was a mixture hiding still more elements. Gadolin’s paper is the doorway into a long house of discoveries; the quarry had been dug for ordinary minerals, and it handed chemistry a puzzle that lasted a century.

trivia.title: Four Names, One Quarry
trivia.summary: Ytterby did not stop at yttrium, and ytterbium, terbium, and erbium still carry pieces of the same Swedish village in their names.
trivia.story: Ytterby is a small place with an unreasonable share of the periodic table. Yttrium took the first slice of the village name. As chemists worked through the same family of ores, ytterbium, terbium, and erbium took their names from that place as well, four elements from one quarry. The honor was accidental, the result of a rich rock and of analysts who refused to treat a mixed earth as if it were pure. Students who memorize those four names are memorizing a shoreline in Sweden. Gadolin opened the account, and the village supplied the titles; few places on Earth are spoken so often in a chemistry lesson for so small a spot on the map.

trivia.title: The Metal Came Late
trivia.summary: Yttria was known in the 1790s, yet metallic yttrium stayed out of reach until chemists could finally pull it free from a stubborn oxide.
trivia.story: Naming an earth is not the same as holding a metal in tongs. Yttrium metal was isolated long after Gadolin’s yttria, once chemists could pull the element free from its stubborn oxide. That delay was ordinary in this corner of the table. The rare earths cling to one another, so early samples called yttrium were still mixtures even when their owners felt confident. Analyst after analyst shaved those mixtures down with repeated crystallizations and fresh tests. A reasonably pure metal arrived only after the village name was already famous for the confusion; Yttrium’s late metallic life is part of its character, a slow unveiling rather than a single lucky day.

trivia.title: A Garnet That Lasers
trivia.summary: Yttrium aluminium garnet became a standard host crystal for laser rods, a clear lattice that lets another element do the shining.
trivia.story: Yttrium’s best-known crystal is yttrium aluminium garnet, usually called YAG. The garnet is a host, a clear and tough lattice that can hold a small amount of another element, often neodymium, and then help amplify light. Surgeons, engineers, and serious laser tools all met this crystal during the late twentieth century. It is a long way from a black rock in a Swedish quarry. Gadolin separated an earth, and instrument makers later grew that chemistry into a rod that emits a controlled beam. The element’s modern reputation is optical as much as it is chemical; a village quarry ended up inside devices that cut, measure, and illuminate.

trivia.title: Above Liquid Nitrogen
trivia.summary: A ceramic of yttrium, barium, and copper carried electricity with no resistance at a temperature that liquid nitrogen could reach.
trivia.story: In 1987 a ceramic of yttrium, barium, copper, and oxygen became the first superconductor to work above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen. Before that, the strange loss of electrical resistance belonged to temperatures near absolute zero, expensive and awkward to maintain. Liquid nitrogen is still very cold, but teaching labs and hospitals can handle it. The discovery set off a rush, with laboratories racing to confirm the composition of the crystal and to find superconductors that worked even warmer. Yttrium behaves a bit like a heavy lanthanide even though it sits in group 3, and suddenly it was on the front page. The quarry element had entered physics.

applications.title: Lasers and phosphors
applications.body: Yttrium aluminum garnet is a host crystal for many lasers, and yttrium phosphors help some lamps and screens glow.

applications.title: Alloys
applications.body: Small amounts of yttrium strengthen some aluminum and magnesium alloys used where the metal must stay light.

applications.title: With the rare earths
applications.body: Yttrium is separated from the same ores as the lanthanides, because its chemistry matches theirs. The metal is a specialty product.

elements.name: Zirconium

summary.beginner:
Zirconium is element 40, a metal that resists corrosion and does not soak up neutrons easily. Nuclear reactors use it as a jacket around fuel.

Its symbol is Zr. At room temperature zirconium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 4. In class those are called period 5 and group 4.

Zirconium also appears in some ceramics and in fake diamonds made of zirconium dioxide. The metal looks ordinary. Its value is that it survives harsh conditions.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral zirconium atom has 40 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Zirconium is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 4. Zirconium is corrosion-resistant, and its low neutron capture is why reactor cladding is a zirconium alloy.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d2 5s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 10, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4.

Hafnium, the element below it, is the opposite for neutrons and must be removed from reactor zirconium. The two are famously hard to separate.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Zirconium (Z = 40) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d2 5s2. Zircaloy works because zirconium's neutron-capture cross section is small.

Hafnium's is large. Chemically the two are almost twins after the lanthanide contraction, which is exactly why the separation is difficult.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Zirconium: say the name, write Zr, find Z=40 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — nuclear cladding and ceramics.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Zirconium: electron configuration [Kr] 4d2 5s2, Typical oxidation states: +4. It sits in group 4. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. corrosion-resistant; low neutron capture.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Zirconium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Zr vs Hf are famously hard to separate If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found in zircon; Berzelius isolated a purer sample later.

elements.history:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth identified a new earth in the gem zircon in 1789 and named it zirconium, from the mineral. Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated an impure metal in 1824. A ductile metal came only with the iodide process in the twentieth century.

Zirconium’s oxide is a refractory ceramic. The metal’s low neutron capture made it the cladding of water-cooled reactor fuel, once it could be separated from its chemical twin hafnium.
elements.howDiscovered:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth fused powdered zircon from Ceylon with alkali, dissolved the cake, and removed the silica. In 1789 an earth remained that was not alumina and not the rare earths he knew. He could not reduce it to a metal.

Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated an impure metal in 1824 by heating the potassium fluoride salt with potassium, the same pattern he used for silicon. A ductile metal came only with the iodide process in the twentieth century. The discovery is the earth that survived after silica had been taken out of the gem.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Zirconium is mostly that same slow-process peak. Zirconium-90, the common isotope, is built in giant stars. Zirconium-96 is the exception: it is neutron-rich and takes a substantial share from the rapid process, so a sample of zirconium is not quite a single story.

The slow process also makes zirconium-93, which is radioactive, with a half-life near 1.5 million years. It decayed to niobium-93 before the planets finished forming. The zirconium metal in reactor cladding is the stable mix, dominated by the giant-star isotopes.

trivia.title: An Earth Inside the Gem
trivia.summary: Martin Heinrich Klaproth found a new earth in the gem zircon and built the element’s name directly from the mineral people already wore.
trivia.story: Martin Heinrich Klaproth had a gift for finding new earths in minerals other people thought they already understood. In 1789 he examined zircon, a gem known for centuries, and announced a new earth in it. He named that earth zirconium, taking the word from the mineral, so the gem and the element would share a family name. He had an oxide, or something close to it, and not yet a workable metal. The gemstone had been hiding an element in plain sight, worn as jewelry while chemists walked past. Zircon was the clue, and the name still shows it; a decorative stone turned out to be a chemical announcement.

trivia.title: A Brittle Metal in 1824
trivia.summary: Jöns Jacob Berzelius produced zirconium metal in 1824, but the sample was impure and brittle, and a ductile metal waited another century.
trivia.story: Klaproth’s earth waited more than thirty years for anything a smith would call a metal. Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated an impure form of zirconium in 1824, a real step and still a disappointment if you wanted a bar you could bend. The element clings to oxygen and to other impurities, so early samples were brittle lumps. A ductile metal, the kind that can be drawn and shaped, arrived only in the twentieth century. Berzelius had proved that a metal existed, and engineers still waited about a century before zirconium could be trusted in a tube. That long delay is why the element can feel modern even though its name is old.

trivia.title: Zirconia Beside the Diamond
trivia.summary: Zirconium dioxide became both a ceramic that survives great heat and, as cubic zirconia, a sparkling stand-in that jewelers still have to test.
trivia.story: Zircon, the silicate gem, is only the beginning of the oxide’s career. Zirconia, which is zirconium dioxide, is a refractory ceramic, able to face temperatures that would wreck ordinary pottery. Cut and stabilized, the same oxide becomes cubic zirconia, the diamond substitute that filled jewelry shops in the late twentieth century. It sparkles, it resists scratches better than glass, and a jeweler can still tell it from a diamond. Klaproth’s earth had become a crucible and a costume gem. The element’s oxide is often more famous than the gray metal itself; a gemstone mystery of 1789 grew into both a high-temperature ceramic and a look-alike on a ring.

trivia.title: Cladding That Spares Neutrons
trivia.summary: Reactor builders needed a metal around hot fuel that would not swallow the neutrons keeping the chain reaction alive, and zirconium could do that.
trivia.story: Zirconium’s great industrial role arrived when nuclear reactors needed a special metal. It barely captures neutrons, so a thin tube of it can hold hot fuel while neutrons pass and keep the reaction going. Hafnium, the chemical twin that shares its ores, does the opposite and absorbs neutrons eagerly. Leave that twin in the metal, and the cladding spoils the reactor’s neutron economy. Separating the two was difficult, and once industry could do it, zirconium alloys became the usual wrap for water-cooled fuel. A gemstone element earned its nuclear place because it does not steal the neutrons the core needs; the twin, not the zirconium, was the problem hiding in the ore.

trivia.title: A Clock Inside the Crystal
trivia.summary: Zircon crystals take in a little uranium and almost no lead at the start, so geologists can read the lead later and date ancient rocks.
trivia.story: Long before reactors, zircon crystals were already recording time. As they form they take in a little uranium and almost no lead, then hold the lead that later decay produces. Geologists measure the two and calculate how long the crystal has stayed closed, sometimes for billions of years. The method helped date some of the oldest minerals known on Earth. It is a use Klaproth could not have planned when he named an earth inside a gem. The mineral that revealed the element also became one of geology’s best clocks, from jewelry cases to the oldest rocks; beauty and deep time start in the same crystal.

applications.title: Nuclear reactors
applications.body: Fuel rods in many reactors are clad in a zirconium alloy, because the metal resists hot water and does not steal many neutrons.

applications.title: Ceramics
applications.body: Zirconium dioxide is a hard ceramic used in knives, dental crowns, and fake diamonds.

applications.title: Separated from hafnium
applications.body: Reactor zirconium has to be freed of hafnium, which would absorb the neutrons the cladding is meant to ignore.

elements.name: Niobium

summary.beginner:
Niobium is element 41, a metal that stays strong when it is very hot. It goes into steel and into the wires of powerful magnets.

Its symbol is Nb. At room temperature niobium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 5. In class those are called period 5 and group 5.

You will not find niobium in a kitchen, but an MRI machine may contain a magnet made with it. The metal is gray and resists corrosion.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral niobium atom has 41 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Niobium is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 5. Niobium has a high melting point, and its important oxidation state in oxides is +5.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d4 5s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 12, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5.

NbTi and Nb3Sn are the workhorse superconductors in many high-field magnets. Small amounts also strengthen steel.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Niobium (Z = 41) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d4 5s1. The superconducting use is a low-temperature property of the alloy, not a chemical reaction.

In ordinary compounds Nb(V) is the stable high oxidation state, as expected for group 5.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Niobium: say the name, write Nb, find Z=41 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — superconducting alloys; steel.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Niobium: electron configuration [Kr] 4d4 5s1, Typical oxidation states: +5. It sits in group 5. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. high melting; +5 chemistry.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Niobium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; NbTi and Nb₃Sn magnets If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found in columbite; later unified with tantalum chemistry.

elements.history:
Charles Hatchett analyzed a mineral in the British Museum in 1801 and announced a new element, which he called columbium, for Columbia. The ore was later confused with tantalum. Heinrich Rose argued in 1844 that it was distinct and named it niobium, for Niobe, daughter of Tantalus. The two names shared the literature until IUPAC settled on niobium in 1950.

Niobium steels and the superconducting alloys NbTi and Nb3Sn are the uses that justified the long argument over the name.
elements.howDiscovered:
Charles Hatchett examined a heavy black mineral in the British Museum, sent from Connecticut and catalogued as an iron ore. In 1801 he fused it with carbonate, dissolved it, and precipitated an oxide that was neither iron, nor tungsten, nor any earth he could name. He called the element columbium and did not isolate a metal.

The oxide was later tangled with tantalum, because the two metals travel together and resist the same acids. Heinrich Rose separated the chemistries in 1844. The original discovery is Hatchett’s precipitation: one museum specimen, one fusion, and an oxide that matched nothing on the shelf.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Niobium-93 is the only stable isotope, and much of it is a decay product. The slow process in giant stars makes zirconium-93. That nucleus lives about 1.5 million years, long enough to be made in the star and short enough that, by the birth of the solar system, it had become niobium.

A rapid-process contribution to niobium is small beside that decay. The niobium in a superconducting alloy is, in that sense, fossil zirconium from giant stars.

trivia.title: Columbium in a Museum Drawer
trivia.summary: Charles Hatchett analyzed a heavy mineral from Connecticut in the British Museum and announced an element he named for Columbia.
trivia.story: Charles Hatchett was not digging a mine when he found his element. In 1801 he analyzed a heavy black mineral in the British Museum, a specimen that had come from Connecticut. Its chemistry matched no metal he knew, so he announced a new element and called it columbium, for Columbia, a poetic name for America. The ore had crossed the ocean and waited in a collection. A museum shelf was the scene of the find. Columbium entered the journals with a New World name and an Old World laboratory; the rock had been a specimen before it was a discovery, which is an unusual path onto the periodic table.

trivia.title: Niobe Beside Tantalus
trivia.summary: Heinrich Rose argued that the American metal was distinct from tantalum and renamed it for Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus in the myth.
trivia.story: Hatchett’s columbium soon fell into a muddle with tantalum, a metal so similar that some chemists decided the two were one. Heinrich Rose took up the argument in 1844 and insisted they were distinct. He named Hatchett’s element niobium, for Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth. The myth was a chemist’s joke with a point, because the two metals sit side by side and are miserably hard to separate. Rose’s name admitted the family resemblance. It also started a fight about what the rest of the world ought to call the metal; a museum specimen had gained a second name, and both names were about to live for a century.

trivia.title: Two Names Until 1950
trivia.summary: American journals kept saying columbium long after many European journals said niobium, and the quarrel outlived the chemists who started it.
trivia.story: Two names for one metal troubled a science that wanted a single language. Through the nineteenth century and well into the twentieth, columbium and niobium shared the literature. American metallurgists often kept Hatchett’s name, tied to Columbia and to the Connecticut ore, while many European chemists followed Rose. A serious paper sometimes had to translate its own title before the experiment could even be discussed. In 1950 IUPAC chose niobium as the official name. Old books still say columbium, and the metal did not change when the word did; the quarrel no longer has two legal winners, which is as much peace as a naming fight usually gets.

trivia.title: Steel Wire and Cold Magnets
trivia.summary: Niobium toughens steels and, in alloys with titanium or tin, carries huge currents in the superconducting magnets of scanners and accelerators.
trivia.story: Niobium earns its keep in steel, where a small addition toughens alloys used in pipelines and structural parts. It also became indispensable in superconducting magnets. The alloys of niobium with titanium and of niobium with tin carry huge currents without electrical resistance when they are kept very cold, which is why they sit inside MRI scanners and large physics machines. Those uses arrived long after Hatchett and Rose were dead. They also explain why the name fight was worth finishing. A metal with two labels was being wound into magnets, and engineers needed one word on the order form; the Connecticut ore had grown into wire.

trivia.title: Almost Erased by Tantalum
trivia.summary: After the announcement, leading chemists decided columbium was only tantalum, and the element had to be argued back into existence.
trivia.story: The hardest stretch in niobium’s story is the stretch when it almost disappeared. After Hatchett’s announcement, leading chemists, including William Hyde Wollaston, examined similar ores and concluded that columbium was simply tantalum. The element was dropped from lists it had just joined. Rose’s work in 1844 put it back, but only through a separation that others had to repeat before they believed him. Identity, for this metal, was not obvious even to experts. The later fight over names was smaller than the earlier fight over whether the element existed at all; the Connecticut specimen had been right the first time, and it took decades for the rest of chemistry to agree.

applications.title: Superconducting magnets
applications.body: The wire in many MRI and accelerator magnets is a niobium alloy that carries current with no resistance when it is kept very cold.

applications.title: Steel
applications.body: A little niobium in steel makes the grains smaller and the steel stronger. Pipelines use that alloy.

applications.title: A high melting point
applications.body: Niobium stays strong when it is hot, so it also appears in rocket nozzles and in chemical equipment that must resist acid.
