elements.name: Molybdenum

summary.beginner:
Molybdenum is element 42, a hard metal with a very high melting point. Steelmakers add it for toughness, and a trace of it is in some enzymes in living cells.

Its symbol is Mo. At room temperature molybdenum is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 6. In class those are called period 5 and group 6.

A soft gray mineral of molybdenum is used as a dry lubricant, a powder that lets metal parts slide. The pure metal is the opposite of soft: it is used where things get hot.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral molybdenum atom has 42 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Molybdenum is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 6. Molybdenum has a very high melting point and several oxidation states, and MoS2 is a layered lubricant.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d5 5s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 13, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +6.

Nitrogenase, the enzyme that helps some bacteria use nitrogen from the air, contains molybdenum. That is a trace biological role, not a supplement to experiment with.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Molybdenum (Z = 42) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d5 5s1. MoS2 shears between sulfur layers, which is the lubricant.

In nitrogenase the molybdenum is part of a cofactor that reduces N2, a rare example of this metal in biology.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +6. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Molybdenum: say the name, write Mo, find Z=42 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — steel hardener; enzymes in biology.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Molybdenum: electron configuration [Kr] 4d5 5s1, Typical oxidation states: +6. It sits in group 6. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. very high melting; many oxidation states.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Molybdenum: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; MoS₂ lubricant; nitrogenase cofactor If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Identified in molybdenite, distinct from graphite and lead ore.

elements.history:
The mineral molybdenite looks like graphite and was long confused with lead ore, which is why the name comes from the Greek molybdos, lead. Carl Wilhelm Scheele showed in 1778 that the ore was neither graphite nor galena, and Peter Jacob Hjelm reduced the oxide to the metal in 1781.

Molybdenum hardens steel and survives high temperature. In biology it sits in the cofactor of nitrogenase, the enzyme that fixes nitrogen at room temperature.
elements.howDiscovered:
Molybdenite looks like graphite and was used as a pencil ore. Carl Wilhelm Scheele treated it with nitric acid in 1778. Unlike graphite, it gave off sulfuric fumes and left a white acidic solid. The white solid was not lead oxide and not tungstic acid.

Peter Jacob Hjelm heated that acid with charcoal and linseed oil in 1781 and obtained a dark metal. The discovery has two steps that could not be skipped: Scheele showed the greasy mineral was a sulfide of a new acid, and Hjelm reduced the acid. Graphite does neither.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Molybdenum’s isotopes refuse a single channel. Molybdenum-96 is mainly the slow process. Molybdenum-100 is mainly the rapid process. Molybdenum-92 and molybdenum-94 are proton-rich, and they are among the most abundant isotopes of the element. The usual neutron-capture paths do not make them.

The leading account of those proton-rich nuclei is the gamma process, photodisintegration in a supernova, and that account underproduces them. Their origin is an open problem. The molybdenum in an alloy is a blend of at least three histories.

trivia.title: Mistaken for Lead Ore
trivia.summary: A soft gray mineral passed as lead ore and as graphite, which is why molybdenum takes its name from the Greek word for lead.
trivia.story: Molybdenite is soft, gray, and slippery, so miners and scholars filed it under whatever it resembled that week. Sometimes it was called a lead ore, because it looked like galena. Sometimes it was scraped and used as if it were graphite, the mineral in pencils, which it is not. The Greek word molybdos means lead, and that mistake froze into the element’s name. Molybdenum sounds like a lead metal and behaves as nothing of the sort. It is a hard, high-melting metal, and the lead-name is a fossil kept after the confusion was corrected; the ore’s disguise lasted longer than it deserved, and the name still confesses it.

trivia.title: Scheele Names the Acid
trivia.summary: Carl Wilhelm Scheele showed in 1778 that the slippery ore was neither galena nor graphite, and he recognized the acid of a new metal.
trivia.story: Carl Wilhelm Scheele attacked the identity of molybdenite in 1778 and showed that the ore was neither graphite nor the lead ore galena. From it he prepared a distinct acid, molybdic acid, the signature of an element the mineral had been hiding. Scheele was brilliant at taking minerals apart and less interested in forcing every new substance all the way down to a lump of metal. He recognized the acid and left the final reduction to someone else. That division of labor was common, and it was honest. Molybdenum’s discovery has two authors because the ore and the metal were two different jobs; the first job was seeing that the gray flake was new.

trivia.title: Hjelm Wins the Metal
trivia.summary: Peter Jacob Hjelm took Scheele’s acid, reduced the oxide, and in 1781 produced the metal that the lead-colored ore had been concealing.
trivia.story: Peter Jacob Hjelm, a Swedish chemist, finished the work in 1781. He reduced the oxide that came from Scheele’s acid and obtained molybdenum metal. It was not a pretty showcase sample by later standards, but it was the element rather than the slippery ore. The name inherited from lead now sat on a metal that would become famous as a toughener of steel. Hjelm gets the credit for isolation, and Scheele gets the credit for seeing that the mineral was new. Between them they ended a confusion that had lasted as long as people had picked up gray rocks and guessed; the metal was finally allowed to be itself.

trivia.title: The Toughener in Hot Steel
trivia.summary: A little molybdenum in steel helps alloys stay hard when they are hot, which is why tools and armor plate both came to want it.
trivia.story: Molybdenum’s famous job is inside steel. A small percentage hardens the alloy and helps it keep that hardness at temperatures where ordinary steel softens. Tools, armor plate, and high-temperature parts all picked up the habit during the twentieth century, especially when wars demanded metal that would not quit. The element is also at home in high heat on its own, with a melting point far above iron’s. Miners who once set the ore aside as bad lead or bad graphite were looking at a strategic metal. The confusion with galena hid one of the best tougheners on the steelmaker’s list; gray and soft in the ground, it makes other metals stubborn.

trivia.title: A Helper for Living Nitrogen
trivia.summary: Away from the steel mill, a few atoms of molybdenum sit in the enzyme that lets some microbes grab nitrogen straight from the air.
trivia.story: Most of the molybdenum ever mined goes into alloys, but a tiny fraction does something more elegant. It sits in nitrogenase, the enzyme some microbes use to pull nitrogen from the air and make it useful to living things. Factories do a similar job only with high pressure and fierce heat. The microbes manage it in ordinary soil, with molybdenum in the enzyme’s helper group. An element named by mistake for lead is also a trace nutrient. Scheele’s acid and a clover root are two chapters of the same metal; the armor plate and the root nodule do not look related until the periodic table is allowed to connect them.

applications.title: Steel
applications.body: Molybdenum makes steel hard and strong at high temperature. Drill steel and pressure vessels often contain it.

applications.title: A dry lubricant
applications.body: Molybdenum disulfide is a soft gray powder that lets metal parts slide. It is a compound, layered like graphite.

applications.title: Enzymes
applications.body: The enzyme that lets some bacteria use nitrogen from the air contains molybdenum. Animals need a trace of the element for other enzymes.

elements.name: Technetium

summary.beginner:
Technetium is element 43, and it has no stable form. Hospitals use a short-lived version to take pictures of the inside of the body.

Its symbol is Tc. At room temperature technetium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 7. In class those are called period 5 and group 7.

Technetium was the first element made by people rather than found in a mine. The form used in scans disappears quickly, which is why it can be useful and still not stay in the body for long.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral technetium atom has 43 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Technetium is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 7. Technetium has no stable isotope, and technetium-99m is a widely used medical imaging tracer.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d5 5s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 13, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +7.

The 'm' means a long-lived excited nucleus that emits a gamma ray as it settles. The chemistry is arranged so the tracer goes to a particular organ, and then the radioactivity fades.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Technetium (Z = 43) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d5 5s2. Tc-99m decays by gamma emission with a six-hour half-life, long enough to image and short enough to limit the dose.

There is no primordial technetium left from Earth's formation.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +7. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: First element produced artificially, from molybdenum bombarded with deuterons.

elements.history:
Mendeleev’s table had a gap under manganese. Claims to have found that element in minerals failed. In 1937 Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè isolated it from a molybdenum foil that had been bombarded with deuterons in Ernest Lawrence’s cyclotron. They named it technetium, from the Greek technetos, artificial. It was the first element made by people before it was found in nature.

Every isotope is radioactive. The short-lived isomer technetium-99m, milked from a generator, became the most used radioisotope in diagnostic imaging.
elements.howDiscovered:
Emilio Segrè and Carlo Perrier received a molybdenum plate that had been bombarded with deuterons in the Berkeley cyclotron. In 1937, in Palermo, they dissolved the plate and followed the radioactivity through a sequence of precipitations. The activity tracked the chemistry expected for the missing element under manganese, the homolog of rhenium, and it was not any known element.

No stable isotope exists, which is why the element had never appeared in an ore analysis. Earlier claims from minerals did not hold. The discovery was a radioactive tracer in a dissolved cyclotron target, behaving as element 43 should and as nothing else did.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Technetium has no stable isotope. The long-lived ones last millions of years, far short of the age of the Earth, so none from the birth of the solar system remains in the crust. Stars do make it. The slow process in giant stars passes through technetium-99. In 1952 Paul Merrill saw its spectral lines in S-type stars.

Those lines showed that stars build heavy elements while we watch. On Earth the element has to be made again. Reactors produce it when uranium fissions. The stellar atom and the reactor atom are the same missing element, made in two places.

trivia.title: Made Before It Was Found
trivia.summary: Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè identified element 43 in molybdenum that Ernest Lawrence’s Berkeley cyclotron had already bombarded.
trivia.story: Element 43 was a hole in the table under manganese, and digging in minerals had not filled it. In 1937 Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè, working in Italy, studied molybdenum that Ernest Lawrence’s cyclotron at Berkeley had bombarded with deuterons. The radioactivity in that metal was not molybdenum’s own. They separated a new element from the target. It was the first element people made before they found it in nature. A machine in California had finished a search that ordinary rocks had refused to end; the sample crossed an ocean, and the missing square finally had an occupant that laboratories could confirm.

trivia.title: A Name Meaning Artificial
trivia.summary: The discoverers chose a Greek word for artificial, fitting an element that a cyclotron produced before any ore was shown to contain it.
trivia.story: Perrier and Segrè named element 43 technetium, from the Greek technetos, meaning artificial. The word admitted the truth of the experiment. They had not picked the element out of a mine. They had recognized it in metal a cyclotron had altered. Every isotope of technetium is radioactive, so the element does not pile up in ordinary crust the way iron does. Tiny traces were found later in uranium ores, where nature performs nuclear changes of its own; the name still fits that history; people met technetium as a product before they ever met it as a mineral, which is the reverse of almost every older element.

trivia.title: The Blank Under Manganese
trivia.summary: Mendeleev’s eka-manganese stayed empty while gallium and germanium arrived, and element 43 became the table’s awkward missing square.
trivia.story: Mendeleev’s table predicted a metal under manganese, the space he treated as eka-manganese, and left element 43 blank. Gallium and germanium filled their boxes while he lived, and this one stayed empty. Chemists hunted platinum ores and manganese minerals and brought back claims that faded under scrutiny. The blank grew embarrassing: a periodic law that could describe an element the rocks would not hand over. A cyclotron finally closed the gap. Technetium was the prediction that waited until people could manufacture it; the earlier victories of the table made this long absence feel like a personal insult, until a machine supplied what geology withheld.

trivia.title: The Unaccepted Masurium
trivia.summary: A 1925 claim said element 43 had been found in minerals and should be called masurium, and the scientific community did not accept it.
trivia.story: In 1925 the Noddacks, working with Otto Berg, reported element 43 in minerals and proposed the name masurium. The announcement arrived in a century already full of false rare elements. Other laboratories could not confirm the work, and masurium never took a lasting place on the table. Perrier and Segrè’s technetium, twelve years later, did not complete that earlier claim. It replaced an unaccepted report with evidence other people could check. Masurium stayed a historical name for a discovery the community does not accept; the dispute matters because the gap was real, and wishing an element out of a mineral was not the same as proving it.

trivia.title: Pictures from a Short Life
trivia.summary: Hospitals use a short-lived form, technetium-99m, to build images of organs, then rely on the fact that the radioactivity fades quickly.
trivia.story: Technetium’s everyday fame is medical rather than metallic. The form used in hospitals, technetium-99m, gives off radiation that cameras outside the body can map, and it fades quickly enough that the patient does not carry it for long. Scans of bone, heart, and other organs became routine because of that balance. Hospitals receive the isotope ready for imaging, a medical use with a short clock already running. Every isotope is radioactive, so there is no stable lump of technetium in a classroom drawer. The artificial element became the most used radioisotope in diagnostic imaging; a metal the Earth almost refused to keep now draws pictures of living people.

applications.title: Medical images
applications.body: A short-lived form of technetium is the most-used tracer in nuclear medicine. A scanner follows where it goes in the body, and then the radioactivity fades.

applications.title: No stable form
applications.body: Technetium has no stable isotope, so there is no technetium ore to mine. It is made from molybdenum in a generator at the hospital's supplier.

applications.title: A made element
applications.body: Technetium was the first element produced artificially. That history is why the box on the table was empty for so long.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.body: Technetium has no stable form, so a visible piece is rare. The vial holds a very small sample of the element, next to a radiation marker. It is the element itself, not a mineral.

elements.name: Ruthenium

summary.beginner:
Ruthenium is element 44, a rare hard metal in the platinum family. It is used as a catalyst, a material that helps a reaction along without being used up.

Its symbol is Ru. At room temperature ruthenium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 8. In class those are called period 5 and group 8.

Ruthenium is not a coin or a wire you would recognize. Small amounts on a surface, or in a chemical, do the work in industry and in research.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral ruthenium atom has 44 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Ruthenium is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 8. Ruthenium is a corrosion-resistant platinum-group metal with several oxidation states.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d7 5s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 15, 1. Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +3. The one courses meet most often is +4.

It hardens platinum and palladium alloys and serves as a catalyst in some chemical processes. A few ruthenium compounds are studied as dyes that catch sunlight.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Ruthenium (Z = 44) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d7 5s1. The spread of oxidation states, including Ru(VIII) in the volatile and toxic RuO4, is characteristic of the heavier platinum metals.

Catalysis uses the metal surface or a designed complex, not a lump of ruthenium.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +3. The one courses meet most often is +4. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Ruthenium: say the name, write Ru, find Z=44 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — hardest platinum-group catalyst.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Ruthenium: electron configuration [Kr] 4d7 5s1, Typical oxidation states: +4, +3. It sits in group 8. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. resists corrosion; many oxidation states.

discovery.text: Isolated from Ural platinum residues.

elements.history:
Platinum ores from the Urals left a residue after the platinum was extracted. Karl Ernst Klaus, working at Kazan, isolated a new metal from that residue in 1844 and named it ruthenium, from Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia. Gottfried Osann had claimed a similar metal earlier, but Klaus’s work was the one that held.

Ruthenium is a platinum-group metal, hard and chemically versatile. It is a catalyst and a hardener of platinum and palladium alloys.
elements.howDiscovered:
Karl Ernst Claus worked through the insoluble residues of Ural platinum ore after osmium and iridium had been argued over. In 1844, at Kazan, he fused the residues, dissolved them, and obtained a metal whose salts and spectrum were not those of iridium, rhodium, or osmium. He prepared the metal in a coherent sample.

The discovery is that last fraction. Platinum residues were a mixture of six metals, and each discovery was whatever refused to follow the precipitation of the one before it. Ruthenium was the one that remained when the others had been named.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Ruthenium’s seven stable isotopes split among the slow process, the rapid process, and the gamma process. Ruthenium-96 and ruthenium-98 are proton-rich. Ruthenium-104 is neutron-rich and largely a rapid-process isotope. The middle isotopes are mixed.

The metal in an electrical contact is that blend, from giant stars, from neutron-rich blasts, and from the photon-driven rare channel. No one site is asked to make all of it.

trivia.title: A Metal in the Leftovers
trivia.summary: After platinum was taken from Ural ores, Karl Ernst Klaus kept working on the residue and isolated a metal earlier reports had muddled.
trivia.story: Platinum ores from the Urals left a stubborn residue once the platinum itself was extracted. Karl Ernst Klaus, at Kazan, treated that residue as a mine of its own. In 1844 he isolated a new metal and showed it was not just a confused mixture of metals already known. Earlier workers had suspected something new in the same leftovers without making the claim hold. Klaus’s preparation could be repeated and tested by others. Ruthenium joined the platinum group as a hard, rare metal that appears only after the famous one is gone; the residue, which looked like waste, was the real ore for this element; stopping at platinum would have missed it.

trivia.title: A Latin Name for Russia
trivia.summary: Klaus named the metal from Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia, tying a quiet platinum-group element to the country of the Ural ores.
trivia.story: Klaus named the metal ruthenium, from Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia. Like gallium for France and germanium for Germany, the word plants the country of the ore inside the element. The Ural mines had already made platinum a Russian export known across Europe. Ruthenium was the quieter metal in those same rocks, easy to overlook once the platinum was gone. The Latin place name was the one that stayed in the textbooks. Translating it still leads a careful student back to Russia; a residue in a Kazan laboratory received a name large enough for a country, which suits an element that almost slipped away unnamed.

trivia.title: Osann’s Claim Falls Apart
trivia.summary: Gottfried Osann had already announced new metals in platinum leftovers, including a ruthenium, but his mixtures did not convince other chemists.
trivia.story: Gottfried Osann studied platinum residues before Klaus and believed he had found several new metals. One of the names he used was ruthenium. The experiments were hard to repeat, the substances were mixtures, and other chemists could not see a clean element in the reports. Klaus knew that history. He revived the name ruthenium once his own metal was actually in hand and could be tested. Credit follows the work that held, which is Klaus’s isolation in 1844 rather than the earlier announcement; suggesting a metal is not the same as proving one; the episode is a priority dispute with a plain ending, because the careful isolation is the discovery that counts.

trivia.title: Hardener of Dearer Metals
trivia.summary: Ruthenium is too scarce for bulk construction, so it earns its cost by hardening platinum alloys and by serving as a catalyst.
trivia.story: Ruthenium is a platinum-group metal, scarce and expensive, so nobody builds a bridge from it. Small amounts harden platinum and palladium alloys, the way a pinch of a different metal can change a familiar one. It is also a versatile catalyst, used in chemical plants and studied for reactions that the more famous platinum metals also serve. An electrical contact or a catalyst pellet may be the closest a person comes to noticing it. Klaus’s residue metal became an additive and a surface rather than a pile in a warehouse. Its value is out of proportion to its mass; the element hides in other precious metals and makes them harder or more useful.

trivia.title: An Oxide That Travels
trivia.summary: Ruthenium metal is manageable in alloys, but ruthenium tetroxide is volatile, and its vapor can seriously harm eyes and lungs.
trivia.story: The compound ruthenium tetroxide worries chemists more than the hard metal itself. It is volatile, and its vapor can seriously harm the eyes and the lungs of anyone who meets it. Laboratories that handle ruthenium compounds plan for that risk as ordinary business, because the harm is well known. The episode is a standing warning in the platinum group rather than one famous disaster with a single date. A metal that arrives as a residue from platinum ore can still form a dangerous compound. The hard metal from Kazan and that traveling oxide are two moods of a single element, and both belong in any honest account of it.

applications.title: Electronics
applications.body: A thin layer of ruthenium is used in some resistors and hard-disk coatings. The amount in any one device is tiny.

applications.title: Catalysts
applications.body: Ruthenium compounds and surfaces help a number of chemical reactions, including some routes to ammonia and to specialty chemicals.

applications.title: Hardening platinum
applications.body: A little ruthenium makes platinum and palladium alloys harder. Electrical contacts use that hardness.

elements.name: Rhodium

summary.beginner:
Rhodium is element 45, a shiny rare metal. A car's catalytic converter uses it to help clean exhaust gases.

Its symbol is Rh. At room temperature rhodium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 9. In class those are called period 5 and group 9.

Rhodium is one of the most expensive metals because it is scarce and useful. The converter on a car holds only a thin coat, not a solid block.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral rhodium atom has 45 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Rhodium is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 9. Rhodium is a reflective platinum-group metal, and its main public use is in catalytic converters.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d8 5s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 16, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

It reduces nitrogen oxides in exhaust. The metal is also plated where a hard, bright, tarnish-free surface is needed.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Rhodium (Z = 45) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d8 5s1. In the converter, rhodium catalyzes reduction of NOx while platinum and palladium oxidize CO and leftover hydrocarbons.

Homogeneous rhodium catalysts, as in Wilkinson's complex, are a separate solution chemistry.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Rhodium: say the name, write Rh, find Z=45 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — catalytic converters.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Rhodium: electron configuration [Kr] 4d8 5s1, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 9. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. inert, reflective platinum-group metal.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Rhodium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; homogeneous catalysis (Wilkinson-type chemistry) If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from crude platinum.

elements.history:
William Hyde Wollaston, working in secret on platinum residues, isolated rhodium in 1803. He named it from the Greek rhodon, rose, because its chloride solutions are rose colored. He announced it together with palladium.

Rhodium stayed the rarest and most expensive of the classic platinum metals. A thin layer of it is the reflective surface of many mirrors, and it is a catalyst in automobile converters.
elements.howDiscovered:
William Hyde Wollaston dissolved crude platinum in aqua regia, precipitated the platinum as the ammonium salt, and was left with a rose-red solution. In 1803 he reduced that solution and obtained a metal. Its salts stayed red, which no platinum salt did, and the metal was harder and less dense than platinum.

The discovery is a color that survived the precipitation of platinum. The same solution also yielded palladium. Two elements came out of one liquor because Wollaston did not stop when the platinum was gone.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Rhodium-103 is the only stable isotope. Models give a substantial share to the slow process in giant stars and a substantial share to the rapid process. The split is not settled to one number.

Rhodium is odd-numbered and scarce, which is why it is a precious metal. The rhodium in a catalytic converter is neutron-capture ash from both channels, later concentrated into the same ores as platinum.

trivia.title: A Secret in Platinum Ore
trivia.summary: William Hyde Wollaston worked privately on platinum residues and in 1803 isolated a metal he announced together with palladium.
trivia.story: William Hyde Wollaston did not rush to the journals when he started pulling metals from platinum ore. He worked in secret, partly because the chemistry was commercially valuable and easy for a rival to copy. In 1803 he isolated a new metal from those residues. He announced it together with palladium, a pair of discoveries from the same stubborn powders. Smithson Tennant, working on the part of the residue Wollaston set aside, found osmium and iridium around the same time. The platinum ores had been hiding a whole family of metals; Wollaston’s share of that family included the element he would name for the color of its solutions; secrecy delayed the news, and it did not prevent the discovery.

trivia.title: Rose Color in the Flask
trivia.summary: The new metal’s chloride solutions were rose red, and Wollaston took the name rhodium from the Greek word for that flower.
trivia.story: Wollaston named the element rhodium, from the Greek rhodon, rose. He was not describing the metal you can plate onto a mirror, which is silvery, hard, and bright. He was describing its chloride solutions, which are rose colored and were the laboratory sign that he had something new in the flask. A name taken from a solution, rather than from a country or a myth, fits his practical style. Palladium, found beside it, was named for an asteroid, while rhodium took a flower, and both names from that private workshop stuck. The rose is in the chemistry of the salts; the shine people notice later is a different fact about the same element.

trivia.title: A Price That Will Not Sit
trivia.summary: Rhodium stayed the scarcest and costliest of the classic platinum metals, and its price has leapt and crashed with the car industry.
trivia.story: Rhodium is the rarest and most expensive of the classic platinum metals, and its price is famous for wild swings. A little of it goes into automobile catalytic converters, where it helps clean exhaust gases. When carmakers need more than the mines can smoothly supply, the price leaps, and when that demand pauses, the price falls. Mines rarely produce rhodium on purpose, because it comes out of platinum and nickel ores as a side metal. That thin supply is the whole tension in the market. Wollaston’s rose-colored solutions ended up as a line on commodity charts; a secret laboratory metal became one of the most nervous prices in the platinum group.

trivia.title: A Bright Skin on Metal
trivia.summary: A very thin coat of rhodium turns jewelry and optical parts into a hard, bright surface that resists tarnish far better than the metal underneath.
trivia.story: Rhodium’s other public face is literally a surface. A thin layer of the metal is bright, hard, and slow to tarnish, so it becomes the reflective coat on many mirrors and a flashing on jewelry. White gold is often rhodium plated so the piece looks whiter and wears better at the outside. The coating stays thin because the metal is costly, and thin is enough, because light only needs a skin. Searchlights and optical mirrors have used the same idea, a precious film doing the work of a thick plate. Wollaston isolated a rare element, and jewelers now lay a trace of it over cheaper metal so the surface stays bright.

trivia.title: Under the Family Car
trivia.summary: When governments demanded cleaner exhaust, rhodium took a narrow catalytic job that platinum by itself did not cover as well.
trivia.story: Catalytic converters became common when governments told carmakers to cut the poisons leaving the tailpipe. Platinum and palladium were already famous catalysts. Rhodium joined them because it is especially helpful against nitrogen oxides, the choking gases in the mix. A tiny load of the metal, spread in the converter, treats the exhaust of a whole car for years. The amount in one vehicle is small, and millions of vehicles make a market large enough to shake the price. That is why a metal from a secret experiment in 1803 sits under family cars; Wollaston sold platinum as a business, and rhodium became the scarce partner in a much later one.

applications.title: Catalytic converters
applications.body: Rhodium in a car's converter helps turn nitrogen oxides in the exhaust into nitrogen gas. A thin coat does the work.

applications.title: A bright plate
applications.body: Rhodium plating is a hard, silvery finish on some jewelry and on optical mirrors. It does not tarnish.

applications.title: A scarce metal
applications.body: Rhodium is one of the rarest and most expensive metals in use. The converter holds milligrams, not a bar.

elements.name: Palladium

summary.beginner:
Palladium is element 46, a rare metal used in catalytic converters and in some jewelry. It can also soak up a large amount of hydrogen gas.

Its symbol is Pd. At room temperature palladium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 10. In class those are called period 5 and group 10.

Palladium looks like a quiet silver metal. Its useful trick is chemical: it helps reactions happen on its surface, and hydrogen atoms can slip into the solid.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral palladium atom has 46 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Palladium is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 10. Palladium's ground configuration is the exception 4d10, and the metal both catalyzes reactions and absorbs hydrogen.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18. Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +4. The one courses meet most often is +2.

Catalytic converters use it alongside platinum and rhodium. Jewelry uses the metal because it stays bright. The hydrogen uptake is large enough to be a teaching example of a metal hydride.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Palladium (Z = 46) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10. The 4d10 configuration means the 5s orbital is empty in the ground atom, a reminder that configurations of heavy atoms are close calls.

Hydrogen occupies interstitial sites and expands the lattice.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +4. The one courses meet most often is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Isolated from platinum ores; named after the asteroid Pallas.

elements.history:
Wollaston isolated palladium from platinum ore in 1803 and named it for the asteroid Pallas, itself discovered the year before and named for Pallas Athena. He first offered the metal anonymously through a shop, then revealed the discovery in 1805 after a dispute.

Palladium absorbs astonishing volumes of hydrogen, a fact Thomas Graham studied in the 1860s. That property, and its catalytic surface, made it the metal of hydrogenation and of catalytic converters.
elements.howDiscovered:
From the same platinum solution, Wollaston precipitated a yellow cyanide in 1803. He ignited the precipitate and obtained a white metal, lighter than platinum and attackable by nitric acid, which platinum is not. He first sold samples anonymously as a new silver, inviting chemists to tell him what it was, and published the isolation in 1805.

The cyanide precipitation is the method. It pulled one metal out of a solution that still contained others. The anonymous sale was a provocation. The evidence was the metal’s density, its solubility in nitric acid, and its refusal to be platinum or silver.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Palladium’s lighter stable isotopes take more from the slow process in giant stars. Palladium-110, the heaviest, takes more from the rapid process. Palladium-102 is proton-rich, a gamma-process isotope, and a minor part of the metal.

The element therefore records both of the great neutron-capture histories. The palladium in a catalyst is not the product of one kind of star.

trivia.title: Named for the Asteroid
trivia.summary: William Hyde Wollaston tied palladium to Pallas, an asteroid found the year before and named, like so many new bodies then, from classical myth.
trivia.story: Wollaston isolated palladium from platinum ore in 1803 and named it for the asteroid Pallas. Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers had found that asteroid only the year before and named it for Pallas Athena. For a brief season, new bodies in the sky and new metals in the ore were being christened from the same myths. Palladium’s name came from astronomy rather than from a color or a country. A speck in platinum ore and a speck in the solar system were tied together by a classical education. The element still carries 1802 inside a discovery dated 1803; the sky got there first, and the laboratory followed within a year.

trivia.title: Sold Before It Was Claimed
trivia.summary: Samples of a strange new metal appeared in a London shop with no discoverer’s name, and Richard Chenevix called the whole thing an alloy.
trivia.story: Wollaston first offered palladium anonymously through a London shop, as if a mysterious new silver had simply turned up for sale. Richard Chenevix bought a sample and decided it was not an element. He argued in print that it was an alloy of platinum and mercury. The attack forced a reply from the real discoverer. In 1805 Wollaston revealed himself and defended palladium as a true element rather than a mixture. A metal that began as an anonymous shop item had to win a public argument before chemists would keep it on the list; the dispute is part of the discovery; secrecy made the first announcement look like a trick, until the chemist stepped forward.

trivia.title: A Sponge for Hydrogen
trivia.summary: Thomas Graham showed in the 1860s that palladium absorbs astonishing volumes of hydrogen, a habit that still shapes how the metal is used.
trivia.story: Thomas Graham, in the 1860s, showed that palladium absorbs astonishing volumes of hydrogen. The gas seems to vanish into the solid metal, which swells slightly and still looks like metal rather than like a chemical sponge. Few elements do anything like it, and none of the common ones do it so eagerly. The fact made palladium a curiosity of physics and, later, a practical surface for reactions that involve hydrogen. Graham’s nineteenth-century measurements explain why the metal shows up wherever hydrogen needs a place to sit. The asteroid’s namesake turned out to have an appetite; that appetite is the property industry actually buys.

trivia.title: Converters and White Jewelry
trivia.summary: Palladium became a hydrogenation catalyst, a partner in car exhaust converters, and a white jewelry metal standing in where platinum was wanted.
trivia.story: Once Graham had shown how eagerly palladium holds hydrogen, industry found jobs for the appetite. The metal became a catalyst for hydrogenation, the adding of hydrogen to molecules in factories that make everyday chemicals. Late in the twentieth century it also went into catalytic converters, cleaning exhaust beside platinum and rhodium. Jewelry makers adopted it as a white precious metal that could stand in for platinum. The usual form is a coating or a small addition, not a large lump in the hand. The anonymous shop sample grew into a quiet industrial habit; a dispute about whether it was even an element ended in parts per car and rings on fingers.

trivia.title: The Cold Fusion Dispute
trivia.summary: Two chemists said in 1989 that palladium electrodes had produced fusion in a jar, and laboratories around the world did not accept the claim.
trivia.story: In 1989 Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons announced that they had produced nuclear fusion at room temperature using palladium electrodes in heavy water. The claim was enormous. A small cell, they said, was giving off more energy than it took in. Laboratories around the world tried to see the same effect and could not establish it. The results did not convince the scientific community, and cold fusion was not accepted as a working power source. Palladium’s real gift, its hunger for hydrogen, had made it the stage for a hope that failed; the episode remains a famous dispute, and it never became a working source of power.

applications.title: Catalytic converters
applications.body: Palladium, like platinum, oxidizes leftover fuel and carbon monoxide in exhaust. Many converters now use more palladium than platinum.

applications.title: Jewelry
applications.body: Palladium is a white jewelry metal that stays bright and is lighter than platinum.

applications.title: Hydrogen
applications.body: Palladium metal can absorb a very large volume of hydrogen. That property is used in some purifiers and is a classic teaching demonstration of a metal hydride.

elements.name: Silver

summary.beginner:
Silver is element 47, the bright metal of jewelry, mirrors, and some coins. It conducts electricity better than any other element.

Its symbol is Ag. At room temperature silver is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 11. In class those are called period 5 and group 11.

Silver tarnishes in air that contains a little sulfur, turning dark on the surface. For a long time photographs used silver compounds that darkened in the light.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral silver atom has 47 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Silver is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 11. Silver is the best electrical conductor, and its common ion is Ag+.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10 5s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

Sterling silver is an alloy, not the pure metal. The black tarnish is silver sulfide. Old black-and-white photography reduced silver halide grains to tiny particles of silver metal.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Silver (Z = 47) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s1. The conductivity record is a bulk property of the metal.

Ag+ is a soft Lewis acid, which is why it binds sulfur and why the photographic and antimicrobial chemistry both start from that ion.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Silver: say the name, write Ag, find Z=47 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — jewelry, coins, photography history.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Silver: electron configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s1, Typical oxidation states: +1. It sits in group 11. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. best electrical conductor.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Silver: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Ag⁺ photography and antimicrobial ions If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Native metal of jewelry and coinage.

elements.history:
Silver is a native metal and was worked as jewelry and coinage from early antiquity. No discovery date belongs to one person. The symbol Ag is from the Latin argentum, related to a word for shining.

It is the best electrical conductor of all the elements and the whitest of the precious metals. Silver halides made photography possible, and the ion is still an antimicrobial agent.
elements.howDiscovered:
Silver occurs native, and the sulfide ores yield the metal when roasted and reduced, or when lead is used to collect it and then oxidized away in a cupel. Those operations are ancient. The metal that remains in the cupel is silver because lead oxide soaks into the hearth and silver does not.

There is no modern discoverer. The element was established by the invariance of that bead: dissolve it, precipitate the chloride, reduce the chloride, and the same white metal returns. The original finding was a metal in the ore that cupellation could not remove.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Silver-107 and silver-109 are fed by both neutron-capture channels, in amounts that are roughly comparable in solar-system material. The slow process runs in giant stars. The rapid process runs in neutron-rich blasts, with merging neutron stars the leading site.

Both isotopes are odd-numbered, so silver stays rarer than palladium or cadmium. Native silver and silver ores are that mixed yield, gathered by hot fluids in the crust.

trivia.title: Shining in the Latin
trivia.summary: Silver was jewelry and coinage in early antiquity, and its symbol Ag still comes from the Latin argentum, a word tied to shining.
trivia.story: Silver is a native metal, found already metallic, and people worked it into jewelry and coins from early antiquity. No discovery date and no single discoverer belong to it. The symbol Ag comes from the Latin argentum, related to a word for shining, which fits a surface that throws light back with unusual force. The English word silver traveled a different road, a Germanic one, while chemists kept the Latin in the symbol. That split is common among the ancient metals. Argentum is the old word hiding in every formula that starts with Ag; the element was named by use and by gleam long before anyone wrote a discovery paper.

trivia.title: The Easiest Path for Current
trivia.summary: Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other element, so a costly metal still appears in contacts where copper is not quite enough.
trivia.story: Silver is the best electrical conductor of all the elements, and it is the best conductor of heat as well. Copper is close behind and much cheaper, so copper won the wires inside ordinary walls. Silver is reserved for places where a little extra performance is worth the price: precise contacts, some electronics, and conductors that must not waste a signal. It is also the whitest of the precious metals, a different kind of brilliance from conductivity. Ancient coins and modern circuits use the same element for two kinds of value. One is beauty that a mint can stamp; the other is the easiest path an electron can take through a solid.

trivia.title: Light Caught in a Salt
trivia.summary: Silver halides darken in light, and nineteenth-century inventors built photography on that reaction until digital sensors changed the craft.
trivia.story: Silver halides, especially the chloride, bromide, and iodide, darken when light hits them. Nineteenth-century inventors built photography on that reaction. Louis Daguerre and William Henry Fox Talbot, working in the same era, made practical processes that held an image on a silver-bearing surface. For more than a century, cameras meant silver, whether the image sat on a metal plate or in a gelatin film. Digital sensors later took over everyday cameras, though museums and some photographers still use the older chemistry. A metal mined for coins became a way to keep light; no heist is required for the story; the picture itself was the adventure.

trivia.title: A Color That Would Not Fade
trivia.summary: Silver compounds can fight microbes, but people who swallowed too much of them were left with blue-gray skin that washing does not remove.
trivia.story: Silver ions disturb microbes, which is why the metal and its compounds have been used as antimicrobial agents, from wound dressings to coatings on equipment. That reputation tempted people to swallow silver preparations as if they were general cures. Take in too much for too long, and silver can lodge in the skin and turn it a blue-gray color. The condition is called argyria, and it does not simply fade when the swallowing stops. The element that makes a bright mirror can mark a face. Medicine still uses silver in forms chosen by clinicians, because the old casual tonics wrote their warning where everyone could see it; shine and stain are both real.

trivia.title: Money That Slowly Blackens
trivia.summary: Empires stamped silver into money for centuries, while sulfur compounds in ordinary air slowly turned the same bright metal dark.
trivia.story: For long stretches of history, silver was money as much as it was a chemical element. Empires mined it, stamped it, and argued over how many silver coins should equal one gold coin. Underneath the economics, the metal kept reacting. Sulfur compounds in air, from pollution or even from a cooked egg, tarnish silver to a dark sulfide film. A polishing cloth became part of housekeeping because the shining surface will not stay shining by itself. The dark film is a slow chemical change, a reminder that the coin metal is still alive as an element; tarnish is not a catastrophe; it is silver doing chemistry on the dinner table.

applications.title: Jewelry and coins
applications.body: Silver has been jewelry and money for thousands of years. It stays bright until sulfur in the air darkens the surface.

applications.title: The best conductor
applications.body: Silver conducts electricity better than any other element. Some high-end electrical contacts use it where copper is not quite enough.

applications.title: Old photographs
applications.body: Black-and-white film was a silver-salt process. Light reduced the salt to tiny grains of silver metal, and those grains made the dark parts of the picture.

elements.name: Cadmium

summary.beginner:
Cadmium is element 48, a soft metal, and it is toxic, so its uses are limited and carefully controlled. Older rechargeable batteries used it.

Its symbol is Cd. At room temperature cadmium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 12. In class those are called period 5 and group 12.

Cadmium was also used in some yellow pigments and metal coatings. Those uses have been cut back because the element builds up in the body and causes harm.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral cadmium atom has 48 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Cadmium is a solid transition metal in period 5 and group 12. Cadmium behaves a little like zinc, with oxidation state +2, and it is toxic enough that many older uses have been restricted.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10 5s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

Nickel-cadmium batteries were the familiar example. Cadmium sulfide was a yellow pigment. Neither is a reason to collect the metal.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Cadmium (Z = 48) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2. Cd2+ replaces Zn2+ in some enzymes and proteins because the ions are similar in charge and not wildly different in size, and that mimicry is part of the toxicity.

The 4d10 shell makes the ion colorless.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Cadmium: say the name, write Cd, find Z=48 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — batteries and coatings; toxic.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Cadmium: electron configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It sits in group 12. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. like zinc but softer; +2.

discovery.text: Found as an impurity in zinc carbonate.

elements.history:
Friedrich Stromeyer, inspecting a shipment of zinc carbonate that turned yellow on heating, traced the color to a new element in 1817. He named it cadmium, from cadmia, the old name for calamine. Karl Hermann and J. C. H. Roloff found it independently the same year.

Cadmium plating and nickel–cadmium batteries spread the metal through the twentieth century. Its toxicity, especially of the oxide fumes, then pulled it back out of consumer products.
elements.howDiscovered:
Friedrich Stromeyer, inspecting apothecaries, found zinc carbonate that turned yellow when heated instead of staying white. In 1817 he dissolved the carbonate, precipitated the zinc, and was left with an oxide that reduced with charcoal to a bluish metal, softer and more volatile than zinc. The metal and its sulfide were yellow where zinc’s are white.

Karl Hermann and J. C. H. Roloff found the same impurity in zinc oxide the same year. The discovery is a color that should not have been there, followed by a reduction of the fraction zinc sulfate would not keep.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Cadmium is weighted toward the slow process. Several of its isotopes are built in giant stars, on the path that climbs from the strontium peak toward barium. Cadmium-116, the heaviest stable isotope, takes a larger rapid-process share.

Cadmium-106 and cadmium-108 are proton-rich and belong to the gamma process. They are a small fraction of the metal. The cadmium in a coating or a battery is mostly the giant-star share.

trivia.title: Yellow in the Zinc Ore
trivia.summary: Friedrich Stromeyer followed a zinc carbonate that turned yellow on heating and found that an uninvited metal was causing the color.
trivia.story: Friedrich Stromeyer was inspecting medicines when a shipment of zinc carbonate misbehaved in the heat. The material turned yellow, which the zinc ore calamine should not have done. He traced the color to an impurity and in 1817 showed that the impurity was a new element. What everyone had filed as a zinc mineral had been carrying a second metal. Cadmium’s discovery is the story of a sample that looked slightly wrong and was. That unexpected yellow tint was enough to open the whole case; a routine inspection became a discovery because someone refused to ignore a color the textbook did not predict.

trivia.title: Taken from the Word Cadmia
trivia.summary: Stromeyer named cadmium from cadmia, an old word for the zinc ores that had been hiding it, in a year when others found it too.
trivia.story: Stromeyer named the element cadmium, from cadmia, the old name for calamine and related zinc ores. The word already belonged to the mineral that had concealed the new metal. It was a precise choice: cadmium is what you find when cadmia is not as pure as the label claims. Karl Hermann and Roloff found the element independently in the same year, which shows how ready the zinc trade was to reveal it. A contaminated shipment was enough for more than one laboratory. The name remembers the ore, and 1817 remembers a crowded discovery; two paths reached the same yellow impurity, and the ore’s old name became the element’s.

trivia.title: Plated, Then Pulled Back
trivia.summary: Cadmium plating and nickel-cadmium batteries spread the metal through the twentieth century, until toxicity pushed it out of ordinary goods.
trivia.story: Through the twentieth century cadmium became useful and common, first as a thin plate that protected steel from rust. Nickel-cadmium batteries then put it into cameras, tools, and emergency lights. The usefulness came with a cost, because cadmium compounds are toxic and the fumes of the oxide are especially dangerous to people who heat the metal. Regulators and manufacturers began taking it out of ordinary consumer goods. Being useful had not made the element safe. Its industrial chapter reads as a rise followed by a forced retreat; the yellow impurity in a zinc ore grew into a global product and then into a substance many industries were told to stop using.

trivia.title: It Hurts by the River
trivia.summary: Cadmium in mine wastewater reached the Jinzu River basin in Japan, and a painful bone disease in that community was traced to the metal.
trivia.story: Along the Jinzu River basin in Japan, wastewater from metal mines carried cadmium into water used on the fields. Rice and drinking water then carried the metal into people’s bodies over many years. Residents developed a severe bone disease, with deep pain that gave the illness its name, itai-itai, meaning it hurts, it hurts. Doctors and officials traced the suffering to cadmium from the mines. In 1968 the Japanese government recognized the disease as cadmium poisoning caused by that pollution. The warning was written in a whole river basin; a community’s health was the cost of letting the element leave the mine uncontrolled.

trivia.title: Yellow Paint, Later Limited
trivia.summary: Artists adopted cadmium sulfide as a brilliant yellow, and studios later had to reckon with the toxic metal inside a favorite color.
trivia.story: Cadmium’s yellow, the same sort of color that betrayed it in Stromeyer’s ore, became a pigment painters trusted. Cadmium sulfide gave artists a strong yellow, and with selenium it gave oranges and reds that stayed bright on the canvas. Painters from the nineteenth century onward reached for those colors when they wanted a yellow that would not fade. The beauty was real, and so was the toxic metal inside the tube. Schools and factories later restricted cadmium pigments for health and for the environment. A color that started as an impurity in zinc became a famous paint and then a regulated one; the element keeps returning as yellow, first as a clue and then as a caution.

applications.title: Older batteries
applications.body: Nickel-cadmium rechargeable batteries used cadmium in one electrode. Many countries have restricted them because cadmium is toxic.

applications.title: Coatings, now limited
applications.body: Cadmium was plated onto steel to stop rust, and cadmium sulfide was a bright yellow pigment. Both uses have been cut back.

applications.title: A metal to treat carefully
applications.body: Cadmium accumulates in the body. There is no hobby use that justifies heating or sanding it.

elements.name: Indium

summary.beginner:
Indium is element 49, a very soft metal that is part of the clear coating on many touch screens. It melts at a low temperature.

Its symbol is In. At room temperature indium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 13. In class those are called period 5 and group 13.

You do not see a bar of indium in a phone. You see a whisper-thin layer of indium tin oxide that conducts electricity and still lets light through.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral indium atom has 49 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Indium is a solid post-transition in period 5 and group 13. Indium is a soft, low-melting metal, and indium tin oxide is a transparent conductor.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 3. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The usual oxidation state is +3. The pure metal can be cut with a knife and makes a squeak when bent, a curiosity rather than a use.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Indium (Z = 49) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p1. Transparent conduction in ITO is a compromise: enough free electrons to conduct, and a wide enough gap that visible light passes.

Indium's scarcity is why display makers look for alternatives.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Indium: say the name, write In, find Z=49 on the table, note the family (Post-transition), and connect it to one real use — solders and ITO coatings.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Indium: electron configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p1, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 13. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. low melting; +3.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Indium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; transparent conductors as indium tin oxide If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Detected by an indigo spectral line in zinc ores.

elements.history:
Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymous Theodor Richter examined zinc ores spectroscopically in 1863, looking for thallium. They found instead a brilliant indigo line. Richter isolated the metal, and they named it indium, from indigo.

Indium is soft enough to mark paper and wets glass. Those odd properties made it a seal and a solder. Indium tin oxide became the transparent conductor of screens.
elements.howDiscovered:
Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymus Theodor Richter were looking for thallium in zinc ores from Freiberg. Reich, who was colorblind, asked Richter to watch the spectroscope. In 1863 a bright indigo line appeared that was not thallium’s green and not any mapped line. They concentrated the chloride and reduced the oxide with charcoal.

A small ingot showed the same indigo line in the spark. The discovery is that line, found while hunting a different element, and a reduction that produced a metal whose spark put the line back.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Indium-115 is about 96 percent of natural indium, and it is mainly a rapid-process product. It is also very slightly radioactive, with a half-life so long that the metal can be held and worked. Indium-113, the minor isotope, is fed more by the slow process.

The rapid process is the channel associated with neutron-star mergers and with rare supernovae. The indium in a transparent conductor is, in bulk, that rapid-process isotope.

trivia.title: Indigo Instead of Thallium
trivia.summary: Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymous Theodor Richter searched zinc ores for thallium in 1863 and found a brilliant indigo line instead.
trivia.story: Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymous Theodor Richter examined zinc ores with a spectroscope in 1863, hoping to find thallium. Thallium was new, and it might have been hiding in those same minerals. The line that appeared was a brilliant indigo, an unexpected color rather than the green they had been ready to celebrate. That unexpected color meant a different element, whether the plan had asked for one or not. Richter isolated the soft metal, and the failed thallium hunt became indium’s discovery. Careful looking had caught an element the experiment did not include; spectroscopy rewarded the people who watched the line they were not seeking.

trivia.title: A Color One Man Could See
trivia.summary: The indigo line named the element, and because Reich was color-blind, Richter had to be the eyes that identified the stripe.
trivia.story: Reich and Richter named the metal indium, from indigo, the color of the spectral line that gave the element away. The name points at a real clue, a deep blue stripe in the spectroscope. Reich himself could not judge that color, because he was color-blind. Richter watched the instrument and identified the indigo line while his partner ran the chemistry. The discovery was a partnership between hands and eyes. Indium reached the table through the person who could tell that blue from the green they had expected of thallium; a name taken from a dye is, in this case, a name taken from a disability and a friendship as well.

trivia.title: Soft Enough to Mark Paper
trivia.summary: Indium bends under a fingernail and leaves a streak on paper, odd habits that later made it a seal and a solder.
trivia.story: Indium is absurdly soft for a metal that industry bothers to refine. A fingernail can dent it, and a bar of it can leave a mark on paper the way a pencil does. It also wets glass, spreading across a surface instead of beading up and rolling away. Those odd habits made it a seal and a solder, especially where a joint must fill a gap and stay reliable when the equipment is cold. The metal looks like a toy and behaves like a gasket. What began as a spectral curiosity later went into seals, including equipment where glass and metal both have to be trusted; softness, for once, was the useful property.

trivia.title: Invisible Wires on Glass
trivia.summary: Indium tin oxide is clear and still conducts electricity, which let it become the unseen conductive coat on modern screens.
trivia.story: Indium oxide mixed with a little tin oxide makes a strange conductor. The coating is almost clear, so light passes through, and it still carries electricity. Touchscreens, flat displays, and some solar cells use that combination, called indium tin oxide, as a transparent electrode. A finger’s touch and a pixel’s job can happen on a layer a person barely sees. The metal that marks paper like a pencil now helps draw pictures on glass. Demand for the coating turned indium, once a spectroscopic oddity, into a strategic trace in pockets and on desks; the indigo line of 1863 became the invisible wiring of a screen.

trivia.title: Dust in the Display Factory
trivia.summary: Workers who handled fine indium compounds while making clear conductive coatings developed serious lung disease linked to that dust.
trivia.story: The clear coating on screens created a workplace hazard that nineteenth-century chemists never met. Workers who ground or sprayed fine indium compounds, especially indium tin oxide, breathed a dust their lungs handled badly. Some of them developed a serious lung disease that doctors linked to the metal. Indium had skipped the ancient reputation of arsenic and still found a way to injure people in a modern factory. A soft bar on a laboratory bench is only a curiosity. As a powder in the air, the same element is a health risk that factories have to respect; the screen’s invisible wire had a visible human cost in the rooms where the powder was made.

applications.title: Touch screens
applications.body: The clear layer that conducts electricity on many screens is indium tin oxide. It lets light through and still carries a current.

applications.title: Solder
applications.body: Indium alloys melt at low temperatures, so they can solder parts that must not get hot.

applications.title: A soft metal
applications.body: Pure indium is soft enough to cut with a knife and squeaks when it is bent. Those are curiosities. The industrial use is the thin oxide film.

elements.name: Tin

summary.beginner:
Tin is element 50, a familiar metal in solder and in the coating on a tin can. People have mixed it with copper to make bronze for thousands of years.

Its symbol is Sn. At room temperature tin is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 14. In class those are called period 5 and group 14.

A tin can is steel with a thin coat of tin so the food does not taste of iron. Solder melts easily and joins wires and pipes.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral tin atom has 50 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Tin is a solid post-transition in period 5 and group 14. Tin has two common oxidation states, +2 and +4, and the metal has a gray and a white allotrope.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 4. Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +2. The one courses meet most often is +4.

White tin is the familiar metal. Gray tin is a crumbly form that can appear in long, severe cold. Bronze is copper plus tin.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Tin (Z = 50) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p2. The gray allotrope is the diamond structure, a semiconductor, and the white form is metallic.

That allotropic shift is the 'tin pest' story. Organotin compounds are a large, and often toxic, chapter of their own.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +2. The one courses meet most often is +4. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Tin: say the name, write Sn, find Z=50 on the table, note the family (Post-transition), and connect it to one real use — solder, tin plate, pewter.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Tin: electron configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p2, Typical oxidation states: +4, +2. It sits in group 14. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. allotropes gray/white tin.
