discovery.text: Worked as bronze and pewter for thousands of years.

elements.history:
Tin is ancient. Bronze is its alloy with copper, and pewter and solder followed. The symbol Sn is from the Latin stannum. The English word tin is Germanic. There is no modern discoverer.

The metal has a famous allotrope problem: below about 13 °C, white tin can crumble into gray tin, the so-called tin pest. Organotin chemistry and tin plate on steel are the later industrial chapters.
elements.howDiscovered:
Tin was smelted from cassiterite in antiquity. The oxide is reduced by charcoal at a temperature a simple furnace reaches, and the metal runs and can be cast. Alloyed with copper it makes bronze, and that use is older than any written chemistry.

No discoverer is assigned. The element was recognized as distinct from lead and silver because the metal was softer than copper, harder than lead, and gave its own oxide. The original discovery is a reduction of a heavy sand, done wherever the sand and the fuel occurred together.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Tin has ten stable isotopes, more than any other element, because it sits on a closed proton shell. The slow process in giant stars flows through several of them and piles material up. The rapid process feeds the neutron-richer isotopes, tin-122 and tin-124 especially. Tin-112 and tin-114 are proton-rich and minor.

A bar of tin is a stack of different events: giants, rapid blasts, and a trace of the gamma process. The slow process is the largest contributor to the common middle isotopes. Bronze Age tin and modern solder are the same stellar blend.

trivia.title: The Partner in Bronze
trivia.summary: Tin is ancient, with no modern discoverer, and its early fame was joining copper to make bronze, the alloy that named an age.
trivia.story: Tin has been known since antiquity, and no modern chemist gets to claim the discovery. Its symbol, Sn, comes from the Latin stannum, while the English word tin is Germanic, two names for a metal that moved with trade. Bronze, the alloy of copper and tin, was hard enough and castable enough to remake tools and weapons. That partnership is why a whole age carries tin’s influence even when people only say the word bronze. Pewter and solder came later, with more tin in the mix and quieter domestic jobs. The element’s origin story is a workshop rather than a paper in a journal; someone smelted it long before anyone defined an element.

trivia.title: The Cry of a Bent Bar
trivia.summary: Bend a bar of ordinary white tin and it crackles, a sound called the tin cry that comes from crystals shifting inside the metal.
trivia.story: Bend a bar of ordinary white tin and it crackles, a sound chemists call the tin cry. The noise is the metal’s crystals rubbing and shifting as the bar changes shape. It is a real property of the solid, not a defect in a bad sample and not a trick hidden in the bar. Students remember the sound longer than they remember many quieter facts about the element. The cry belongs with classroom demonstrations, something a person can hear without a spectrometer or a flame. An ancient alloying metal still knows how to startle a modern room; the voice of tin is structure, made audible for a moment when the bar is persuaded to bend.

trivia.title: Gray Crumbs in the Cold
trivia.summary: Below about 13 °C, white tin can slowly turn into brittle gray tin, a real change known as tin pest that ruins objects left in the cold.
trivia.story: White tin is the familiar metal of coatings and solder, and it has another crystal form waiting in the cold. Below about 13 °C, white tin can slowly convert into gray tin, a brittle material that crumbles. The change is called tin pest. Once it starts, the gray form can spread through an object, which is why the name sounds like a disease even though no germ is involved. Objects left in a long, hard cold have been found weakening and crumbling at the surface. The pest is real chemistry, slow and tied to temperature; it is an element rearranging its crystals when winter lasts, and the damage can be permanent for the object even though the atoms are the same.

trivia.title: Buttons of a Winter Legend
trivia.summary: A popular tale says tin pest destroyed the buttons of Napoleon’s army in 1812, and historians treat that tale as a legend.
trivia.story: Tin pest is real enough to invite legends, and one legend went too far. People say Napoleon’s soldiers lost their buttons to crumbling tin in the Russian winter of 1812, and that the failure helped doom the army. The picture is vivid, and it is useful mainly as a warning about bad history. The buttons of that campaign have not been shown to be pure tin waiting to disintegrate, and the retreat had much larger causes than clothing. What remains true is the chemistry: white tin can fail in a lasting cold. The army story is a legend attached to that fact; classrooms can keep the pest and still refuse the buttons.

trivia.title: A Coat on the Steel Can
trivia.summary: A thin layer of tin let steel hold food without rusting, while other tin compounds used on ship hulls harmed life in the water.
trivia.story: Tin’s later industrial chapter is often a coating rather than a solid bar. Steel rusts, and food should not sit against rust, so makers learned to cover steel sheet with a thin layer of tin. The familiar tin can is a steel can wearing a tin coat, cheap strength plus a surface that tolerates the meal. A different branch of tin chemistry, the organotin compounds, later spread into plastics and into antifouling paints on ships, then met bans after those paints harmed living things in the water. The plain metal on a can and the harmful compounds once painted on hulls are both tin, and they earned separate reputations. One protects food; the other had to be limited.

applications.title: Solder and cans
applications.body: Solder is often a tin alloy that melts easily and joins wires. A tin can is steel with a thin coat of tin so the food does not taste of iron.

applications.title: Bronze
applications.body: Bronze is copper with tin, hard enough for bells, bearings, and historical tools.

applications.title: A coat, not the can
applications.body: The metal you think of as tin is usually a coating or an alloy. The pure element has a gray form that can crumble in severe, prolonged cold.

elements.name: Antimony

summary.beginner:
Antimony is element 51, a brittle silvery element used in some alloys and in flame retardants. It is not a metal you would bend into a wire.

Its symbol is Sb. At room temperature antimony is a solid. It is a metalloid, between the metals and the nonmetals in the way it behaves. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 15. In class those are called period 5 and group 15.

Antimony makes lead harder in some older alloys, and its compounds help some plastics resist fire. The pure element shatters rather than bends.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral antimony atom has 51 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Antimony is a solid metalloid in period 5 and group 15. Antimony is a metalloid with oxidation states +3 and +5, and it is used to harden alloys.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p3. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 5. Oxidation states in this dossier are --3, +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is --3.

Stibnite, an antimony sulfide, was an ancient cosmetic pigment. Modern uses are industrial, and several compounds are toxic.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Antimony (Z = 51) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p3. The layered structure and the +3/+5 pair resemble arsenic more than a typical metal.

Flame-retardant oxides act in the solid as the plastic heats, which is a materials use, not a household chemical.

Oxidation states in this dossier are --3, +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is --3. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Antimony: say the name, write Sb, find Z=51 on the table, note the family (Metalloid), and connect it to one real use — alloys and flame retardants.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Antimony: electron configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p3, Typical oxidation states: -3, +3, +5. It sits in group 15. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. metalloid; +3/+5.

discovery.text: Known in stibnite cosmetics and alloys.

elements.history:
Stibnite, antimony sulfide, was a cosmetic and a medicine in the ancient Mediterranean, called stibium. The free metal was known in the medieval period. The symbol Sb keeps the Latin name. The English name antimony is from the medieval Latin antimonium, of disputed origin.

Antimony hardens lead in type metal and in battery grids. It is a metalloid, and its +3 and +5 chemistry is the heavier echo of phosphorus and arsenic.
elements.howDiscovered:
Stibnite, the black sulfide, was ground as a cosmetic and was reduced to metal early. Heat the sulfide, or roast it and reduce the oxide with charcoal, and a brittle silvery metal runs out. That metal was known to medieval metallurgists and was often confused with lead and with bismuth.

The distinction was practical. Antimony is brittle, forms a characteristic sulfide, and alloys with lead in a way lead does not mimic. By the time elements were listed, antimony was already a metal on the shelf. The discovery was a reduction of a cosmetic ore.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Antimony-121 and antimony-123 are each a mixture of the slow process and the rapid process. The heavier isotope takes the larger rapid-process share. Antimony is odd-numbered, scarcer than tin or tellurium.

The antimony of stibnite is that mixture. Geology concentrated it into the sulfide. The nuclei were made in giant stars and in neutron-rich blasts before the Earth existed.

trivia.title: Kohl from a Black Sulfide
trivia.summary: Long before modern chemistry, people ground the mineral stibnite into dark cosmetic lines and also treated preparations of it as medicine.
trivia.story: Stibnite, antimony sulfide, was ground into kohl, the dark cosmetic used around the eyes in the ancient Mediterranean and beyond. Physicians and healers also put preparations of the same mineral into their medicines. People knew the substance as stibium long before they argued about chemical elements. The symbol Sb still keeps that Latin name, even though the English name of the element is antimony. A line of ancient makeup and a square on the periodic table are linked by a black sulfide. Familiarity began with the compound, and the idea of the element came later; the cosmetic is the oldest chapter, and it is still the easiest one to picture.

trivia.title: A Name with No Clear Root
trivia.summary: Antimony comes from medieval Latin antimonium, and the catchy tale that the word means anti-monk is folk etymology, not a settled origin.
trivia.story: The English name antimony comes from the medieval Latin antimonium, and the origin of that word is disputed. A folk etymology says it means anti-monk, from a tale in which monks were poisoned by an antimony medicine. The tale is memorable, and scholars reject it as folk etymology even though casual books keep repeating it. The careful statement is that the origin is uncertain. The symbol Sb, from stibium, is the clearer trail, leading back to the ancient sulfide and the cosmetic. The grim joke about monks should be labeled as a joke; uncertainty is the honest answer, and it is more interesting than a false translation.

trivia.title: The Monk Who Was Legend
trivia.summary: Old books credit a monk called Basil Valentine with deep writings on antimony, but historians treat that author as a legendary figure.
trivia.story: Early modern books on antimony often cite Basil Valentine, supposedly a monk with a famous treatise on the metal and its medicines. Historians treat that author as a legend, not as a documented discoverer with a laboratory anyone could visit. The free metal was already known in the medieval period and had passed through many hands. Later chemists, including Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin, studied antimony with the sharper methods of a newer age. No single modern person gets to discover antimony the way a nineteenth-century chemist discovers a gas. The legend grew in the space a clean discovery paper would have filled; a good story moved in where the archive was thin.

trivia.title: Type Metal and Battery Grids
trivia.summary: Antimony mixed into lead made printing type hold a sharp face, and a related alloy later stiffened the lead grids inside batteries.
trivia.story: Antimony’s classic job is to harden lead. Printing type needed a metal that would cast a sharp letter and resist crushing, and type metal was a lead alloy containing antimony and often tin. That extra metal is why a letter could be printed thousands of times and still look like itself. Battery grids later used a related idea, with antimony stiffening the lead so the plates survive charging and use. A cosmetic sulfide had become an additive in technology. The element is a metalloid, with a chemistry that echoes both metals and nonmetals, which suits a substance living this double life; it strengthens other metals while keeping a character of its own.

trivia.title: Cups That Sickened the Sick
trivia.summary: Early physicians used antimony so harshly that special cups and strong medicines became part of the element’s dangerous medical reputation.
trivia.story: Antimony’s medical history is a warning more than a model for anyone to follow. Physicians once prescribed harsh antimony compounds as purges, and some of those treatments harmed the patients they were meant to help. Antimony cups were sold on the idea that a drink kept in them would sicken the body and thereby cure it. People were hurt by medicines that were really a form of poisoning. Modern practice abandoned those cups and those casual uses. Type metal is a controlled use of the element, while the old cup was a reckless one; the metalloid that sharpens a printed letter was, in the wrong compound, a way to make a sick person sicker.

applications.title: Flame retardants
applications.body: Antimony oxide is combined with some halogenated plastics so the plastic resists catching fire. The use is in the factory formulation.

applications.title: Alloys
applications.body: Antimony hardens lead in some older batteries and type metal. The element itself is brittle.

applications.title: An old pigment
applications.body: Stibnite, an antimony sulfide, was ground as a black cosmetic in the ancient world. Modern compounds are handled as industrial chemicals, several of them toxic.

elements.name: Tellurium

summary.beginner:
Tellurium is element 52, a rare silvery element added to some steels and to some solar-cell materials. You are unlikely to meet a piece of it outside a lab or a factory.

Its symbol is Te. At room temperature tellurium is a solid. It is a metalloid, between the metals and the nonmetals in the way it behaves. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 16. In class those are called period 5 and group 16.

Tellurium sits under selenium and sulfur. A little of it changes how steel machines. Some solar panels use a compound of cadmium and tellurium.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral tellurium atom has 52 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Tellurium is a solid metalloid in period 5 and group 16. Tellurium is a metalloid analog of selenium, used in alloys and in cadmium telluride solar cells.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p4. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 6. Oxidation states in this dossier are --2, +4, +6. The one courses meet most often is --2.

The element itself is uncommon in the crust. Compounds can be toxic and some smell very unpleasant, which is another reason it stays in industry.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Tellurium (Z = 52) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p4. CdTe is a II-VI semiconductor with a band gap suited to sunlight.

Tellurium's chemistry parallels selenium, including a -2 state in tellurides and positive states in oxides.

Oxidation states in this dossier are --2, +4, +6. The one courses meet most often is --2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Tellurium: say the name, write Te, find Z=52 on the table, note the family (Metalloid), and connect it to one real use — steel alloys and solar.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Tellurium: electron configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p4, Typical oxidation states: -2, +4, +6. It sits in group 16. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. metalloid analog of selenium.

discovery.text: Found in Transylvanian gold ore; Klaproth confirmed it.

elements.history:
Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein suspected a new metal in Transylvanian gold ore in 1782. Martin Heinrich Klaproth confirmed it in 1798 and named it tellurium, from the Latin tellus, Earth. Müller is credited with the discovery.

Tellurium is a metalloid, rare, and chemically the heavy analog of selenium. It alloys with steel and appears in some solar-cell and thermoelectric materials.
elements.howDiscovered:
Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein, working on gold ores from Zlatna in Transylvania, obtained in 1782 a metal he could not identify as antimony, bismuth, or any metal the ore was supposed to contain. He sent material to Torbern Bergman, who died before the question was settled. The substance sat unresolved for years.

Martin Heinrich Klaproth repeated the analysis in 1798, isolated the same metal, and named it. The procedure was a wet analysis of a gold ore: dissolve, precipitate, and compare the product with every metal that might have been expected. The discovery is the product that survived that comparison.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Tellurium is weighted toward the rapid process. Tellurium-128 and tellurium-130 are the two most abundant isotopes, and both are made almost only by rapid neutron capture. The slow process and the gamma process account for the lighter, less abundant isotopes.

Those two heavy isotopes decay by a double-beta path so slow that they behave as stable in any mineral. The tellurium in an alloy is, in the main, rapid-process ash from neutron-rich blasts older than the Sun.

trivia.title: A Puzzle in Gold Ore
trivia.summary: Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein found that Transylvanian gold ores did not behave like antimony, and his sample waited years for a full answer.
trivia.story: Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein was studying gold ores in Transylvania in 1782 when the assays refused to match antimony. He suspected a new metal and kept testing the idea for years. He sent material to Torbern Bergman in Sweden, who was too ill to finish the work and died soon after. The question paused, sitting in a sample nobody else was ready to finish. Müller already had the right suspicion and still lacked the world’s agreement. Tellurium begins as a gold-ore puzzle whose confirmation had to wait; a miner’s odd metal and a chemist’s unfinished letter are the start of the element, not a sudden flash of proof.

trivia.title: Klaproth Names the Earth
trivia.summary: Martin Heinrich Klaproth confirmed the metal in 1798, named it for the Earth, and left the credit for the discovery with Müller.
trivia.story: Martin Heinrich Klaproth took up Müller’s substance and confirmed it as a new element in 1798. He named it tellurium, from the Latin tellus, the Earth. Müller is the one credited with the discovery, and Klaproth is the one who gave the name and the confirmation other chemists trusted. That split is fair and a little untidy, which is common when a find waits sixteen years. Earth was a grand name for a rare metalloid pulled from gold ore. Selenium, found later and at first mistaken for this element, would be named for the Moon in reply; the pair still teaches that order: the planet first, then its companion in the name.

trivia.title: Garlic on the Breath
trivia.summary: Chemists who take in even a little tellurium can develop a garlic odor on the breath that lingers long after they leave the bench.
trivia.story: Tellurium’s most personal hazard is not a flame and not a blast. People who absorb even small amounts of the element, or of some of its compounds, can develop a garlic-like odor on the breath and in the sweat. The smell can linger long after the work is over, and colleagues notice it before any instrument does. Chemists sometimes call the effect tellurium breath, and it made the element unpopular with anyone who had plans after the laboratory. The effect is unpleasant and real, a consequence in the body rather than dirt on a coat. A rare metal is supposed to feel distant; this one can announce itself across a room, which is a strange fame for a metalloid from a gold ore.

trivia.title: A Pinch in Special Steel
trivia.summary: Tellurium is scarce, yet a little of it helps some steels machine cleanly, and it also appears in a few solar and thermoelectric materials.
trivia.story: Tellurium is a metalloid, the heavy chemical cousin of selenium, and it is much rarer in the crust. Even so, a little of it improves some steels, changing how they cut and machine, and it shows up in certain solar-cell and thermoelectric materials. These are specialty uses, not bulk ones. There is never a mountain of tellurium waiting, so engineers spend it carefully. Müller’s impurity in a gold ore became a deliberate additive. The garlic breath is the human cost of handling it, and the alloy is the industrial reason people handle it anyway; scarcity kept the element from ever becoming ordinary; a pinch is the usual dose of its fame.

trivia.title: Two Finders, One Credit
trivia.summary: Paul Kitaibel also met the strange metal in ore, and when Klaproth confirmed it the quiet argument was about who had been first.
trivia.story: Müller was not the only person to stumble on the odd metal in gold-bearing ore. The Hungarian chemist Paul Kitaibel also encountered it and recorded what he saw. When Klaproth confirmed the element, the quiet dispute was about priority rather than about whether the substance was new. The earlier work belonged to Müller, and that is the credit textbooks kept. Kitaibel’s effort shows how an element can be met more than once when letters travel slowly. Tellurium’s early years are a chain of interrupted handoffs; Bergman died before he could finish, Kitaibel overlapped the trail, and Klaproth closed the case in 1798 with a name and a confirmation.

applications.title: Solar cells
applications.body: Some thin-film solar panels use cadmium telluride. Tellurium is the scarce ingredient in that compound.

applications.title: Steel and copper
applications.body: A little tellurium makes some steels and coppers easier to machine. The addition is small and is done at the mill.

applications.title: A rare element
applications.body: Tellurium is uncommon in the crust and is mostly recovered as a byproduct of copper refining. It is not a shop metal.

elements.name: Iodine

summary.beginner:
Iodine is element 53, a dark solid that gives off a violet vapor when it is warmed. Your thyroid needs a little of it, and it has been used as an antiseptic.

Its symbol is I. At room temperature iodine is a solid. It is a halogen, a reactive nonmetal in the column next to the noble gases. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 17. In class those are called period 5 and group 17.

Table salt is sometimes iodized, which means a tiny amount of an iodine compound is added. The pure crystals are not a food. They stain skin and should not be handled as a toy.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral iodine atom has 53 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Iodine is a solid halogen in period 5 and group 17. Iodine is the solid halogen, I2, with a violet vapor, and the body uses iodide to make thyroid hormone.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p5. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 7. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1.

The antiseptic is usually a solution or a complex, not the dry element. Iodide and iodate are the common ions. Starch turns blue-black with iodine, a classic test.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Iodine (Z = 53) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p5. The violet color of the vapor is molecular I2 absorbing visible light.

Thyroid hormones are organoiodine compounds. Radioiodine is a separate, medical use of particular isotopes.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Iodine: say the name, write I, find Z=53 on the table, note the family (Halogen), and connect it to one real use — thyroid hormone and antiseptic.

discovery.text: Released from seaweed ash as a violet vapor.

elements.history:
Bernard Courtois, manufacturing saltpeter from seaweed ash in 1811, added too much sulfuric acid and watched a violet vapor rise. The vapor condensed to dark crystals. Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Humphry Davy studied them, and Gay-Lussac named the element iodine, from the Greek iodes, violet.

Iodine was soon recognized in the thyroid. Tincture of iodine became an antiseptic, and the element is the heaviest halogen that is still available as a bottle on a shelf.
elements.howDiscovered:
Bernard Courtois was extracting sodium carbonate from the ash of seaweed, for saltpeter manufacture. In 1811 he added too much sulfuric acid to the liquor. A violet vapor rose and condensed as dark crystals on the cool parts of the vessel. The crystals sublimed without melting into a liquid first.

He handed the observation to Charles Bernard Desormes and Nicolas Clément. Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Humphry Davy, independently, showed in 1813 that the crystals were an element analogous to chlorine. The discovery itself was an accident of an excess of acid on a kelp liquor, and a vapor with a color nobody had recorded.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Iodine-127 is the only stable isotope, and it is mainly a rapid-process product. The slow process contributes a smaller share. Iodine-129, with a half-life near 16 million years, was also made by the rapid process and was present when the solar system formed. It has since decayed to xenon-129.

The excess of xenon-129 in meteorites is the evidence of that extinct iodine. The iodine in thyroid hormone is the stable isotope, from the same family of neutron-rich events.

trivia.title: Violet Over Seaweed Ash
trivia.summary: Bernard Courtois, making saltpeter from seaweed ash in 1811, used too much sulfuric acid and watched a violet vapor rise and crystallize.
trivia.story: Bernard Courtois was manufacturing saltpeter in 1811, using ash from seaweed as part of the work. He added too much sulfuric acid, and a violet vapor rose out of the mixture. That vapor cooled into dark crystals with a metallic shine. Courtois could tell the substance was unusual, so he passed samples to chemists better placed to study what might be a new element. He had been trying to supply a nitrate works, not to rewrite the table of elements. The violet cloud over a seaweed ash is how iodine actually entered chemistry; a manufacturing slip produced the first sight of it, and the color was impossible to mistake once it filled the air.

trivia.title: Paris and London Race
trivia.summary: Humphry Davy and Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac both rushed to understand the violet crystals, and Gay-Lussac’s name from the Greek for violet stuck.
trivia.story: The crystals from Courtois’s workshop did not sit quietly on a shelf. Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac in Paris and Humphry Davy in Britain both took up the substance and argued, in a polite and hurried way, about what it was. Davy pressed the case that it was a new element, in the same family as chlorine. Gay-Lussac gave it the name that won, iodine, from the Greek iodes, meaning violet. Naming rights and scientific credit were tangled, as they often were when Paris and London studied the same surprising sample. Both men helped show that the vapor was an element; Courtois remained the manufacturer who first watched it rise, which is the start the name does not erase.

trivia.title: Needed by the Thyroid
trivia.summary: Doctors tied iodine to the thyroid, and a shortage in the diet was linked to goiter, which many countries later tried to prevent with salt.
trivia.story: Iodine’s place in the body became clear when doctors connected the element with the thyroid, the gland in the neck that needs it. Where diets lacked iodine, goiter, a swelling of that gland, was common. The link turned a seaweed vapor into a question of public health. In the twentieth century many countries began adding a little iodine to table salt so that everyday food would supply what some soils do not. The policy was about preventing a deficiency, not about inviting kitchens to experiment. The crystals had become a nutrient, and because too much iodine causes harm of its own, the public story is about balance; enough is the goal, and more is not automatically better.

trivia.title: The Brown Antiseptic Bottle
trivia.summary: Tincture of iodine became a household antiseptic, a stinging brown liquid whose stain and vapor reminded families that the element is active.
trivia.story: Tincture of iodine, the familiar solution in alcohol, sat in medicine cabinets for generations. It stings on a cut, it stains skin brown, and it kills many microbes on a surface. That made it a famous antiseptic long before most households had heard about iodine in the thyroid. The bottle is also a hazard if it is misused, because the element is not harmless merely because a family owns a small amount. Vapor from the solid crystals irritates eyes and lungs. The same violet substance that surprised Courtois became both a nutrient and a disinfectant; ordinary shelves made it familiar; they did not make it gentle, which is why the brown stain still teaches respect.

trivia.title: A Radioactive Form in Fallout
trivia.summary: After serious nuclear accidents, radioactive iodine can collect in the thyroid, which is why that gland became part of the public warning.
trivia.story: The iodine in salt is a stable nutrient the thyroid is built to collect. Iodine-131, produced in reactors and released in serious accidents, is a different matter. The gland pulls iodine in, usefully in ordinary life and dangerously when the iodine is radioactive. After events such as the Chernobyl disaster, worry about thyroid exposure became a public part of the news. Health authorities focused on keeping that radioisotope away from the glands of children especially. Families learned the danger from the aftermath; the element that rose as a violet vapor over seaweed ash also has a radioactive form the body can mistake for the nutrient it wants.

applications.title: The thyroid
applications.body: Thyroid hormone contains iodine, and iodized salt is how many people get enough. The amount in the salt is a compound, measured in micrograms.

applications.title: Antiseptic
applications.body: Iodine solutions and iodine complexes have been painted on skin as antiseptics. The dark crystals themselves stain and are not a first-aid toy.

applications.title: A violet vapor
applications.body: Warm iodine crystals give off a violet gas. That vapor, and the blue-black color iodine makes with starch, are the classroom observations.

elements.name: Xenon

summary.beginner:
Xenon is element 54, a heavy noble gas used in very bright lamps and in some spacecraft thrusters. Unlike helium, it can be pushed into forming a few compounds.

Its symbol is Xe. At room temperature xenon is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a noble gas. Left alone, it almost never joins other elements to make compounds. On the periodic table it is in row 5, column 18. In class those are called period 5 and group 18.

Xenon is rare in air. In a lamp it produces an intense white flash. The compounds are a laboratory subject, not something a lamp needs.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral xenon atom has 54 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Xenon is a noble gas in period 5 and group 18. Xenon is a noble gas that does form fluorides and oxides, and it is used in high-intensity lamps and ion thrusters.

The electron configuration is [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p6. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 8. Oxidation states are not listed for this entry.

XeF2 is a real, reactive solid taught as proof that noble gases are not absolutely inert. Most of the element in service is still the uncombined gas.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Xenon (Z = 54) has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p6. XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, and XeO4 show xenon in positive oxidation states with fluorine or oxygen.

The lamp and the thruster use the gas and its ions, not those compounds.

Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Xenon: say the name, write Xe, find Z=54 on the table, note the family (Noble gas), and connect it to one real use — bright lamps and ion propulsion.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Xenon: electron configuration [Kr] 4d10 5s2 5p6, Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. It sits in group 18. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. noble gas that forms fluorides and oxides.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Xenon: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; XeF₂, XeO₄; high-intensity lamps If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from liquefied air; named for the strange new gas.

elements.history:
Ramsay and Travers isolated xenon in 1898 from the least volatile fraction of liquid air. They named it from the Greek xenos, stranger. For sixty years it was the noble gas that proved the group really was inert.

In 1962 Neil Bartlett prepared a xenon compound, and the fluorides and oxides followed within a year. Xenon is also the filling of high-intensity lamps and of ion thrusters.
elements.howDiscovered:
Ramsay and Travers distilled the krypton fraction of liquid air still further. In July 1898 a heavier residue, sparked under low pressure, gave a blue glow and a spectrum of lines that belonged neither to krypton nor to argon. The density was higher than krypton’s.

The amount was minute. The method was the same fractional distillation, pushed to the last drops. Xenon was discovered because the residue of a residue still had a spectrum of its own.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Xenon’s isotopes split cleanly enough to be useful. Some are slow-process, some are rapid-process, and xenon-124 and xenon-126 are proton-rich. Xenon-129 is partly the decay product of iodine-129, so meteorites preserve a record that the rapid process ran shortly before the solar system formed.

The xenon in a lamp is the trapped planetary share of that mix. Like the other noble gases, it was inherited as a gas. The Earth did not manufacture it.

trivia.title: The Stranger in Liquid Air
trivia.summary: William Ramsay and Morris Travers isolated a last scarce gas from the heaviest fraction of liquid air and named it with the Greek for stranger.
trivia.story: William Ramsay and Morris Travers isolated xenon in 1898 from the least volatile fraction of liquid air, the portion that refused to boil away with the lighter gases. Krypton had already come from that same kind of patient work. Xenon was scarcer still, a small yield from a large amount of air. They named it from the Greek xenos, stranger. The name suited a gas that barely seemed to belong to ordinary chemistry at all. It had been present in the atmosphere the whole time, in traces, waiting for anyone patient enough to distill the sky; stranger was a welcome of sorts; it described how foreign the gas felt, and how hidden it had stayed.

trivia.title: The Gas That Proved Inert
trivia.summary: For about sixty years xenon was the noble gas that seemed to prove the whole family would never form a genuine chemical compound.
trivia.story: After 1898, xenon became evidence in a larger claim about the noble gases. They looked chemically aloof, and xenon, heavy and available in small cylinders, still refused to react in ordinary experiments. Textbooks hardened the observation into a rule that these gases do not form compounds. For about sixty years that rule held in the classroom and in the laboratory. Xenon was the stranger used to prove that the family was truly inert, or so it seemed. Ramsay’s generation found the gases, and a later generation had to break the rule xenon had helped to teach; the proof was sincere, and it was also temporary.

trivia.title: Bartlett Makes a Compound
trivia.summary: Neil Bartlett reasoned that xenon might bond as oxygen had, and in 1962 he obtained xenon hexafluoroplatinate, the first noble-gas compound.
trivia.story: Neil Bartlett noticed that xenon gives up an electron about as easily as oxygen does, and he had already combined oxygen with a fierce platinum fluoride. In 1962 he brought xenon into that chemistry, and a solid compound formed. It was xenon hexafluoroplatinate, the first real compound of a noble gas. Fluorides and oxides of xenon followed within a year. Classrooms had to drop the absolute claim that noble gases never bond. The stranger named in 1898 had finally joined a molecule; Bartlett did not merely add a curiosity to a list; he removed a ban that had organized the teaching of a whole group of elements for sixty years.

trivia.title: Flashes and Ion Thrusters
trivia.summary: A discharge through xenon makes intense white light for lamps, and the same heavy gas is the propellant in some spacecraft ion thrusters.
trivia.story: Xenon is scarce in air, and a little of it still does loud work. A discharge through the gas makes the white flash of studio lamps and the bright arc of some headlights and projectors. The same heavy gas flies on spacecraft. Ion thrusters push by accelerating xenon ions, a gentle thrust that can last a long time on a mission. The element is not burned the way a rocket fuel is burned. It is a noble gas that can shine in a lamp or leave a nozzle as a beam of charged atoms; scarcity sets the price of both jobs; the stranger became useful without ceasing to be rare.

trivia.title: Too Thin to Catch in a Jar
trivia.summary: Every breath contains a trace of xenon, yet the amount is so small that only distillation of huge volumes of air can collect a sample.
trivia.story: A breath of air contains xenon, but so little that no nose and no simple jar could ever find it. Ramsay and Travers reached it by liquefying air and saving the heaviest fraction that remained when the rest had boiled. Its spectrum showed a new element, distinct from krypton, which is why the stranger received a separate name. That scarcity still sets the price of flash lamps and of ion thrusters. The gas is free in the atmosphere and expensive in a cylinder because freeing it takes an enormous plant. Dilute is not the same thing as absent, which is the lesson of 1898; the sky was full of a gas nobody could see until the air was taken apart.

applications.title: Bright lamps
applications.body: Xenon arc lamps are the intense white source in some cinema projectors, car headlights, and scientific instruments.

applications.title: Ion thrusters
applications.body: Some spacecraft push themselves by accelerating xenon ions. The gas is heavy and unreactive, which suits an engine that runs for months.

applications.title: A few real compounds
applications.body: Xenon fluorides are genuine compounds of a noble gas. They are reactive laboratory chemicals, not the filling of the lamp.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.title: The pure element
sample.body: Pure xenon, sealed in glass. The gas has no color of its own, so the sample looks like a clear tube. This is the element by itself, not a compound.
sample.credit: RTC, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

elements.name: Caesium

summary.beginner:
Cesium is element 55, a gold-tinged metal that melts on a warm day. It is extremely reactive, so you meet it in atomic clocks and in special instruments, not in a drawer at home.

Its symbol is Cs. At room temperature caesium is a solid. It is an alkali metal: soft, and quick to react with water. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 1. In class those are called period 6 and group 1.

Cesium reacts violently with water. The famous clocks use the light from cesium atoms to keep time, not a lump of the metal sitting on a shelf.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral caesium atom has 55 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Caesium is a solid alkali metal in period 6 and group 1. Cesium has the lowest ionization energy of the stable elements, and the metal is liquid on a warm day.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 6s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 8, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

The single 6s electron is easily removed, which is why Cs+ salts exist and the metal must be sealed from air. Cesium atomic clocks define the second.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Caesium (Z = 55) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 6s1. The second is defined from a hyperfine transition of cesium-133, a property of the nucleus and the electron together.

Chemically, cesium is the softest, most electropositive stable alkali metal.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Caesium: say the name, write Cs, find Z=55 on the table, note the family (Alkali metal), and connect it to one real use — photocells; most electropositive stable metal.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Caesium: electron configuration [Xe] 6s1, Typical oxidation states: +1. It sits in group 1. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. lowest ionization energy of stable elements.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Caesium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; liquid near room temperature If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Detected by sky-blue spectral lines in mineral water.

elements.history:
Bunsen and Kirchhoff found sky-blue spectral lines in mineral water from Dürkheim in 1860 and named the element caesium, from the Latin caesius, sky blue. Carl Setterberg isolated the metal by electrolysis in 1882. It is the most electropositive of the stable elements.

Caesium melts just above room temperature. The second is defined by a hyperfine transition of caesium-133, which made this reactive metal the time standard of the world.
elements.howDiscovered:
Bunsen and Kirchhoff evaporated tens of tonnes of mineral water from Dürkheim and examined the residue in the spectroscope. In 1860 two blue lines appeared, close together, that no known alkali produced. They concentrated the new alkali by fractional crystallization of the chloroplatinate, the same tedious separation later used for rubidium.

The metal was not isolated until 1882, when Carl Setterberg electrolyzed the molten cyanide. The discovery in 1860 was the pair of blue lines and a salt that put those lines back into the flame. The water had held a trace. The prism found it.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Cesium-133 is the only stable isotope, and it is mainly a product of the slow process in giant stars, near the climb toward the barium peak. A rapid-process contribution is allowed and is not the bulk.

Cesium-135 and cesium-137 are radioactive fission products of reactors. They are not the cesium of minerals. The cesium in an atomic clock is the giant-star isotope, odd-numbered and scarce.

trivia.title: Sky Blue in Spa Water
trivia.summary: Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff saw sky-blue spectral lines in mineral water from Dürkheim and named the hidden element for that color.
trivia.story: Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff turned their spectroscope on mineral water from Dürkheim in 1860 and saw sky-blue lines that belonged to no known element. They named it caesium, from the Latin caesius, sky blue. As with rubidium, the name remembers the light rather than the color of the metal in a bottle. The metal itself, isolated later, is pale and extremely reactive. A spa water had been hiding an element, and the blue lines were the only practical way to see it. Caesium entered chemistry as that blue announcement, years before anyone could safely pass the metal around a room; the water tasted like a resort, and the spectrum said it was also a mine.

trivia.title: Setterberg Isolates the Metal
trivia.summary: The blue lines were known for years before Carl Setterberg, using electrolysis, isolated caesium metal and showed how eager it is to react.
trivia.story: Seeing caesium in a spectrum was the victory of 1860. Holding the metal was harder, because it is the most electropositive of the stable elements and pulls itself back into compounds at the first chance. Carl Setterberg isolated caesium in 1882 by electrolysis of a molten salt. The sample proved that the blue lines had a real metal behind them, soft, pale, and eager. It melts just above room temperature, low enough to surprise anyone who thinks only gallium does that, and far more violent in every other way. Bunsen and Kirchhoff had found the signal, and Setterberg, twenty-two years later, produced the metal itself; two kinds of discovery share the credit.

trivia.title: The Second in the Atom
trivia.summary: The world’s second is defined by a hyperfine transition of caesium-133, so a fiercely reactive metal became the international standard of time.
trivia.story: Caesium melts almost as soon as a warm room reaches it, and it reacts fiercely with water, which makes it a strange candidate for the world’s clock. Even so, a hyperfine transition in atoms of caesium-133 defines the second. Atomic clocks count 9,192,631,770 of those microwave ticks as one second, and navigation systems inherit the count. The metal in the clock is not a lump sitting in a dish. It is a carefully controlled vapor of atoms. The reactive element and the time standard are the same substance under very different discipline; the blue lines that named it were gentle; the timekeeping is strict, and the laboratory that runs the clock refuses to treat the element casually.

trivia.title: A Glow in Goiânia
trivia.summary: A medical source of caesium-137 left behind in Goiânia became a radiological accident after scavengers found it and the material spread.
trivia.story: In 1987, in the Brazilian city of Goiânia, a scavenged medical source of caesium-137 was broken open. The material inside glowed blue, and that strange beauty drew people to handle it, carry it home, and share it. Contamination spread through a neighborhood. People died, and many more were harmed or had to be watched, while buildings and soil were removed for disposal. The caesium in an atomic clock is caesium-133, a stable atom used as a timekeeper. The isotope in Goiânia was a hospital source, abandoned and then dispersed; the accident showed what an abandoned hospital source can do once it leaves the building.

trivia.title: Stored Away from Water
trivia.summary: Caesium is the most electropositive stable element, and chemists keep the pure metal away from air and water because the reaction is violent.
trivia.story: Caesium is the most electropositive of the stable elements, which means it gives away its outer electron with extreme ease. Air attacks the metal, and water reacts with it so violently that the hydrogen can ignite. Chemists store it away from both, often sealed or kept under a dry protective liquid. That care is the hazard story for the pure metal, separate from the radiological disaster of the abandoned medical source. The blue lines that gave caesium its name were a gentle discovery. The metal itself is not gentle; a clock can use caesium atoms only because a laboratory refuses to let the element meet the room; beauty in the spectrum and violence in the flask are both true.

applications.title: Atomic clocks
applications.body: The second is defined by a property of cesium atoms. Cesium clocks are the reference other clocks are checked against.

applications.title: A metal that melts easily
applications.body: Cesium melts on a warm day and reacts violently with water. It is sealed in the devices that use it.

applications.title: Drilling fluids
applications.body: A cesium salt solution is dense enough to be used as a specialty drilling fluid in some oil wells. The salt is not the free metal.

elements.name: Barium

summary.beginner:
Barium is element 56, a metal whose compounds can make fireworks green. A special barium drink was used so X-rays could outline the stomach, and that compound had to be the kind that does not dissolve.

Its symbol is Ba. At room temperature barium is a solid. It is an alkaline-earth metal. These metals react, but less wildly than the alkali metals beside them. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 2. In class those are called period 6 and group 2.

Soluble barium compounds are poisonous. The white sulfate used in medical images does not dissolve, which is why it can be swallowed under medical supervision. Fireworks use the color, not the pure metal.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral barium atom has 56 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Barium is a solid alkaline-earth metal in period 6 and group 2. Barium is a heavy alkaline-earth metal, always Ba2+ in compounds, and soluble barium salts are toxic.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

BaSO4 is extremely insoluble, which is why a suspension of it can be used as an X-ray contrast. The green firework color is a flame emission, a different use entirely.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Barium (Z = 56) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 6s2. The medical contrast works only because the solubility product of BaSO4 keeps free Ba2+ negligible.

Chloride and nitrate salts do the opposite and are poisons. The flame test is atomic emission of barium.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Neighbors differ because each added proton changes how tightly the electrons are held as the shells fill.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Barium: say the name, write Ba, find Z=56 on the table, note the family (Alk. earth), and connect it to one real use — X-ray contrast historically; green fireworks.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Barium: electron configuration [Xe] 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It sits in group 2. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. heavy alkaline earth; +2.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Barium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; soluble toxic salts; sulfate is insoluble If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from baryta by electrolysis.

elements.history:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele distinguished a heavy earth, baryta, from lime in the 1770s. Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808 and named it barium, from the Greek barys, heavy. The mineral barite was already known as a dense stone.

Barium sulfate is insoluble enough to be the contrast agent of X-ray images of the gut. Soluble barium salts are toxic. The green flame of barium is a firework color.
elements.howDiscovered:
A dense mineral, Bologna stone, was already famous for glowing after it had been heated with charcoal. Carl Wilhelm Scheele showed in the 1770s that the earth in it was not lime. The sulfate was insoluble, the earth was heavy, and the salts burned green.

Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808 by electrolyzing the moistened earth with a mercury cathode and distilling off the mercury. The metal regenerated the earth when it burned. Baryta was discovered by distinguishing a heavy earth from lime. The metal was discovered by the current.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Barium sits on the second peak of the slow process, where a closed shell of 82 neutrons stalls further capture. Giant stars make most of the barium, especially barium-138, the common isotope. Barium lines are strong enough that a whole class of giant stars is named for them.

The rapid process adds a minority share, notably to barium-135 and barium-137. Astronomers use barium against europium to separate the two channels in a star. The barium in a glass or a drilling mud is mostly the giant-star peak.

trivia.title: Heavier Than Ordinary Lime
trivia.summary: Carl Wilhelm Scheele separated a dense earth, baryta, from lime in the 1770s, matching the heft people already felt in the mineral barite.
trivia.story: Carl Wilhelm Scheele, in the 1770s, distinguished a heavy earth he called baryta from ordinary lime. The minerals had been confusing chemists because both earths can look pale and both sit in rocks that seem ordinary until you lift them. Barite was already known as a dense stone, heavy in the hand out of proportion to its size. Scheele’s work said the heaviness belonged to a distinct earth, not to a dirty form of lime. Barium’s story starts as a weighing puzzle. The metal itself was still locked inside compounds, but the earth had been given its own identity; a stone that felt wrong in the hand was the beginning of an element.

trivia.title: Davy Names the Heavy Metal
trivia.summary: Humphry Davy isolated barium in 1808 and named it from the Greek for heavy, so the mineral’s most obvious trait stayed in the element.
trivia.story: Humphry Davy isolated barium metal in 1808, during the same electrical campaign that produced several other reactive metals. He named it barium, from the Greek barys, heavy. The name agreed with barite and with Scheele’s baryta, so the element carried its most obvious property in a single word. The pure metal is soft and reactive, which surprises anyone who knows only the dense, quiet mineral. Heaviness belonged to the compounds people had been picking up for years. The pure metal is the restless form of that same element, and Davy was the chemist who forced it into view; heavy described the stone; reactive describes what he finally isolated.

trivia.title: The Chalky Picture Drink
trivia.summary: Doctors use insoluble barium sulfate to outline the gut on X-rays, while soluble barium salts are toxic and must never be confused with it.
trivia.story: Barium sulfate is the contrast agent in a barium meal, the chalky drink used before some X-ray images of the gut. It works because the salt is extremely insoluble. It passes through the body as a suspension and blocks X-rays, so the outline of the digestive tract shows on the picture. Soluble barium salts are toxic, and they are not the salt in that cup. The whole medical use depends on the difference between a compound that barely dissolves and compounds that do. Confusing the insoluble sulfate with a soluble barium salt would turn a diagnostic drink into a poisoning; the insolubility is the safety, and that contrast is what doctors rely on.

trivia.title: Green in the Firework
trivia.summary: Barium salts burn with a green flame, so firework makers use them for that color, far from the warning attached to the soluble salts.
trivia.story: Barium’s flame test is green, and firework makers use its salts when they want that color in a burst. The display is the friendly public face of an element whose soluble compounds are poisonous. People watching the show are not swallowing the salt, and the chemistry in the sky is a hot glow rather than a dose. The green is as traditional on the firework chart as strontium’s crimson red. Scheele’s heavy earth became both a color and a medical contrast agent. Both of those uses depend on compounds, not on handing around the pure reactive metal Davy isolated; the element can entertain, can outline a stomach on film, and, in the wrong salt, can harm.

trivia.title: Heavy Spar in the Mud
trivia.summary: Ground barite thickens drilling muds and fills paints because it is dense and insoluble, the safer industrial face of a toxic element.
trivia.story: Barite, also called heavy spar, found jobs that use the weight Scheele noticed and the insolubility that makes some barium compounds safer. Finely ground, it thickens drilling muds that have to hold pressure in a deep hole, and it fills paints and plastics wherever density is useful. Those uses rely on the insoluble mineral. Workers still treat barium dust and any soluble salts as occupational hazards, because a legitimate industry does not cancel the element’s toxicity. A dense white powder can be a product or a mistake, depending entirely on which compound it is. The Greek word for heavy is the first fact a student learns; solubility is the fact that decides whether heavy is tolerable.

applications.title: Green fireworks
applications.body: Barium compounds give fireworks a green color. The pure metal is not what is packed in the shell.

applications.title: Medical images
applications.body: A suspension of barium sulfate is swallowed so an X-ray can outline the stomach. That particular compound does not dissolve. Other barium salts are poisonous.

applications.title: Drilling mud
applications.body: Barium sulfate is also the dense mineral added to drilling mud so the fluid can hold back pressure in a well.

elements.name: Lanthanum

summary.beginner:
Lanthanum is element 57, the first of the rare-earth row under the main table. Camera lenses and some catalysts use it.

Its symbol is La. At room temperature lanthanum is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 3. In class those are called period 6 and group 3.

Lanthanum is a silvery metal, softer and more reactive than iron. In a lens it is part of the glass, not a shiny piece you can see.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral lanthanum atom has 57 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Lanthanum is a solid lanthanide in period 6 and group 3. Lanthanum starts the lanthanide series in teaching tables, and the ion is La3+.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 5d1 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 18, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

La2O3 improves the refractive index of some optical glass. The metal is also a component of some nickel-metal hydride battery electrodes and of fluid-cracking catalysts.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Lanthanum (Z = 57) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 5d1 6s2. La3+ has an empty 4f shell, so it is colorless and only weakly magnetic.

Later lanthanides add 4f electrons one at a time. That is the series lanthanum opens.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Lanthanum: say the name, write La, find Z=57 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — camera lenses and catalysts.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Lanthanum: electron configuration [Xe] 5d1 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 3. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. start of the f-block story in teaching tables.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Lanthanum: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; often 5d¹ 6s²; +3 ion If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from cerium earths.

elements.history:
Carl Gustaf Mosander, a student of Berzelius, separated a new earth from cerium nitrate in 1839. He named it lanthanum, from the Greek lanthanein, to lie hidden, because it had been concealed in ceria. The metal came later.

Lanthanum is the first of the series that bears its name. Those fifteen metals were peeled apart through the nineteenth century by repeated crystallization, one of the hardest separations in classical chemistry.
elements.howDiscovered:
Carl Gustaf Mosander suspected that ceria was not a single earth. In 1839 he heated cerium nitrate gently, so that only part of it decomposed, and leached the mass with dilute nitric acid. The soluble portion held an earth that was not cerium. Its sulfate and its atomic weight differed.

He announced it, briefly withdrew the claim, and then confirmed it. The method is a partial decomposition: the new earth dissolved under conditions that left ceria behind. Lanthanum was hidden inside a sample chemists had been calling pure.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Lanthanum-139 is the only stable isotope, and it is mainly a slow-process product, made with barium in giant stars. A rapid-process share is present and smaller. Lanthanum-138 is a long-lived trace, with a half-life near 100 billion years.

The lanthanum in a camera lens is the common isotope. It belongs to the same neutron-capture peak as barium, which is why the two elements track each other in many stars.

trivia.title: Hidden in Cerium Nitrate
trivia.summary: Carl Gustaf Mosander, a student of Berzelius, separated cerium nitrate until a new earth appeared inside a salt everyone had trusted.
trivia.story: Carl Gustaf Mosander had studied with Berzelius, and he inherited the problem of the rare earths, which refused to stay pure. In 1839 he separated a new earth from cerium nitrate. What laboratories had been calling cerium was hiding another element inside the crystals. Mosander’s skill was patience, repeating a separation until the fractions stopped behaving as one substance. Lanthanum arrived not as a nugget in a river but as a discrepancy in a salt everyone thought they understood. The teacher’s element had been a mixture, and the student proved it; a nitrate that looked finished was the ore, in a sense, and the new earth was the prize for not stopping.

trivia.title: A Word for Lying Hidden
trivia.summary: Mosander named the earth from a Greek verb meaning to lie hidden, an honest label for an element that had been concealed in ceria.
trivia.story: Mosander named the new earth lanthanum, from the Greek lanthanein, to lie hidden. The name admits how the discovery felt to the person who made it. The element had been concealed in ceria, sharing salts with cerium until someone refused to stop separating. That same hiding is the habit of the rare earths, a crowd of similar ions that crystallize together and fool the eye. Lanthanum is the first of the series later called the lanthanides. A word about secrecy became the family’s title, which is as honest as a chemical name can be; Mosander did not pretend the find had been obvious; he named the difficulty, and the difficulty became the brand of a whole row.

trivia.title: Weeks of Nearly Same Dishes
trivia.summary: The lanthanides came apart through the nineteenth century by repeated crystallization, a slow method that made tiny chemical differences finally visible.
trivia.story: Once lanthanum was known, the series that would carry its name still had to be peeled apart. Nineteenth-century chemists did the work by repeated crystallization, returning salts to solution and to solid again until one element preferred the crystals and another preferred the liquid. The work was weeks of nearly identical dishes, not a single dramatic afternoon. Mosander himself would later show that fractions which seemed finished could be split again. Lanthanum’s discovery was the start of that long unpicking, one of the hardest separations in classical chemistry. The hidden element taught a method as much as it filled a square; patience was the apparatus.

trivia.title: Lenses and Mixed Flints
trivia.summary: Lanthanum oxide helps special optical glasses bend light, and the metal also rides along with cerium in the alloys of lighter flints.
trivia.story: Lanthanum’s modern uses are quiet and mostly optical. Its oxide goes into some camera and telescope glasses that need a high refractive index, bending light more sharply without a thicker lens. The metal also appears in mischmetal, the mixed rare-earth alloy used in lighter flints, usually as a companion to cerium. Neither use looks like Mosander’s rows of nitrate dishes. Both depend on having finally separated a metal that spent years hidden inside someone else’s element. A lens that focuses a sharp image may contain the earth he teased out of cerium nitrate; the spark in a flint may contain its relatives; hidden, in industry, often means well mixed on purpose.

trivia.title: A Secret Inside the Secret
trivia.summary: Pulling lanthanum out of cerium did not end the surprises, because material from that work still concealed the mixture later called didymium.
trivia.story: Mosander’s lanthanum explained one impurity in what had been called cerium, and then the explanation frayed. Further separation showed that material from this same family of earths still contained another component, later called didymium. The element named for hiding had stood next to another hiding place. That is the tense pattern of the rare earths: every time a chemist declared a fraction pure, a better separation might prove it was a pair. Didymium itself would eventually split into praseodymium and neodymium. Lanthanum stayed a real element through all of those later cuts; its discovery was true, and it was also the first door in a hallway of doors that the nineteenth century had to open one by one.

applications.title: Camera lenses
applications.body: Lanthanum oxide raises the refractive index of some optical glass, so a lens can bend light more in a thinner piece.

applications.title: Catalysts
applications.body: Lanthanum compounds are part of the catalysts in oil refining and in some catalytic converters.

applications.title: Lighter flints
applications.body: The sparking flint in many lighters is a mix of rare-earth metals rich in cerium and lanthanum, alloyed with iron.

elements.name: Cerium

summary.beginner:
Cerium is element 58, the most common rare-earth metal. It is in lighter flints and in the catalytic converters that help clean car exhaust.

Its symbol is Ce. At room temperature cerium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

A flint spark comes from a little cerium mixed with iron. In a converter, a cerium compound stores and releases oxygen as the engine runs.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral cerium atom has 58 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Cerium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Cerium is unusual among lanthanides because both +3 and +4 are important.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f1 5d1 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 19, 9, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +4. The one courses meet most often is +3.

CeO2 is the oxygen-storage material in many three-way catalysts. Mischmetal flints are a cerium-iron alloy.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Cerium (Z = 58) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f1 5d1 6s2. The +4 state is available because cerium can empty the 4f shell to reach the xenon core.

CeO2 then cycles between Ce(IV) and Ce(III) as it stores and releases oxygen.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +4. The one courses meet most often is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Cerium: say the name, write Ce, find Z=58 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — catalytic converters and lighter flints.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Cerium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f1 5d1 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3, +4. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. 4f¹; +3 and +4.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Cerium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; CeO₂ oxygen-storage material If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found in cerite; the first of the lanthanide series to be isolated as an earth.

elements.history:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger, and independently Martin Heinrich Klaproth, found a new earth in the mineral cerite in 1803. They named it cerium, for the asteroid Ceres, discovered two years earlier. Mosander later showed that ceria was a mixture and split lanthanum and didymium from it.

Cerium is the most abundant lanthanide. Its oxide stores and releases oxygen, which is why it sits in catalytic-converter washcoats and in lighter flints.
elements.howDiscovered:
Wilhelm Hisinger and Jöns Jacob Berzelius analyzed the heavy mineral cerite from Bastnäs, and Martin Heinrich Klaproth analyzed it independently, in 1803. After removing silica and iron, an earth remained that was not yttria and not any earth then listed. Both laboratories found it.

The earth later proved to contain lanthanum and didymium as well, so the 1803 oxide was a mixture whose major constituent was real. The discovery is that analysis of cerite. The metal was prepared decades later by reduction.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Cerium is mostly the slow process. Cerium-140, the dominant isotope, is built in giant stars just after the barium peak. Cerium-136 is proton-rich and rare. Cerium-142 takes a rapid-process share.

The cerium in a catalytic converter and in lighter flints is, in bulk, giant-star ash. The proton-rich and rapid-process pieces ride along in the same metal.

trivia.title: Found Twice in One Year
trivia.summary: In 1803 Berzelius and Hisinger in Sweden, and Klaproth in Germany, each separated a new earth from the mineral cerite.
trivia.story: Cerium was found twice, on two sides of Europe, in 1803. Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger in Sweden, and Martin Heinrich Klaproth in Germany, each examined the mineral cerite and separated a new earth. Neither laboratory had copied the other’s notes. The mineral itself was doing the announcing, and skilled analysts on both sides were ready to hear it. A double discovery can turn into a quarrel about pride and priority. In this case the shared year became the story, and the element was accepted rather than fought into exhaustion; cerite had a name before the element did; the earth inside it soon received a namesake more famous than the rock.

trivia.title: Borrowed from the Asteroid
trivia.summary: The discoverers named the earth cerium for Ceres, the asteroid Giuseppe Piazzi had found in 1801, two years before the chemical papers.
trivia.story: Berzelius, Hisinger, and Klaproth named the new earth cerium, for the asteroid Ceres. Giuseppe Piazzi had found Ceres in 1801, two years before the chemical papers, and astronomers were still excited by that moving point of light. Naming an element after a new planet, which is what asteroids were called at the time, was a way of saying that chemistry was keeping up with the sky. Palladium would later borrow the asteroid Pallas in a similar spirit, but cerium reached a heavenly name first. The mineral cerite and the asteroid are different kinds of rock, joined only by the word. A European ore and an astronomer’s discovery share a name on purpose.

trivia.title: The Earth Was a Crowd
trivia.summary: Carl Gustaf Mosander later showed that ceria was a mixture, pulling lanthanum and the material called didymium out of the old earth.
trivia.story: The earth of 1803 did not stay single. Mosander showed that ceria was a mixture and separated lanthanum from it, with didymium emerging as yet another component of material that had been treated as one element. Cerium itself remained real. It had simply been accompanied, in the original rocks, by neighbors that crystallize in almost the same way. The first discovery was corrected without being thrown out. That kind of correction stings, because Berzelius, Hisinger, and Klaproth had worked carefully and still held a crowd in their samples; Cerium is the most abundant lanthanide, and in those early samples it had been sheltering the rest; abundance made the hiding easier.

trivia.title: Sparks in a Pocket Flint
trivia.summary: Cerium-rich mischmetal throws sparks in lighter flints, and cerium oxide stores oxygen in the catalysts that clean car exhaust.
trivia.story: Cerium is the most abundant lanthanide, which is why it can show up in something as ordinary as a lighter. Mischmetal, an alloy rich in cerium together with other rare earths, is the flint that throws sparks when a wheel scrapes it. The scrape produces a shower of hot fragments, which is all a pocket lighter needs. Cerium oxide has a more serious talent for oxygen. It stores oxygen and gives it back inside the washcoat of catalytic converters, helping the catalyst cope when the exhaust changes. A lighter and a car’s converter both rely on cerium, in different chemical moods; the asteroid’s element ended up in a pocket and under a hood.

trivia.title: Powder for a Clear Lens
trivia.summary: Cerium oxide became a standard polish for optical glass, removing fine scratches from lenses without the harsh cut of harder grits.
trivia.story: Long before it sat in exhaust systems, cerium oxide was a powder for polishing glass. Opticians use it to finish lenses and mirrors because it clears fine scratches without the wild cutting of harder grits. The same abundance that puts cerium into mischmetal makes the polishing powder affordable enough for a workshop. A rare-earth name does not always mean a rare object on the shelf. Cerium is the common lanthanide, and common is what a polishing room needs. What Berzelius and Klaproth separated from a mineral later became a dust that opticians rub across glass until the reflection is clean; the heavenly name has a very practical powder.

applications.title: Catalytic converters
applications.body: Cerium oxide stores oxygen and gives it back as a car's exhaust changes. That keeps the converter working.

applications.title: Lighter flints
applications.body: The sparks from a lighter flint are burning bits of a cerium-iron alloy. The metal is pyrophoric when it is finely divided.

applications.title: Glass polishing
applications.body: Cerium oxide powder polishes glass, from telescope mirrors to the screens of phones. The powder is a compound, not a lump of the metal.
