elements.name: Praseodymium

summary.beginner:
Praseodymium is element 59, a rare-earth metal used in strong magnets and in the glass of some safety goggles. Its compounds can be green.

Its symbol is Pr. At room temperature praseodymium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

The name means green twin, from the color of its salts and from the element it was separated from. You meet it inside a magnet or a piece of glass, not as a labeled bar.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral praseodymium atom has 59 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Praseodymium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Praseodymium is a typical +3 lanthanide, and it is used in magnets and in didymium glass.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f3 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 21, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

Didymium glass absorbs the yellow glare of glassblowing. The metal also partners with neodymium in some permanent magnets.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Praseodymium (Z = 59) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f3 6s2. The 4f2 ion has a characteristic absorption in the yellow, which is the glassblower's filter.

Magnet alloys use the metal for its magnetic anisotropy, not for that color.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Praseodymium: say the name, write Pr, find Z=59 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — magnets and lighter flints.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Praseodymium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f3 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. typical +3 lanthanide.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Praseodymium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; used in didymium glass If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from didymium as a distinct earth.

elements.history:
Mosander’s didymium, the twin of lanthanum, was itself a mixture. Carl Auer von Welsbach split it in 1885 into a green fraction and a rose fraction. He named the green one praseodymium, from the Greek prasinos didymos, green twin.

The separation was done by repeated crystallization of double nitrates, not by a single dramatic experiment. Praseodymium is a typical +3 lanthanide, used in magnets, glasses, and lighter flints.
elements.howDiscovered:
Mosander’s didymium was accepted as one element until Carl Auer von Welsbach split it. In 1885 he fractionally crystallized the double ammonium nitrate hundreds of times. Two fractions separated: one gave green salts, the other rose-pink salts, and their absorption spectra were different.

The green fraction was praseodymium. The evidence was the spectrum that changed as the crystallization proceeded, and the failure of either fraction to produce the other’s bands. No new mineral was involved. The discovery was a separation pushed far past the point where the sample had looked pure.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Praseodymium-141 is the only stable isotope. It is mainly a slow-process product of giant stars, on the path from the barium peak toward lead. The rapid process contributes a lesser share.

Praseodymium is odd-numbered and scarcer than cerium or neodymium. The green salts that gave the element its name, and the metal in a magnet alloy, are that giant-star nucleus.

trivia.title: The Twin That Was Two
trivia.summary: Mosander’s didymium held a place as one element, the twin of lanthanum, until later work showed the twin itself was a mixture.
trivia.story: Mosander’s didymium was named as a twin, the partner separated from the same rare-earth mixture as lanthanum. For decades it held a place as if it were a single element. The salts looked consistent enough, and the separations of that era had done what they could. Didymium was a truthful report of a fraction and a misleading report of an element. The tension sat in the lanthanide row, where everyone using the name was actually handling a blend. The blend’s undoing waited for a chemist willing to push the same salts past the point where others had stopped; a twin on the table can still be a crowd; that was didymium’s secret, and it lasted for decades.

trivia.title: Green Twin in the Name
trivia.summary: Carl Auer von Welsbach split didymium in 1885 and named the green fraction praseodymium, from Greek words meaning green twin.
trivia.story: Carl Auer von Welsbach split didymium in 1885. One fraction gave green salts, and the other gave rose-colored salts, and the difference survived when the purification continued. He named the green fraction praseodymium, from the Greek prasinos didymos, green twin. The modern name still carries didymium inside it, so the old mistake remains visible in the word. He had not found a new rock in a field. He had refused to let a famous element remain an unseparated pair; Praseodymium’s birth is a correction, which is a less glamorous kind of discovery and a very solid one; green was the proof you could see without a new theory, only with a careful eye and a great deal of patience.

trivia.title: Patience Instead of Drama
trivia.summary: The separation used repeated crystallization of double nitrates, a patient campaign rather than one sudden experiment a class could watch once.
trivia.story: Von Welsbach separated the twins by repeated crystallization of double nitrates. There was no single dramatic experiment that a class can replay between bells. Fractions that looked the same had to be processed until the green salts and the rose salts finally stopped traveling together. Praseodymium, once it was alone, behaves as a typical lanthanide in the +3 state, chemically orderly rather than exotic. The difficult part had been believing that didymium was unfinished business. The green color was the visible proof that the old twin had been two substances sharing a name; heroism, in this corner of the table, looked like endurance and careful labels on a row of dishes.

trivia.title: Lenses for the Glassblower
trivia.summary: Glassblowers still wear didymium lenses, named for the old mixture, because the blend cuts the yellow glare of hot glass in the flame.
trivia.story: Didymium did not vanish from workshops when it vanished from the list of elements. Glassblowers still wear didymium glasses, made from a blend of praseodymium and neodymium that filters the intense yellow light of hot sodium in a flame. The glare drops, and the worker can see the glass being shaped. It is a use that keeps the retired name on purpose. The two twins, separated in 1885, go back into the same lens because together they do this optical job. Praseodymium’s green identity matters in the chemical story; in the workshop, Mosander’s old mixture is allowed to return under the name he gave the blend; separation and reunion are both useful.

trivia.title: Flints, Glass, and Magnets
trivia.summary: Once it could be sold as itself, praseodymium went into colored glass, lighter flints, and some strong magnets beside its former twin.
trivia.story: Praseodymium is a typical lanthanide with a few bright industrial corners. It gives some glasses and ceramics a yellow-green tint, echoing the salts that earned it the name green twin. It is also one of the metals in mischmetal lighter flints, beside cerium, and it appears in certain strong magnets, sometimes alongside neodymium. None of these uses required a legendary new continent. They required the 1885 split to be real, so a seller could say which twin was in the shipment. A mixture cannot be quality-controlled forever, so the green fraction had to become an ingredient with its own name; Von Welsbach’s patience turned a correction into a catalog entry that factories can order.

applications.title: Magnets
applications.body: Praseodymium is paired with neodymium in many strong magnets. The two metals are neighbors and are often used together.

applications.title: Glassblowers' goggles
applications.body: Didymium glass, which contains praseodymium, blocks the yellow glare of hot glass so the worker can see the piece.

applications.title: A green salt
applications.body: Praseodymium compounds are green, which is what the name records. The color is the salt, not the silvery metal.

elements.name: Neodymium

summary.beginner:
Neodymium is element 60, the metal in many of the strongest magnets you can buy. Headphones, hard drives, and wind turbines use those magnets.

Its symbol is Nd. At room temperature neodymium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

A neodymium magnet is an alloy, not pure neodymium, and it is strong enough to pinch skin. The pure metal would corrode in damp air. The magnet is coated.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral neodymium atom has 60 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Neodymium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Neodymium is the lanthanide in Nd2Fe14B, the strongest common permanent magnet.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f4 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 22, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The +3 ion is the chemical form in compounds. The magnet's strength comes from the crystal and from neodymium's unpaired f electrons working with iron.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Neodymium (Z = 60) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f4 6s2. Nd2Fe14B combines a high saturation magnetization from iron with strong anisotropy from neodymium.

The Curie temperature is a limit, which is why dysprosium is sometimes added for hot uses.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Neodymium: say the name, write Nd, find Z=60 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — powerful magnets (NdFeB).
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Neodymium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f4 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. +3; 4f⁴.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Neodymium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; high magnetic anisotropy in Nd₂Fe₁₄B If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from didymium with praseodymium.

elements.history:
The other half of von Welsbach’s 1885 split of didymium was neodymium, the new twin, from the Greek neos didymos. The rose-colored salts distinguished it from the green praseodymium fraction. The two had shared one place on the table for forty years.

Neodymium’s later fame is magnetic. The Nd2Fe14B magnets developed in the 1980s are the strongest permanent magnets in common use.
elements.howDiscovered:
The rose-pink fraction of the same crystallization was neodymium. Von Welsbach obtained it alongside praseodymium in 1885, from didymium that had been extracted from cerite. The absorption bands of the pink salts were not the bands of the green ones, and further crystallization did not split the pink fraction again.

The method was identical to the praseodymium separation because the two elements were the two products of one experiment. Neodymium was discovered when didymium, recrystallized often enough, stopped being a single spectrum.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Neodymium’s isotopes divide. Neodymium-142, a large share of the element, is a slow-process product. The heavier isotopes, from 143 through 150, carry a much larger rapid-process share, and neodymium-150 is almost purely rapid-process.

Neodymium-142 also receives a little from the decay of samarium-146, which was alive in the early solar system. A neodymium magnet is a real blend: giant stars for the light isotope, neutron-rich blasts for the heavy ones.

trivia.title: The Rose Half of the Twin
trivia.summary: The other fraction of von Welsbach’s 1885 split was rose-colored, and he named that half neodymium, the new twin, beside the green one.
trivia.story: The other half of Carl Auer von Welsbach’s 1885 split of didymium was neodymium. He named it from the Greek neos didymos, the new twin, and the rose-colored salts marked it off from green praseodymium. For about forty years the two had shared one place under Mosander’s old name. A student in the years before the split who memorized didymium was memorizing a blend. A student afterward had two elements to learn and a clearer laboratory. Neodymium’s origin is that division: it was distinguished, by color and by patience, from a twin that had shared its label; it was not dug up as a new pebble on a hillside; it was recognized inside a substance chemistry already thought it knew.

trivia.title: New Twin, Already Present
trivia.summary: Neodymium means new twin, a humble name admitting that the element was new to the table and already old as the hidden half of didymium.
trivia.story: Neos didymos is a humble sort of name for an element. New twin admits that neodymium was not a stranger from outside the known list but the unrecognized half of something already taught. The rose color of its salts was the everyday clue in von Welsbach’s dishes, set beside the green of praseodymium. Color is a thin thread on which to hang a claim of a new element, and in this case the thread held through further purification. Later chemistry confirmed that the two fractions were different elements, not merely different tints of one. Neodymium is the twin that arrived by being separated; the word new records the surprise of finding a second metal where the books had allowed only one.

trivia.title: Magnets from the 1980s
trivia.summary: Two industrial groups in the 1980s combined neodymium with iron and boron to make permanent magnets stronger than the common ones before them.
trivia.story: Neodymium’s later fame is magnetic. In the 1980s two industrial groups, one around Masato Sagawa and one around John Croat, developed NdFeB magnets from neodymium, iron, and boron. Those magnets became the strongest permanent magnets in common use. Headphones, disk drives, motors, and generators could shrink because a small piece did the work of a much larger older magnet. The metal once hidden inside didymium became a strategic material, and a nineteenth-century separation sat underneath a late-twentieth-century industry. Nothing about the rose-colored salts looked like a motor, and the link is real all the same; a correction in 1885 became a magnet the world now depends on.

trivia.title: Light from a Clear Rod
trivia.summary: Neodymium ions in glass or in garnet crystals became a standard source of powerful infrared laser light for workshops and medicine.
trivia.story: Before the famous magnets, neodymium was already earning a living inside lasers. A small amount of the element, held in glass or in a yttrium aluminium garnet crystal, can take in light and then emit a powerful infrared beam. Workshops, surgeons, and research laboratories all met neodymium lasers even when they never saw the metal itself. The rose-colored ion is doing optical work inside a host that looks like plain glass or a clear rod. It is a quieter fame than a motor magnet, and it is an earlier one. Didymium’s new twin turned out to be good at storing energy and releasing it in a very orderly flash; the beam is the part the public notices.

trivia.title: A Glass That Changes Mood
trivia.summary: Glass containing neodymium shifts its apparent color between daylight and indoor lamps, because the ions swallow narrow bands of the spectrum.
trivia.story: A piece of glass that contains neodymium plays a quiet color trick that needs no accident to be interesting. Its apparent color shifts between daylight and indoor lamps, because the ions absorb sharp bands of light and leave a different mix for the eye. That trick is a cousin of the rose salts that helped von Welsbach tell the twins apart in 1885. The element spent about forty years disguised inside didymium before it had a name of its own. It later became a laser ion and the heart of the strongest magnets in common use. Color was its first identity in the laboratory, and color never entirely left the story; the new twin is still something people notice by looking.

applications.title: Strong magnets
applications.body: The magnets in headphones, hard drives, and many wind turbines are a neodymium-iron-boron alloy. They are strong enough to be dangerous if two of them snap together.

applications.title: Lasers
applications.body: Neodymium in a crystal is the heart of a common infrared laser, used in industry and in some medical tools.

applications.title: Colored glass
applications.body: Neodymium glass absorbs yellow light and is used in some welding goggles and in decorative glass that looks different under different lamps.

elements.name: Promethium

summary.beginner:
Promethium is element 61, and every form of it is radioactive. It is not found in ordinary rocks, and it has to be made.

Its symbol is Pm. At room temperature promethium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

The name recalls Prometheus, who stole fire, because the element is obtained from nuclear reactions rather than from a mine. Tiny amounts have been used in specialized batteries.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral promethium atom has 61 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Promethium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Promethium has no stable isotope, so any sample is radioactive and must be produced.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f5 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 23, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

It is a fission product and a gap in the list of stable elements. A few nuclear batteries have used the heat or the radiation from a promethium isotope.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Promethium (Z = 61) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f5 6s2. The absence of a stable isotope follows from nuclear shell structure, not from the 4f chemistry, which is an ordinary +3 lanthanide.

Macroscopic samples are a radiological problem first.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Promethium: say the name, write Pm, find Z=61 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — no stable isotopes; reactor product.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Promethium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f5 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. all isotopes radioactive.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Promethium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; named for stealing fire — it has to be made If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from fission products; named for Prometheus.

elements.history:
The periodic table had a gap at element 61. Claims from minerals, under names such as illinium and florentium, were not confirmed. Jacob Marinsky, Lawrence Glendenin, and Charles Coryell isolated the element from uranium fission products at Oak Ridge in 1945. They named it promethium, for Prometheus, because it had to be made.

No isotope is stable. Promethium is the missing lanthanide, present on Earth only as a short-lived product of other decays and of reactors.
elements.howDiscovered:
Jacob Marinsky, Lawrence Glendenin, and Charles Coryell took fission products from uranium fuel at Oak Ridge and passed them through an ion-exchange column, eluting with citrate. In 1945 a radioactive fraction came off between neodymium and samarium, the gap where element 61 had been predicted and where earlier mineral claims had failed.

The fraction’s radiation and its elution position identified it. There was no weighable sample. Promethium was discovered as a band on a column and a decay, because every isotope is radioactive and no ore retains it.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Promethium has no stable isotope. The longest-lived last about twenty years, not geological ages, so none survives from the birth of the solar system. The slow process in a giant star steps through the promethium numbers and beta-decays onward. The element is a doorway on that path, not a destination that accumulates.

On Earth, promethium is a fission product. Reactors make it when uranium splits. A star can hold a trace for a short time. A planet cannot inherit a stock.

trivia.title: The Box That Stayed Empty
trivia.summary: Chemists kept offering a new rare earth for the blank box among its neighbors, and each proud sample failed when another laboratory tried to repeat the work.
trivia.story: The periodic table had a hole among the rare earths, and that hole tempted everyone who could boil a mineral and watch the colors change. Announcements arrived with confident names, illinium from one group and florentium from another, as if the missing metal had finally agreed to be caught. Other laboratories repeated the separations and found only familiar neighbors. A discovery that cannot be repeated does not earn a permanent box, so those names slipped into footnotes. Element 61 stayed the missing one, a place on the chart with no accepted sample a teacher could hold up.

trivia.title: Fire That Had to Be Taken
trivia.summary: Wartime chemists at Oak Ridge were sorting the broken pieces of uranium atoms when a long-empty place on the table finally answered them.
trivia.story: Jacob Marinsky, Lawrence Glendenin, and Charles Coryell were not cracking a hillside rock the way rare-earth chemists usually worked. They were sorting fission products at Oak Ridge, the pieces left when uranium atoms had been split. In 1945 those separations identified element 61 at last. They named it promethium, after Prometheus, because this fire was an element people had to make rather than find in a mine. Earlier claims had already failed, and the new name marked a discovery that began in the ashes of fission.

trivia.title: An Element That Vanishes
trivia.summary: The neighboring rare earths can sit in a rock for the age of the Earth, but element 61 never offers a sample that simply waits.
trivia.story: Lanthanum, neodymium, and the other rare earths include atoms that do not decay, so a mountain can hold them quietly. Promethium is different in a way that explains the empty years. Not one of its isotopes is stable. Any trace formed in nature, or left behind by some other decay, is already on its way to becoming another element. That is why the metal appears on Earth only as a short-lived product of those decays and of reactors, and why nobody ever mined a promethium vein.

trivia.title: Batteries Smaller Than a Coin
trivia.summary: Some instruments must keep working for years where nobody can change a cell, so engineers looked for a power source that carries its own fuel.
trivia.story: An ordinary battery waits on a chemical reaction and eventually goes flat. Promethium offered a stranger bargain, because a speck of the radioactive metal releases energy as it decays, and that energy can be turned into a small electric current. Engineers built tiny nuclear batteries on that idea for instruments that had to run far from a socket. The amounts were always small, which is the only scale on which this element is practical. Nobody raised a power station from promethium, but a grain of it could keep a quiet device alive.

trivia.title: Glow Painted on a Dial
trivia.summary: Instrument makers wanted marks that could be read in the dark without a lamp, and a scarce made metal seemed small enough to stir into paint.
trivia.story: A dial is useless if the reader cannot see it when the lights fail. One later use of promethium mixed a tiny amount into luminous paint, so the radioactivity stirred a phosphor and the mark glowed on its own. The idea was a younger cousin of the old radium paints, with an element that had to be manufactured and that would not last forever. It never became a mining trade. The glow itself repeated the story of the name, borrowed fire, put to work in a thin coat and then allowed to fade.

applications.title: Made, not mined
applications.body: Promethium has no stable form, so every sample is produced in a reactor. There is no promethium ore.

applications.title: Nuclear batteries
applications.body: A few specialized batteries have used the heat or the radiation from a promethium isotope. The amounts are sealed and small.

applications.title: A gap in the table
applications.body: For a long time element 61 was the missing rare earth. Finding it in fission products, rather than in a rock, closed that gap.

elements.name: Samarium

summary.beginner:
Samarium is element 62, a rare-earth metal used in magnets that stay strong when they get hot. Nuclear reactors also use it because it absorbs neutrons.

Its symbol is Sm. At room temperature samarium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

Samarium-cobalt magnets were famous before neodymium magnets became common, and they still win when the magnet must survive heat. The metal is not a household object.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral samarium atom has 62 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Samarium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Samarium is used in SmCo magnets and as a neutron absorber in reactor control.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f6 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 24, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The chemical ion is Sm3+. The magnet is an alloy. Neutron capture is a nuclear property of particular isotopes, not a chemical reaction.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Samarium (Z = 62) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f6 6s2. SmCo5 and Sm2Co17 keep useful coercivity at temperatures where NdFeB weakens.

High neutron-capture cross sections of some samarium isotopes are why the element also appears in control rods.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Samarium: say the name, write Sm, find Z=62 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — magnets and nuclear-control rods.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Samarium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f6 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. +3; high neutron capture.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Samarium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; SmCo magnets If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated spectroscopically from didymium earths.

elements.history:
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found a new set of spectral lines in a didymium sample in 1879 and separated the oxide. He named the element samarium, for the mineral samarskite, itself named for the Russian mining official Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets.

Samarium is a lanthanide with a high neutron-capture cross section, which put it into nuclear control rods. Samarium–cobalt magnets were the high-performance magnets of the 1970s, before neodymium iron boron.
elements.howDiscovered:
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran was recording the absorption spectra of didymium fractions from the mineral samarskite. In 1879 extra bands remained after the known didymium bands were accounted for. He separated an earth, by fractional precipitation and crystallization, that carried those bands and left the didymium bands behind.

The earth came from the same mineral family as the other rare earths, and the only reason it had been missed was that its spectrum was buried in theirs. Samarium was discovered by a spectrum that fractional separation could peel off.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Samarium is a blend, and one isotope is a clock. Samarium-144 is proton-rich. Samarium-147 decays to neodymium-143 with a half-life near 100 billion years, and that decay dates rock. Samarium-152 and samarium-154 take a large rapid-process share. The middle isotopes are fed by the slow process as well.

The samarium in a magnet is that mixture. The dating method reads one radioactive isotope inside an otherwise ordinary rare earth. The nuclei came from giant stars, from the gamma process, and from rapid blasts.

trivia.title: Lines in a Didymium Sample
trivia.summary: A French chemist was examining a sample that other people thought they already understood when new spectral lines refused to match the known earths.
trivia.story: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran was reading the light from a didymium sample in 1879 when extra spectral lines appeared, lines that did not belong to the earth he thought he was holding. Light was the witness, the way a fingerprint is a witness, long before a jar of pure metal existed. He worked the sample until he had separated a new oxide. The didymium that classrooms had treated as one substance was still a mixture, and this was another tenant hiding in it. Samarium entered the table not with a nugget but with a set of lines and a patient separation.

trivia.title: A Mineral Named for an Officer
trivia.summary: The new element's name did not honor the man who found it, and the trail of that name runs through a mineral back to a Russian mining officer.
trivia.story: Boisbaudran did not put his own name on the element he had separated. He called it samarium, after the mineral samarskite, the rock in which the new earth could hide. That mineral had already been named for Colonel Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets, a Russian mining official. So the element carries a compliment that traveled from a person to a rock and only then to the periodic table. It is an unusual path for a name. Most discoverers sign their find directly, but here the honor stopped one step earlier, with the ore.

trivia.title: Magnets Before Neodymium
trivia.summary: Engineers wanted permanent magnets stronger than the old steel ones, and a rare-earth alloy held that crown for a while before a famous successor arrived.
trivia.story: Samarium stayed a specialist metal until magnets gave it a public job. Alloys of samarium and cobalt, developed as the high-performance magnets of the 1970s, could hold a strong field in a small piece. Motors, headphones, and early compact machines used that strength. Then neodymium iron boron magnets arrived and took the everyday crown. Samarium-cobalt did not disappear, because it keeps its grip when the temperature rises in ways that embarrass cheaper magnets. The older champion became the one you choose when the work gets hot.

trivia.title: A Metal That Swallows Neutrons
trivia.summary: Reactor designers needed materials that could catch flying neutrons and slow a chain of fissions, and one lanthanide turned out to be hungry for them.
trivia.story: Inside a reactor, neutrons are the messengers that keep fissions going, and engineers need a way to catch those messengers when the power should fall. Samarium's nucleus is unusually willing to grab a passing neutron. That appetite, a high capture of neutrons, is what put the element into control rods. The rod is not a fuel and not a bomb. It is a brake. A metal found by reading spectral lines in 1879 ended up with a hand on the throttle of machines its discoverer could not have imagined.

trivia.title: The Honor Hidden in a Name
trivia.summary: Students often assume an element's name remembers its discoverer, but this one remembers a mineral, and the mineral remembers somebody else entirely.
trivia.story: Ask a class who samarium is named for, and the first guess is usually the chemist with the long French name. The guess is reasonable and wrong. Boisbaudran found the element and then pointed the name at samarskite. Samarsky-Bykhovets never separated the earth, never published a spectrum, and still walks into the lesson whenever the mineral is explained. The story is a reminder that names on this row of the table are often geological. The quarry, the ore, and the officer can outlast the afternoon of the experiment.

applications.title: Magnets that stay hot
applications.body: Samarium-cobalt magnets keep their strength at temperatures where many other magnets weaken. They are used in motors that run hot.

applications.title: Reactor control
applications.body: Some samarium isotopes absorb neutrons strongly, so the element is used in control rods that slow a reactor.

applications.title: Headphones, an older design
applications.body: Before neodymium magnets were common, samarium-cobalt was the strong small magnet in many headphones and pickups.

elements.name: Europium

summary.beginner:
Europium is element 63, a rare-earth metal that helps phosphors glow red. Screens and lamps have used that glow.

Its symbol is Eu. At room temperature europium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

A phosphor is a powder that takes in energy and gives out colored light. Europium is a small ingredient in that powder, not the glass of the screen.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral europium atom has 63 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Europium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Europium is unusual because both Eu2+ and Eu3+ are stable enough to matter, and the two ions glow different colors.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f7 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 25, 8, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +3.

Eu3+ is a classic red emitter. Eu2+ can emit blue. That pair is why europium shows up in lighting phosphors.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Europium (Z = 63) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f7 6s2. The half-filled 4f7 shell stabilizes Eu2+, which is why europium, like ytterbium later, has a real +2 chemistry.

The red lines of Eu3+ are sharp f-f transitions.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Europium: say the name, write Eu, find Z=63 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — red phosphors; Eu²⁺/Eu³⁺ color.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Europium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f7 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3, +2. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. can be +2 as well as +3.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Europium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; the half-filled 4f⁷ ion is relatively stable If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from samarium fractions.

elements.history:
Eugène-Anatole Demarçay suspected a new element between samarium and gadolinium for years. In 1901 he separated it and named it europium, for Europe. The spectral lines, not a bulk sample, were the evidence.

Europium is unusual among the lanthanides in forming a reasonably stable +2 ion as well as +3. That pair of oxidation states is why europium phosphors can be both red and blue, and why they colored television screens.
elements.howDiscovered:
Eugène-Anatole Demarçay fractionated samarium magnesium nitrate, crystallizing it repeatedly and watching the spark spectrum of each crop. Between 1896 and 1901 a set of lines grew stronger in the head fractions while the samarium lines weakened. He concentrated an earth that showed those lines almost alone.

The lines were the discovery. The crystallization was the separation. Europium sits in samarium ores in small amount, and only a spectrum made the enrichment visible before the earth was pure enough to weigh as its own oxide.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Europium is the classical tracer of the rapid process. Europium-151 and europium-153 are both made mostly that way. The slow process contributes a small share. Astronomers compare europium with iron, or with barium, to ask whether a star’s heavy elements came from a neutron-rich blast or from the slow trickle of giants.

The rapid process needs a blast so neutron-rich that captures outrun beta decay. Merging neutron stars are the leading site. The europium in a red phosphor was made in events of that kind before the Sun formed, not in a merger observed in our own time.

trivia.title: Years of a Suspicious Line
trivia.summary: A spectroscopist kept seeing hints of something between two rare earths, and for years the hint was too faint to count as a discovery.
trivia.story: Eugène-Anatole Demarçay spent years suspecting that a new element sat between samarium and gadolinium. The suspicion lived in spectral lines, extra marks of light that would not match the neighbors, rather than in a lump he could weigh. In 1901 he finally separated the new earth and the lines held still. He named it europium, for Europe. There was no nugget to pass around a lecture hall. The evidence was the light, and the name chose a continent instead of a village, a person, or a mine.

trivia.title: A Name for a Continent
trivia.summary: While nearby elements remember a Swedish quarry or a single chemist, this one was given the name of a whole continent after a long spectral hunt.
trivia.story: Most of the rare earths carry the name of Ytterby, or of a chemist who suffered through their separations. Europium is the odd one that looks at a map of nations. Demarçay, having chased the element through spectra until 1901, chose Europe as its namesake. The choice has a quiet boldness. He did not carve his own surname into the table. He attached the new metal to a continent, as if the years of uncertain lines had been a European project even though the decisive separations were his.

trivia.title: The Red in the Television
trivia.summary: Color screens needed a red that stayed red, and a lanthanide phosphor became the glow behind countless television pictures and lamps.
trivia.story: A color television has to make red that looks like red, not a tired orange, every time the screen lights. Europium phosphors became that red. A little of the element, spread in a coating, takes energy and hands back a sharp red light, and lamp makers borrowed the same trick. Living rooms of the late twentieth century were full of a metal most owners never knew they were watching. The discovery had been a faint line in a spectroscope. The use was a color steady enough to build a picture on.

trivia.title: Two Charges One Phosphor
trivia.summary: Most rare earths are content with a single usual charge, but this one keeps a second option, and that quirk is why its glow can change color.
trivia.story: Lanthanides usually settle as ions with a charge of three, and europium does that too. It is unusual because a charge of two is also reasonably stable. That pair of personalities is not a textbook footnote only. It is why europium phosphors can be coaxed toward red in one arrangement and blue in another. The same element that painted television red could also supply a blue, which is a lot of work for a metal that began as a suspicious spectral line. Demarçay separated an earth, and engineers later separated its colors.

trivia.title: A Glow Hidden in the Banknote
trivia.summary: Bank designers needed a mark that ordinary light would not reveal, and they hid a fluorescent metal where a cashier's lamp could find it.
trivia.story: Euro banknotes have to survive photocopiers, careful forgers, and a quick look in bad light. One of the quiet defenses is europium. Compounds of the element sit in the printing and fluoresce when ultraviolet light hits them, a glow the eye does not see under the shop lamp. A cashier's special lamp wakes the mark. The same red fluorescence that once colored television screens became a security tell. Europe's namesake element ended up guarding Europe's cash, which is a neater ending than Demarçay could have planned in 1901.

applications.title: Red phosphors
applications.body: The red glow in many fluorescent lamps and older screens comes from a europium phosphor. A little of the element goes a long way.

applications.title: Anti-counterfeiting
applications.body: Euro banknotes have used a europium compound that glows under ultraviolet light, as a mark that is hard to fake.

applications.title: Two ions, two colors
applications.body: Europium can glow red in one ionic form and blue in another. Lamp makers use that pair on purpose.

elements.name: Gadolinium

summary.beginner:
Gadolinium is element 64, a rare-earth metal used in the contrast dye for some MRI scans. It also goes into certain magnets.

Its symbol is Gd. At room temperature gadolinium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

The dye is a compound that a doctor injects, not a piece of metal. It changes the MRI picture. People with kidney trouble need special care with that dye, which is a medical decision.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral gadolinium atom has 64 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Gadolinium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Gd3+ has more unpaired electrons than any other simple ion, which is why it is an MRI contrast agent.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f7 5d1 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 25, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The same unpaired electrons make gadolinium useful in magnetic refrigeration research. Some isotopes also absorb neutrons strongly.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Gadolinium (Z = 64) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f7 5d1 6s2. Seven unpaired 4f electrons make Gd3+ an S-state ion with a huge magnetic moment and slow electronic relaxation, the combination MRI contrast needs.

The ligand around the ion is what makes the injection tolerable.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Gadolinium: say the name, write Gd, find Z=64 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — MRI contrast (Gd³⁺) and magnets.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Gadolinium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f7 5d1 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. 8 unpaired electrons in Gd³⁺.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Gadolinium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; high neutron capture; used in shielding If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from yttria; named for Gadolin.

elements.history:
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac separated a new earth from yttria in 1880. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran prepared a purer sample in 1886 and proposed the name gadolinium, for Johan Gadolin, who had started rare-earth chemistry at Ytterby. Marignac agreed.

The Gd3+ ion has more unpaired electrons than any other simple ion, which made gadolinium compounds the contrast agents of magnetic-resonance imaging.
elements.howDiscovered:
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac examined fractions from yttria and from samarskite with a spectroscope. In 1880 he found lines that matched neither samarium nor the earths already named. He separated an oxide that carried them. Lecoq de Boisbaudran confirmed the spectrum.

The separation was the usual one: fractional precipitation of the oxalates and crystallization of the double salts, repeated until the lines were stable. Gadolinium was discovered as a spectrum that survived that repetition.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Gadolinium’s heavier isotopes dominate the element, and they are largely rapid-process. Gadolinium-158 and gadolinium-160 are the abundant ones. Gadolinium-152 and gadolinium-154 are fed by the slow process and are minor. Gadolinium-152 is also weakly radioactive.

The gadolinium used for magnetic resonance is, in bulk, rapid-process ash, with a slow-process minority in the same sample. The same neutron-rich events that supply europium supply most of this metal.

trivia.title: The Quarry Chemist Remembered
trivia.summary: Rare-earth chemistry began with a man who studied odd minerals from a Swedish village, and a later element was named so that work would not be forgotten.
trivia.story: Johan Gadolin, working with minerals from Ytterby, opened the rare-earth story that would occupy chemists for the next century. He did not live to see every earth separated, and he did not find gadolinium himself. The name came later, as a thank-you. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran proposed gadolinium for him, and Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac agreed. A quarry village and a patient chemist are both in that choice. The element remembers the person who showed that yttria was a door, not a single room.

trivia.title: A Cleaner Sample Years Later
trivia.summary: One chemist separated a new earth from yttria, and another needed several more years before the sample was pure enough to name with confidence.
trivia.story: Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac separated a new earth from yttria in 1880. The rare earths never came apart in one dramatic afternoon, so a first separation was a beginning rather than a finished portrait. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran prepared a purer sample in 1886 and proposed the name gadolinium. Marignac agreed, which spared the element a long fight over what to call it. The method was the familiar one, repeated crystallization and a careful eye, until the new earth stopped being a stain in yttria and became itself.

trivia.title: Brightening a Body Scan
trivia.summary: Hospital scans of soft tissue can look like fog, and a rare-earth ion with a crowd of unpaired electrons became a way to sharpen the picture.
trivia.story: Magnetic-resonance imaging looks at soft parts of the body that a plain X-ray barely notices. The pictures improve when a contrast agent changes how those tissues respond to the scanner's magnets. Gadolinium compounds became the usual agents because the gadolinium ion carries more unpaired electrons than any other simple ion. Those electrons make the ion a strong little magnet. A metal separated from Swedish yttria in the 1880s walks into the hospital as a dissolved salt, does its brightening, and is meant to leave again. The scan is clearer because the ion is magnetically loud.

trivia.title: The Champion Neutron Catcher
trivia.summary: Among elements that have a stable form, one lanthanide stands out for the way its nucleus grabs passing neutrons, a fact reactor physicists like to quote.
trivia.story: Neutrons slip into some nuclei and bounce off others, and the difference matters wherever a reactor is controlled. Gadolinium is the stable element that captures neutrons most readily. A thin presence of it can swallow a crowd of them. That is a talking point in nuclear lessons and a practical reason the metal appears in certain controls and shields. It is also a cousin of the samarium story, two lanthanides with an appetite, gadolinium the hungrier of the stable pair. The same element that brightens a medical scan can, in another job, quiet a flux of neutrons.

trivia.title: Contrast With a Caution
trivia.summary: The scan-brightening salts became routine in hospitals, and then doctors learned that a particular group of patients could be harmed if the choice was casual.
trivia.story: Gadolinium contrast made many magnetic-resonance pictures good enough to trust, and for years it felt almost ordinary. Then physicians learned that some patients with badly damaged kidneys could be harmed by certain of these agents. The ion that is so useful in a scanner is not a harmless dye for every body. Hospitals tightened who receives it and which compound is chosen. Nothing in that lesson requires a recipe or a dose recited in class. The story is enough: a remarkable tool stayed in use, and a real risk taught the users to be selective.

applications.title: MRI contrast
applications.body: Some MRI scans use a gadolinium compound, injected so that particular tissues stand out in the picture. The metal itself is not injected.

applications.title: Magnets
applications.body: Gadolinium alloys are studied for magnetic refrigeration, a way of cooling with a changing magnetic field.

applications.title: Neutrons
applications.body: Gadolinium absorbs neutrons very strongly, so it is used in some reactor shielding and in neutron radiography.

elements.name: Terbium

summary.beginner:
Terbium is element 65, a rare-earth metal used in green phosphors and in alloys that change shape in a magnetic field. You will not find a lump of it at home.

Its symbol is Tb. At room temperature terbium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

The green in some fluorescent lamps has come from terbium. Another use is an alloy that grows or shrinks slightly when a magnet is brought near, which can drive a precise actuator.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral terbium atom has 65 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Terbium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Terbium provides green phosphor emission and the large magnetostriction of Terfenol-D.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f9 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 27, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The ion in ordinary compounds is Tb3+. A less common +4 state exists. The actuator alloy is terbium with dysprosium and iron.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Terbium (Z = 65) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f9 6s2. Terfenol-D's magnetostriction is a bulk alloy effect, hundreds of times larger than that of pure iron.

The green emission is Tb3+ f-f lines, a separate use of the ion.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Terbium: say the name, write Tb, find Z=65 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — green phosphors and magnetostriction.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Terbium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f9 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. 4f⁸; +3 and some +4.

discovery.text: Separated from yttria as erbia, later renamed.

elements.history:
Carl Gustaf Mosander split yttria further in 1843 and found a rose-colored fraction he associated with terbium, named for Ytterby. The names terbium and erbium were later swapped in the literature and then fixed. The element that kept the name terbium is the one isolated cleanly in the later nineteenth century.

Terbium’s green phosphor line, and the giant magnetostriction of terfenol, are the modern reasons to separate this scarce lanthanide from its neighbors.
elements.howDiscovered:
Carl Gustaf Mosander, in 1843, dissolved yttria and precipitated it in fractions with dilute ammonia. The first and last precipitates were not the same earth. One fraction was pink, one was yellow, and what remained was a third. He named two new earths, terbia and erbia.

Later chemists swapped and split those fractions, and the name terbium settled on one of the products only after holmium, erbium, and the others had been peeled away. The original discovery was the fractional precipitation: yttria was not one earth, and the yellow fraction was the start of terbium.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Terbium-159 is the only stable isotope. It is mainly a rapid-process product, with a slow-process share from giant stars. The odd proton number makes it one of the scarcer rare earths.

The terbium in a green phosphor is that mostly rapid-process nucleus. The heavy rare earths often occur in the same minerals because geology gathered them together. Their nuclei were made in overlapping, not identical, stellar channels.

trivia.title: A Rose Color From Yttria
trivia.summary: A Swedish chemist kept splitting an earth that was supposed to be one substance, and a rose-colored fraction pointed toward a village name.
trivia.story: Carl Gustaf Mosander did not trust yttria to be simple. In 1843 he split it further and found a rose-colored fraction, which he associated with a new element. He named it terbium, for Ytterby, the quarry village that was already becoming a factory of element names. The color was the clue a student could imagine, pinkish salts where a white earth had been expected. A pure story took longer than the first split, because this row of the table hides inside itself. Mosander's rose fraction was a door, and later chemists still had to decide what stood on the other side.

trivia.title: When Two Names Traded Places
trivia.summary: Two rare earths from the same village spent years with their labels swapped in the journals, and students of the old papers can still get lost.
trivia.story: Terbium and erbium were born in the same 1843 splitting of yttria, and then the literature played a long trick. Chemists swapped the two names in their papers, so a salt called one thing in one decade was the other thing in the next. The confusion was not a small spelling quarrel. It meant the rose fraction and the pinker story traded labels while everyone was still separating impurities. Eventually the names were fixed, and the element that kept the name terbium is the one isolated cleanly later in the nineteenth century. Ytterby had donated the words, and the journals had muddled them.

trivia.title: Green Light From a Village
trivia.summary: Screen makers needed a green as reliable as the reds already glowing in their phosphors, and a scarce lanthanide from a Swedish quarry supplied it.
trivia.story: Once europium had a claim on red, display makers still needed a green that would not wander. Terbium's phosphor line gave them that green. A coating doped with the element takes energy and returns a color good enough for lamps and screens. The amounts in any one device are small, which is fortunate, because terbium is scarce and tiresome to separate from its neighbors. Mosander's village name therefore sits in the glow of machines he never saw. The rose-colored salts of 1843 and the green light of a modern lamp are the same element, cleaned up and given a job.

trivia.title: A Metal That Changes Shape
trivia.summary: Most metals shrug at a magnet, but one terbium alloy changes size so strongly that engineers can build motion into a solid piece.
trivia.story: A magnet usually pulls on a metal from the outside. Terfenol, an alloy that takes its name from terbium, does something more theatrical. In a magnetic field the solid changes shape by a giant amount, for a metal, and then changes back. Engineers use that motion in precise small actuators, where a screw would be clumsy. The effect is called magnetostriction, which sounds like a textbook label until a rod visibly lengthens. Terbium's modern life includes green light, and it also includes a metal that listens to a magnet and answers by moving.

trivia.title: The Quarry in the Name
trivia.summary: A small Swedish village lent its sound to several elements, and terbium is one of the words carved out of that single place name.
trivia.story: Ytterby was a feldspar quarry, not a capital, and yet its syllables were cut apart to name elements. Yttrium took one piece, terbium another, erbium another, ytterbium another. Terbium is the slice that begins with the middle of the village. Mosander's 1843 choice tied a rose-colored earth to that quarry even though the pure element took decades more work. Standing at the pit, a miner would have seen ordinary rock. The chemists saw fractions, and between them they turned one place-name into a handful of boxes on the chart.

applications.title: Green phosphors
applications.body: Terbium compounds provide the green in many fluorescent lamps, next to europium's red.

applications.title: Actuators
applications.body: An alloy called Terfenol-D, which contains terbium, changes shape in a magnetic field. That motion can drive a precise device.

applications.title: A specialist metal
applications.body: There is no terbium hardware in a kitchen. The uses are the phosphor and the magnetostrictive alloy.

elements.name: Dysprosium

summary.beginner:
Dysprosium is element 66, a rare-earth metal added to magnets so they keep their strength when hot. The name comes from a Greek word meaning hard to get.

Its symbol is Dy. At room temperature dysprosium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

A wind-turbine magnet may contain a little dysprosium for that reason. The pure metal is not something a hardware store sells, and separating it from its neighbors is the hard part.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral dysprosium atom has 66 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Dysprosium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Dysprosium is added to NdFeB magnets to raise the temperature at which they stay magnetized.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f10 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 28, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The ion is Dy3+. The metal has a high magnetic moment. Both facts come from a partly filled 4f shell.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Dysprosium (Z = 66) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f10 6s2. Dysprosium increases coercivity at the cost of some remanence, which is why magnet makers use as little as the operating temperature allows.

The name records the difficulty of the historical separation.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Dysprosium: say the name, write Dy, find Z=66 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — magnets and phosphors.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Dysprosium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f10 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. high magnetic moment.

discovery.text: Separated from holmium earths.

elements.history:
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran separated dysprosium from holmium oxide in 1886, after a long series of crystallizations. He named it from the Greek dysprositos, hard to get at. The name is a comment on the work.

Dysprosium is a typical heavy lanthanide, strongly magnetic at low temperature. It is added to neodymium magnets so they keep their strength when they get hot.
elements.howDiscovered:
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran started from holmium oxide that still showed foreign lines. In 1886 he precipitated it fractionally, again and again, until a set of absorption bands could be followed into one fraction and out of the holmium. He named the earth for the difficulty.

There was no new mineral and no single decisive crystal. The discovery was the persistence of the fractionation. Dysprosium appeared when the holmium spectrum finally shed a set of bands that refused to leave.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Dysprosium’s abundant isotopes are weighted toward the rapid process, and the slow process contributes. Dysprosium-164, 163, 162, and 161 carry most of the mass. Dysprosium-156 and dysprosium-158 are proton-rich and rare.

The metal in a magnet alloy is this blend, dominated by the neutron-rich channel. The gathering of rare earths into odd minerals is terrestrial. The assembly of the nuclei is stellar, and for dysprosium it is mostly the rapid process.

trivia.title: Hard to Get At
trivia.summary: After a weary separation, a French chemist chose a Greek name that sounds less like a celebration than a complaint about the work itself.
trivia.story: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran separated a new earth from holmium oxide in 1886, after crystallizations that seemed unwilling to finish. He named the element dysprosium, from the Greek dysprositos, hard to get at. The words comment on the labor instead of honoring a city, a god, or the chemist himself. Each crop of crystals had promised a clean salt and then returned a mixture with one more impurity squeezed out. The name still tells the truth about the heavy rare earths, which yield only to someone ready to repeat the same slow step.

trivia.title: Crystallizing a Hidden Earth
trivia.summary: The new metal did not announce itself with a single bright flame test, and the path to it started in an oxide that was already rare.
trivia.story: Dysprosium's discovery was a slow enrichment, the kind of campaign rare-earth chemists knew too well. Boisbaudran began with holmium oxide, itself the product of earlier separations, and teased another earth out of that oxide. Repeated crystallization sorted salts that leave a solution at slightly different moments, one crop a little richer than the last. By 1886 the fraction was distinct enough to stand as its own element on the table. Patience, more than any dramatic piece of apparatus, is the method that the name still remembers.

trivia.title: Magnets That Survive the Heat
trivia.summary: The strongest everyday magnets can lose their grip when an engine bay grows hot, and a scarce lanthanide is added so they keep their strength.
trivia.story: Neodymium magnets are famous for their strength, and they have a weakness when the temperature climbs. Dysprosium is added so those magnets keep their grip in the heat of a motor or a generator. The amount in each magnet is small, and the difference it makes is large, which is why a hard-to-isolate metal became strategically interesting. Boisbaudran's tedious crystals now sit inside machines that must not fade on a hot day. The element that was difficult to extract is valued because it refuses to let a magnet give up.

trivia.title: Magnetism in the Deep Cold
trivia.summary: Warm to the touch, this metal seems ordinary, but when the temperature falls far enough its magnetic behavior becomes extreme.
trivia.story: Dysprosium is a typical heavy lanthanide in a classroom sample, gray and unremarkable on the bench. Cool it deeply, and the magnetism becomes intense, among the strong low-temperature magnetic behaviors in the periodic table. That cold personality is a research tool and a reminder that this row of elements hides its drama in electrons. The same metal that steadies a hot neodymium magnet is, in a cryostat, a specialist magnet material of its own. Heat and deep cold are both part of its working life. The 1886 separation was only the beginning of finding out when the metal wakes up.

trivia.title: A Name That Complains
trivia.summary: Students laugh at a label that means hard to get at, and then the separations of the heavy rare earths show them the joke was earned.
trivia.story: A humorous translation can still be accurate chemistry. Dysprositos means hard to get at, and anyone who has watched rare-earth fractions creep apart understands the sigh in the word. Boisbaudran could have chosen a place or a patron. He chose a description of difficulty, almost as a warning to the next person who would try to purify the salts. The warning aged well. Modern industry still spends real effort pulling dysprosium away from its neighbors because magnets want it and the rocks do not offer it freely.

applications.title: Magnets in hot places
applications.body: A little dysprosium in a neodymium magnet helps the magnet keep its strength when a motor or a turbine runs hot.

applications.title: Control rods
applications.body: Dysprosium absorbs neutrons and is used in some nuclear control rods, for the same reason samarium is.

applications.title: Hard to separate
applications.body: The name means hard to get. Dysprosium is separated from the other rare earths for those two uses, not sold as a pure bar in a shop.

elements.name: Holmium

summary.beginner:
Holmium is element 67, a rare-earth metal with some of the strongest magnetic behavior of any element. Lasers for surgery use a compound of it.

Its symbol is Ho. At room temperature holmium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

The surgical laser is a crystal containing holmium, not a rod of the metal. The magnetic record is a laboratory fact about the element, not a magnet you can buy in a toy.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral holmium atom has 67 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Holmium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Holmium has a very high magnetic moment, and Ho:YAG is a medical laser crystal.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f11 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 29, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The laser wavelength is useful for cutting soft tissue in surgery. The ion is Ho3+. The metal itself is a specialist material.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Holmium (Z = 67) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f11 6s2. The large moment is the 4f10 configuration of Ho3+.

The laser is a sharp f-electron transition in a garnet host, the same reason rare-earth lasers have precise colors.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Separated from erbia; named for Stockholm.

elements.history:
Per Teodor Cleve and, independently, Marc Delafontaine and Jacques-Louis Soret, separated a new earth from erbia in 1878. Cleve named it holmium, for Holmia, the Latin name of Stockholm. The spectral band was the first evidence. A pure sample took longer.

Holmium has one of the highest magnetic moments of any element. Holmium-doped YAG is a medical laser, and the metal is a specialist magnet material.
elements.howDiscovered:
Marc Delafontaine, Jacques-Louis Soret, and Per Teodor Cleve, working separately, found a new set of absorption bands in erbia in 1878. Soret saw the bands. Cleve separated an earth that carried them and was neither erbium nor thulium. The earth formed its own salts, and the bands stayed with those salts.

The discovery is the band spectrum of a fraction. A pure metal was not the point, and a pure earth took longer than the first observation. Holmium was established when the bands and the earth traveled together through a separation.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Holmium-165 is the only stable isotope, and it is mainly a rapid-process product. The slow process adds a minority. Holmium is odd-numbered and scarce even by the standard of the rare earths.

The holmium in a magnetic alloy was made in neutron-rich blasts, most plausibly neutron-star mergers, and waited in the interstellar gas until the solar system formed. Giant stars are a side contribution here.

trivia.title: Named for Stockholm
trivia.summary: A Swedish chemist needed a name for a new earth, and he reached for the Latin name of his own capital city.
trivia.story: Per Teodor Cleve named the new earth holmium, for Holmia, the Latin name of Stockholm. The choice put a capital city on the table beside villages and gods. Cleve was separating rare earths from erbia, and a name from home fitted a discovery made in Sweden. Holmia sounds grander than the little dish of earth that carried it, which is part of the charm. A spectral band and a salt became a city. Students who visit Stockholm can say they have stood in the namesake of a laser metal.

trivia.title: The Band Called Element X
trivia.summary: Two laboratories noticed a new earth in the same season, and one of them could only label the evidence with a temporary letter.
trivia.story: In 1878 Per Teodor Cleve and, independently, Marc Delafontaine and Jacques-Louis Soret, drew a new earth out of erbia. Soret and Delafontaine had seen an absorption band they called element X, a placeholder for a substance not yet named. Cleve's name, holmium, is the one that lasted. The first evidence was that band of light, not a bottle of pure metal, and a truly pure sample took longer than the announcement. Two paths reached the same hidden earth. The letter X retired, and Stockholm remained.

trivia.title: A Laser in the Operating Room
trivia.summary: Surgeons wanted a beam that could work in living tissue with control, and a crystal doped with a rare earth became one answer.
trivia.story: Holmium-doped YAG is a medical laser, a crystal that takes in light and gives back a beam surgeons can aim. The element that began as a faint band in erbia now does precise work in operating rooms. Nothing about Cleve's 1878 separation predicted a scalpel made of light. The connection is the electrons of holmium, which offer a useful optical transition once the metal is seated in a crystal. A city-named earth became a clinical tool. The sample that once existed only as a spectrum now has a job at the end of a fiber.

trivia.title: One of the Strongest Magnets
trivia.summary: Among the elements, this one is famous for an enormous magnetic moment, a quiet superlative that shows up when physicists compare the row.
trivia.story: Holmium carries one of the highest magnetic moments of any element, a superlative easy to skip past on a poster. The unpaired electrons are the reason, lined up in a way that makes each atom a strong little magnet. At very low temperature the metal itself becomes a specialist magnetic material. Cleve and the element X observers were chasing a spectral band, not a record. The record appeared later, when instruments could ask the atoms how magnetic they were. Stockholm's element turned out to be loud in a magnetic sense.

trivia.title: Waiting for a Pure Sample
trivia.summary: The spectrum announced a newcomer before anyone could hold a clean salt, and the gap between those two moments was real work.
trivia.story: A colored band in a spectrum can prove that something new is present and still leave the chemist without a pure earth. Holmium's early story has that shape. The band came first, in the work of 1878, and the unmixed sample lagged behind, because erbia was a nest of neighbors. Holmium, thulium, and what remained as erbium had to be peeled apart. Naming the element for Stockholm did not finish the purification. It marked the moment the band was believed, while the bottles caught up later.

applications.title: Surgical lasers
applications.body: A holmium laser is used in some surgeries, including work on soft tissue and kidney stones. The holmium is a dopant in a crystal, not a rod of metal.

applications.title: Magnetic pole pieces
applications.body: Holmium has an unusually high magnetic moment, so it is used in the pole pieces of some very strong laboratory magnets.

applications.title: A rare-earth metal
applications.body: The ordinary chemistry is a +3 ion in a specialty salt. The public uses are the laser and the magnet.
