elements.name: Erbium

summary.beginner:
Erbium is element 68, a rare-earth metal that can tint glass pink. A more important use is in the fiber cables that carry internet signals, where it helps the light stay strong over long distances.

Its symbol is Er. At room temperature erbium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

The pink glass is the visible curiosity. The amplifier in a cable is a short stretch of fiber with a little erbium in it, pumped by another laser so the signal does not fade.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral erbium atom has 68 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Erbium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Erbium-doped fiber amplifies infrared light near 1.5 micrometers, the band used in long-distance communications.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f12 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 30, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The pink color of erbium glass is a visible absorption of Er3+. The telecom use is an emission in the infrared, where silica fiber is most transparent.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Erbium (Z = 68) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f12 6s2. The 1.5 micrometer transition sits in the low-loss window of silica.

An EDFA is that transition, pumped and stimulated, not a piece of erbium metal in the cable.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Erbium: say the name, write Er, find Z=68 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — optical fibers and pink glass.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Erbium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f12 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. +3; optical amplifier at 1.5 μm.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Erbium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Er-doped fiber amplifiers If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from yttria; the name later settled on erbium.

elements.history:
Mosander’s 1843 split of yttria produced a fraction he named erbium, for Ytterby. Later chemists found that this fraction still contained holmium, thulium, and ytterbium. The name erbium stayed with the pink oxide that remained.

Erbium’s optical transition near 1.5 micrometers sits in the low-loss window of silica fiber. Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers, developed around 1987, made long-distance optical communication practical.
elements.howDiscovered:
Erbium began as one of Mosander’s 1843 fractions of yttria, the pink one. The fraction was not pure. Over the next forty years holmium, thulium, and ytterbium were removed from it, each time by fractional crystallization or precipitation, each time taking some bands away and leaving the pink.

The name stayed with what remained. Erbium was discovered as a colored fraction of an earth that had been thought simple, and it was purified by the same kind of repetition that discovered its neighbors.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Erbium is mixed. The rapid process supplies a large share of the heavier isotopes, including erbium-166, 167, 168, and 170. The slow process contributes across the set. Erbium-162 and erbium-164 are proton-rich and minor.

The erbium in an optical fiber is this mixture. The pink of erbium glass is the same nuclei. Nothing in the color records which channel made a given atom.

trivia.title: Pink Salts From Ytterby
trivia.summary: Another fraction from an already famous earth came out pink, and the chemist tied that color to the quarry village once again.
trivia.story: Carl Gustaf Mosander's 1843 split of yttria produced a fraction he named erbium, for Ytterby. The salts that stayed with that name are pink, a color distinctive enough to anchor the element while its neighbors were still being sorted out. Ytterby was handing chemists more elements than a single quarry seems able to hold. Erbium was one of the words cut from the village name, beside yttrium, terbium, and later ytterbium. The pink oxide was the visible signature. A student who sees those salts understands why color, in this chapter of chemistry, counted as evidence.

trivia.title: Neighbors Hiding in the Fraction
trivia.summary: The earth labeled erbium still had guests in it, and later chemists kept finding new elements where one name had seemed enough.
trivia.story: Mosander's erbium fraction was real, and it was also crowded. Later chemists found holmium, thulium, and ytterbium still inside what had been called erbia. Each discovery was a separation from a separation, a reminder that yttria had been a suitcase. The name erbium stayed with the pink oxide that remained when those guests had left. That survival of the name was a choice, made after the famous swap with terbium had been untangled. The pink salt is what the word means now, and the earlier bottles marked erbium held a small crowd.

trivia.title: Light Boosted Along the Cable
trivia.summary: Long glass cables were losing the messages they carried, until a rare-earth amplifier gave the light a fresh push without turning it back into electricity.
trivia.story: A telephone conversation turned into laser light can travel far in a glass fiber, and still the light fades. Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers, developed around 1987, catch that tired pulse and strengthen it while it is still light. They made long-distance optical communication practical, the kind that runs under oceans and between cities. Mosander's pink salts had no such ambition in 1843. The electrons that color those salts also match a wavelength silica fiber carries especially well. A quarry element became a relay station for the modern world, dissolved in a thread of glass.

trivia.title: The Window in the Glass
trivia.summary: Silica fiber has a wavelength where the glass wastes unusually little light, and erbium's glow happens to sit in that same window.
trivia.story: Glass is not equally transparent to every color. Silica fiber has a low-loss window near one and a half micrometers, in the infrared, where a signal can travel with less waste. Erbium's useful optical transition sits in that window, which is why the amplifier and the cable are such a fortunate pair. Engineers did not have to force an awkward wavelength through a stubborn glass. The element and the fiber already agreed. That agreement, more than any single cable, is why erbium shows up in lessons about the internet's physical layer.

trivia.title: The Name That Stayed Pink
trivia.summary: Labels wandered between two rare earths for years, and when the confusion settled, one name remained attached to the pink oxide.
trivia.story: Erbium and terbium traded places in the literature after Mosander's split, and a careful reader of old papers can follow the wrong salt. When the names were fixed, erbium was the pink one that remained after holmium, thulium, and ytterbium had been removed. Color saved the story for students, and a pink jar, a village syllable, and a fiber amplifier are one element at three ages. The quarry donated the sound of the name, the pink oxide defended it, and the glass fiber gave it a twentieth-century career nobody in Ytterby could have described.

applications.title: Internet cables
applications.body: A short stretch of optical fiber doped with erbium amplifies the infrared signal that carries data under the ocean and across continents.

applications.title: Pink glass
applications.body: Erbium oxide tints glass pink. That is the visible form of an element whose important job is invisible infrared light.

applications.title: Lasers in medicine
applications.body: Erbium lasers are also used in some skin and dental treatments. Again the element is a dopant in a crystal.

elements.name: Thulium

summary.beginner:
Thulium is element 69, one of the scarcer rare-earth metals. A radioactive form of it has been used in small portable X-ray machines.

Its symbol is Tm. At room temperature thulium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

Thulium is a dense silvery metal, and there is little of it in any one product. The X-ray use is the radioactive isotope under controls, not the ordinary metal.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral thulium atom has 69 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Thulium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Thulium is a dense late lanthanide, usually Tm3+, and thulium-170 has been a portable X-ray source.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f13 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 31, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The metal's ordinary chemistry is the typical +3 ion. The X-ray source is a nuclear-decay product sealed in a device.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Thulium (Z = 69) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f13 6s2. Tm-170 emits useful X-rays as it decays, which is why a small source can replace a tube in some field instruments.

The metal's high melting point is a separate materials fact.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Thulium: say the name, write Tm, find Z=69 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — portable X-ray; research metal.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Thulium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f13 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. dense +3 lanthanide.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Thulium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; high melting among the late lanthanides If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from erbia.

elements.history:
Per Teodor Cleve separated thulium from erbia in 1879, after holmium had already been removed. He named it for Thule, the classical name for a far northern land. It was the scarcest of the stable rare earths he was sorting, and the samples were tiny.

Thulium has no large-scale use. A portable X-ray source based on thulium-170 is one of the few technologies that asks for the pure element.
elements.howDiscovered:
After holmium had been taken out of erbia, Per Teodor Cleve continued the crystallization. In 1879 a small fraction remained whose spectrum was neither holmium nor erbium. The oxide was pale, the amount was tiny, and the bands were its own.

Thulium was the last of the major fractions Cleve sorted from that earth. The method added nothing new in kind. It was fractional crystallization carried past the point where most chemists would have stopped, on a sample that was almost gone.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Thulium-169 is the only stable isotope, and it is mainly a slow-process product of giant stars, unlike several of its rare-earth neighbors. The rapid process contributes a smaller share. The capture path passes through thulium on the way toward lead.

Thulium is one of the least abundant rare earths partly because it is odd-numbered and partly because capture does not stall on it. The thulium in a small X-ray source is that giant-star isotope.

trivia.title: A Name From the Far North
trivia.summary: The chemist who isolated this earth reached past his own city and named it for a legendary land at the edge of the map.
trivia.story: Per Teodor Cleve named thulium for Thule, the classical name for a far northern land at the edge of the known world. Holmium had taken Stockholm, and thulium took the mythic north, which suited an element found in tiny amounts at the end of a long separation. The name is geography turning into poetry. Thule may never have been one real island, and the element is very real and very scarce. Cleve attached a rumor of distance to a salt he could barely accumulate. The far north, in this case, was a place in a book and a speck in a dish.

trivia.title: The Scarcest of Those Earths
trivia.summary: After holmium had been taken out of the mixture, one more earth remained, and the samples of it were painfully small.
trivia.story: Cleve separated thulium from erbia in 1879, after holmium had already been removed. It was the scarcest of the stable rare earths he was sorting, and the samples were tiny. A discovery can be certain and still look like almost nothing in the vial. Spectral evidence and a slight residue had to carry the claim. Students who picture discovery as a gleaming bar of metal will miss what Cleve actually had. He had a trace that behaved as its own earth, at the end of a queue of separations, and he had a name ready for it.

trivia.title: X-rays From a Small Source
trivia.summary: Hospitals have large machines for pictures of bone, but some jobs need an X-ray source that can travel, and one isotope took that role.
trivia.story: Thulium has no large everyday industry, which makes its one famous technical use stand out. A portable X-ray source based on the isotope thulium-170 can take pictures where a hospital machine cannot go. The use is the point of the story, not a plan for building the source. A scarce element, isolated in traces in 1879, turns out to matter when the device must be small and the radiation must be dependable. Cleve's far-northern name sits on a tool for field pictures. Most of the periodic table never gets asked to do that particular job.

trivia.title: An Element Without a Crowd
trivia.summary: Neighbors on the row went into magnets, phosphors, and glass cables, while this one remained a specialist with almost no mass market.
trivia.story: Abundance decides careers on the rare-earth row. Elements that mines can supply by the tonne find their way into magnets and lamps. Thulium, scarce even among that group, never gathered a large-scale use. The portable X-ray source is one of the few technologies that specifically asks for it. That quietness is simply what scarcity looks like, and Cleve's tiny samples predicted the modern situation with accidental accuracy. The element remains a small-print metal, known to specialists and to students who like the legend of Thule.

trivia.title: Thule on the Periodic Table
trivia.summary: Ancient writers used Thule for the most distant north they could imagine, and a nineteenth-century chemist borrowed that distance for a speck of salt.
trivia.story: Greek and Roman geographers spoke of Thule as a land beyond the familiar seas, more direction than address. Cleve borrowed that word in 1879 for an earth he had just distinguished from holmium. The borrowing fits a chemist in Stockholm reaching for a name more remote than his own city. Holmium was home, and thulium was the horizon. Nothing in the oxide is icy or nautical, of course. The romance is entirely in the label, and it has kept a scarce element memorable long after the vial Cleve held was gone.

applications.title: Portable X-ray
applications.body: A sealed thulium isotope has been used as a small X-ray source where a full X-ray tube is impractical.

applications.title: Lasers
applications.body: Thulium-doped fiber lasers emit in the infrared and are used in surgery and in materials work.

applications.title: One of the scarcer rare earths
applications.body: Thulium is a small fraction of rare-earth ores. There is no bulk consumer product made of the metal.

elements.name: Ytterbium

summary.beginner:
Ytterbium is element 70, a soft rare-earth metal used in some stainless steels and in atomic clocks. Most people never see the pure metal.

Its symbol is Yb. At room temperature ytterbium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

Ytterbium can form a +2 ion more easily than most of its neighbors, which makes its chemistry a little special. The clock use is about particular atoms, not about a bar of metal.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral ytterbium atom has 70 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Ytterbium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Ytterbium has a filled 4f shell in the atom, and both +3 and +2 matter.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 8, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +3.

Small additions change the grain of some steels. Ytterbium-171 is an atomic-clock isotope. The +2 ion is colorless and resembles a heavy alkaline earth.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Ytterbium (Z = 70) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 6s2. The filled 4f14 shell stabilizes Yb2+, analogous to Eu2+.

Optical lattice clocks use a narrow transition of ytterbium atoms, a metrology experiment rather than a metallurgical one.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +2. The one courses meet most often is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Ytterbium: say the name, write Yb, find Z=70 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — stainless alloys and clocks.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Ytterbium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3, +2. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. full 4f¹⁴; can be +2.

discovery.text: Separated from erbia as ytterbia.

elements.history:
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac separated a new earth from crude erbia in 1878 and named it ytterbium, the fourth element named for Ytterby. Georges Urbain and Carl Auer von Welsbach later showed that Marignac’s ytterbia still contained lutetium.

Ytterbium can be +2 as well as +3, a consequence of the filled 4f shell. The optical clock transition of ytterbium-171 is one of the most precise frequency standards now in use.
elements.howDiscovered:
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac, in 1878, crystallized crude erbia as the nitrate and found that the mother liquor held a colorless earth. Its atomic weight and its spectrum differed from erbium’s. The pink had stayed in the crystals. The colorless earth had stayed in the solution.

That earth still contained lutetium, which Urbain and von Welsbach separated in 1907. Marignac’s discovery was real even so: a colorless oxide where erbium’s is pink, obtained by leaving the pink salt to crystallize and examining what did not.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Ytterbium’s isotopes need both the slow process and the rapid process. Ytterbium-174, 172, and 173 are abundant and mixed. Ytterbium-168 and ytterbium-170 include a proton-rich contribution and are less common.

The ytterbium in an alloy or a laser is that blend. It sits just before the last slow-process climb through lutetium and hafnium into the lead peak.

trivia.title: The Fourth Name From Ytterby
trivia.summary: A Swiss chemist drew one more earth out of crude erbia and gave it a village name that three other elements were already sharing.
trivia.story: Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac separated a new earth from crude erbia in 1878 and named it ytterbium. It was the fourth element named for Ytterby, after yttrium, terbium, and erbium. The quarry's name had been stretched, sliced, and reused until it covered a whole neighborhood of the table. Marignac's choice was deliberate continuity with that story, and a new salt joined a family of labels from one Swedish pit. The village itself stayed small, while its syllables traveled farther than any cartload of feldspar.

trivia.title: A Twin Still Hiding Inside
trivia.summary: The earth called ytterbium looked finished, and then two later chemists showed that one more element was still sitting in it.
trivia.story: Marignac's ytterbia was a triumph in 1878, and it was not the end of the separations. Georges Urbain and Carl Auer von Welsbach later showed that this earth still contained lutetium. The pattern is the whole history of the rare earths in miniature. A chemist isolates what the tools of the day can isolate, names it, and a finer method finds a roommate. Ytterbium kept its name and its place, while lutetium moved into the next box. The quarry element had been a house with a hidden tenant.

trivia.title: A Filled Shell and Two Charges
trivia.summary: A completed shell of electrons lets this lanthanide do something most of its neighbors resist, and the second charge follows from that fullness.
trivia.story: Ytterbium can be an ion of charge two as well as the usual charge of three. The reason is a filled 4f shell, a completed set of electrons that makes the extra arrangement unusually calm. Most lanthanides cling to the charge of three and make the alternatives costly. Ytterbium's filled shell opens the door, which sounds bookish until it explains why the element's chemistry branches. Marignac separated an earth, and the shell structure, understood much later, explains why that earth does not behave like a strict copy of its neighbors.

trivia.title: The Clock Made of Light
trivia.summary: Timekeeping moved from pendulums to atoms, and one isotope of a Ytterby element became one of the steadiest ticks now in use.
trivia.story: An optical clock uses the vibration of light from a chosen atom as its tick, and ytterbium-171 provides one of the most precise frequency standards now in use. The isotope is cooled, trapped, and questioned with lasers, a scene far from Marignac's crystallizing dishes. Precision is the use. A metal named for a feldspar quarry helps define the second more finely than any gear could. Students do not need the laser layout to grasp the plot. An element once known as a contamination in erbia became a standard of time.

trivia.title: Four Labels One Quarry
trivia.summary: Yttrium, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium sound like a rhyme for a reason, and the reason is a single pit outside Stockholm.
trivia.story: Say the four names aloud and the echo is the point, because yttrium, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium all come from Ytterby. Ytterbium is the fourth and the most literal, the village name worn almost whole. The minerals from that quarry launched rare-earth chemistry, and the labels are the souvenirs. Marignac's 1878 separation added the last of those four words. Later work showed his earth still hid lutetium, but lutetium took a Roman city's name instead. Ytterby stopped at four, which is already an astonishing haul for one hole in the ground.

applications.title: Atomic clocks
applications.body: One isotope of ytterbium is used in some of the most accurate atomic clocks. The clock uses trapped atoms, not a piece of metal.

applications.title: Stainless steel
applications.body: A small addition of ytterbium improves the grain and the strength of some stainless steels.

applications.title: A softer rare earth
applications.body: Ytterbium metal is softer than its neighbors and can form a +2 ion. Both facts matter to chemists more than to a hardware store.

elements.name: Lutetium

summary.beginner:
Lutetium is element 71, the last of the lanthanide row. It is scarce and expensive, and it turns up in a few catalysts and in detectors for medical scans.

Its symbol is Lu. At room temperature lutetium is a solid. It is a lanthanide, one of the rare-earth metals in the row under the main table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 6.

Lutetium behaves a bit more like an ordinary metal of the middle block than like the lanthanides before it. There is still no everyday object made of it.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral lutetium atom has 71 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Lutetium is a solid lanthanide in period 6, in the row under the main table. Lutetium is the end of the lanthanide contraction, usually Lu3+, and it is used in PET-scan crystals and in some catalysts.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d1 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

Lutetium oxyorthosilicate is a detector crystal. The metal is sometimes argued to be the first of the next d-block column rather than a lanthanide. Both labels appear in textbooks.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Lutetium (Z = 71) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d1 6s2. The 4f shell is full, so Lu3+ has no f electrons left and the chemistry looks like a group 3 metal.

The detector crystal uses the dense host, not an f-f glow from lutetium itself.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. The lanthanides are hard to separate because the outer electrons are almost the same. The 4f electrons sit inside and change the chemistry only a little from one element to the next.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Lutetium: say the name, write Lu, find Z=71 on the table, note the family (Lanthanide), and connect it to one real use — catalysts and phosphors.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Lutetium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d1 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. d-block-like after 4f¹⁴.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Lutetium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; sometimes classed as a d-block metal If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from ytterbia; named for Lutetia (Paris).

elements.history:
In 1907 Georges Urbain, Carl Auer von Welsbach, and Charles James independently separated the last rare earth from ytterbia. Urbain named it lutetium, for Lutetia, the Roman name of Paris. Von Welsbach’s name cassiopeium persisted in some German literature. Urbain’s name is the one IUPAC kept, with Urbain credited.

Lutetium closes the lanthanide series. With a filled 4f shell it behaves more like a group-3 metal, which is why some tables argue about whether it, not lanthanum, belongs under scandium and yttrium.
elements.howDiscovered:
Georges Urbain crystallized ytterbium nitrate many times and watched the spark spectrum. In 1907 the mother liquors enriched a set of lines that ytterbium did not have, and the atomic weight of the enriched oxide rose. Carl Auer von Welsbach and Charles James arrived at the same separation independently.

The evidence was a spectrum that grew stronger as the crystallization rejected ytterbium, plus a density and an atomic weight that moved with the lines. Lutetium was the last rare earth separated by this classical method. There was nothing left in the liquor that still split.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Lutetium-175 is almost all of natural lutetium, and it is mainly a slow-process product. Lutetium-176 is a few percent, with a half-life near 37 billion years, and it is a thermometer. In a giant star, the temperature decides how much lutetium-176 survives instead of capturing another neutron.

Lutetium-176 decays to hafnium-176. The pair dates rocks and diagnoses the stars that ran the slow process. The lutetium in a catalyst is mostly the stable 175, with that clock isotope inside it.

trivia.title: Three Chemists One Earth
trivia.summary: Around 1907, three chemists each pulled the last rare earth out of ytterbia, and the question of who arrived first became its own dispute.
trivia.story: Georges Urbain, Carl Auer von Welsbach, and Charles James each separated the last rare earth from ytterbia around 1907. They were working independently, which is how a priority dispute is born, three laboratories reaching the same hidden salt. Urbain named the element lutetium and received the credit that the international tables kept. James and von Welsbach had real claims, and the argument was about priority rather than about whether the earth existed. The last rare earth arrived as a quarrel as much as a discovery, which fits an element that had been hiding inside another element's bottle.

trivia.title: The Roman Name of Paris
trivia.summary: The name that won the dispute looks back to Roman Paris, a city label chosen by the chemist whose word the official tables kept.
trivia.story: Urbain called the new element lutetium, taking the name from Lutetia, the old Roman name of Paris. A capital city joined Stockholm, Ytterby, and the Rhine as a place-name on this stretch of the table. The choice was patriotic in a quiet way, a French chemist signing his find with his city's older name. Von Welsbach had a different label ready, but Lutetia is the one students learn. Paris therefore sits in the last box of the lanthanides, a long way from the Swedish quarry where the parent earth was first dug.

trivia.title: The Name That Lost
trivia.summary: A second name circulated in German writings for years, and then the official tables closed the contest in favor of the Paris label.
trivia.story: Carl Auer von Welsbach called the same new element cassiopeium, naming it after the constellation Cassiopeia. The name persisted in some German literature even after other countries had settled on lutetium. A lost name can linger in textbooks the way an old street name lingers on a map. The international body kept Urbain's name lutetium and credited Urbain with the discovery, so cassiopeium lost the official contest. Students who meet the older word in a German paper are seeing the dispute still warm on the page, long after the element itself had been accepted.

trivia.title: Closing the Lanthanide Row
trivia.summary: With this box filled, the rare-earth row was complete, and a filled electron shell started an argument about where the element belongs.
trivia.story: Lutetium closes the lanthanide series, the long row that begins after barium and ends before hafnium. With a filled 4f shell it behaves more like a group 3 metal than like a typical rare earth in the middle of the row. Some tables therefore place lutetium, alongside scandium and yttrium, in the main group 3 column. Other tables leave lanthanum there and tuck lutetium at the end of the f block. The dispute is about arrangement, both sides looking at the same filled shell, and an element from a 1907 priority fight is still rearranging the furniture of the table.

trivia.title: Found Inside Ytterbium's Earth
trivia.summary: The parent earth had already been named and filed, and the last lanthanide was still inside it, waiting on a finer separation.
trivia.story: Ytterbium's earth, separated by Marignac in 1878, still held one more element that nobody had yet named. Urbain, von Welsbach, and James were finishing a separation that the previous generation's crystallizations could not complete. Pushed further than before, fractional crystallization let the last tenant move out into salts of its own. That is why lutetium feels like an ending rather than a beginning on this row. The rare-earth story that began at Ytterby closed when the hidden metal in ytterbia finally received its own box and its own argument about a name.

applications.title: PET scanners
applications.body: A crystal containing lutetium detects the gamma rays in a PET scan. The dense crystal is the use, not a lutetium tool.

applications.title: Catalysts
applications.body: A few petroleum catalysts use lutetium compounds. The amounts are small and the metal is expensive.

applications.title: The end of the row
applications.body: Lutetium is the last lanthanide, and it is scarce. Its uses stay in instruments and catalysts.

elements.name: Hafnium

summary.beginner:
Hafnium is element 72, a metal that absorbs neutrons, which is the opposite of zirconium in that one important way. Nuclear control rods use it, and it forms extremely hard carbides.

Its symbol is Hf. At room temperature hafnium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 4. In class those are called period 6 and group 4.

Hafnium hides in zirconium ores because the two metals are so alike. Separating them matters: one is for fuel cladding, the other for stopping neutrons.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral hafnium atom has 72 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Hafnium is a solid transition metal in period 6 and group 4. Hafnium is zirconium's twin after the lanthanide contraction, except that hafnium captures neutrons strongly.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d2 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 10, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4.

HfC is among the highest-melting materials known. Reactor zirconium has to be freed of hafnium before it is used as cladding.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Hafnium (Z = 72) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d2 6s2. Chemically, Hf4+ and Zr4+ are nearly the same size, so classical separation is hard.

Neutron capture is a nuclear difference, not a valence difference. Relativistic effects on the 6s electrons add to that similarity.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Hafnium: say the name, write Hf, find Z=72 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — nuclear control rods and plasma blades.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Hafnium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d2 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +4. It sits in group 4. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. twin of zirconium after lanthanide contraction.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Hafnium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; very high melting; HfC ceramics If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found in Norwegian zircon by X-ray spectroscopy; predicted as ekazirconium.

elements.history:
Mendeleev’s table implied a missing heavy analog of zirconium. Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy found it in 1923 by X-ray spectroscopy of Norwegian zircon, in Niels Bohr’s laboratory in Copenhagen. They named it hafnium, from Hafnia, the Latin name of the city. It had been hiding in every zirconium mineral.

The two metals are hard to separate, which is exactly why reactor-grade zirconium has to be cleaned of hafnium. Hafnium carbide is among the most refractory materials known.
elements.howDiscovered:
Henry Moseley’s X-ray work had given each atomic number a predictable wavelength. Element 72, still missing, had to sit under zirconium if Bohr’s arrangement was right, and its K lines could be calculated before anyone had seen them. Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy dissolved Norwegian zircon in Copenhagen and concentrated the fraction that was not zirconium.

In 1923 the X-ray plate showed the predicted lines. Optical spectra had failed because zirconium and the new element are almost inseparable by chemistry and their arc lines are a forest. The discovery instrument was the X-ray tube. The sample was an ordinary zircon, which had contained the element all along.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Hafnium is mixed. The slow process and the rapid process both feed it, and hafnium-176 has an extra source: the decay of lutetium-176. That is why the lutetium-hafnium pair dates rocks and also traces the slow process through the Galaxy.

Hafnium-174 is proton-rich and rare. The hafnium that must be separated from zirconium for reactor cladding is the ordinary mix, the two neutron-capture channels plus that slow radioactive trickle from lutetium.

trivia.title: Hiding in Every Zirconium Rock
trivia.summary: Chemists thought their zirconium was pure, and a sister metal had been sitting in those samples the whole time, almost impossible to notice.
trivia.story: Hafnium had been hiding in every zirconium mineral chemists handled, a passenger nobody had learned to see. The two metals are so alike that ordinary analysis treated the pair as a single element called zirconium. A jar on the shelf was quietly a mixture, and the mixture was simply the natural state of the ore. That camouflage explains the long delay, because the missing element was never actually rare inside those rocks. The discovery felt less like finding a new mountain and more like noticing a companion who had been in every old photograph.

trivia.title: X-rays in Bohr's City
trivia.summary: Two researchers in a Copenhagen laboratory examined Norwegian zircon with X-rays and gave the new metal the Latin name of that city.
trivia.story: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy went looking in Norwegian zircon, in Niels Bohr's laboratory in Copenhagen. They used X-ray spectroscopy, reading the characteristic lines of the atoms rather than waiting for a new color in a test tube. In 1923 the characteristic lines of element 72 appeared clearly enough to end the search. They named it hafnium, from Hafnia, the Latin name of Copenhagen. A metal that had hidden inside zirconium was identified by its light, in the city whose old name it still carries.

trivia.title: The Gap Under Zirconium
trivia.summary: The table had implied a heavy partner for zirconium, and a newer theory of electrons told the searchers which minerals were worth opening.
trivia.story: Mendeleev's table had already implied a missing heavy analog of zirconium, an empty seat under a familiar metal. Bohr's newer picture of the electrons went further and predicted that element 72 would closely resemble zirconium. The older hope, that it might be another rare earth, pointed at the wrong neighborhood. That prediction sent Coster and de Hevesy into zircon ores instead of back into another round of yttria. Theory told the chemists where the hider was standing, and the X-ray lines in Copenhagen answered a gap the table had advertised for decades.

trivia.title: The Impurity Reactors Cannot Keep
trivia.summary: Nuclear engineers need zirconium that lets neutrons pass, and the sister metal in the ore does the opposite, so the two must be parted.
trivia.story: Zirconium is valued in reactors because it lets neutrons pass, which is what a fuel cladding should do. Hafnium, its constant companion in the ore, swallows neutrons instead. Reactor-grade zirconium therefore has to be cleaned of hafnium, a separation required because the two metals spent geological time mixed together. The same likeness that hid hafnium from nineteenth-century chemists becomes a strict specification in a modern plant. The lesson stops at that outcome, with one metal allowed near the fuel and the other removed before the parts are built.

trivia.title: A Carbide That Barely Melts
trivia.summary: Even among materials chosen for extreme heat, a compound of this metal is named when engineers want something that almost refuses to melt.
trivia.story: Hafnium carbide sits among the most refractory materials known, substances that stay solid when almost everything else has melted. The parent metal was easy to overlook inside zirconium, and its carbide is hard to overlook once heat becomes the problem. Furnace linings and the hottest experimental hardware are the conversations where this compound comes up. Coster and de Hevesy were reading X-ray lines in 1923, not sketching a nozzle or a crucible. The path from a Copenhagen spectrum to a material that stays solid in extreme fire is one of the longer journeys on the table.

applications.title: Control rods
applications.body: Hafnium absorbs neutrons, so it is used in control rods that regulate a reactor. That is the opposite job from zirconium cladding.

applications.title: Very hard materials
applications.body: Hafnium carbide is among the most heat-resistant materials known. It is studied for surfaces that must survive extreme temperature.

applications.title: Separated on purpose
applications.body: Hafnium has to be removed from the zirconium used in fuel cladding. The two metals are chemical twins with opposite nuclear jobs.

elements.name: Tantalum

summary.beginner:
Tantalum is element 73, a metal that resists almost every acid. Tiny capacitors in phones use it, and surgeons use it because the body tolerates it.

Its symbol is Ta. At room temperature tantalum is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 5. In class those are called period 6 and group 5.

A phone capacitor contains a little tantalum, not a visible piece. The same resistance to corrosion is why a surgical implant can be made from it.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral tantalum atom has 73 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Tantalum is a solid transition metal in period 6 and group 5. Tantalum is extremely corrosion-resistant, and Ta2O5 is the insulator in tantalum capacitors.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d3 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 11, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5.

The +5 oxidation state dominates. The metal shrugs off aqua regia at room temperature, which is a famous classroom fact and a real industrial advantage.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Tantalum (Z = 73) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d3 6s2. The capacitor is a sintered powder with a Ta2O5 dielectric film grown on it, so the oxide, not the bulk metal, stores the charge.

Biocompatibility follows from the same passive oxide.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Tantalum: say the name, write Ta, find Z=73 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — capacitors and surgical tools.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Tantalum: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d3 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +5. It sits in group 5. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. extremely corrosion resistant.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Tantalum: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Ta₂O₅ dielectric films If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from tantalite; named for Tantalus.

elements.history:
Anders Gustaf Ekeberg isolated a new metal from a Finnish mineral in 1802 and named it tantalum, for Tantalus, because the oxide would not drink acid. For decades many chemists, including Wollaston, thought tantalum and columbium were the same element. Heinrich Rose separated the two stories in the 1840s.

Tantalum’s oxide film is an excellent dielectric, which put the metal into capacitors. It is also almost immune to body fluids, so it is a surgical metal.
elements.howDiscovered:
Anders Gustaf Ekeberg analyzed yttrotantalite from Ytterby and a heavy mineral from Kimito in Finland. In 1802 he obtained an oxide that would not dissolve in the acids that dissolved the look-alike columbium earth, even when he fused the sample and tried again. He took the insolubility as the property that defined a new metal.

William Hyde Wollaston later argued the two oxides were the same, and the argument lasted decades. Heinrich Rose and then Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac separated them, Marignac by the different solubilities of the potassium double fluorides. The original discovery was an oxide that refused the acids. The confirmation was a fluoride crystallization that finally divided the two metals.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Tantalum-181 is almost all of the element, and it is mainly a slow-process product of giant stars. Tantalum-180 is a trace. The atom found in nature is a long-lived excited state, the rarest primordial isotope, and the ground state is short-lived. Neutrino reactions, or the gamma process, are the accounts offered for that trace.

The tantalum in a capacitor is the common isotope, the giant-star product. The rare isomer rides in the same metal at a very small fraction and does not change the bulk origin.

trivia.title: The Metal That Would Not Drink
trivia.summary: A Swedish chemist found a new metal in a Finnish mineral and named it for a mythical king whose punishment was endless, unsatisfied thirst.
trivia.story: Anders Gustaf Ekeberg isolated a new metal from a Finnish mineral in 1802. He named it tantalum, for Tantalus, who in the Greek story stood in a pool he could not drink. The oxide would not take up acid, as if it too refused the drink placed in front of it. A familiar myth made that chemical stubbornness easy for a classroom to remember. Students who forget the Finnish ore can still remember a thirsty king, and from him remember an oxide that would not dissolve when chemists insisted.

trivia.title: Decades of One Element or Two
trivia.summary: A respected chemist decided two stubborn metals were the same, and it took another generation before the pair was properly untangled.
trivia.story: For decades many chemists, William Wollaston among them, thought tantalum and columbium were a single element. The metals behave like twins, and early samples were messy enough to excuse the mistake. Heinrich Rose separated the two stories in the 1840s and showed that niobium, long called columbium in America, was distinct from Ekeberg's tantalum. Crossed labels filled the textbooks for years while the argument lasted. Tantalum kept the mythic name, and the other twin had to survive a naming quarrel of its own before niobium became the settled word.

trivia.title: A Film Inside the Capacitor
trivia.summary: A thin skin of oxide on this metal stores electric charge unusually well, which is why tiny components in modern circuits depend on it.
trivia.story: Tantalum grows an oxide film that is an excellent dielectric, a thin insulator able to hold electric charge. That talent put the metal into capacitors, the small parts that store a brief electrical pulse in phones and other circuits. Those pieces stay small because the metal is costly, and a thin film is exactly what a small part wants. Ekeberg's stubborn oxide, the one that would not take up acid, becomes an advantage when a stable skin is the whole point. A myth about refusal becomes a component that must keep its charge, and the circuit board repeats the chemical story from 1802.

trivia.title: A Metal Surgeons Could Trust
trivia.summary: Implants have to survive the chemistry of a living body, and this metal's indifference to those fluids made it a material for surgery.
trivia.story: Body fluids attack many metals, and a piece left inside a person has to survive without dissolving as the years pass. Tantalum is almost immune to those fluids, which made it a surgical metal for devices meant to stay. The corrosion resistance is the practical face of the oxide that refused acid in Ekeberg's laboratory. He saw stubbornness in a Finnish mineral, and surgeons later saw a surface that living chemistry could not easily ruin. The same film links a rock described in 1802 to an implant designed to be quiet inside the body.

trivia.title: Pipes That Acids Do Not Eat
trivia.summary: Chemical plants needed vessels that harsh acids would leave alone, and the metal named for a thirsty king turned out almost indifferent.
trivia.story: Tantalum's refusal to react goes beyond the oxide film inside a capacitor or the surface of an implant. In chemical plants the metal is built into equipment that must stand in hot aggressive acids without being eaten away. The corrosion resistance that surgeons trust is the same trait a factory trusts when a vessel has to last. Ekeberg chose Tantalus because the oxide would not take up acid, and industry later chose the metal for that same stubbornness. A laboratory disappointment in 1802 became a specification, and the myth still fits equipment that harsh acids do not consume.

applications.title: Phone capacitors
applications.body: A tiny tantalum capacitor stores charge in phones and computers. The insulator is a thin layer of tantalum oxide on tantalum powder.

applications.title: Surgery
applications.body: Tantalum is used in some implants and skull plates because the body tolerates the metal and it does not corrode.

applications.title: Acid plants
applications.body: Tantalum equipment survives hot acids that would destroy steel. The metal is reserved for those harsh jobs.

elements.name: Tungsten

summary.beginner:
Tungsten is element 74, the metal with the highest melting point. The filament of an old light bulb was tungsten, and it is still the hard tip in many cutting tools.

Its symbol is W. At room temperature tungsten is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 6. In class those are called period 6 and group 6.

Tungsten wire can be white-hot without melting, which is why it lit bulbs. Mixed with carbon it becomes tungsten carbide, hard enough to cut steel.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral tungsten atom has 74 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Tungsten is a solid transition metal in period 6 and group 6. Tungsten has the highest melting point of the metals, and WC is the hard carbide in cutting tools.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d4 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 12, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +6.

The filament works because the metal is strong even near 3000 K and evaporates slowly in a sealed bulb. The carbide is a compound, much harder than the pure metal.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Tungsten (Z = 74) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d4 6s2. The melting point, about 3695 K, reflects strong metallic bonding in a 5d metal.

Cemented carbide is WC grains in a cobalt binder. The bulb filament is the pure metal, a different microstructure entirely.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +6. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Tungsten: say the name, write W, find Z=74 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — light-bulb wire and hard alloys.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Tungsten: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d4 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +6. It sits in group 6. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. highest melting point of the metals.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Tungsten: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; WC carbides; dense d-block packing If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Reduced from wolframite; Scheele had prepared the oxide.

elements.history:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele prepared tungstic acid from the Swedish mineral tungsten, heavy stone, in 1781. The brothers Juan José and Fausto Elhuyar reduced a related ore, wolframite, to the metal in 1783 and are credited with the discovery. The symbol W is from wolfram. The English name tungsten kept Scheele’s mineral.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, which is why it was the filament of the incandescent lamp. Tungsten carbide is the hard edge of cutting tools.
elements.howDiscovered:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele digested the mineral then called tungsten, calcium tungstate, with acid in 1781 and obtained a new acidic oxide, distinct from molybdic acid. He did not reduce it. In 1783 Juan José and Fausto Elhuyar dissolved wolframite, precipitated the same acid, mixed it with charcoal, and heated it. A hard, dense metal remained.

The metal regenerated the acid when it was oxidized, and the acid was the one Scheele had described. The discovery of the element as a metal is the charcoal reduction. The discovery of its acid is Scheele’s digestion of the heavy stone.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Tungsten is a mix of the slow and rapid processes. Tungsten-182, 183, 184, and 186 are all significant. Tungsten-180 is proton-rich and rare. Tungsten-182 has a further chapter: hafnium-182, with a half-life near 9 million years, was alive in the early solar system and decayed to tungsten-182.

The excess of that daughter in some meteorites times how quickly the first planetary bodies formed. The tungsten in a filament is the neutron-capture blend. The extinct-radioactivity signal is readable only in isotope ratios of the oldest samples.

trivia.title: The Stone That Was Heavy
trivia.summary: Swedish miners had a name for an unusually dense rock, and a chemist turned that rock into a new acid before anyone held the pure metal.
trivia.story: Carl Wilhelm Scheele, in 1781, prepared a new acid from a Swedish mineral the miners called tungsten, a name meaning heavy stone. The rock was dense enough to surprise a hand that had expected the weight of ordinary stone. Scheele held tungstic acid, a clear chemical clue, and still did not have a bead of metal he could hammer. The English name of the element remembers that heavy stone and the mineral Scheele used. The isolation of the metal itself would come from another ore a year or two later, so the weight in the palm stayed the opening chapter.

trivia.title: Brothers and the Wolf Ore
trivia.summary: Two brothers reduced a different ore to a real metal, and the letter on the table still comes from that ore's older name.
trivia.story: The brothers Juan José and Fausto Elhuyar reduced the ore wolframite to the metal in 1783, and they are credited with the discovery. The symbol W comes from wolfram, the element's other name, taken from that same ore. English kept Scheele's word tungsten, heavy stone, while several other languages stayed with wolfram. Two names for one gray metal have trailed students ever since the brothers' reduction in Spain. Scheele supplied an acid and the English word, and the Elhuyars supplied the metal itself together with the letter in the equations.

trivia.title: The Filament That Stayed Solid
trivia.summary: Lamps needed a wire that could glow white-hot without collapsing, and a metal with a record melting point finally made that wire practical.
trivia.story: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, so a thin wire can glow white-hot in a bulb without collapsing into a droplet. Earlier filament materials sagged, burned through, or simply broke after a short life. Early in the twentieth century, Coolidge's ductile tungsten made fine, durable filaments practical, and incandescent lamps spread into ordinary rooms. The bulb put an obscure metal, first known as a heavy stone, into daily life on a huge scale. Newer lamps have taken much of that household job, and the melting point remains the record of a metal that keeps its shape in extreme heat.

trivia.title: Ore That Wartime Governments Wanted
trivia.summary: Hard steel needed a scarce ore during a world war, and much of the supply sat in two neutral countries that both sides tried to sway.
trivia.story: During the Second World War, tungsten was wanted for hard steel and for cutting tools that had to survive heat. Much of the ore that could be purchased sat in Portugal and Spain, neutral countries courted over their shipments. The tension stayed diplomatic and commercial, a contest about cargoes rather than a scene of combat. Engineers on each side needed the metal in tough alloys, and governments tried to guide where the ore would go. A heavy stone known since the eighteenth century had become a strategic mineral, a wartime chapter told at the level of trade.

trivia.title: The Hard Edge of a Tool
trivia.summary: Workshop tools that chew metal and rock need an edge that stays sharp, and a compound of this element became that durable edge.
trivia.story: Tungsten carbide is the hard edge on many cutting tools, a compound that keeps its bite when ordinary steel would have dulled. Drill bits and machining inserts rely on that hardness every day in ordinary workshops. The element that once filled light bulbs also arms the machines that cut metal and the tools that grind rock. Scheele's heavy stone therefore lives in two rooms, one remembered as a glow inside glass and one still throwing sparks at a lathe. A record melting point and a fierce hardness are the same reluctance to yield, shown once in a filament and once along a cutting edge.

applications.title: Light-bulb filaments
applications.body: The wire in an old incandescent bulb is tungsten. It can be white-hot without melting.

applications.title: Cutting tools
applications.body: Tungsten carbide is the hard tip on drill bits and lathe tools. It is a compound, much harder than the pure metal.

applications.title: The highest melting point
applications.body: Among the metals, tungsten melts at the highest temperature. That is why it survives where other wires would fail.

elements.name: Rhenium

summary.beginner:
Rhenium is element 75, a very rare metal that stays strong at the temperatures inside a jet engine. It was one of the last stable elements chemists discovered.

Its symbol is Re. At room temperature rhenium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 7. In class those are called period 6 and group 7.

There is very little rhenium in Earth's crust, so it is used in thin layers and in alloys, not as big parts. It lets turbine blades run hotter.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral rhenium atom has 75 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Rhenium is a solid transition metal in period 6 and group 7. Rhenium is a refractory metal, and Re2O7 shows the group oxidation state +7.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d5 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 13, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +7.

Nickel superalloys for turbines contain a few percent of rhenium. The pure metal is dense and has a melting point second only to tungsten among the metals.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Rhenium (Z = 75) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d5 6s2. Re2O7 is volatile and is the structural relative of Mn2O7, a reminder of the group.

The alloy use is solid-solution strengthening at temperatures where most metals have already softened.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +7. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Rhenium: say the name, write Re, find Z=75 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — jet-engine alloys.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Rhenium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d5 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +7. It sits in group 7. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. refractory; +7 in Re₂O₇.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Rhenium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; one of the last stable elements found If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found in molybdenite by X-ray spectroscopy.

elements.history:
The gap under manganese stayed empty longer than Mendeleev expected. In 1925 Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, and Otto Berg detected element 75 by X-ray spectroscopy in platinum ores and molybdenite, and named it rhenium, for the Rhine, Rhenus. It was the last stable element to be discovered.

Rhenium is rarer in the crust than many radioactive elements. A few percent of it in a nickel superalloy is what lets a jet-engine turbine blade run hotter.
elements.howDiscovered:
Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, and Otto Berg concentrated large masses of molybdenite, columbite, and platinum residues, looking for the two gaps under manganese. In 1925 their X-ray plates showed lines at the wavelengths predicted for element 75. They pursued the fraction chemically until a weighable oxide and then a metal could be prepared.

Their claim for element 43 did not survive. The claim for 75 did, because the lines repeated in different ores and the chemistry could be carried far enough to yield a sample. Rhenium was discovered by an X-ray wavelength in a concentrate, and confirmed by isolating the oxide. It was the last stable element found.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Rhenium-187 is most of natural rhenium, and it is mainly a rapid-process product. It decays to osmium-187 with a half-life near 41 billion years. Rhenium-185 takes a slow-process share. The pair is the rhenium-osmium clock, used on iron meteorites and on the age of the Galaxy’s heavy elements.

The rhenium in a superalloy is this mostly rapid-process metal, still slowly becoming osmium. The decay is irrelevant in a workshop and useful, over billions of years, for dating.

trivia.title: A Line From the Rhine
trivia.summary: Three researchers searching ores with X-rays found the missing metal and named it for a great European river that runs past several nations.
trivia.story: In 1925 Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, and Otto Berg detected element 75 by X-ray spectroscopy in platinum ores and in molybdenite. The lines were the evidence, a light-signature of the same family that had revealed hafnium two years earlier. They named the new element rhenium, for the river Rhine, whose Latin name is Rhenus. A European river lent its name to a metal found at the end of a long empty seat under manganese. The discovery arrived as a spectrum convincing enough to close a gap that had stood open for decades.

trivia.title: The Last Stable Discovery
trivia.summary: Elements found after this one are radioactive in a way classrooms cannot ignore, and this metal was the last discovery that still had a stable form.
trivia.story: Rhenium was the last stable element to be discovered, a quiet superlative attached to the work of 1925. The boxes that remained after that year belonged to elements with no permanent isotope. Promethium and the artificial elements made later have to be produced, and they decay. Rhenium can sit in a bottle the way iron can, which felt almost old-fashioned for a find so late. It is a hinge in the story, the last discovery that still offered a form stable enough to keep on a shelf.

trivia.title: Mendeleev's Empty Manganese Slot
trivia.summary: The table's architect had left a placeholder under manganese, a paper name that waited decades for a real element to claim the seat.
trivia.story: Mendeleev left a space two places under manganese and called the missing metal dvi-manganese, a placeholder rather than a sample. He expected a heavier element with manganese's family traits and a much higher atomic mass. The space stayed empty far longer than that confident nineteenth-century grid had suggested. Noddack, Tacke, and Berg finally set rhenium in the seat in 1925, and the placeholder could retire. A river's name replaced the theoretical nickname, which is what a sound prediction is for, a seat kept until the evidence arrives.

trivia.title: A Claim That Did Not Hold
trivia.summary: Before the accepted discovery, a researcher in Japan announced an element under another name, and that claim is not counted as this metal.
trivia.story: Students sometimes meet an earlier claim, Ogawa's nipponium, and wonder if element 75 was found before 1925. That earlier claim is not accepted as the discovery of rhenium, whatever curiosity the old name stirs. A name printed in a journal still has to be tied, by evidence others can test, to the correct box on the table. The detection that counts is the 1925 X-ray work of Noddack, Tacke, and Berg. Nipponium stays a historical aside, while the accepted element carries the name of the Rhine.

trivia.title: The Metal in a Hot Blade
trivia.summary: Jet engines push metal parts close to their limit, and a small amount of a very rare element lets the turbine blades run hotter.
trivia.story: Rhenium is rarer in Earth's crust than many elements that are famous for being radioactive. Its notable modern use is in nickel superalloys for the turbine blades of jet engines. A small addition of the metal lets those blades run hotter without sagging, and hotter running can mean a more efficient engine. The 1925 discoverers were reading X-ray lines in ores, not designing a passenger aircraft. Scarcity keeps rhenium a specialist addition, and the last stable element found earns its keep in those very hot blades.

applications.title: Jet engines
applications.body: A few percent of rhenium in a turbine-blade alloy lets the blade stay strong at a higher temperature. Hotter engines use less fuel.

applications.title: Catalysts
applications.body: Rhenium catalysts help turn crude oil into high-octane fuel. The metal is recovered and reused because it is so scarce.

applications.title: A rare stable metal
applications.body: Rhenium was one of the last stable elements discovered. There is very little of it in the crust, so every use is a thin addition, not a solid part.

elements.name: Osmium

summary.beginner:
Osmium is element 76, the densest stable element, a hard blue-gray metal. Tiny amounts harden pen tips and electrical contacts, and one of its oxides is dangerously toxic.

Its symbol is Os. At room temperature osmium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 8. In class those are called period 6 and group 8.

Osmium is twice as dense as lead, so a small piece feels startlingly heavy. The pure metal is rare. The oxide OsO4 is a serious hazard and is not a curiosity to make.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral osmium atom has 76 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Osmium is a solid transition metal in period 6 and group 8. Osmium is the densest stable element, and the volatile tetroxide OsO4 is both a useful stain and a severe toxin.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d6 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 14, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +8. The one courses meet most often is +4.

Fountain-pen tips and instrument pivots used a hard osmium alloy. The tetroxide is a laboratory reagent for staining microscope samples, handled in a hood.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Osmium (Z = 76) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d6 6s2. Density near 22.6 g/cm3 is a consequence of the lanthanide contraction plus a heavy nucleus.

OsO4 is Os(VIII), a covalent molecular oxide, which is why it is volatile unlike ordinary metal oxides.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +8. The one courses meet most often is +4. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Osmium: say the name, write Os, find Z=76 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — densest stable metal; fountain-pen tips.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Osmium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d6 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +4, +8. It sits in group 8. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. hexagonal metal; toxic volatile tetroxide.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Osmium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; OsO₄ used (carefully) in staining If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from platinum residues as a very dense metal.

elements.history:
Smithson Tennant dissolved crude platinum in aqua regia in 1803 and examined the black residue that would not dissolve. From it he isolated two metals. One of them formed a volatile, sharp-smelling oxide, so he named it osmium, from the Greek osme, smell.

Osmium is the densest stable element. The tetroxide that gave it its name is toxic and was used, carefully, as a biological stain. The metal itself tips pen nibs and phonograph needles.
elements.howDiscovered:
Smithson Tennant dissolved crude platinum in aqua regia. A black powder remained. In 1803 he fused that powder with alkali, acidified, and distilled a volatile oxide with a penetrating smell. The oxide contained a new metal. Reducing it gave a dense, hard bead.

The volatility was the separation. No other metal in the residue distilled so readily as that oxide. Osmium was discovered by driving it out of the undissolved scrap of platinum ore and condensing the vapor.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Osmium’s isotopes split among the slow process, the rapid process, and the decay of rhenium. Osmium-187 is enlarged by that decay, which is how the clock is read. Osmium-186 is mainly slow-process. Osmium-188, 189, 190, and 192 carry rapid-process material. Osmium-184 is proton-rich and rare.

The osmium in a hard alloy is that blend. Part of the osmium-187 in an old metal was still rhenium when the solar system formed.

trivia.title: What the Acid Left Behind
trivia.summary: Crude platinum dissolved in a fierce acid mixture, and the black residue that refused to dissolve still held two unknown metals.
trivia.story: Smithson Tennant, in 1803, dissolved crude platinum in aqua regia and turned his attention to the black residue that would not dissolve. Most chemists of the day wanted the platinum that went into solution, and Tennant wanted the leftover. From that dark powder he isolated two new metals and announced them together. One of them formed a volatile oxide with a sharp, unpleasant smell. The residue that looked like dirt was a pair of elements, and the smell would give the first of them its name.

trivia.title: Named for a Sharp Smell
trivia.summary: The name comes from a Greek word for smell, because a volatile oxide announced the new metal to the nose as soon as it formed.
trivia.story: Tennant named that metal osmium, taking the word from the Greek osme, meaning smell. The volatile oxide was impossible to ignore, a sharp odor bound to a newly isolated element. Naming a metal for a smell is unusual on a table full of places, gods, and personal names. The odor was a warning as well as a label, even before the danger was fully respected. A gentle Greek root names an ungentle substance, and it still tells a student that this oxide is more than a curiosity.

trivia.title: An Oxide Treated as a Warning
trivia.summary: The volatile oxide behind the name is highly toxic, and laboratories that once used it as a stain had to treat it as a serious hazard.
trivia.story: The volatile oxide that gave osmium its name is highly toxic, which is the hazard to remember. Its reputation is a warning earned by real harm, and the warning is the whole of what a school story should carry. Laboratories used it carefully as a biological stain, because it marks specimens in a way microscopists valued. The metal itself found calmer work at the tips of pen nibs and phonograph needles, where hardness was the point. The lesson pairs a real danger in the oxide with a quieter use of the metal, and it keeps those two roles distinct.

trivia.title: The Densest Title on the Table
trivia.summary: Two neighboring metals are so close in density that the ranking depends on the measurement, though one of them usually wears the crown.
trivia.story: Osmium is usually listed as the densest of the elements, the name most tables put at the top of that contest. Iridium sits so close beside it that the two can trade the title, depending on how density is measured. Calling them essentially tied is fair, and calling osmium slightly denser matches the usual listing. Tennant found both metals in the same platinum residue in 1803, so the rivalry began in a single experiment. A small piece feels wrongly massive in the hand, and the ranking of the pair still depends on the measurement.

trivia.title: Tips of Pens and Needles
trivia.summary: Hardness put this dense metal at the point of old pens and phonograph needles, a small job for an element won from residues.
trivia.story: A pen nib has to stay hard at the very tip, where paper would otherwise wear a softer metal away. Osmium, often alloyed with iridium, tipped those nibs and also tipped phonograph needles that tracked a groove again and again. The amounts were tiny, which suited an element recovered from platinum residues rather than dug from a great mine of its own. Tennant's dark powder of 1803 eventually became a point that met paper and a point that met a record. The oxide stayed a laboratory warning, and the hard tip became the public face of an otherwise seldom-seen metal.

applications.title: Pen tips and contacts
applications.body: A hard osmium alloy has been used for fountain-pen tips and for electrical contacts that must not wear away.

applications.title: The densest stable element
applications.body: Osmium is the densest stable element, about twice as dense as lead. A small piece feels startlingly heavy.

applications.title: A dangerous oxide
applications.body: Osmium tetroxide is used, carefully, to stain samples for electron microscopes. The vapor is toxic, and the compound is not a curiosity.
