elements.name: Iridium

summary.beginner:
Iridium is element 77, a metal that resists corrosion better than almost anything else. Spark plugs and laboratory crucibles use it, and a thin layer of it in old rock is a clue to an ancient asteroid impact.

Its symbol is Ir. At room temperature iridium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 9. In class those are called period 6 and group 9.

Iridium is rare in Earth's crust and more common in meteorites. The layer at the end of the age of dinosaurs is famous for that reason. The metal itself is dense, hard, and quiet.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral iridium atom has 77 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Iridium is a solid transition metal in period 6 and group 9. Iridium is among the most corrosion-resistant metals, with +3 and +4 the oxidation states usually met.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d7 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 15, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +3. The one courses meet most often is +4.

A spark-plug electrode may be tipped with a tiny amount. Crucibles of iridium survive reactions that destroy platinum. The dinosaur-extinction clue is an iridium anomaly in clay.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Iridium (Z = 77) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d7 6s2. Chemical inertness is a kinetic fact of the surface as much as a thermodynamic one.

The K-Pg iridium spike is a geochemical marker of extraterrestrial material, not a property of iridium chemistry in water.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +4, +3. The one courses meet most often is +4. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Iridium: say the name, write Ir, find Z=77 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — spark plugs and crucibles.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Iridium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d7 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +4, +3. It sits in group 9. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. most corrosion-resistant metal.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Iridium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; high melting; +3/+4 chemistry If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated with osmium from platinum ores.

elements.history:
The other metal in Tennant’s 1803 platinum residue gave salts of many colors. He named it iridium, from Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow. He announced osmium and iridium together.

Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant metal: even aqua regia leaves it alone at room temperature. A thin layer of extra iridium in the rocks at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary is the geochemical trace of the impact that ended the dinosaur age.
elements.howDiscovered:
After the volatile oxide had been distilled from the platinum residue, Tennant was left with a metal that still would not dissolve and that gave salts of several colors: red, green, and black. In 1803 he showed that this metal was not osmium and not platinum. Its density was extraordinary, and its spectrum of salt colors was its own.

Iridium was discovered in the same black powder as osmium, by staying behind when osmium left. The two announcements came together because they were the two products of one residue.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Iridium-191 and iridium-193 are both mainly rapid-process products. The slow process adds little, because the capture path does not pile up here. Iridium belongs with platinum and gold among the metals the rapid process is asked to explain.

Iridium is scarce in the crust and richer in some meteorites, which is why an iridium-rich layer marks the asteroid impact at the end of the Cretaceous. The nuclei were made in neutron-rich blasts. The layer records a delivery, long after the making.

trivia.title: Salts the Color of a Rainbow
trivia.summary: The second metal from the platinum residue formed salts of many colors, and its name remembers the Greek goddess of the rainbow.
trivia.story: The other metal in Tennant's 1803 platinum residue gave salts of many colors, unexpected shades from a single element. He named it iridium, from Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because the colors asked for that myth. Osmium and iridium were announced together, two elements drawn from one black powder. A sharp smell named the first metal, and a palette of colored salts named the second. Platinum's leftover, the part aqua regia would not dissolve, was generous enough to remake a corner of the table.

trivia.title: Left Alone at Room Temperature
trivia.summary: The acid mixture that dissolves gold leaves this metal alone when the room is merely warm, which became a symbol of chemical stubbornness.
trivia.story: Iridium is among the most corrosion-resistant metals, a reputation it earns by ignoring attacks that ruin its neighbors. Aqua regia, the fierce mixture that dissolves gold and attacks platinum, leaves iridium alone at room temperature. Tennant had already met that stubbornness, because the black residue itself had refused to dissolve. A rainbow of colorful salts belongs to a metal that, in the lump, barely agrees to react. The resistance lets iridium serve where a lesser metal would pit, which is a practical sequel to the 1803 residue.

trivia.title: A Layer Where the Dinosaurs Ended
trivia.summary: A thin rock layer around the world is oddly rich in this rare metal, and in 1980 that layer became evidence of a giant impact.
trivia.story: In 1980 the Alvarez team described a thin layer of extra iridium in rocks at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary. Iridium is scarce in Earth's crust and more common in asteroids, so a worldwide sprinkle asked for an unusual explanation. The layer became chemical evidence for a giant impact at the end of the dinosaur age. A metal Tennant had separated from platinum residue was suddenly a clue read in a cliff. The asteroid itself did not have to be sitting there, because a rare element had written the event into the strata.

trivia.title: The Metal of the Standard Weights
trivia.summary: The official meter bar and the kilogram cylinder were alloys of platinum with this metal, chosen so the standards would not corrode.
trivia.story: The international prototypes of the meter and the kilogram were platinum-iridium, chosen because the alloy stays bright and holds its shape. For generations the official kilogram was one such cylinder, kept with care and compared against national copies. Iridium's refusal to corrode was the reason to mix it into the platinum in the first place. A metal from Tennant's residue became part of how the world defined length and mass. In 2019 the kilogram left its metal cylinder for a definition based on constants, and the platinum-iridium alloy stayed behind as history.

trivia.title: A Tip in the Spark Plug
trivia.summary: Engines and harsh laboratory melts both ask for a metal that survives heat and chemistry, and this one took those small, durable jobs.
trivia.story: Iridium often hides in daily life at the tip of a spark plug, where a spark must jump in a hot, corrosive engine. A high melting point and a famous resistance to attack let that tiny tip last far longer than a cheaper metal would. Laboratory crucibles for harsh melts have trusted the same pair of virtues. The rainbow belongs to the salts, and the lump of metal is valued for the reactions it declines. Tennant's 1803 residue metal became a point in an engine and a cup on a bench, both chosen because they endure.

applications.title: Spark plugs
applications.body: The tip of a long-life spark plug may be a tiny amount of iridium. The metal resists the spark and the heat.

applications.title: Crucibles
applications.body: Iridium crucibles survive chemical reactions that eat through platinum. Laboratories use them for those few jobs.

applications.title: A clue in the rocks
applications.body: A thin layer of iridium-rich clay marks the time an asteroid struck Earth at the end of the age of dinosaurs. The metal is rare in the crust and more common in meteorites.

elements.name: Platinum

summary.beginner:
Platinum is element 78, a dense silver-white metal that does not tarnish. Jewelry is the famous use, and catalytic converters are the larger one.

Its symbol is Pt. At room temperature platinum is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 10. In class those are called period 6 and group 10.

Platinum stays bright in air and resists most acids. A car holds a thin coat of it that helps turn exhaust into less harmful gases. A few platinum compounds are used as cancer medicines, under a doctor's care.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral platinum atom has 78 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Platinum is a solid transition metal in period 6 and group 10. Platinum is a noble, unreactive metal and a major catalyst, and cisplatin is a Pt(II) anticancer drug.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d9 6s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 17, 1. Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +4. The one courses meet most often is +2.

The converter chemistry is a surface catalysis. Jewelry uses the bulk metal. Cisplatin is a specific square-planar complex, not platinum metal dissolved in water.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Platinum (Z = 78) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d9 6s1. Cisplatin cross-links DNA.

That is coordination chemistry of Pt(II), and the metal in a ring is unrelated. Catalysis and the drug share an element and almost nothing else about the mechanism.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +4. The one courses meet most often is +2. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Platinum: say the name, write Pt, find Z=78 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — catalysts and jewelry.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Platinum: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d9 6s1, Typical oxidation states: +2, +4. It sits in group 10. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. unreactive; excellent electrode.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Platinum: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; cisplatin is a Pt(II) anticancer complex If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Described in South American ores; later isolated in Europe.

elements.history:
Platinum was worked in South America before European chemists had a name for it. Antonio de Ulloa described the unworkable white metal in 1735, and Charles Wood brought samples to Europe. The name is from the Spanish platina, little silver. Wollaston’s refining method, early in the nineteenth century, made the pure metal available.

Platinum became the metal of crucibles, electrodes, and catalysts. Cisplatin, a platinum complex introduced in the 1970s, is an anticancer drug.
elements.howDiscovered:
Grains of a white metal turned up in the gold sands of the Chocó, in New Granada. They would not melt in a goldsmith’s fire and would not behave as silver. Antonio de Ulloa described them in 1735. Charles Wood brought samples to England, and William Brownrigg and William Watson showed in the 1750s that the grains dissolved in aqua regia and precipitated as a metal distinct from gold and from silver.

The original finding was a grain that survived the operations used to part gold. The demonstration that the grain was a single new metal, and not an alloy, was the European dissolution and precipitation. Platinum was discovered as an inconvenience in a gold washing, then established with aqua regia.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Platinum is mainly a rapid-process metal. Platinum-194, 195, and 196, the abundant isotopes, are built when neutron captures run faster than beta decay. The slow process adds a minority. Platinum-190 is proton-rich and rare.

Merging neutron stars are the leading site of that rapid capture. The platinum in a crucible was made in blasts of that kind, or in whatever rarer supernovae also manage the rapid process, and was inherited by the solar cloud.

trivia.title: Little Silver Unripe Gold
trivia.summary: Miners in South America kept finding a heavy white metal they could not work, and some Europeans decided the gold had not finished ripening.
trivia.story: Platinum was already known in South America before European chemists had a settled name or use for it. Spanish speakers called the heavy white metal platina, little silver, because it turned up in gold workings and would not behave like gold. Some Europeans treated it as unripe gold, a noble metal that simply had not finished becoming itself. That belief captured their frustration, while the chemistry said they were holding a different element. Difficult to melt and stubborn to work, it kept the dismissive nickname, and the word platinum still carries little silver inside it.

trivia.title: Samples Carried Across the Ocean
trivia.summary: A Spanish scientist described the awkward white metal, and another traveler brought pieces to Europe, where the samples could finally be studied.
trivia.story: Antonio de Ulloa described the unworkable white metal in 1735, putting a miner's nuisance into a scientific report. Charles Wood brought samples to Europe, where the metal could be heated, dissolved, and argued over in person. A written description and a real specimen are different kinds of arrival, and platinum needed both before it was believed. The Spanish name platina, little silver, traveled with those pieces into European laboratories. Once scholars could hold it, the notion of unripe gold weakened, because waiting never turned the metal yellow.

trivia.title: A Business in the Residues
trivia.summary: Two English chemists turned the difficult white metal into a trade, and the sludge from purifying it still hid further discoveries.
trivia.story: Early in the nineteenth century, William Wollaston worked out how to make platinum malleable enough to be genuinely useful. He and Smithson Tennant built a business on the metal and on the residues left after it was refined. The purified platinum became crucibles and apparatus that lesser metals could not survive. The residues held osmium and iridium, which Tennant separated in 1803 from the powder that aqua regia left behind. A saleable metal and two new elements came from the same ore, once someone was willing to study the sludge.

trivia.title: Cleaning the Exhaust of a Car
trivia.summary: A thin coat of this metal, often with its neighbors, sits in the exhaust path so harmful gases can be changed before they leave the car.
trivia.story: A catalytic converter passes engine exhaust over a thin coat of platinum, often shared with palladium and rhodium. Those metals help change harmful gases into milder ones before the exhaust leaves the tailpipe. Only a thin coat is required, which matters because platinum has always been too costly to use by the kilogram in a car. Wollaston's enduring crucibles and a modern exhaust system rely on the same talents, chemical activity and resistance to attack. The metal once dismissed as unripe gold became part of the machinery of cleaner air on ordinary roads.

trivia.title: From Crucibles to a Cancer Drug
trivia.summary: The scarce metal anchored a standard of mass, survived as laboratory ware, and later appeared in a medicine used against cancer.
trivia.story: The international kilogram was long a platinum-iridium cylinder, a standard chosen to last without corroding or changing mass. Crucibles and electrodes used the pure metal because it survived chemical treatments that destroy ordinary steel. In the 1970s a platinum complex called cisplatin became an anticancer drug, far from jewelry and far from river gravel. One element therefore lived in a vault as a definition of mass and in a clinic as a medicine. The span fits a metal that was painfully hard to work and, once worked, painfully hard to replace.

applications.title: Catalytic converters
applications.body: Platinum helps oxidize carbon monoxide and leftover fuel in a car's exhaust. Jewelry is the famous use. The converter is the larger one.

applications.title: Jewelry
applications.body: Platinum stays bright and does not tarnish, so it is a jewelry metal. It is denser and usually more expensive than gold.

applications.title: A cancer medicine
applications.body: Cisplatin, a platinum compound, is a chemotherapy drug. It is a specific molecule given by a doctor, not platinum metal.

elements.name: Gold

summary.beginner:
Gold is element 79, the yellow metal of coins, rings, and electrical contacts that must not corrode. It is soft, dense, and unusually unwilling to react.

Its symbol is Au. At room temperature gold is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 11. In class those are called period 6 and group 11.

Gold stays yellow and shiny in air and water, which is why it was money and jewelry before anyone had a periodic table. A thin layer on a connector keeps the contact reliable.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral gold atom has 79 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Gold is a solid transition metal in period 6 and group 11. Gold is a soft noble metal, an excellent conductor, and yellow because of relativistic effects on its electrons.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 1. Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +1. The one courses meet most often is +3.

Aqua regia dissolves it, which is the famous exception to its inertness. Oxidation states +1 and +3 both matter in compounds. The metal itself is the form in coins and contacts.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Gold (Z = 79) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s1. The color comes from a relativistic contraction of the 6s orbital that shifts the reflectivity.

Without that effect gold would look like silver. Softness is a large-scale crystal fact: the metal deforms easily.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +1. The one courses meet most often is +3. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Gold: say the name, write Au, find Z=79 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — money, electronics, inert electrodes.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Gold: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s1, Typical oxidation states: +3, +1. It sits in group 11. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. very unreactive; excellent conductor.

discovery.text: Native metal of currency, electronics, and ornament.

elements.history:
Gold is a native metal and was gathered before written history. The symbol Au is from the Latin aurum. There is no discoverer and no discovery year. Its refusal to tarnish is why it was money and ornament in every culture that found it.

The yellow color is a relativistic effect: the 6s electrons move fast enough that the reflectivity drops in the blue. Modern use adds corrosion-free electrical contacts to the old uses of coinage and jewelry.
elements.howDiscovered:
Gold occurs native, and the oldest method is mechanical: wash a sand, and the heavy yellow grains remain. Cupellation and parting with acid came later. Gold stays in the cupel when lead is oxidized away, and it stays undissolved when silver is removed with nitric acid.

There is no discoverer. The element was established by that refusal to change. Heat it, dissolve its alloys, and the yellow metal returns with the same weight. The original discovery was a heavy yellow grain in a river.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Gold-197, the only stable isotope, is a rapid-process nucleus. The slow process in giant stars does not reach it in any useful amount, and fusion in stellar cores stops at the iron peak, far below. The captures have to be rapid, in a neutron-rich blast.

Merging neutron stars are the leading site. The glow after some of those mergers fits the heavy rapid-process elements. The gold already in the Earth came from events of that kind before the Sun formed. Geology later gathered it into quartz veins. A merger watched today did not mint that gold.

trivia.title: Gathered Before Written History
trivia.summary: People picked this metal from gravel before science kept written dates, so the table lists neither a discoverer nor a discovery year.
trivia.story: Gold is a native metal, found as itself in river gravel and quartz, and people gathered it before written history began. There is no discoverer and no discovery year, a blank that makes gold unusual on a poster full of dates. The symbol Au comes from the Latin aurum, while the English name is older than any laboratory that might have claimed it. Because it refuses to tarnish, it became ornament and money in cultures that found the metal in their rivers. A yellow metal that stays yellow needed no chemist to introduce it, only someone willing to notice a gleam in the gravel.

trivia.title: A Rush Toward California Rivers
trivia.summary: A find in a California mill in the late 1840s pulled a huge migration west, aimed at metal already sitting native in the gravel.
trivia.story: In 1848 James Marshall noticed gold at Sutter's mill in California, and the rush of 1849 carried a crowd west to wash the rivers. The fever worked because the metal was already metal, ready to pan, not locked in an ore that demanded a furnace. Camps and towns appeared at a speed that ordinary settlement did not match. Many seekers found less than the rumors promised, and what they found was the same native gold people had gathered for ages. An element with no scientific discoverer still gained a nineteenth-century chapter, written in gravel and in the movement of that crowd.

trivia.title: The Acid Mixture Called Royal Water
trivia.summary: Ordinary acids leave this metal untouched, and one famous mixture is the exception, known by a Latin name that means the water of kings.
trivia.story: Gold shrugs at most acids, which is one reason coins can survive burial, seawater, and long use. A mixture called aqua regia, Latin for royal water, is the famous exception that dissolves it. The story needs that name and that fact, and it does not need the proportions of the mixture. Royal water is a boast, and the boast is accurate enough that every careful textbook pairs the phrase with gold. The metal that ignores ordinary bench acids yields to that one mixture, which is the whole of the exception.

trivia.title: Coins That Refused to Tarnish
trivia.summary: A surface that stays bright made the metal into ornaments, coins, and treasury reserves, and the same calm surface later served electrical contacts.
trivia.story: Choosing a coin metal is a chemical decision as well as a political one. Gold does not tarnish, so a piece stays recognizable after years in a purse, a vault, or a shipwreck. Empires struck it into coins, banks stored bars, and jewelry carried the same metal into private life. The color and the weight made the pieces easy to trust and difficult to imitate with a cheap substitute. A clean electrical contact is a newer use of that same untarnished surface, a circuit's version of an old coin.

trivia.title: Why the Metal Looks Yellow
trivia.summary: The familiar color comes from the metal itself, and the explanation involves electrons moving strangely fast near a very heavy nucleus.
trivia.story: Gold is yellow for a reason that surprises students who expect the color to be a simple surface coating. Electrons near its heavy nucleus move so fast that relativity changes which colors the metal reflects. Blue is diminished in that shuffle, and the familiar yellow is what remains for the eye. The color is a property of the element itself, not a finish that could flake away with time. Coinage, jewelry, and corrosion-free electrical contacts are all uses of a metal whose electrons behave in this unusual way.

applications.title: Jewelry and coins
applications.body: Gold stays yellow and shiny in air and water, which is why it has been jewelry and money for thousands of years.

applications.title: Electronics
applications.body: A thin coat of gold on a connector resists corrosion, so a computer contact still works years later.

applications.title: Not just decoration
applications.body: Gold is also an excellent reflector of infrared light and a reliable conductor. The softness that makes it easy to shape is the same softness that makes a pure coin wear away.

elements.name: Mercury

summary.beginner:
Mercury is element 80, the silvery metal that is a liquid at room temperature. It is poisonous, so thermometers and switches that used it have been replaced.

Its symbol is Hg. At room temperature mercury is a liquid, which is unusual for an element. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 12. In class those are called period 6 and group 12.

Mercury vapor is the danger people do not see. A broken old thermometer is a cleanup problem, not a toy. The metal also forms alloys called amalgams with other metals.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral mercury atom has 80 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Mercury is a liquid transition metal in period 6 and group 12. Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature because its 6s electrons are held unusually tightly, and the vapor is toxic.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +1. The one courses meet most often is +2.

The filled 5d10 6s2 shell and a relativistic contraction make the atoms bind weakly to each other, so the metal melts at 234 K. Amalgams are solutions of other metals in that liquid.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Mercury (Z = 80) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2. The low melting point is a relativistic effect on the 6s pair, not a molecular liquid like bromine.

Chronic toxicity is from the element, from inorganic salts, and from organomercury compounds, three different hazards.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +1. The one courses meet most often is +2. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Mercury: say the name, write Hg, find Z=80 on the table, note the family (Transition metal), and connect it to one real use — thermometers historically; toxic liquid metal.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Mercury: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2, Typical oxidation states: +2, +1. It sits in group 12. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. liquid at room temperature.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Mercury: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; filled 5d¹⁰ 6s²; amalgam chemistry If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Known as quicksilver in cinnabar; distilled for millennia.

elements.history:
Cinnabar was roasted for mercury in the ancient world, and the liquid metal was called quicksilver. The symbol Hg is from the Latin hydrargyrum, water silver. No modern discoverer is assigned. Alchemists used it for centuries as the supposed principle of metallicity.

Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature and pressure. Thermometers, barometers, and dental amalgam spread it, and the toxicity of the vapor and of methylmercury pulled it back out of those uses.
elements.howDiscovered:
Cinnabar, the red sulfide, releases mercury when it is roasted. The sulfur leaves as a gas, and the metal vapor condenses on a cool surface as a liquid. That distillation was practiced in the ancient world, at Almaden and elsewhere, and the liquid metal was collected in flasks.

No modern discoverer is assigned. The element was recognized as simple because the liquid could be boiled, condensed, and recovered unchanged, and because cinnabar always gave the same liquid. Mercury was discovered by a roast and a condensation.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Mercury’s isotopes are a blend of the slow process and the rapid process, close to the lead peak where slow capture is about to end. Mercury-196 is proton-rich and rare. The common isotopes, 202, 200, 199, and 198, are mixed.

The mercury distilled from cinnabar is that blend. Giant stars and neutron-rich blasts both contribute, and the liquid metal does not record which atom came from which channel.

trivia.title: Liquid Silver and a Fast Planet
trivia.summary: Ancient people knew a rolling liquid metal, linked the drops with a swift planet, and kept a Latin name that means liquid silver.
trivia.story: Mercury was known to the ancient world as quicksilver, the metal that flows and beads at ordinary room temperature. People linked those fast drops with the fast planet Mercury, and the English name of the element remembers the planet. The symbol Hg comes from the Latin hydrargyrum, liquid silver, a second name that simply describes the look of the metal. No modern discoverer is assigned, because the element was already famous when chemistry became a formal science. Alchemists set the shining liquid at the center of their theories, a real metal asked to stand for the idea of metallicity itself.

trivia.title: Won From a Red Ore
trivia.summary: The usual source was a red mineral, and ancient workers obtained the flowing metal by heating that ore until the liquid gathered.
trivia.story: Cinnabar, a red mineral, was the great ore of mercury in the ancient world. Workers won the liquid metal by heating that ore, and they called the result quicksilver. A school telling keeps the method at that plain fact and does not turn it into a workshop procedure. The outcome was a heavy, mobile liquid that invited people to play with it and to store it in open vessels. The shine encouraged trust, and trust was risky, because the vapor and many compounds of the metal can do real harm.

trivia.title: The Hatters and Their Shakes
trivia.summary: Felt hats were prepared with a mercury compound, and the workers' trembling and confusion became familiar enough to earn a grim nickname.
trivia.story: Hat makers used mercury nitrate to treat animal fur so the felt would mat into a dense, smooth hat. Day after day the work put the metal's compounds on their hands and into the air of the shop. A pattern of illness called erethism, trembling and confused behavior, became familiar in the trade. People spoke of the mad hatter, a phrase that sounds playful and named a real occupational disease. Elegant hats left for the street, and the harm stayed with the workers, a documented chapter that stories later borrowed.

trivia.title: A Bay That Turned Dangerous
trivia.summary: People in a Japanese coastal town fell ill after eating local fish, and the illness was traced to mercury leaving a factory in wastewater.
trivia.story: Physicians in Minamata, Japan, recognized a severe illness in the 1950s among people who had eaten local fish. A factory had released mercury in its wastewater, and in the bay that mercury became methylmercury, which built up in the fish. Families were harmed by a waste stream they did not choose and could not see in the catch. The history is a warning about pollution, and it is not a set of chemical steps for anyone to follow. A metal that looks clean in a bottle had moved through a food chain, and a coastal town made that danger impossible to ignore.

trivia.title: Pulled Back Out of the Instruments
trivia.summary: Thermometers, barometers, and dental fillings spread a liquid metal through daily life, and toxicity pushed it back out of those casual jobs.
trivia.story: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature and pressure, so a silver thread rose neatly in thermometers and barometers. Dental amalgam carried it into ordinary dentistry as well, a daily contact far from any mine. Toxicity of the vapor, and of compounds such as methylmercury, pulled the element back from those casual uses. A school thermometer that once seemed harmless became a reason to switch instruments and to treat spills with respect. The liquid alchemists admired is still extraordinary, and its public life has been a long retreat from rooms where people breathe.

applications.title: Old thermometers
applications.body: Mercury's even expansion made it the liquid in many thermometers. Those thermometers are being retired because the vapor is poisonous.

applications.title: Old switches and lamps
applications.body: A tilt switch could use a drop of mercury to close a circuit, and fluorescent lamps contain a small amount of mercury vapor. Broken lamps are a disposal problem.

applications.title: Amalgams
applications.body: Mercury dissolves some other metals to make an amalgam. Dental amalgam is a historical filling material that dentistry has been moving away from.

elements.name: Thallium

summary.beginner:
Thallium is element 81, a soft gray metal, and it is highly poisonous. It belongs in a controlled laboratory, not in a home.

Its symbol is Tl. At room temperature thallium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 13. In class those are called period 6 and group 13.

Thallium was once used in pest poisons. That use was stopped because the element harms people. There is no safe household experiment with it.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral thallium atom has 81 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Thallium is a solid post-transition in period 6 and group 13. Thallium shows the inert-pair effect: +1 is more important than the +3 you might expect from the column.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 3. Oxidation states in this dossier are +1, +3. The one courses meet most often is +1.

Tl+ resembles the alkali ion K+ in size and charge, and that resemblance is part of why thallium is so poisonous. The metal itself is soft and tarnishes in air.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Thallium (Z = 81) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p1. The 6s pair stays put, so Tl+ is the common ion and Tl3+ is the oxidizing one.

Mimicry of potassium lets thallium into biological pathways that expect K+.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +1, +3. The one courses meet most often is +1. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Thallium: say the name, write Tl, find Z=81 on the table, note the family (Post-transition), and connect it to one real use — electronics; toxic heavy metal.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Thallium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p1, Typical oxidation states: +1, +3. It sits in group 13. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. +1 and +3; inert-pair effect.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Thallium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; Tl⁺ resembles K⁺ — that is why it is poisonous If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Detected spectroscopically in sulfuric-acid residues.

elements.history:
William Crookes, searching spectroscopically for tellurium in a sulfuric-acid residue in 1861, found a bright green line instead. He named the element thallium, from the Greek thallos, a green shoot. Claude-Auguste Lamy isolated the metal the next year.

Thallium was briefly a rodenticide and a depilatory, then withdrawn because the ion mimics potassium and is poisonous. The inert pair, which favors Tl+, is the textbook example of that effect in period 6.
elements.howDiscovered:
William Crookes was examining the residue of a sulfuric-acid works with a spectroscope, looking for tellurium. In 1861 a bright green line appeared that was not tellurium and not sulfur. He followed the line through precipitations of the mud. Claude-Auguste Lamy isolated a larger quantity the next year and melted a button of metal, which showed the same green line in the spark.

The discovery is the line in the chamber mud. The metal followed, once enough residue had been worked to plate and melt. Thallium was found the way rubidium and caesium were found, by a prism, in a waste that industry had concentrated.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Thallium-205 and thallium-203 lie just before the lead peak. Both take a large share from the slow process, which is funneling material toward lead-208, and both take a rapid-process share. Thallium-205 can also receive the decay of lead-205, a long-lived radioactive nucleus.

Thallium is odd-numbered and scarce. The thallium once used in infrared optics is this end-of-the-line neutron-capture mix.

trivia.title: A Green Line Instead
trivia.summary: A chemist hunting for tellurium in a factory residue found a brilliant green spectral line, and the color became the new element's name.
trivia.story: William Crookes, in 1861, was searching with a spectroscope for tellurium in a residue from sulfuric acid manufacture. A brilliant green line appeared where he had hoped to see the signs of tellurium. He named the element thallium, from the Greek thallos, a green shoot, because the color suggested new growth. The discovery was a line of light, the kind of evidence that can arrive before any weighable bead of metal. A botanical word was attached to an element whose later fame would be as a notorious poison.

trivia.title: The Metal the Next Year
trivia.summary: A green line announced the element, and isolating an actual piece of metal took a second chemist and the following year.
trivia.story: Claude-Auguste Lamy isolated metallic thallium the year after Crookes observed the green line. Spectroscopy had announced the element, and a chemical isolation produced a sample that could be melted and kept. One man worked with light, and the other worked with a specimen, at nearly the same moment in the early 1860s. Thallium therefore has a discoverer of the spectral line and a chemist who first held the metal. The second arrival, the following year, showed that the green shoot in the spectrum was a substance you could weigh.

trivia.title: Sold Once as a Rat Killer
trivia.summary: Salts of this element were sold to kill rodents and were even mixed into hair-removal creams, until poisonings forced the products off the market.
trivia.story: Thallium salts were once sold as rodent killers, an ordinary commercial product aimed at rats and mice. For a time the same element was put into depilatory creams that promised to remove hair. Both uses were withdrawn, because thallium is a notorious poison and the accidents of ordinary sale were too grave. The ion can mimic potassium, so a body may take it up along paths meant for an essential element. The mimicry is the lesson, and the green line of 1861 had introduced a metal that could not stay on a shop shelf.

trivia.title: A Poison in a Detective Plot
trivia.summary: A famous mystery writer built a novel around this metal, using a real and already notorious poison as the hidden cause of an illness.
trivia.story: Agatha Christie placed thallium poisoning at the center of her detective novel The Pale Horse. In the plot, an illness that looks mysterious has this metal as its hidden cause. The novel is literature history, worth telling because the poison itself is real and had already been sold and withdrawn. Readers met thallium as a clue on the page and could then discover it was not a writer's fantasy. A name taken from a green shoot, and a salt once sold as a rat killer, had become a plot that pointed back at the chemistry.

trivia.title: A Charge That Mimics Potassium
trivia.summary: This metal prefers a single positive charge, and that habit helps explain why living tissue can mistake it for a salt the body needs.
trivia.story: Thallium shares a column with metals that often carry a higher charge, yet it prefers ions with a single positive charge. Chemists call the habit the inert pair, and thallium is the classroom example of that effect in this row of the table. The preference connects to the poisonings, because a single charge lets the ion resemble potassium. Living tissue can take the impostor up along routes meant for an element the body actually needs. Crookes saw a green line in 1861, and the later electron story helps explain why tissue was willing to absorb what he had found.

applications.title: Electronics, limited
applications.body: A little thallium has been used in some specialty electronics and in infrared optics. The amounts are controlled because the element is very toxic.

applications.title: Old poisons, withdrawn
applications.body: Thallium salts were once rodenticides. That use was stopped after people were poisoned. There is no safe home use.

applications.title: A medical isotope
applications.body: A radioactive thallium isotope has been used in heart imaging. The dose is a medical decision, and the metal is not a reagent to keep.

elements.name: Lead

summary.beginner:
Lead is element 82, a heavy soft metal used in car batteries and in shields that block X-rays. It is toxic, which is why it was taken out of house paint and gasoline.

Its symbol is Pb. At room temperature lead is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 14. In class those are called period 6 and group 14.

A car battery contains lead plates and a lead compound, sealed so you do not touch them. Lead dust and old paint chips are a health hazard, especially for children. The metal is useful and not casual.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral lead atom has 82 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Lead is a solid post-transition in period 6 and group 14. Lead's common oxidation state is +2 because of the inert pair, and the metal is both a battery material and a radiation shield.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 4. Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +4. The one courses meet most often is +2.

Tetraethyllead in gasoline was an anti-knock additive and a public-health disaster. X-ray rooms use the dense metal, not a lead compound. Pb2+ in old paint is the exposure people still watch for.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Lead (Z = 82) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p2. The inert 6s pair makes Pb2+ stable and Pb4+ oxidizing, the reverse of the light group-14 elements.

Density, not chemistry, is why a lead apron stops X-rays. Toxicity is the chemistry of the ion.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +4. The one courses meet most often is +2. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Lead: say the name, write Pb, find Z=82 on the table, note the family (Post-transition), and connect it to one real use — batteries and radiation shielding; toxic.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Lead: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p2, Typical oxidation states: +2, +4. It sits in group 14. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. inert-pair +2 vs +4.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Lead: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; tetraethyllead history; Pb²⁺ in minerals If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Worked as plumbing, solder, and weights; toxic in modern use.

elements.history:
Lead is prehistoric. The Romans piped water through it, sweetened wine with its salts, and named it plumbum, which is the symbol Pb. The English word lead is Germanic. No one is credited with a discovery.

The metal’s density and softness made it solder, shot, and radiation shielding. Tetraethyllead in gasoline, introduced in the 1920s and removed late in the century, is the cautionary chapter. The inert pair makes +2 the common state, unlike the +4 of lighter group-14 elements.
elements.howDiscovered:
Galena, the sulfide, was roasted to the oxide and reduced with charcoal in antiquity, and the metal was also recovered by heating the sulfide with iron. The metal is soft, dense, and low-melting, and it can be cast in molds. Roman pipes and weights are the scale of that knowledge.

There is no discoverer. Lead was classed as an element because the metal could be oxidized and reduced in a cycle that always returned the same substance, and because it parted from silver in the cupel as the part that was absorbed, not the part that remained. The original discovery was a smelt of a common sulfide.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Lead is where the slow process ends. Lead-208 has 82 protons and 126 neutrons, both closed shells, and nuclei that reach it by slow capture tend to stop. Giant stars pile lead up. That primordial lead includes smaller slow-process shares of lead-206 and lead-207, plus a rapid-process contribution.

On Earth a second source dominates many ores. Uranium-238 decays to lead-206, uranium-235 to lead-207, and thorium-232 to lead-208. The isotope ratios in a galena record the age of the ore as well as the stars. A piece of lead is part stellar ash and part the daughter of those radioactive metals.

trivia.title: Pipes That Gave the Metal a Name
trivia.summary: Roman builders ran water through this soft metal, and their Latin word for it still sits inside the English word for the pipes.
trivia.story: Lead is prehistoric, a metal with no discoverer and no year that anyone can call a discovery. The Romans piped water through it, sweetened wine with some of its salts, and named it plumbum. That Latin word still sits in the symbol Pb and in the English word plumbing. Soft, dense, and easy to cast, the metal became pipes, roofs, shot, and weights across many centuries. Usefulness delayed caution, and a material that bends in the hands was built into daily life long before its harm was faced.

trivia.title: A Bargain in the Gasoline
trivia.summary: An additive quieted knocking engines and spread this metal through city air, and the practice ended only after a long, late phase-out.
trivia.story: Midgley and others, in the 1920s, promoted tetraethyllead as an additive that would quiet knocking engines. Gasoline then carried lead into the air of busy streets, a use that touched everyone near traffic. Workers who produced the additive fell ill, an early warning that came from the factories themselves. The compound stayed in fuel for decades, defended because engines ran more smoothly and the habit was hard to quit. Late in the twentieth century, countries phased tetraethyllead out, a long removal after a long and documented harm.

trivia.title: Dust in the Paint and the Shop
trivia.summary: Tough white paints hid this metal in walls and in workshop dust, and the people who sanded or lived with that dust bore the harm.
trivia.story: Lead pigments made paint white, tough, and long lasting, which is why older houses still hide the metal in their walls. The danger arrived as dust, as flakes under a sander, and as powder in the air where painters worked. Workers and children met it in that quiet form, a pigment rather than a pipe they could point to. The poisoning was slow enough to argue about and widespread enough to force lead out of household paint. A clean-looking surface was the disguise, and the campaign to retire it lasted longer than any single law.

trivia.title: Water That Picked Up the Pipes
trivia.summary: After a city changed its water source, old pipes lost their protection, and lead reached kitchen taps before the alarm was fully believed.
trivia.story: In 2014 the city of Flint, Michigan, changed the source of its drinking water and set an old problem loose. The newer supply was not treated in the way that keeps a protective film on old lead pipes. Lead from those pipes reached household taps, and residents reported water that looked and smelled wrong. Officials were slow to treat the rising lead measurements as the emergency the taps had already become. Plumbing, the word inherited from the Romans' plumbum, had returned as a failure of a modern public water system.

trivia.title: Useful Enough to Linger
trivia.summary: Solder, shot, and radiation shields made the metal hard to abandon, so each handy use became another place where the retreat had to be negotiated.
trivia.story: Density and softness made lead the metal of solder, of shot, and of shields against radiation. Each of those jobs was a reason for workshops to keep it even after the health evidence had grown loud. Solder joined pipes and circuits, and shielding stopped rays that would have required a much thicker wall of a lighter material. Phasing tetraethyllead and household paint out of daily life did not cancel every remaining use in a single year. The twentieth-century story is a sequence of useful habits meeting the evidence, and then, unevenly, letting go.

applications.title: Car batteries
applications.body: A lead-acid battery, the kind that starts a car, uses lead plates and a lead compound in sulfuric acid. The case stays sealed.

applications.title: Radiation shields
applications.body: Lead is dense enough that a sheet of it stops X-rays. Aprons in a radiology room and the walls of some labs use that density.

applications.title: Taken out of daily life
applications.body: Lead pigment in house paint and tetraethyllead in gasoline were banned because lead harms the nervous system, especially in children. Old paint is still a reason to be careful when renovating.

elements.name: Bismuth

summary.beginner:
Bismuth is element 83, a brittle metal with a faint pink shine. It is used in low-melting alloys and in some stomach medicines, and it is the last element that is essentially stable.

Its symbol is Bi. At room temperature bismuth is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 15. In class those are called period 6 and group 15.

Bismuth crystals grow in stairstep shapes and can look rainbow-colored from a thin coat on the surface. The medicine is a compound, not a lump of metal to taste.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral bismuth atom has 83 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Bismuth is a solid post-transition in period 6 and group 15. Bismuth is essentially stable, with +3 the usual oxidation state, and it is used in low-melting alloys and in bismuth subsalicylate.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p3. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 5. Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is +3.

The rainbow on a crystal is an oxide film, like a soap bubble, not a bulk color of the metal. Wood's metal and similar alloys melt in hot water.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Bismuth (Z = 83) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p3. Bismuth-209 was long called the heaviest stable isotope.

It does decay by alpha emission, with a half-life far longer than the age of the universe, so for every practical purpose it is stable.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +3, +5. The one courses meet most often is +3. Neighbors differ because of shell filling, the lanthanide contraction, and relativistic effects on the inner electrons.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Bismuth: say the name, write Bi, find Z=83 on the table, note the family (Post-transition), and connect it to one real use — low-melting alloys; some medicines history.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Bismuth: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p3, Typical oxidation states: +3, +5. It sits in group 15. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. last stable element; ²⁰⁹Bi is nearly stable.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Bismuth: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; alpha activity is extremely slow If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Shown to be distinct from tin and lead.

elements.history:
Bismuth minerals were known in the Middle Ages and often confused with lead, tin, or antimony. Claude François Geoffroy showed in 1753 that bismuth was a distinct metal. The name comes from the German Wismut, of uncertain origin, possibly a corruption of a phrase meaning white mass.

Bismuth was long called the last stable element. In 2003 its only primordial isotope, bismuth-209, was found to decay by alpha emission with a half-life of about 2 × 10^19 years, so the element is radioactive only in a technical sense.
elements.howDiscovered:
Bismuth turned up in the ores of the Erzgebirge and was cast as a brittle, low-melting metal that miners knew from lead and from tin by experience. The written distinction is Claude François Geoffroy’s, in 1753. He compared the metal’s density, its fracture, its oxide, and its behavior on the cupel with lead and with tin, and the properties matched neither.

The discovery, as a demonstration, was that comparison. The metal had already been on the bench. Geoffroy’s experiments took it off the list of impure leads.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Bismuth-209 is the heaviest nucleus that survives on a cosmic timescale, and only barely: its half-life is about 2 × 10^19 years, far longer than the age of the Universe. It is the last stop of the slow process. Capture beyond it makes polonium, which alpha-decays, and the chain falls back toward lead. Giant stars therefore pile material at bismuth as well as at lead.

A rapid-process share exists and is smaller. The bismuth in an alloy is mostly that terminal slow-process nucleus. The decay is real, and no laboratory lasts long enough to watch a sample of it.

trivia.title: Confused With Lead for Centuries
trivia.summary: Workshops filed this pretty crystalline metal with lead, tin, or antimony until an eighteenth-century chemist showed that its reactions were its own.
trivia.story: Bismuth minerals were known through the Middle Ages and were constantly confused with lead, tin, or antimony. The crystals can look striking, and a striking look still does not prove which metal is in the hand. Claude François Geoffroy showed in 1753 that bismuth was its own metal, with reactions that missed the lookalikes. After that distinction, the odd properties had a box of their own instead of a borrowed name. Easy melting, brittleness, and a faint iridescent color belonged to bismuth itself, no longer filed under lead.

trivia.title: A German Name of Uncertain Origin
trivia.summary: The word arrived from German mining speech, and scholars still do not share one settled story about the older phrase inside it.
trivia.story: The name bismuth comes from the German Wismut, and nobody has a single agreed story for the older meaning. One suggestion derives it from a phrase for a white mass, which would suit a pale metal, and the suggestion stays a guess. Unlike hafnium or holmium, the element does not commemorate a city that a map can settle. Miners were using the word well before Geoffroy, in 1753, showed the metal was distinct from lead. The workshop recognized the substance more readily than scholars could finish explaining the name.

trivia.title: The Stable Element That Was Not
trivia.summary: Textbooks once called this the last stable element, until a very slow decay showed that the final natural isotope does break down.
trivia.story: For a long time bismuth was called the heaviest stable element, the last box that seemed not to decay. In 2003 that long comfort failed, and it failed by a measurement rather than by a surprise in the hand. The only natural isotope, bismuth-209, was shown to decay by emitting an alpha particle. The half-life is about 2 × 10^19 years, far longer than the age of the universe, so the loss is almost imaginary. A lump still behaves as if permanent, radioactive only in the technical sense and stable for every ordinary human purpose.

trivia.title: An Alloy That Melts in Hot Water
trivia.summary: A workshop alloy of this metal lets go at a temperature hot water can reach, which put it into fuses and fire-sprinkler links.
trivia.story: Wood's metal, an alloy built around bismuth, melts in hot water, well below the point where ordinary solder softens. The low melting point put it into fire-sprinkler links and into fuses that should open when equipment overheats. The useful fact is physical, a metal that yields at the temperature of a kettle rather than the temperature of a furnace. Because its reputation is gentler than lead's, bismuth sometimes replaces lead in solders and in shotgun pellets. A metal once confused with lead became one of the materials chosen when people wanted a softer exit from lead's old jobs.

trivia.title: The Pink Bottle in the Cabinet
trivia.summary: A familiar medicine for an upset stomach is built on a compound of this metal, a household role far from any medieval mine.
trivia.story: Pepto-Bismol, the pink medicine kept for upset stomachs, is built on a compound of bismuth. The element therefore has a household fame that tungsten, hafnium, and rhenium never reached. A person using it is unlikely to be thinking of Geoffroy in 1753 or of a half-life longer than the universe. Feeling better is still a real use, and it is the use most families actually meet. The path from a mineral confused with lead to a mild bottle in a cabinet is the long public journey of bismuth.

applications.title: Stomach medicine
applications.body: Bismuth subsalicylate is the active ingredient in some upset-stomach medicines. It is a compound, taken as directed, not a chunk of metal.

applications.title: Low-melting alloys
applications.body: Bismuth alloys can melt in hot water. They are used in fire-sprinkler links and in metal casts that must not get extremely hot.

applications.title: A pretty crystal
applications.body: Bismuth crystals grow in stair steps and flash rainbow colors from a thin oxide film. The color is that film, like a soap bubble.

elements.name: Polonium

summary.beginner:
Polonium is element 84, a rare radioactive metal found in uranium ores in tiny amounts. There is no everyday object made of it.

Its symbol is Po. At room temperature polonium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 16. In class those are called period 6 and group 16.

Marie and Pierre Curie separated it from pitchblende. It is intensely radioactive. Handling it is a specialist job with serious controls, not a school demonstration.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral polonium atom has 84 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Polonium is a solid post-transition in period 6 and group 16. Polonium is a radioactive chalcogen, all of whose isotopes decay, and it occurs as a daughter in uranium and thorium chains.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p4. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 6. Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +4. The one courses meet most often is +2.

A few industrial antistatic devices once used a sealed polonium source. That is a historical use of the radiation, not of polonium chemistry.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Polonium (Z = 84) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p4. The famous isotope is Po-210, an intense alpha emitter.

Chemistry resembles tellurium, but the radioactivity dominates every practical decision long before the oxidation state does.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +2, +4. The one courses meet most often is +2. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Polonium: say the name, write Po, find Z=84 on the table, note the family (Post-transition), and connect it to one real use — radioactive; historically in antistatic devices.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Polonium: electron configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p4, Typical oxidation states: +2, +4. It sits in group 16. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. all isotopes radioactive.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Polonium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; daughter of uranium/thorium chains If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from pitchblende as a radioactive product of uranium.

elements.history:
Marie and Pierre Curie, following the radioactivity of pitchblende beyond uranium, announced a new element in July 1898. Marie named it polonium, for Poland, her birth country, which was not then on the map as a state. They isolated it by following the activity through chemical separations, not by collecting a visible lump.

Polonium is intensely radioactive. A milligram is hot to the touch from its own alpha decay. Later sources were made by irradiating bismuth rather than by mining.
elements.howDiscovered:
Marie and Pierre Curie measured the radioactivity of pitchblende and found it several times higher than the uranium content allowed. In 1898 they dissolved the ore and separated it by the analytical groups. The extra activity followed the bismuth fraction, and it could be enriched further by fractional precipitation and by sublimation, which bismuth’s own activity, having none, could not imitate.

The detector was an electrometer, not a balance. They never had a visible piece of the new element in that first year. Polonium was discovered as an activity that refused to stay proportional to any known element in the ore and that clung to the bismuth group while exceeding bismuth.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Polonium has no isotope that lasts. In a star, the slow process steps through polonium and the polonium alpha-decays, which is part of why the capture chain terminates near lead and bismuth. The rapid process makes polonium too, and it decays onward or, in an extreme blast, fissions.

On Earth the only polonium is what uranium and thorium decay chains produce now, especially polonium-210, and it disappears on a scale of months. There is no primordial polonium in a mineral. The atoms are daughters, constantly replenished, of uranium and thorium the rapid process made long ago.

trivia.title: Named for a Country Off the Map
trivia.summary: Two researchers following extra radioactivity in an ore announced a new element and named it for a homeland that was not then a free state.
trivia.story: Marie and Pierre Curie, in July 1898, announced a new element hidden in pitchblende, beyond the uranium already accounted for. Marie named it polonium, for Poland, her birth country, which was not then a free state on the political map. The name was an act of loyalty as well as a chemical label. They had no visible lump to pass around, only an activity that remained after uranium and thorium were removed. A country missing from the map of states was written onto the periodic table by following those rays.

trivia.title: Activity That Led Through the Ore
trivia.summary: After uranium and thorium were accounted for, the ore was still fiercely active, and the Curies followed that remainder through their separations.
trivia.story: Pitchblende was more radioactive than its uranium could explain, even after thorium had been accounted for. Marie and Pierre Curie followed that extra activity through chemical separations, keeping every fraction their instruments still found hot with rays. They were tracking a property, radioactivity, rather than gathering a lump a visitor could admire. Polonium announced itself by staying in the active portion after the known radioactive elements had been removed. The discovery was a thread pulled through a dark ore until the thread was strong enough to deserve a country's name.

trivia.title: Years of Work and a Heavy Cost
trivia.summary: A tiny amount of the new element heats itself by its own rays, and the long labor of the research harmed the two people who led it.
trivia.story: Polonium is intensely radioactive, and a milligram is hot to the touch from the alpha particles it emits. That outcome shows how fierce a speck can be, and it is an outcome rather than a set of instructions. The Curies' long work with pitchblende, and with the elements they separated from it, harmed their health. The damage was the slow cost of years spent among strong sources, not one invented blast or one single day. An element named for a homeland extracted a personal price from the two people who gave it that name.

trivia.title: London and a Radioactive Trail
trivia.summary: A documented crime in London used this element as a poison, and investigators reconstructed the events from the rays left behind.
trivia.story: In 2006 Alexander Litvinenko was poisoned with polonium in London, and the poisoning killed him. Investigators followed the radioactivity through places tied to the crime, because instruments can find what the eye cannot see. The case is recorded history, a real crime, and the telling here stays at that level. A classroom account stops short of any amount and any procedure, because those details are not the history worth keeping. The lasting point is stark enough, a speck can kill, and the rays themselves can reconstruct where it went.

trivia.title: No Longer Won From the Mine
trivia.summary: Digging the element out of uranium ore was a miserable bargain, and later supplies were produced on purpose from a different metal.
trivia.story: Separating polonium from pitchblende meant moving huge masses of ore for a yield too small to see. Later supplies were produced by irradiating bismuth, so the element was made on purpose instead of being chased through uranium rock. The shift is a historical outcome, the end of a miserable mining bargain. Polonium became a specialist source of alpha particles, still intensely radioactive and still handled as a danger. The classroom stops at that change of origin, from ore to a prepared source, and does not continue into a method.

applications.title: No everyday product
applications.body: Polonium is too radioactive for any ordinary material. There is no polonium pan, pigment, or school sample.

applications.title: A historical static eliminator
applications.body: A few industrial devices once used a sealed polonium source to neutralize static charge. Those sources are regulated and are not a consumer part.

applications.title: A decay product
applications.body: Polonium forms in uranium ores as the ore decays. The amount in the rock is tiny, and separating it was the Curies' work.

sample.title: A thin deposit
sample.body: Polonium is so radioactive that a lump of the pure metal is rarely kept. This sealed piece is polonium deposited on a small brass sheet, which is how a visible sample of the element is handled.

elements.name: Astatine

summary.beginner:
Astatine is element 85, the halogen under iodine, and it is so radioactive that a visible piece has never been gathered. What chemists know comes from tiny traces made in accelerators.

Its symbol is At. At room temperature astatine is a solid. It is a halogen, a reactive nonmetal in the column next to the noble gases. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 17. In class those are called period 6 and group 17.

On the table it sits where a halogen should. In a bottle it does not exist. Any sentence about its color or its melting point is an inference, not a sample you could point at.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral astatine atom has 85 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Astatine is a solid halogen in period 6 and group 17. Astatine has no stable isotope, and its chemistry is known from tracer experiments rather than from a bulk sample.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p5. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 7. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1.

It is expected to be a halogen, with a tendency toward positive oxidation states that iodine already hints at. The half-lives are short enough that the element never accumulates.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Astatine (Z = 85) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p5. Tracer chemistry suggests both At- and positive states, so astatine is a halogen drifting toward metallic behavior.

No macroscopic property has been measured on a visible piece, and predictions should be labeled as predictions.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.
