discovery.text: Produced by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles.

elements.history:
The gap under iodine was filled in 1940 at Berkeley. Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie, and Emilio Segrè bombarded bismuth with alpha particles and chemically followed the product, which behaved as a halogen. They named it astatine, from the Greek astatos, unstable. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of about 8 hours.

No one has seen a visible piece of astatine. Its chemistry is inferred from tracer experiments: it is the heaviest halogen, metallic in tendency, and present in nature only as a fleeting decay product.
elements.howDiscovered:
Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie, and Emilio Segrè bombarded bismuth with alpha particles in the Berkeley cyclotron in 1940. The target became radioactive with a half-life of hours. They dissolved it and the activity followed the chemistry of a halogen: it could be extracted and coprecipitated with iodine, and it distilled the way a heavy halogen should.

No weighable amount was produced. The chemical behavior plus the radiation identified element 85, the gap under iodine, which had been sought in minerals and missed because every isotope is short-lived. Astatine was discovered as a radioactive tracer that behaved as iodine’s heavier neighbor.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Astatine is only a brief step. Every isotope lives for hours or less. Neutron-capture paths may pass through astatine, and the nucleus decays before a star can mix it into space in any stored form. Uranium and thorium chains also produce it, for seconds, inside minerals that contain those parents.

There is no astatine ore and no primordial stock. Atoms made in accelerators, and atoms flickering inside uranium minerals, are the inventory. The universe does not accumulate this element.

trivia.title: Made for a Moment at Berkeley
trivia.summary: Three researchers struck bismuth with helium nuclei and then followed a product that behaved like the heaviest member of iodine's family.
trivia.story: Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie, and Emilio Segrè filled the gap under iodine in 1940, working at Berkeley. They bombarded bismuth with alpha particles and then followed the new activity through a series of chemical separations. It behaved as a halogen, iodine's family, which matched the place the periodic table had saved for it. The amount was tiny, far below anything a person could see or weigh on an ordinary balance. The evidence was tracer chemistry, a radioactivity that moved through the tests like a heavy cousin of iodine.

trivia.title: A Name That Means Unstable
trivia.summary: The discoverers chose a Greek word for something that will not hold still, and the word describes the samples more honestly than a place name would.
trivia.story: Corson, MacKenzie, and Segrè named element 85 astatine, from the Greek astatos, which means unstable. Towns, gods, and continents name many of the neighbors, and this element was named for its own refusal to last. A classical adjective became a warning label, readable by anyone who asks what the word means. The translation tells a student not to expect a jar of it in the stockroom beside iodine. The Berkeley product was real, and the most important fact about it was already sitting inside the name.

trivia.title: Never Enough to See
trivia.summary: Every sample that has ever existed has been vanishingly small, and the world has never held a visible piece of the element at one time.
trivia.story: Only tiny amounts of astatine have existed at any one moment, in targets or in the whole crust of the Earth. Nobody has seen a visible piece, and tales of a speck you could point to go beyond what the experiments held. In nature it appears only as a fleeting decay product, formed and lost while longer-lived elements carry on. Chemists learned it by watching where the radioactivity traveled, not by scraping a solid out of a beaker. The 1940 trace earned its box by behaving as element 85 should, and then it was gone.

trivia.title: Gone Again in Hours
trivia.summary: The longest-lived form fades on the scale of a school day, which is why nobody can save a sample for the next morning's class.
trivia.story: The longest-lived isotope of astatine has a half-life of about eight hours, a clock shorter than a school day and night. Material made in the morning is largely transformed by the next day into elements that are no longer astatine. A stockroom bottle is therefore impossible, because the contents would not survive until the next class. The Greek name, unstable, is a schedule as much as a description. The Berkeley chemists had to work quickly, since their product would not wait through a leisurely week of tests.

trivia.title: Chemistry Done With a Trace
trivia.summary: What the element does in a flask was learned from invisible quantities, by noticing which chemical company the radioactivity preferred.
trivia.story: Astatine's chemistry was inferred from tracer experiments rather than from a pile of crystals. Researchers noted which solution or solid carried the radioactivity, and from those choices they described a halogen with a metallic leaning. It is the heaviest halogen, and it leans toward metal more than iodine, the neighbor above it, ever does. The description is genuine knowledge, gathered without a crucible full of powder. Every chemical statement about it rests on amounts too small to see, which makes the evidence strange and still solid.

applications.title: No bulk use
applications.body: Astatine has never been gathered into a visible piece. There is no product, pigment, or medicine made from a bottle of it.

applications.title: Tracer studies
applications.body: What chemists know comes from following a few radioactive atoms. That is research, not a use in the ordinary sense.

applications.title: A halogen on paper
applications.body: On the table, astatine sits under iodine. Any guess about its color or its chemistry is an inference from that place.

sample.body: Astatine has never been gathered into a piece large enough to see as a solid or a liquid. The blue glow is light from a microscopic sample of the element. The empty vial beside it is only there for scale.

elements.name: Radon

summary.beginner:
Radon is element 86, a radioactive noble gas that can seep out of rock and soil into a house. It has no color and no smell, which is why test kits exist.

Its symbol is Rn. At room temperature radon is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a noble gas. Left alone, it almost never joins other elements to make compounds. On the periodic table it is in row 6, column 18. In class those are called period 6 and group 18.

Radon comes from the decay of uranium and thorium in the ground. Breathing it for years raises the risk of lung cancer. Venting a basement is the practical response, not collecting the gas.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral radon atom has 86 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Radon is a noble gas in period 6 and group 18. Radon is a radioactive noble gas, and radon-222 from the uranium series is the indoor-air hazard.

The electron configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p6. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 8. Oxidation states are not listed for this entry.

The half-life of Rn-222 is 3.8 days. It is an alpha emitter. The danger is the decay chain in the lungs, not a chemical reaction with the gas.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Radon (Z = 86) has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p6. Rn-222's short half-life means the gas itself fades quickly, but its solid decay products stick to dust and deliver the alpha dose.

Chemically it is a noble gas. Biologically it is a radiological problem.

Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Observed as the radioactive gas from radium decay.

elements.history:
Friedrich Ernst Dorn noticed in 1900 that radium gave off a radioactive gas. Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy studied the related emanation from thorium and showed that these gases were a new element in the radium and thorium decay chains. The name radon was adopted in 1923, from radium, replacing emanation and niton.

Radon-222, with a half-life of 3.8 days, seeps from uranium-bearing rock into houses. It is the noble gas people measure for health, not for chemistry.
elements.howDiscovered:
Friedrich Ernst Dorn collected the gas that bled out of a radium preparation in 1900 and found that the gas itself was radioactive. Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy studied the similar emanation from thorium. The gases could be condensed with liquid air, transferred from vessel to vessel, and they decayed with characteristic half-lives while the parent salt grew a fresh supply.

Diffusion rates suggested a heavy monatomic gas. The discovery was the transfer: the activity moved as a gas, condensed as a gas, and came back when the radium decayed, so it was a daughter element and not a dust of the parent.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Radon is a decay-chain gas. Radon-222 comes from radium-226, itself a daughter of uranium-238. Radon-220 comes from the thorium chain. A neutron-capture blast can make a radon nucleus, and that nucleus decays in days or less, so it never joins the gas a new solar system inherits.

The radon in indoor air is terrestrial and current. It exists because uranium and thorium are still decaying. Its cosmic story is the story of those parent metals.

trivia.title: A Gas That Escaped From Radium
trivia.summary: A physicist noticed that radium was giving off a radioactive gas, and the gas was a new element someone might later breathe without seeing it.
trivia.story: Friedrich Ernst Dorn noticed in 1900 that radium gives off a radioactive gas as it decays. The gas was a new element, not dust and not a leak in the apparatus, and early workers called it radium emanation. The first name described the behavior, a something seeping out, and it was not yet the permanent word. A solid radioactive element was exhaling another element, which is a startling kind of parenthood. The later danger starts there, because the child element is a gas a person can breathe without ever seeing it.

trivia.title: Emanation Then Niton Then Radon
trivia.summary: The gas wore a description, then another formal name, then the label used now, and that last word is the one public warnings could share.
trivia.story: Before it reached the name used now, the radioactive gas collected a small stack of earlier labels. Emanation described how it seeped from radium and from thorium, a behavior treated as a label. Niton was a later formal name, taken from a word for shining, and it also failed to last. In 1923 the name radon, built from radium, was adopted, and emanation and niton stepped aside. One shared word let scientists and, later, homeowners talk about the same gas, which is why the renaming mattered.

trivia.title: The Same Surprise From Thorium
trivia.summary: Thorium was giving off a similar gas, and two physicists showed that these emanations were a new element inside the decay chains.
trivia.story: Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy studied the gas thorium gives off, together with the emanation Dorn had found from radium. They showed that these gases were a new element appearing in the decay chains of those metals. The result tied a laboratory curiosity to the larger fact that elements transform into other elements. Radon was evidence for that transformation, a noble gas born out of a solid parent as the parent decayed. A radioactive member of helium's family shook the assumption that every noble gas was automatically gentle.

trivia.title: The Noble Gas in the Basement
trivia.summary: A short-lived isotope seeps from ordinary rock into houses, and years of living with high levels raise the risk of lung cancer.
trivia.story: Radon-222 seeps from uranium-bearing rock and soil into houses, and its half-life is just under four days. As a noble gas it does not cling to walls or announce itself with a smell or a color. People who live for years with high levels face a real increase in the risk of lung cancer. Health officers therefore measure it more often than research chemists ever bottle it. A gas first noticed above radium in 1900 turned out to be an invisible guest in ordinary basements.

trivia.title: Testing and an Open Window
trivia.summary: The public answer to this household gas is ordinary on purpose, and it starts by finding out whether the air indoors is carrying it.
trivia.story: The public-health answer to radon is deliberately plain, and it begins with a measurement of the air in the house. Test low rooms over ground that may supply the gas, and ventilate so the gas does not linger and build up. Those two steps, testing and ventilation, are protection for residents, not a laboratory procedure for concentrating the element. Dorn's 1900 emanation became, a century later, a reason to use a home detector and to keep fresh air moving. The advice sounds like housekeeping because housekeeping, in this case, is the response that lowers the risk.

applications.title: A gas to vent, not to use
applications.body: Radon seeping into a house is a health risk, not a resource. The practical response is to test and, if needed, to vent the foundation.

applications.title: How it gets indoors
applications.body: Uranium and thorium in soil decay through a chain that includes radon. The gas can move through cracks that a liquid or a dust cannot.

applications.title: Old medical uses, abandoned
applications.body: Radon was once sealed into small tubes for medical treatments. That practice belongs to the history of radiation, not to a current household product.

elements.name: Francium

summary.beginner:
Francium is element 87, an alkali metal so radioactive that only tiny amounts exist at any moment. You will not hold a sample.

Its symbol is Fr. At room temperature francium is a solid. It is an alkali metal: soft, and quick to react with water. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 1. In class those are called period 7 and group 1.

It would behave like cesium if you could collect it: a soft metal, eager to lose one electron. The atoms decay before anyone can gather a visible piece.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral francium atom has 87 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Francium is a solid alkali metal in period 7 and group 1. Francium is the heaviest alkali metal, and every isotope is short-lived.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 7s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 8, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

The longest-lived isotope lasts about 22 minutes. Chemistry is inferred from a few atoms and from the group trend: a single outer electron and a +1 ion.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Francium (Z = 87) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 7s1. Francium is expected to be the most electropositive element, but relativistic effects on the 7s electron complicate a simple extrapolation from cesium.

No bulk property has been measured.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Isolated from actinium decay as a short-lived alkali metal.

elements.history:
Marguerite Perey, working at the Curie Institute, found a short-lived alkali metal among the decay products of actinium in 1939. She named it francium, for France. It was the last element discovered in a natural decay chain rather than made in an accelerator.

The longest-lived isotope lasts about 22 minutes. Francium is the most electropositive element, and also one that no one will ever hold: the whole Earth’s crust contains grams of it at any moment.
elements.howDiscovered:
Marguerite Perey followed the decay products of actinium-227 at the Curie Institute. In 1939 a small fraction of the activity coprecipitated with caesium perchlorate, the way an alkali metal does, and that fraction decayed with a half-life of about 22 minutes. It grew back in from purified actinium, so it was a daughter, not a contamination.

The chemistry excluded every known alkali, and the half-life excluded the other daughters. Francium was discovered by a precipitation that alkalis undergo and by a clock that started when actinium decayed. It was the last element found in a natural decay series.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Francium lasts minutes. Francium-223, the longest-lived isotope, is a rare branch of actinium-227 in the uranium-235 chain. A neutron-rich blast can assemble a francium nucleus, and it beta-decays before any star can deliver it as francium.

There is no mineral and no primordial stock. At any moment the crust holds grams of francium, made and destroyed continuously. The original nuclei, as a stock from before the Earth, do not exist.

trivia.title: The Last Element Found in Nature
trivia.summary: A chemist sorting the decay of a heavier element found a new alkali metal, the last element discovered in a natural chain.
trivia.story: Marguerite Perey, at the Curie Institute, found a short-lived alkali metal among actinium's decay products in 1939. She named the new alkali metal francium, choosing France as its namesake. It was the last element discovered in a natural decay chain, rather than created first by an accelerator. With her result, the old hunt for new elements in ores and decay series came to its end. Later boxes were filled by machines that made atoms on purpose, so francium closes the era of finding elements already at work in nature.

trivia.title: An Alkali Metal in the Decay
trivia.summary: The new substance behaved like sodium's family, which told the discoverer which empty box at the bottom of that column she had filled.
trivia.story: Perey studied the decay products of actinium, work done with chemistry rather than with a new accelerating machine. One component acted as an alkali metal, in the family of sodium and caesium, which pointed to a particular empty box. The box was element 87, and the amount available was minute. A short lifetime meant the tests had to be quick, finished while the atoms were still the new element. Actinium's own breakdown supplied the source, and a chemical separation supplied the proof that the alkali metal was real.

trivia.title: Work in the Curie Institute
trivia.summary: The discoverer was working in the laboratory tradition Marie Curie had built, and the new metal extended that long hunt through radioactive residues.
trivia.story: Perey worked in the Curie Institute, in the tradition Marie Curie had established for chasing radioactive substances. Polonium and radium had come from that same line of work at the end of the nineteenth century. Francium came from a later generation still willing to sort decay products that looked used up. The institute's habit was to follow rays with careful chemistry, and Perey applied that habit to actinium. From those separations came an alkali metal named for France, evidence that a laboratory's training can outlast one career.

trivia.title: Minutes Long and Almost Nowhere
trivia.summary: The longest-lived form disappears in minutes, and the whole rocky crust of the Earth holds only a tiny stock at any moment.
trivia.story: The longest-lived isotope of francium lasts about twenty-two minutes before it decays further. In that short span an atom can be detected, and then it is no longer francium. The entire crust of the Earth holds only grams of it at any moment, nothing a mine could collect. No museum will ever set a bead of the metal in a case, because a bead cannot be assembled. The scarcity is the arithmetic of a brief life fed by a slow parent decay, a metal always arriving and always leaving.

trivia.title: The Metal Nobody Will Hold
trivia.summary: On paper this is the most extreme alkali metal, eager to give up an electron, and in practice there is never a piece to pass around.
trivia.story: Francium is the most electropositive element, the most willing in principle to give up an electron like a classic alkali metal. That ranking is a fact about its place at the bottom of the column. The practical limit is stricter, since no sample is large enough or long-lived enough to pass around a classroom. Perey established the identity in 1939 without producing a souvenir anyone could keep. An extreme metallic personality and an extreme scarcity arrived together, completing the column without ever filling a jar.

applications.title: No product
applications.body: Francium decays so quickly that there is never enough of it to make an object. It has no use as a material.

applications.title: Research atoms
applications.body: Physicists study a few francium atoms when they want the heaviest alkali metal. The sample is a beam or a trap, not a bottle.

applications.title: What the column predicts
applications.body: If it could be collected, francium would behave like cesium: one outer electron, and a violent reaction with water. The atoms do not last long enough to test that in bulk.

elements.name: Radium

summary.beginner:
Radium is element 88, a metal that is intensely radioactive. It was once painted onto watch dials so they would glow, and that use was abandoned because it harmed the workers.

Its symbol is Ra. At room temperature radium is a solid. It is an alkaline-earth metal. These metals react, but less wildly than the alkali metals beside them. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 2. In class those are called period 7 and group 2.

Radium sits under calcium and barium, so the body can mistake it for those metals and put it into bone. The Curies separated it from uranium ore. It is not a glow-in-the-dark craft material.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral radium atom has 88 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Radium is a solid alkaline-earth metal in period 7 and group 2. Radium is an alkaline-earth radioelement, chemically Ra2+, and radium-226 was the historical luminous-paint isotope.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

The glow of old paint came from radiation hitting a phosphor, not from radium shining by itself like a flame. The medical and industrial uses of that era are a cautionary history.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Radium (Z = 88) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 7s2. Ra-226 decays by alpha emission to radon-222, so a sealed radium source also becomes a radon source.

The bone-seeking behavior is the group-2 chemistry of Ra2+ plus a radiological consequence.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Separated from pitchblende; intensely radioactive.

elements.history:
In December 1898, months after polonium, Marie and Pierre Curie announced a second, far more radioactive element in pitchblende. They named it radium, from the Latin radius, a ray. Isolating a tenth of a gram of the chloride from tonnes of ore took until 1902.

Radium’s glow put it into watch dials and patent medicines before the danger was understood. The same element gave Rutherford the alpha particles he used to probe the nucleus, and it defined the curie as a unit of activity.
elements.howDiscovered:
After polonium had been traced into the bismuth fraction of pitchblende, Marie and Pierre Curie found a second excess of activity in the barium fraction. In late 1898 they fractionally crystallized barium chloride. The least soluble crops grew more radioactive with each crystallization, and the atomic weight of the salt crept upward. Eugène Demarçay photographed a new spectral line in the enriched sample.

The work consumed tonnes of Joachimsthal residues to yield a tenth of a gram of radium chloride by 1902. The discovery in 1898 was the crystallization: radioactivity and a spectral line concentrating together, in the crystals, away from barium.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Radium does not survive on its own from the stars. Radium-226, with a half-life near 1,600 years, is produced continually by the decay of uranium-238. Radium-228 comes from thorium-232. Any radium the rapid process made directly was gone long before the solar system formed.

The radium separated from pitchblende was young in geologic terms, even though its uranium parent was made in neutron-rich blasts billions of years earlier. As long as the uranium lasts, the radium is replenished. The element’s cosmic origin is the origin of uranium.

trivia.title: A Second Ray in the Pitchblende
trivia.summary: Months after their first new element, the same two researchers announced another in the ore and named this one for the rays themselves.
trivia.story: Marie and Pierre Curie, in December 1898, announced a second element in pitchblende, months after polonium and far more radioactive. They named it radium, from the Latin radius, a ray, taking the label from the phenomenon that revealed it. The instruments were already showing an activity much stronger than the uranium in the ore could explain. Pitchblende still held this fiercer remainder after the known radioactive portions had been considered. The name was not decoration, because rays were the evidence, the guide, and the reason the search continued.

trivia.title: Tonnes of Ore a Speck of Salt
trivia.summary: Announcing the element was only the opening, and isolating a visible salt required years of labor and a mountain of rock.
trivia.story: Isolating radium was a harsher task than announcing it in the first excited paper. The Curies processed tonnes of ore to obtain about a tenth of a gram of the chloride, and the work lasted until 1902. A great mass of rock had become a speck of salt that could sit in a small tube. The speck glowed and ionized the air, which made a trivial-looking quantity feel miraculous to visitors. Wonder moved faster than caution, and that imbalance shaped radium's early life in public.

trivia.title: Brushes Pointed With the Lips
trivia.summary: Dial painters in the United States tipped glowing brushes on their lips after being told the work was harmless, and years later they were gravely ill.
trivia.story: In the United States during the 1910s and 1920s, young women painted watch dials with radium so the numbers would glow. They pointed the fine brushes with their lips, and the employers told them the paint was harmless. The radium remained in their bodies, and in the years afterward they became gravely ill. The workers are remembered as the radium girls, a plain name for a workplace disaster. A glow marketed as delicate work was radioactive material taken up day after day, and the illnesses exposed the assurance as false.

trivia.title: A Tonic That Was Not Medicine
trivia.summary: Radioactive water was bottled and sold as a vigor drink, and the death of a well-known user in 1932 made the fashion indefensible.
trivia.story: Radium was also sold, recklessly, as a health drink to people chasing energy and a feeling of vigor. A commercial product called Radithor put radioactive water in bottles and wrapped it in a promise of health. Eben Byers, a wealthy American customer, used the Radithor tonic and died in 1932. His death made the whole fashion for drinking radioactive water much harder to defend in public. A scientific triumph had been bottled by sellers who treated rays as a tonic, and 1932 exposed that mistake.

trivia.title: A Laboratory Tool and a Fad
trivia.summary: The same rays that reckless sellers bottled also gave a physicist the particles he used to probe the atom, and they defined a unit.
trivia.story: Radium's life in the laboratory was as serious as its life in the marketplace was reckless. Rutherford used the alpha particles streaming from it to probe atoms, work that led toward the nuclear model. The curie, a unit of radioactivity, was defined from radium's activity, so the element helped name the measurement. The same substance therefore sat in patent medicines and in the founding experiments of nuclear science. People had to learn the difference between a research source and a drink, and that education came at a high human cost.

applications.title: A use that was stopped
applications.body: Radium paint made watch dials glow. The workers who painted it were harmed, and the use was abandoned. Old dials are a disposal problem, not a collectible to scrape.

applications.title: Why it was dangerous
applications.body: Radium behaves a little like calcium, so the body can deposit it in bone. The glow was never worth that.

applications.title: Research sources
applications.body: Sealed radium sources still exist in some legacy medical and industrial equipment. They are regulated radioactive objects.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.title: A tiny radium source
sample.body: Pure radium metal is rarely photographed. This sliver, about 1.5 by 3 millimetres, is a radium-226 source of the kind once fitted to a Geiger counter. It is a real sample of the element, not a drawing.
sample.credit: grenadier, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

elements.name: Actinium

summary.beginner:
Actinium is element 89, the start of the actinide row, and it is radioactive. It is scarce, and its uses are in research rather than in products you buy.

Its symbol is Ac. At room temperature actinium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 3. In class those are called period 7 and group 3.

Actinium is present in uranium ores in tiny amounts because it is part of a decay chain. The metal itself is not something a museum puts in a case for visitors to lean on.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral actinium atom has 89 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Actinium is a solid actinide in period 7 and group 3. Actinium is the prototype actinide, usually Ac3+, and it is the parent of one natural decay series.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 6d1 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The chemistry resembles lanthanum: a +3 ion with no f electrons in the common state. Samples large enough to see are a radiological project.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Actinium (Z = 89) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 6d1 7s2. The 6d1 7s2 configuration makes Ac3+ a closed-shell ion like La3+.

Later actinides fill 5f. Actinium itself is the name-bearer, not the element with the famous f-electron chemistry.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Actinium: say the name, write Ac, find Z=89 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — start of the actinide series.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Actinium: electron configuration [Rn] 6d1 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It sits in group 3. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. 5f/6d boundary; +3.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Actinium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; parent of the actinium decay series If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Separated from pitchblende residues.

elements.history:
André-Louis Debierne, a colleague of the Curies, found a new radioactive substance in pitchblende residues in 1899 and named it actinium, from the Greek aktis, a ray. Friedrich Oskar Giesel discovered it independently in 1902. The chemistry was hard because actinium follows the rare earths.

Actinium gave its name to the series of elements that fill the 5f orbitals. It is also the parent of the actinium decay chain, which ends at lead-207.
elements.howDiscovered:
André-Louis Debierne examined the rare-earth fraction of pitchblende after uranium, polonium, and radium had been removed. In 1899 a radioactivity remained that precipitated with ammonia and followed lanthanum, and that was not radium and not thorium. Friedrich Oskar Giesel found the same activity independently.

The chemistry was awkward because actinium and lanthanum are hard to part, so early samples were dilute. The evidence was an activity that survived every removal of the known radioactive elements and that stayed with the rare-earth precipitate. Actinium was discovered as what was left in that precipitate.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Actinium-227, with a half-life near 22 years, belongs to the uranium-235 decay chain. Uranium minerals produce it continuously. None of it survives from the formation of the Earth as actinium. The rapid process that made the uranium is the original event.

Other actinium isotopes are shorter-lived. Blasts can make them, and they decay. Actinium in a laboratory was milked from a uranium or radium parent, or made in a reactor. It is not a primordial metal.

trivia.title: Another Ray in the Residues
trivia.summary: A colleague of the Curies found yet another radioactive substance in the ore residues and named it, as radium had been named, for the rays.
trivia.story: André-Louis Debierne, working with the Curies, found a new radioactive substance in pitchblende residues in 1899. He named it actinium, from the Greek aktis, a ray, echoing the idea Marie and Pierre had used for radium. The chemistry was awkward, because actinium follows the rare earths and disappears into their separations. Detecting those rays in the residues was far easier than preparing a salt anyone would call clean. From the start it was scarce, a trace in uranium ores rather than a mineral mined for itself.

trivia.title: Found Again a Few Years Later
trivia.summary: Another chemist came upon the same radioactivity independently, and the second finding made the first much harder to dismiss as a private mistake.
trivia.story: Friedrich Oskar Giesel came upon actinium independently in 1902, several years after Debierne had named it. Pitchblende residues were being examined in more than one city, so a second, independent encounter was entirely possible. Giesel's result showed that the activity was not a private mistake on a single bench. Priority remains with Debierne in 1899, and the repetition still strengthened the claim. A scarce trace earns trust when a different chemist finds it again, which is the old standard applied to a faint element.

trivia.title: Scarce Company in the Uranium Ore
trivia.summary: Uranium minerals hold only a whisper of this element, which is why it was found by chasing rays instead of by opening a mine of its own.
trivia.story: Actinium has never gathered into a rich ore that miners could hunt for the element itself. It occurs as a scarce companion in uranium minerals, present because decay chains pass through it. Debierne found it in the residues only after the more plentiful radioactive elements had been wrestled out of the way. No hillside of actinium was ever waiting to be crushed, washed, and bagged. The element is a brief stop on the way from uranium toward lead, a trace to detect rather than a crate to fill.

trivia.title: The Element That Named a Row
trivia.summary: A scarce radioactive metal lent its name to the whole row of heavy elements that fills the bottom of the modern table.
trivia.story: Actinium gave its name to the actinides, the row of elements that fill the 5f orbitals beneath the lanthanides. Thorium, uranium, and the elements made later in reactors all sit in the family that word created. A scarce substance found in 1899 became the heading on an entire line of the table. What began as a word for rays grew into a label for a shared electron structure and a shared chemistry. Students meet the word actinide more often than the element itself, a quiet success for the name Debierne chose.

trivia.title: Following the Rare Earths Down
trivia.summary: Separations were difficult because this element tagged along with the rare earths, and its chain of decays eventually finishes at lead.
trivia.story: Chemists struggled to separate actinium because it follows the rare earths, sharing their solutions and their precipitates. The rays could be measured while the material still looked like a mixture of lanthanides. The decay chain that begins with actinium ends at lead-207, a stable isotope and a quiet finish. Francium appears on that same chain, which is how Perey later found her short-lived alkali metal. A trace in uranium ore is the start of a route the table can draw from a ray, through francium, down to lead.

applications.title: Research
applications.body: Actinium is scarce and radioactive. The work done with it is research, including studies of how such a heavy atom behaves in solution.

applications.title: A parent of a decay series
applications.body: One natural radioactive series is named for actinium because the chain passes through it on the way from uranium to lead.

applications.title: No consumer product
applications.body: There is no actinium alloy in a device you can buy. Samples large enough to see are a radiological project.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.title: A sample that glows
sample.body: Actinium is intensely radioactive, and a visible sample glows from its own radiation. This vial holds a small amount of the element in solution. The blue light is the sample, not a lamp behind the glass.
sample.credit: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

elements.name: Thorium

summary.beginner:
Thorium is element 90, a radioactive metal that once made gas-lantern mantles glow brightly. It can also be part of a nuclear fuel cycle.

Its symbol is Th. At room temperature thorium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

The mantle use is historical. Thorium oxide glowed when heated, and the radioactivity was a reason to stop using it so casually. The metal is dense and silvery when freshly cut.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral thorium atom has 90 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Thorium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Thorium is a long-lived radioactive actinide, usually +4, and thorium-232 can breed uranium-233.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 6d2 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 10, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4.

Gas mantles used ThO2 mixed with a little cerium. The nuclear interest is that thorium-232 absorbs a neutron and, after decays, becomes fissile uranium-233.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Thorium (Z = 90) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 6d2 7s2. Th4+ has no 5f electrons, so the chemistry looks like a heavy group-4 metal.

The breeding chain to U-233 is a nuclear-engineering proposal, not a property of the oxide in a lantern.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Thorium: say the name, write Th, find Z=90 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — gas-lantern mantles historically; nuclear fuel cycle.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Thorium: electron configuration [Rn] 6d2 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +4. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. all isotopes radioactive; ²³²Th is long-lived.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Thorium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; breeder to ²³³U; oxide ceramics If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from thorite.

elements.history:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated a new earth from a Norwegian mineral in 1828 and named the element thorium, for the Norse god Thor. The mineral was later called thorite. Thorium was a chemical element for seventy years before radioactivity was known. Marie Curie and Gerhard Schmidt showed independently, in 1898, that it is radioactive.

Thorium nitrate made the mantles of gas lamps glow white. Thorium-232 is long-lived enough to be primordial, and it is a possible breeder fuel because it absorbs a neutron to become fissile uranium-233.
elements.howDiscovered:
A Norwegian mineral, later called thorite, was sent to Jöns Jacob Berzelius. In 1828 he decomposed it, removed silica and the known earths, and was left with an earth whose sulfate and whose atomic weight were new. He reduced the fluoride with potassium and obtained an impure gray metal.

Radioactivity was not part of the discovery. That was shown seventy years later, by Marie Curie and by Gerhard Schmidt, independently. Thorium was discovered the way zirconium was: an earth that remained after the mineral had been taken apart, and a potassium reduction of its fluoride.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Thorium is a rapid-process element. Thorium-232, the isotope found in nature in bulk, has a half-life near 14 billion years, so a useful fraction of what the Galaxy made is still here. The slow process ends around lead and bismuth and does not reach thorium.

Merging neutron stars are the leading site of the rapid process, and some rare supernovae are still discussed. Thorium and uranium together make a clock, because they are made together and decay at different rates. The thorium in a gas mantle is that survivor.

trivia.title: Named for the God of Thunder
trivia.summary: A Swedish chemist isolated a new earth from a Norwegian mineral and gave the element the name of a Norse god of the sky.
trivia.story: Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated a new earth from a Norwegian mineral in 1828 and named the element thorium, for Thor. The mineral later took the name thorite, and the oxide is the earth called thoria. Radioactivity was not a word in that laboratory, so the sample was a chemical prize and nothing more ominous. A god of thunder was a grand namesake for a powder sitting in a crucible. The name's drama became more literal only decades later, when the same element was found to emit rays.

trivia.title: Known Long Before the Rays
trivia.summary: For about seventy years the element was simply a chemical earth, until two researchers independently showed that it gives off radiation.
trivia.story: Thorium was treated as an ordinary chemical element for about seventy years after Berzelius described it in 1828. In 1898 Marie Curie and Gerhard Schmidt showed, independently of each other, that the element is radioactive. The original chemical identification had been sound, and a new property had been waiting for a way to be seen. The radioactivity is weak beside radium's, which is why thorium could sit in reagents and lamps without announcing itself. A metal named for thunder had been easy to handle as a mere earth until instruments made the rays obvious.

trivia.title: Mantles That Turned the Flame White
trivia.summary: Street lamps and parlor lamps grew bright when a fragile ash, loaded with thorium and cerium oxides, was held in an ordinary gas flame.
trivia.story: Carl Auer von Welsbach's gas mantles turned a pale flame into a strong white light for streets and parlors. The glow came from thorium and cerium oxides, carried on a fragile ash skeleton left when the cloth burned away. An ordinary gas burner became, with that ash in place, a lamp bright enough to change a street at night. The trick was a commercial triumph of the late nineteenth century, built on Berzelius's earth and a rare-earth partner. It also put a weakly radioactive material into ordinary shops, a success that later knowledge would have to reconsider.

trivia.title: When the Lamp Trade Stepped Back
trivia.summary: Once the weak radioactivity was treated as a real concern, mantle makers moved away from the oxide that had made their lamps famous.
trivia.story: Once thorium's radioactivity was treated as a real concern, the gas-mantle industry began to leave the element behind. Dust from used mantles and from the factories was no longer shrugged off as ordinary lamp ash. Makers shifted toward other oxides that could glow in a gas flame without that radioactive burden. The change was a slow commercial retreat, not a single disaster added for drama. A famous nineteenth-century product stepped back, and thorium left the hardware shop while remaining fully present on the table.

trivia.title: A Long Life and a Quiet Risk
trivia.summary: The main natural form has lasted since the Earth formed, and some energy plans have looked at the metal as a possible future fuel.
trivia.story: Thorium-232 is long-lived enough to be primordial, present since Earth formed, and only weakly radioactive. It can take up a neutron and become uranium-233, which is why some plans have treated thorium as a possible nuclear fuel. The statement is an outcome and a proposal, and it is not a design for building anything. No criticality accident belongs in the story, and the record does not need an invented one. The element's firm place in history is simpler, a named earth, a bright mantle, and a radioactivity the lamp trade later left behind.

applications.title: Old lantern mantles
applications.body: Gas-lantern mantles once glowed because they were made of thorium oxide. That use has been dropped because the ash is radioactive.

applications.title: A possible nuclear fuel
applications.body: Thorium-232 can be converted in a reactor into uranium-233, which can split. A few reactor designs are built around that idea.

applications.title: Welding electrodes
applications.body: Some welding rods used thorium oxide to help the arc start. Many shops have switched to electrodes that are not radioactive.

sample.title: The pure element
sample.body: A tenth of a gram of thorium metal, sealed in glass. Thorium is a soft, dense metal. This square is the element itself, not the oxide used in old gas mantles.
sample.credit: Alchemist-hp, Free Art License, via Wikimedia Commons

elements.name: Protactinium

summary.beginner:
Protactinium is element 91, a scarce radioactive metal between thorium and uranium. It appears in the decay of uranium, and it has no household use.

Its symbol is Pa. At room temperature protactinium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

The name means parent of actinium, because it decays into actinium. Only a little of it exists in a ton of uranium ore. It is a research element.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral protactinium atom has 91 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Protactinium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Protactinium is a scarce actinide with a dominant +5 oxidation state, occurring as protactinium-231 in the uranium series.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f2 6d1 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 20, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5.

The +5 chemistry resembles niobium and tantalum more than a typical later actinide. There is no commercial product.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Protactinium (Z = 91) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f2 6d1 7s2. Pa(V) is the stable oxidation state in water, and Pa(IV) is harder to keep.

The isotope of interest, Pa-231, is a decay product of U-235, which is why the element is scarce rather than absent.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Protactinium: say the name, write Pa, find Z=91 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — scarce radioelement between Th and U.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Protactinium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f2 6d1 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +5. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. +5 chemistry; ²³¹Pa.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Protactinium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; exists as a uranium decay product If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found as a uranium decay product; later named protactinium.

elements.history:
Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring identified a short-lived member of the uranium decay chain in 1913 and called it brevium. Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner isolated the longer-lived isotope in 1917, as did Frederick Soddy and John Cranston independently. The name became protactinium, the parent of actinium, because the 231 isotope decays to actinium-227.

Protactinium is scarce, intensely radioactive, and chemically awkward. Aristid von Grosse isolated a visible amount of the oxide in 1927 and the metal in 1934. It sits between thorium and uranium and is not mined for its own sake.
elements.howDiscovered:
Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring, in 1913, found a short-lived activity in the uranium series, lasting about a minute, and followed it through precipitations. Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner looked for a longer-lived parent of actinium. In 1917 they processed pitchblende residues with tantalum as a carrier, then separated an alpha activity that was not tantalum and that decayed with a half-life of tens of thousands of years. Frederick Soddy and John Cranston found it independently.

The detector was a counter, not a spectrum. The chemistry used a carrier because the amount of the element was invisible. Protactinium was discovered as an alpha activity that could be parted from its carrier and that sat in the decay series where a parent of actinium had to sit.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Protactinium-231, with a half-life near 32,000 years, belongs to the uranium-235 decay chain. It stays scarce in uranium ores because the parent is scarce and the daughter does not accumulate over geologic time. No protactinium remains from the birth of the solar system as protactinium.

The rapid process can make protactinium during a blast. Those nuclei decay. The protactinium that has been isolated grew, in the mineral, from uranium, or was made later in a reactor.

trivia.title: The Element Called Brevium
trivia.summary: Two chemists followed a radioactive signal that faded within minutes and chose a name for what they thought they had caught.
trivia.story: In 1913 Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring followed radioactivity through the uranium family and met an isotope that vanished within minutes. They believed they had found a new element, and they named it brevium, taking the word from Latin for something brief. The name matched the clock, because this isotope was gone almost before a lesson could begin. Fajans and Göhring were right that a new element was speaking, but they had heard only its shortest-lived voice. A longer-lived isotope of the same element still lay in uranium ore, and it would demand a different name.

trivia.title: Parent of Actinium
trivia.summary: Working far apart, two pairs of chemists closed in on a stubborn isotope and had to decide what its long life meant.
trivia.story: Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner spent 1917 isolating a longer-lived isotope of element 91 from uranium material in Berlin. Far from that bench, Frederick Soddy and John Cranston reached the same isotope without borrowing the Berlin notes. Because the work was independent, the credit could not be handed to only one laboratory. The isotope they had, numbered 231, decays into actinium, and that family relationship gave the element its lasting name. Protactinium means the parent of actinium, a better description than brevium once chemists could see an isotope that lingered.

trivia.title: One of the Rarest Elements
trivia.summary: Chemists knew element 91 sat in uranium minerals, yet the amount in ordinary rock was almost too small to picture.
trivia.story: Protactinium does occur in nature, yet it is one of the rarest elements that Earth made on its own. It hides in the same minerals that supply thorium and uranium, the neighbors miners already know how to dig. The protactinium itself is a thin radioactive trace, chemically awkward to separate, and too scarce to justify a mine. A chemist can prove it is present and still finish the day with no visible speck in the dish. That scarcity explains the long hunt, and it explains why protactinium is still not gathered for its own sake.

trivia.title: A Speck You Could See
trivia.summary: For years element 91 was only a signal in a detector, until one chemist tried to collect enough to look at.
trivia.story: Aristid von Grosse wanted more than a radioactive click from element 91, and he set out to collect a quantity a person could see. In 1927 he isolated a visible amount of protactinium oxide from uranium material, after chemical work that was slow and difficult. The oxide proved the element could be gathered, yet he still did not have the metal itself. In 1934 he prepared a small sample of protactinium metal, intensely radioactive and finally something with a real surface. That speck did not make protactinium common, but it retired the idea that the element was only a ghost in a decay chain.

trivia.title: Left in the Rock
trivia.summary: A visible sample of element 91 settled a scientific argument and left a practical question sitting on the bench.
trivia.story: Once protactinium could be seen, the practical question was what anyone would do with it, and the honest answer was very little. The element is intensely radioactive, so even a small piece demands care that ordinary reagents never require. Its chemistry is awkward, and it follows other elements through a separation until the last frustrating steps. No industry had a task worth that cost, since thorium and uranium were already the prizes in the ore. Protactinium stayed a laboratory element, studied so the table would be complete, and otherwise left in the rock.

applications.title: No household use
applications.body: Protactinium is too scarce and too radioactive for a product. A ton of uranium ore holds only a fraction of a gram.

applications.title: Part of the uranium chain
applications.body: Protactinium-231 is a decay product of uranium-235. That is why it exists in the ore at all.

applications.title: Research chemistry
applications.body: The chemistry that has been studied is mostly the +5 oxidation state, compared with niobium and tantalum. It is a specialist subject.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.title: A very small sample
sample.body: Protactinium is scarce, and a photograph usually shows a speck rather than an ingot. The dark fragment in the tube is a sample of the element.
sample.credit: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

elements.name: Uranium

summary.beginner:
Uranium is element 92, a heavy radioactive metal and the fuel of nuclear reactors. Most of it is a quieter isotope, and only a small fraction can split and release energy.

Its symbol is U. At room temperature uranium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

Uranium ore does not look like a glowing green rod from a cartoon. The metal is dense and silvery before it oxidizes. Reactor fuel is a carefully prepared solid, handled under strict rules.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral uranium atom has 92 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Uranium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Natural uranium is mostly uranium-238, and the fissile fraction is uranium-235, about 0.7 percent.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f3 6d1 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 21, 9, 2. Oxidation states in this dossier are +6, +4. The one courses meet most often is +6.

The important oxidation states are +6 and +4. Yellow cake and uranyl compounds are the +6 chemistry of the nuclear fuel cycle. The fission is a property of particular nuclei, not of every uranium atom.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Uranium (Z = 92) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f3 6d1 7s2. U-235 is fissile with slow neutrons.

U-238 is fertile: it breeds plutonium-239. The uranyl ion, UO2 2+, dominates aqueous +6 chemistry. Those are two different layers, nuclear and chemical, of the same element.

Oxidation states in this dossier are +6, +4. The one courses meet most often is +6. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Uranium: say the name, write U, find Z=92 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — nuclear fuel and glass color historically.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Uranium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f3 6d1 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +6, +4. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. last primordial actinide in quantity.

discovery.text: Identified in pitchblende; the metal was isolated in 1841.

elements.history:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth examined pitchblende in 1789, decided it contained a new element, and named it uranium for the planet Uranus, found eight years earlier. He had isolated the oxide. Eugène-Melchior Péligot prepared the metal in 1841. Radioactivity was discovered in uranium salts by Henri Becquerel in 1896.

The nucleus came apart in 1938, when Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium in neutron-irradiated uranium and Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained the result as fission. Uranium-235 is the fissile isotope. Uranium-238 is 99.3 percent of the natural metal.
elements.howDiscovered:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth dissolved pitchblende in acid and precipitated a yellow compound with alkali. In 1789 the yellow oxide matched no known earth. He heated it with charcoal and took the black product to be the metal. It was an oxide still.

Eugène-Melchior Péligot prepared uranium tetrachloride in 1841 and reduced it with potassium. The result was a metal with a different weight from Klaproth’s black powder, and the stoichiometry showed that Klaproth had been handling the dioxide. Uranium was discovered as the yellow oxide. The metal was discovered when the chloride was reduced, half a century later. Radioactivity, found by Henri Becquerel in 1896, came later still.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Uranium is a rapid-process element. Uranium-238, with a half-life near 4.5 billion years, and uranium-235, with a half-life near 700 million years, were both present when the solar system formed. The shorter life of uranium-235 is why it is only about 0.7 percent of natural uranium now, and a larger fraction when the Earth was young.

The slow process cannot build them. The captures have to be rapid, and merging neutron stars are the leading site. Some of the material fissioned before it could reach uranium. What reached uranium and survived is the uranium of pitchblende.

trivia.title: Named for a New Planet
trivia.summary: A chemist examining a dark ore decided he had a new element, and he looked upward for a name that was just as new.
trivia.story: In 1789 Martin Heinrich Klaproth examined pitchblende, a heavy dark mineral, and decided it held an element nobody had named. He called it uranium after the planet Uranus, found in 1781, only eight years earlier, so the name was as new as the sky. What he actually isolated was the oxide, a compound, and the pure metal was still out of reach. Even so, the name stuck, and uranium entered science through a dark ore and a newly found planet. Pitchblende remained the mineral miners and chemists meant whenever they went looking for it.

trivia.title: The Metal behind the Oxide
trivia.summary: Decades after uranium received its name, the pure metal was still missing, and another chemist set out to free it.
trivia.story: Klaproth had named uranium from an oxide in pitchblende, and decades later the pure metal was still missing from the shelf. In 1841 Eugène-Melchior Péligot prepared metallic uranium and gave the element a form a person could recognize as metal. The gray sample finished what 1789 had started, joining the planet's name to the element in its own right. In 1896 Henri Becquerel showed that uranium salts give off radiation by themselves, which was the discovery of radioactivity. From that year on, the metal from pitchblende was also the element in which radioactivity first announced itself to science.

trivia.title: Barium in the Dish
trivia.summary: A Berlin experiment kept producing an element far too light to be a chip off uranium, and the explanation waited abroad.
trivia.story: In December 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann irradiated uranium with neutrons and found barium among the products. A uranium nucleus is much heavier than barium, so the result looked at first like a mistake in the analysis. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, working through the physics in 1939, realized the nucleus had split, and they named that split fission. Nearly all natural uranium is isotope 238, while the scarcer isotope 235 is the one that can split when a slow neutron hits it. The 1944 Nobel Prize for the discovery went to Hahn alone, and Meitner, who had explained the barium, was not included.

trivia.title: A Chain under Control
trivia.summary: In Chicago a team waited to learn whether a uranium reaction could be started by hand and then shut down again.
trivia.story: On 2 December 1942, Enrico Fermi and his team in Chicago started the first controlled nuclear chain reaction. The device was called a pile, and the point of the afternoon was control rather than any kind of blast. Instruments watched the neutron count rise and then hold steady at a level the operators were willing to allow. When Fermi decided the test was finished, the reaction was shut down. The afternoon showed that uranium could feed a chain people could start and stop, which is the idea a power reactor is built on.

trivia.title: Green Glass on the Shelf
trivia.summary: Old decorative glass made with a uranium compound looks ordinary until someone carries an ultraviolet lamp into the room.
trivia.story: Long before anyone called uranium a fuel, glassmakers stirred its compounds into bowls, cups, and other decorative pieces. In daylight those pieces often look yellow or pale green, like any old dish waiting on a shelf. Under an ultraviolet lamp the same glass glows a vivid green. The light is fluorescence from the uranium in the glass, a quiet household sight on a table. Collectors still seek those cups and marbles, because a lamp, a shelf, and a green glow make the gentlest story this element has.

applications.title: Reactor fuel
applications.body: Nuclear reactors use uranium, usually enriched so there is more of the isotope that can split. The fuel is a ceramic pellet, handled under strict rules.

applications.title: A long-lived isotope
applications.body: Most natural uranium is uranium-238, which is only weakly radioactive. The energy comes from the much smaller share of uranium-235.

applications.title: Historical glass
applications.body: Uranium compounds once colored glass yellow-green. That glass is a collector's item and is mildly radioactive. It is not a craft glaze to revive.

elements.name: Neptunium

summary.beginner:
Neptunium is element 93, the first element beyond uranium, and it is made rather than mined as a product. It is radioactive.

Its symbol is Np. At room temperature neptunium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

Neptunium is named for the planet Neptune, the next planet out from Uranus, just as the element is the next one out from uranium. Its role is in research and in the nuclear fuel cycle.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral neptunium atom has 93 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Neptunium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Neptunium is the first transuranic element, with several oxidation states and no stable isotope.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f4 6d1 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 22, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5.

It is produced when uranium captures neutrons. The +5 state, as NpO2+, is a characteristic aqueous ion. There is no civilian product made of neptunium metal.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Neptunium (Z = 93) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f4 6d1 7s2. The 5f electrons start to matter here, and oxidation states from +3 to +7 are known.

Np-237 is the long-lived isotope that dominates separated neptunium. It is a radiological and safeguards problem, not a structural metal.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Neptunium: say the name, write Np, find Z=93 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — first transuranic; research only.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Neptunium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f4 6d1 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +5. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. 5f⁴; several oxidation states.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Neptunium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; produced from uranium, not mined as a commodity If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Produced by neutron irradiation of uranium.

elements.history:
Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson produced element 93 in 1940 by irradiating uranium with neutrons at Berkeley. A beta decay of uranium-239 gave a new element that was not the ekarhenium some chemists had expected. They named it neptunium, for the planet beyond Uranus.

Neptunium was the first transuranic element. It showed that the elements past actinium form a 5f series, parallel to the lanthanides, rather than a fourth row of ordinary transition metals.
elements.howDiscovered:
Edwin McMillan irradiated a thin layer of uranium oxide with neutrons from the Berkeley cyclotron in 1940. A 2.3-day radioactivity recoiled out of the layer onto a catcher sheet, so it was a decay product and not the uranium itself. Philip Abelson joined him for the chemistry. The activity did not follow rhenium, which is where the periodic table of the time had placed element 93. It could be oxidized and reduced through states of its own.

The recoil separated the atoms from the target. The chemistry showed they were not an isotope of a known element. Neptunium was discovered as a daughter that jumped out of the uranium and then refused the chemical slot everyone had reserved for it.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
The same rapid captures that make uranium can make neptunium. Every neptunium isotope then decays. Neptunium-237, the longest-lived, has a half-life near 2 million years, short beside the 4.6 billion years since the solar system formed. No primordial neptunium remains.

Traces in uranium ore are made in place, by neutrons from spontaneous fission and from alpha particles on light nuclei. Neptunium in a laboratory was made by adding neutrons to uranium. The cosmic path leaves daughters, not a stock of neptunium.

trivia.title: The Planet past Uranus
trivia.summary: At Berkeley, two chemists sent neutrons into uranium and needed a name for the new radioactivity that grew in the target.
trivia.story: In 1940 Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson irradiated uranium with neutrons at Berkeley and watched a new radioactivity grow in the target. They traced it to a beta decay of uranium-239, a step that turned that nucleus into element 93. The name they chose was neptunium, for Neptune, the next planet out beyond Uranus. Uranium had taken its name from a planet, and element 93 walked one orbit farther along the same sky. It was the first transuranium element, made from uranium before the wider world had heard of the work.

trivia.title: The Metal That Was Missing
trivia.summary: Textbooks had saved a seat for a heavier kind of rhenium, and the new element declined to sit in it.
trivia.story: Before neptunium was made, some chemists expected element 93 to behave like a heavy form of rhenium. They even used a placeholder name, ekarhenium, for the metal they thought would stand under rhenium. McMillan and Abelson tested for that familiar chemistry and watched the new element decline the role. Neptunium had habits of its own, closer to uranium than to the old transition metals above it. The miss mattered, because the elements past uranium were not going to form another row of ordinary metals.

trivia.title: A Row of Their Own
trivia.summary: Element 93 forced a layout question that the familiar periodic table had been answering in the wrong way.
trivia.story: Students had learned a table where transition metals march in rows, and element 93 was expected to keep that march going. Neptunium's chemistry pointed somewhere else, toward elements filling 5f orbitals in a series of their own. The rare earths already showed what such a series looks like, higher up in the table. Actinium would lend the new row its name, and uranium would sit inside that family. The 1940 target redrew the bottom of the table, and every heavier element still unmade would have to live there.

trivia.title: Born inside a Target
trivia.summary: The newest element did not come from a hillside, and the people who found it had started with a familiar metal.
trivia.story: Neptunium never came from a mine, because the experiment started with uranium and a stream of neutrons. Some uranium nuclei captured a neutron and became uranium-239, an isotope with only a short time to remain itself. A beta decay then lifted the atomic number by one, and element 93 was sitting in that same target. McMillan and Abelson recognized it by the radiation it gave off and by chemical steps that pulled it away from the uranium. Nature had not set neptunium on a shelf, so the first sample was an element people had to make.

trivia.title: A Map rather than a Product
trivia.summary: After the discovery, laboratories still had to ask what neptunium was for, and the first answer was the table itself.
trivia.story: Nobody carried neptunium home in a household gadget, and it was not sold as a reagent for an ordinary school laboratory. McMillan and Abelson had made the element so chemists could see what lay one step past uranium. Its refusal to behave like rhenium was the result that mattered, because it opened the actinide row. They handed the table a correction, and they did not hand industry a new metal to melt and sell. The use of the discovery was the map it drew, showing where the next elements would have to live.

applications.title: A product of reactors
applications.body: Neptunium is made when uranium captures neutrons. It is part of the material a reactor creates, not an ore that is mined for sale.

applications.title: Research
applications.body: Chemists study neptunium because it is the first element beyond uranium and it has several oxidation states. The work is done in specialized labs.

applications.title: No consumer metal
applications.body: There is no neptunium tool or alloy on the market. The element is a nuclear-material question first.
