elements.name: Plutonium

summary.beginner:
Plutonium is element 94, a radioactive metal made in reactors. Some of it can split, so it has been used as nuclear fuel and in weapons, and it is not a classroom sample.

Its symbol is Pu. At room temperature plutonium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

Plutonium does not belong in a school lab or in a curiosity cabinet. It is handled in specialized facilities because it is both radioactive and chemically toxic. The public fact is that it is made from uranium, not dug up as a common ore.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral plutonium atom has 94 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Plutonium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Plutonium-239 is fissile, and the element has an unusually wide range of oxidation states.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f6 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 24, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4.

Reactor plutonium and weapons plutonium differ in isotopic mix. The metal itself has many crystal forms. None of that is a hands-on topic.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Plutonium (Z = 94) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f6 7s2. Oxidation states from +3 to +7 are known, and the ions are colorful.

The nuclear properties of Pu-239 are the reason for the security around the element. Chemistry and criticality are separate hazards that both have to be respected.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Plutonium: say the name, write Pu, find Z=94 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — nuclear weapons and some reactors.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Plutonium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f6 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +4. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. fissile ²³⁹Pu; many oxidation states.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Plutonium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; handling is a radiotoxicity problem, not a classroom demo If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Produced by deuteron bombardment of uranium.

elements.history:
Late in 1940, Glenn Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy, and Arthur Wahl bombarded uranium with deuterons and chemically separated element 94. The work was classified until after the war. The name plutonium, for Pluto, continues the planetary sequence after uranium and neptunium. Plutonium-239, made by neutron capture, is fissile.

The element was produced in wartime quantity before most chemists knew it existed. Its many oxidation states, and the radiotoxicity of the metal, made it a nuclear material rather than a laboratory reagent.
elements.howDiscovered:
Glenn Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy, and Arthur Wahl bombarded uranium with deuterons in the 60-inch cyclotron in late 1940. They dissolved the target and coprecipitated the new radioactivity with rare-earth fluorides. When they oxidized the solution, the activity stayed dissolved under conditions where a rare earth would have precipitated again. That change of behavior isolated it from every element in the target.

The amounts were invisible. Alpha particles were the signal. The discovery is the oxidation cycle: a species that precipitated like a rare earth and, once oxidized, did not. Plutonium’s chemistry, not a visible bead, was the evidence.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Plutonium is a rapid-process product that almost survives. Plutonium-244 has a half-life near 80 million years, too short for a useful stock from the birth of the solar system to remain, and long enough that plutonium-244 was alive then. Meteorites record its decay. Traces attributed to more recent cosmic events have been reported in deep-sea sediments.

The plutonium handled as a fuel was not mined from that fossil. Reactors make it by neutron capture on uranium-238, followed by two beta decays. The universe’s rapid process makes plutonium. The metal in a stockpile was made on Earth.

trivia.title: A Secret from the Cyclotron
trivia.summary: Four chemists pulled a new element out of uranium and then had to keep the news inside the laboratory.
trivia.story: As 1940 drew to a close, Seaborg, McMillan, Kennedy, and Wahl stood at Berkeley and struck uranium with deuterons. Chemical separations pulled element 94 out of the target, and the identification was clear by early 1941. The war had already made nuclear results a secret, so the notebooks stayed closed to the public. Most chemists learned the details only after the fighting ended, when the element was no longer a rumor. By then plutonium existed in a quantity that peacetime chemistry had never been allowed to discuss.

trivia.title: Named for Distant Pluto
trivia.summary: Uranium and neptunium already wore the names of planets, and element 94 was waiting for the next name in that line.
trivia.story: The planetary names had become a pattern, and element 94 was the next piece on that path. Uranium recalled Uranus, and neptunium recalled Neptune, so the new metal took Pluto. Seaborg and his coworkers called it plutonium, a name that sounded like a story even while the work was classified. Plutonium-239, made when uranium captures neutrons, can itself split, which is why the secret was so carefully kept. When the name finally reached textbooks, it still pointed at the sky, and the element under that name had already changed the century.

trivia.title: Two Losses at Los Alamos
trivia.summary: At a wartime laboratory a plutonium core was involved in two separate experiments, and each one went badly wrong.
trivia.story: Harry Daghlian and Louis Slotin were physicists at Los Alamos, and each man worked with a plutonium core. In 1945 Daghlian's experiment slipped into an uncontrolled chain reaction, and the radiation he received killed him. In 1946 Slotin suffered a second, separate accident with a plutonium core, and he died of his injuries as well. The two afternoons were not the same event, and both ended in a death. A piece of plutonium could kill in a laboratory, through radiation from a brief runaway reaction, without any weapon leaving the building.

trivia.title: A City Called Nagasaki
trivia.summary: By the last summer of the war, plutonium was no longer only a laboratory secret, and one city would bear that fact.
trivia.story: In August 1945 a plutonium bomb was used in war against the city of Nagasaki. The blast and fire destroyed much of the city, and a great many people were killed. That weapon and a power reactor both involve a nuclear chain reaction, and they are different machines with different aims. The bomb was a single wartime act, over in moments, with a terrible human cost. Remembering Nagasaki means remembering that cost, and the story stops there, without any account of how such a bomb is built.

trivia.title: Warmth for a Far Probe
trivia.summary: Long after the war, a particular kind of plutonium found a job in machines that had to travel past the Sun's warmth.
trivia.story: Plutonium-238 is valued because it runs hot as it decays, and that heat can be turned into electricity. Spacecraft that travel far from the Sun cannot rely on weak sunlight alone, so they carry a small heat source. Voyager used plutonium-238 this way on its long journey through the outer solar system. The Mars rover Curiosity has relied on the same kind of source to keep working through cold nights. The use is real and narrow, a sealed source of steady warmth, and it is a different story from any weapon.

applications.title: Reactor fuel
applications.body: Some reactors run on a mix that includes plutonium recovered from used fuel. The handling is a national-laboratory and industry task.

applications.title: Weapons, a fact to state plainly
applications.body: Plutonium-239 can split in a chain reaction, and it has been used in nuclear weapons. That is why the metal is guarded. It is not a teaching sample.

applications.title: Made from uranium
applications.body: Plutonium is produced by neutron capture in uranium-238, followed by two decays. It is manufactured in a reactor, not dug out of a plutonium mine.

elements.name: Americium

summary.beginner:
Americium is element 95, a radioactive metal made from plutonium. A tiny amount of one isotope is the source inside many household smoke detectors.

Its symbol is Am. At room temperature americium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

The smoke detector keeps that source sealed. It is not a piece to pry out, pocket, or throw in a fire. The rest of americium's story is research, not household chemistry.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral americium atom has 95 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Americium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Americium-241 in ionization smoke detectors is the one public use, and the common oxidation state is +3.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f7 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 25, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The alpha particles ionize air in the detector. Smoke changes that current. Opening the source is a contamination hazard and is illegal in many places.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Americium (Z = 95) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f7 7s2. Am-241's alpha decay also yields a gamma ray, which is why a discarded source is a radiological object, not scrap plastic.

Chemically, Am3+ starts to resemble the lanthanides as the 5f electrons pull in.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Americium: say the name, write Am, find Z=95 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — smoke-detector sources (²⁴¹Am).
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Americium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f7 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. 6d/5f actinide; +3 common.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Americium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; alpha source in ionization detectors If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Isolated from plutonium irradiated in a reactor.

elements.history:
Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan, and Albert Ghiorso identified element 95 in 1944 in plutonium that had been irradiated in a reactor. The announcement waited until after the war, in 1945. They named it americium, for the Americas, by analogy with europium just above it in the table.

Americium-241, an alpha emitter with a convenient half-life, became the ionization source in household smoke detectors. It is the transuranic element most people have, unknowingly, at home.
elements.howDiscovered:
Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan, and Albert Ghiorso irradiated plutonium with neutrons in a reactor in 1944. The target was dissolved, and the actinide fraction was separated by a cycle of oxidations and by ion exchange. A new alpha activity eluted in the position expected for element 95, beyond plutonium, and it grew in as a daughter of a short-lived parent.

There was no weighable product. The discovery was an elution band and a decay, in a sample of plutonium that had captured neutrons. The column put the new element in a place on the chart. The radiation showed the place was occupied.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Americium lies further along the rapid-process path, and every isotope is too short-lived to inherit. Americium-243, the longest-lived, lasts a few thousand years. A neutron-star merger can assemble such a nucleus during the blast. It decays, or fissions, long before a planet forms.

The americium in a smoke detector was made in a reactor, by neutron capture on plutonium. That is a human copy of a capture chain. It is not a recovery of primordial americium, because none remains.

trivia.title: Hidden until the War Ended
trivia.summary: A new element turned up in irradiated plutonium during the war, and the people who found it had to wait to say so.
trivia.story: In 1944 Seaborg, working with Ralph James, Leon Morgan, and Albert Ghiorso, recognized element 95 in plutonium that had already been through a reactor. The atoms were real, the chemistry was done, and the public announcement still had to wait. Wartime secrecy held the result until 1945, when the fighting was over and the name could be spoken. Students hearing the news were meeting an element that had already existed, quietly, inside a reactor target. The delay was the tense part of the story: a discovery finished in the laboratory and locked away from the classroom.

trivia.title: Named like Europium
trivia.summary: Element 95 needed a name, and the rare earth sitting above it on the table offered a pattern to follow.
trivia.story: Seaborg's group looked one row up, where europium honors Europe, and they borrowed the pattern. Element 95 would honor the Americas, and the name they chose was americium. The analogy was deliberate, because they already believed the new elements formed a family parallel to the rare earths. A continent became a chemical name, just as a continent had done for europium. When the name was released in 1945, alongside curium, americium took its place as the American twin of that older element.

trivia.title: A Foil behind the Alarm
trivia.summary: One isotope of element 95 slipped into ordinary houses, sealed inside a device most families never open.
trivia.story: Americium-241 is an alpha emitter with a half-life convenient for a small, long-lived source. That property put a tiny amount of it inside many household smoke detectors, where its radiation helps the alarm sense smoke. The americium sits in a sealed foil, made to stay inside the detector for the life of the device. The detector should not be taken apart, because the foil is a radioactive source even though the box looks ordinary. Americium became the transuranium element most people own without knowing the name printed in the table.

trivia.title: Four Names on the Paper
trivia.summary: Element 95 was not a solo hunt, and the credit had to stretch across a crowded wartime bench.
trivia.story: Glenn Seaborg is the name people remember, yet americium was a group's discovery. Ralph James, Leon Morgan, and Albert Ghiorso shared the 1944 identification with him. They were working in plutonium that had already been through a reactor, looking for what the neutrons had built. Each new activity had to be pinned to an atomic number, with chemistry done on invisible amounts. The paper that finally told the story carried four names, and the element belonged to that whole bench.

trivia.title: The Element at Home
trivia.summary: Most synthetic elements never leave a nuclear laboratory, which makes the one in the hallway smoke alarm a strange exception.
trivia.story: By the time americium was announced, it might have stayed a research curiosity like its heavier neighbors. Americium-241 changed that, because a sealed speck of it could sit in a plastic detector for years. Families walk past it on the ceiling and think only about batteries and beeping. The scientific story and the household story meet in that foil, which is why the warning matters. Leave the detector closed, replace the whole unit when it fails, and the element remains a quiet helper rather than a project.

applications.title: Smoke detectors
applications.body: Many household smoke detectors contain a tiny sealed source of americium-241. The alpha particles ionize air, and smoke changes the current. The source stays inside the detector.

applications.title: Do not open one
applications.body: Prying the source out, or throwing a detector in a fire, spreads a radioactive material. Detectors are returned or recycled, not broken apart.

applications.title: Made from plutonium
applications.body: Americium is produced by irradiating plutonium. The smoke-detector isotope is a managed byproduct, not a mineral.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.title: The pure element
sample.body: A small piece of americium metal in a sealed vial. Americium is a silvery metal made in reactors. The photograph shows the element, not the oxide used in smoke detectors.

elements.name: Curium

summary.beginner:
Curium is element 96, a radioactive metal named for Marie and Pierre Curie. It is made in reactors and used as a starting material for still heavier elements.

Its symbol is Cm. At room temperature curium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

There is no curium in a product you buy. Scientists make it, measure it, and sometimes use it as a target that a beam of particles hits to make something heavier.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral curium atom has 96 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Curium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Curium is a synthetic actinide, typically Cm3+, and it is a target for producing heavier elements.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f7 6d1 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 25, 9, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The element is named for the Curies. Several isotopes are strong alpha emitters. A few have been used as power sources in specialized instruments.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Curium (Z = 96) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f7 6d1 7s2. Cm3+ has a half-filled 5f7 shell, analogous to Gd3+, which is why the +3 state is especially stable.

Target chemistry for heavier elements is done on milligram or smaller scales.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Curium: say the name, write Cm, find Z=96 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — research; named for Curie.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Curium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f7 6d1 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. produced from plutonium.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Curium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; used as a target to make heavier actinides If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Produced by alpha bombardment of plutonium.

elements.history:
Seaborg, James, and Ghiorso produced element 96 in 1944 by bombarding plutonium with alpha particles. They named it curium, for Marie and Pierre Curie, by analogy with gadolinium, which honors Johan Gadolin. The name was announced with americium in 1945.

Curium is a research element and a target. Heavier actinides were made by starting from curium and adding more helium nuclei, one element at a time.
elements.howDiscovered:
Seaborg, James, and Ghiorso bombarded plutonium-239 with helium ions in the Berkeley cyclotron in 1944. The product was separated with the rare-earth fraction and identified by its alpha radiation and by its behavior on an ion-exchange resin. It eluted just ahead of americium, as element 96 should if the actinides were a real series.

The target and the product were both radioactive, so the separation had to be done quickly and behind shielding, on an invisible quantity. Curium was discovered as an elution position and an alpha energy, from a helium-ion bombardment.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Curium sits on the same rapid-process path. Curium-247 has a half-life near 16 million years, long enough that models ask whether a trace was present in the early solar system, and far too short for any to remain now. The other isotopes are shorter-lived.

Laboratory curium was made by helium nuclei on plutonium, or by neutron capture in a reactor. A merger may make curium nuclei for a while. They do not become a planetary inventory.

trivia.title: Honoring Two Curies
trivia.summary: Element 96 needed a name, and a pair of scientists who had opened the study of radioactivity were waiting in the history.
trivia.story: Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, and Albert Ghiorso produced element 96 in 1944 and looked for a name worthy of it. They chose curium, for Marie and Pierre Curie, the pair whose work on radioactivity had led toward this end of the table. The choice also matched a pattern overhead, where gadolinium honors Johan Gadolin. A person, or in this case two people, could be written into the actinide row just as names had been written into the rare earths. Seaborg's group announced curium with americium in 1945, once wartime silence could be lifted.

trivia.title: Helium Nuclei on Plutonium
trivia.summary: The Berkeley group started with plutonium and a beam of helium nuclei, hoping the target would step two places forward.
trivia.story: Curium was made by bombarding plutonium with alpha particles, the nuclei of helium atoms. Seaborg, James, and Ghiorso were adding those particles to a nucleus that was already past uranium. Each successful hit was a way of climbing the table two boxes at a time, if the new nucleus held together. The product was element 96, identified in 1944 and kept quiet until the following year. The method was a sentence long in the telling and enormous in the machines it required, and it gave the world curium.

trivia.title: A Glow from the Sample
trivia.summary: Curium is so radioactive that chemists talk about it differently from the metals that sit quietly in a drawer.
trivia.story: Curium is fiercely radioactive, far beyond the caution already required for uranium or even for a smoke-detector foil. A visible sample would glow from the energy of its own decays, a light born in the nucleus rather than in a flame. That imagined glow is a warning as much as a wonder, because the same radiation that lights the sample also damages what it touches. Chemists therefore treat curium as a research element, handled in tiny amounts behind shielding. The glow marks the difference between a textbook square and a substance that will not sit still.

trivia.title: The Step toward Heavier Names
trivia.summary: Once curium existed, it became a starting block for people trying to reach elements that were still blank squares.
trivia.story: Curium's main work was not a household device. It became a target, a place to stand while helium nuclei were added in hopes of reaching the next elements. Heavier actinides were built by beginning with curium and climbing one element at a time. Berkelium and californium, among others, belong to that climb. Seaborg's element was both a discovery and a doorway, and the doorway mattered as much as the name. Without that target, the later climb toward berkelium and californium would have started from a poorer foothold.

trivia.title: Spoken after the Silence
trivia.summary: The chemists knew they had element 96 while the war was still on, and the public name had to wait in a drawer.
trivia.story: The 1944 experiments succeeded, and then the result joined americium in the file of things that could not yet be said. A discovery that cannot be published is an odd kind of victory, real on the bench and invisible in the journals. In 1945 the names curium and americium were released together. Listeners heard two new elements at once, both made in secrecy, both named for places and people outside the laboratory. The tense episode was not an explosion in the dish but the long wait between making curium and being allowed to pronounce it.

applications.title: Targets for heavier elements
applications.body: Curium is bombarded to make still heavier actinides. A target is a use, and it is not a product you can buy.

applications.title: Power for instruments
applications.body: A few isotopes of curium have powered specialized instruments where a battery would not last. The source is sealed and radioactive.

applications.title: Named for the Curies
applications.body: The name honors Marie and Pierre Curie. The element is synthetic and is handled as a strong alpha emitter.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.body: Photographs of curium metal are not free to reuse. The violet lines are light curium atoms give off, from a short public list of measured wavelengths. They sit close together, so they look like one band.

elements.name: Berkelium

summary.beginner:
Berkelium is element 97, a radioactive metal made in reactors and accelerators. There is no commercial product, and scientists make it so they can study it and build heavier atoms.

Its symbol is Bk. At room temperature berkelium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

The name comes from Berkeley, California, where it was first made. A visible amount is a major undertaking. Most work is done on invisible quantities.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral berkelium atom has 97 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Berkelium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Berkelium is a late actinide, usually +3, with a less common +4 state, and it is made as a target.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f9 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 27, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

Tennessine was produced by firing calcium at a berkelium target. That sentence is the public use: a few atoms of a heavier element.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Berkelium (Z = 97) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f9 7s2. Bk(IV) is accessible, by analogy with terbium.

The isotopes are short-lived enough that a target has a shelf life, which is why berkelium campaigns are scheduled around the bombardment.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Berkelium: say the name, write Bk, find Z=97 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — research; named for Berkeley.

discovery.text: Produced by alpha bombardment of americium.

elements.history:
Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn Seaborg produced element 97 at Berkeley in 1949 by bombarding americium with alpha particles. They named it berkelium, for the city, following the pattern of ytterbium’s town and europium’s continent. The first samples were a few thousand atoms.

Berkelium’s later public role was as the target for tennessine. In 2010, calcium-48 ions on berkelium-249 made element 117.
elements.howDiscovered:
Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn Seaborg bombarded a target of americium-241 with helium ions in 1949. The recoiling atoms were collected, dissolved, and run down an ion-exchange column with a citrate eluant. A few thousand atoms appeared in the elution position predicted for element 97, with a characteristic alpha decay.

The prediction of the elution order was part of the evidence. The actinide series behaves like the lanthanide series on a resin, so an empty slot in the order could be recognized. Berkelium was discovered as a handful of atoms in that slot.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Berkelium can be assembled only in the most neutron-rich blasts, and fission and beta decay remove it quickly. The longest-lived isotope, berkelium-247, lasts about a thousand years. Nothing like a mineral stock can survive from the formation of the solar system.

The berkelium used as a target for heavier elements was made in a reactor. The cosmic rapid process is the imagined original channel, and it leaves uranium, thorium, and their daughters, not berkelium.

trivia.title: A City on the Table
trivia.summary: Element 97 was made in a California laboratory, and the discoverers reached for the city's name when the atoms were real.
trivia.story: December 1949 found Thompson, Ghiorso, and Seaborg in Berkeley, with element 97 showing up in their experiment. Berkelium was the name they chose, tying the element to the city and echoing place-names already used for the rare earths. Ytterbium remembers a town, and europium remembers a continent, so a city was a fair claim for a new actinide. The name tied the element to the place where the cyclotron and the chemistry benches stood. Berkeley had been making new elements for a decade, and now the town itself sat in the table.

trivia.title: Only a Few Thousand Atoms
trivia.summary: The first sample of element 97 was so small that the usual idea of a bottle or a pinch of powder did not apply.
trivia.story: The first berkelium was not a pinch of powder and not a bead of metal. Thompson, Ghiorso, and Seaborg had a few thousand atoms, an amount that would vanish on a speck of dust. They knew the element was there because radiation and chemical behavior pointed to atomic number 97. A classroom can say the word berkelium easily, and the discoverers could not see the sample that earned the word. The tiny yield was the tense fact of December 1949: a new element, announced by atoms you could count rather than weigh.

trivia.title: Helium Nuclei on Americium
trivia.summary: To reach element 97, the Berkeley team started one square earlier and tried to add the nucleus of a helium atom.
trivia.story: Berkelium was produced by bombarding americium with alpha particles, which are helium nuclei. Americium itself had been new only a few years earlier, and now it was a target for the next step. The idea was simple to say and hard to do: add a helium nucleus and hope element 97 remains long enough to be identified. No recipe belongs in a classroom story, only the plain fact of the method. Thompson, Ghiorso, and Seaborg made that climb in 1949, and the product was the city-named element.

trivia.title: The Target for Element 117
trivia.summary: Decades after its discovery, berkelium was asked to do one famous job, and the clock on that job was already running.
trivia.story: Berkelium's later public role was as a target, not as a material anyone mills or melts. In 2010 a beam of calcium-48 ions was sent into berkelium-249, and the product was element 117. The isotope does not last forever, so the target had to be made and used while it was still berkelium. Oak Ridge prepared that target, and Dubna received it for the experiment. An element discovered as a few thousand atoms in 1949 had become the stepping stone to tennessine.

trivia.title: Following an Old Pattern
trivia.summary: The discoverers of element 97 wanted the name to sound as if it had always belonged among the place-names of the table.
trivia.story: Naming berkelium was partly a joke of geography and partly a serious claim about family resemblance. The rare earths already carried town and continent in their names, and the actinides were the parallel row. If europium could mean Europe, berkelium could mean Berkeley. Thompson, Ghiorso, and Seaborg put that argument in the open by choosing the city. The name still teaches the pattern: place first, then the element, with the laboratory city written into atomic number 97. Listeners in 1949 could hear Berkeley in the word as soon as the discovery was read aloud.

applications.title: A target
applications.body: Berkelium has been made into a target and bombarded with calcium to produce tennessine. That campaign is the public use.

applications.title: Research quantities
applications.body: The amounts are milligrams or less, and the isotope decays while the experiment is planned. There is no stockpile on a shelf.

applications.title: No commercial product
applications.body: Berkelium is not in an alloy, a detector, or a medicine. It exists so heavier atoms, and its own chemistry, can be studied.

sample.body: Berkelium has been prepared as a metal, but the clearest free photograph is of a solution. The green drop in the capillary is a real berkelium sample, small enough to sit in a glass tip.

elements.name: Californium

summary.beginner:
Californium is element 98, a radioactive metal, and some of its isotopes are a strong source of neutrons. Those neutrons are used in research and in a few specialized instruments.

Its symbol is Cf. At room temperature californium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

Californium is made one batch at a time in a high-flux reactor. It is valuable because a tiny amount emits a lot of neutrons. It is not a metal you machine into a part.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral californium atom has 98 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Californium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Californium-252 fissions spontaneously and is used as a compact neutron source.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f10 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 28, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The chemistry is mainly the +3 ion. The neutron emission is a nuclear property of particular isotopes. Microgram quantities are already intense sources.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Californium (Z = 98) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f10 7s2. Cf-252's spontaneous-fission branch is why a microgram rivals a small accelerator as a neutron source.

The metal has been prepared, but the useful form is a sealed source, not a structural piece.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. intense neutron emitter in some isotopes.

discovery.text: Produced by alpha bombardment of curium.

elements.history:
Thompson, Kenneth Street, Ghiorso, and Seaborg made element 98 in 1950 by bombarding curium with alpha particles. They named it californium, for the state and the university. The discovery paper noted that naming an element for a place was already a rare-earth tradition.

Californium-252 fissions spontaneously and sprays neutrons. That made a microgram of it a portable neutron source for reactors, medicine, and assay, and also one of the most expensive materials ever sold by the microgram.
elements.howDiscovered:
Thompson, Kenneth Street, Ghiorso, and Seaborg repeated the helium-ion experiment on a curium target in 1950. The catcher foil was dissolved, and the ion-exchange column showed an activity in the next predicted position, element 98, with its own alpha energy and half-life.

The method differed from berkelium’s only in the target. That was enough, because the elution order and the decay had to both move together to the next place. Californium was discovered as the next band on the same kind of column.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Californium is a possible brief product of the rapid process, on the neutron-rich side, before fission recycling breaks the heaviest nuclei apart. No isotope lives long enough to remain from the birth of the solar system. Californium-251, the longest-lived, lasts about nine hundred years.

The californium in a neutron source was made by intense neutron capture in a reactor, starting from plutonium or curium. That pile of neutrons is a terrestrial stand-in for a much wilder cosmic one, and the product does not outlive the experiment by geological ages.

trivia.title: Named for California
trivia.summary: Element 98 appeared at Berkeley in 1950, and the discoverers had a state as well as a city to honor.
trivia.story: Stanley Thompson, Kenneth Street, Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn Seaborg made element 98 in 1950. Californium was their choice, pointing at the state and at the university that had housed the work. Berkelium had just taken the city, and californium took the larger place around it. In the paper they answered a likely complaint: rare-earth names had already turned towns and regions into elements, so a state was hardly a new kind of boast. California thus joined the table twice in two years, first as a town and then as a state.

trivia.title: A Beam on Curium
trivia.summary: The route to element 98 began with curium, itself only a few years old, and a beam of helium nuclei.
trivia.story: Californium was made by bombarding curium with alpha particles. Thompson, Street, Ghiorso, and Seaborg were repeating a climb they knew, adding a helium nucleus to a heavy target. Curium had been the doorway, and element 98 was one more room along that hall. The amounts were tiny, identified by nuclear signals and chemistry rather than by a lump of metal. In 1950 the periodic table gained californium, named for the place and built from the element named for the Curies.

trivia.title: Neutrons from a Speck
trivia.summary: One isotope of element 98 releases neutrons on its own, and that habit gave a tiny sample an outsized job.
trivia.story: Californium-252 fissions by itself and releases neutrons, which makes a very small amount unusually useful. Engineers have used it as a compact neutron source to help start reactors. The same kind of source appears in some industrial gauges and in assay work, and it has also been used in medicine. The story of the use stops at that sentence, with no account of how the isotope is extracted or installed. A microgram can matter because the neutrons come from the nucleus without a large machine wrapped around it.

trivia.title: Sold by the Microgram
trivia.summary: Element 98 became famous not only for its name but for how little of it money could buy.
trivia.story: Because californium-252 is so radioactive and so hard to make, it has been sold by the microgram. That unit is a joke in ordinary chemistry, where reagents come in jars, and it is the real unit here. A price attached to a microgram made californium one of the most expensive materials ever offered that way. The cost is a consequence of the neutrons and of the struggle to make the isotope, not an invitation to collect it. Classrooms meet californium as a name in the actinides and as a warning that some elements are counted in millionths of a gram.

trivia.title: A Place Name with Cousins
trivia.summary: The people who named element 98 wanted listeners to hear an old tradition, not a sudden boast about one campus.
trivia.story: Street, Thompson, Ghiorso, and Seaborg knew that a state on the periodic table might sound boastful. Their paper pointed back to the rare earths, where towns and regions had already become element names. Californium was a continuation, sitting beside berkelium as place after place. The four names on the discovery are the human part of the story, and the state name is the public part. Together they fixed element 98 as a California element in both the laboratory sense and the geographic one.

applications.title: A neutron source
applications.body: Californium-252 splits on its own and releases neutrons. A tiny sealed source is used in research and in some mining and medical instruments.

applications.title: Made in a reactor
applications.body: Californium is built up by a long chain of neutron captures, starting from plutonium or curium. Only specialized reactors make it.

applications.title: Micrograms matter
applications.body: A microgram of the neutron-emitting isotope is already an intense source. That is why the element is valuable and why it is not a sample to display.

elements.name: Einsteinium

summary.beginner:
Einsteinium is element 99, a radioactive metal first found in the debris of a hydrogen-bomb test. Only tiny amounts are made, for research.

Its symbol is Es. At room temperature einsteinium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

It is named for Albert Einstein. There is no einsteinium alloy in a machine you use. Chemists study small samples to see how such a heavy atom behaves.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral einsteinium atom has 99 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Einsteinium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Einsteinium has no bulk commercial use, and the amounts available are measured in micrograms or less.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f11 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 29, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

It was discovered in fallout from the Ivy Mike test. Today it is made in reactors. The oxidation state in solution is +3.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Einsteinium (Z = 99) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f11 7s2. Es3+ is the aqueous ion.

A +2 state is known in solids. Self-heating and rapid decay limit what any measurement can mean: the sample is changing while you study it.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. einsteinium has no macroscopic civilian use.

discovery.text: Found in debris from the first hydrogen-bomb test.

elements.history:
Element 99 was found in the debris of the Ivy Mike thermonuclear test of 1952. A burst of neutrons on uranium built the nucleus up many steps before it could beta-decay. Albert Ghiorso and coworkers at Berkeley identified it, and the name einsteinium, for Albert Einstein, was published in 1955.

Einsteinium has no civilian bulk use. It was the starting target for mendelevium, the first element identified essentially one atom at a time.
elements.howDiscovered:
The Ivy Mike thermonuclear test of 1952 threw a burst of neutrons onto uranium in the device. Filter papers flown through the cloud were brought to Berkeley, dissolved, and put through ion-exchange columns. Albert Ghiorso and coworkers found an alpha activity past californium, in the place calculated for element 99, with a half-life of about twenty days.

The neutrons had built the nucleus up many mass units before it could beta-decay back down to 99 protons. Einsteinium was discovered in fallout, by a column and a counter. The same element was later made in a reactor, which confirmed the elution and the decay.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Einsteinium is what a furious neutron burst builds if the burst continues past californium. The Ivy Mike thermonuclear test did that on Earth in 1952 and left einsteinium in the debris. A neutron-star merger is the cosmic event asked to do something similar, for a moment.

Einsteinium-252, the longest-lived isotope, lasts about a year. No primordial atoms remain, and none are expected in a planet. The element’s original formation, if it happens in nature, is a transient step inside the rapid process, followed at once by decay.

trivia.title: Atoms in the Debris
trivia.summary: Element 99 was not born on a quiet bench, and the people who identified it had to look in the remains of a giant test.
trivia.story: Atoms of element 99 turned up in material collected after the 1952 test known as Ivy Mike. A huge burst of neutrons struck uranium and built very heavy nuclei before those nuclei could decay back down. Filter papers from the test carried the evidence to Albert Ghiorso and his coworkers at Berkeley. They identified a new element in that debris, made in a moment and recognized afterward in a laboratory. Nothing in this story is a plan for a weapon; it is an account of what the debris contained and who read it.

trivia.title: A Name Kept Quiet
trivia.summary: The Berkeley group knew they had a new element, and the test that made it kept the announcement in the dark.
trivia.story: Ghiorso and the Berkeley team identified element 99 in 1952, and then the discovery had to stay quiet. The source was a secret thermonuclear test, so a public paper would have said too much about that test. The name einsteinium, for Albert Einstein, waited until 1955 to be published. For three years the element existed in classified reports and in the memory of the people who had separated it. The tense episode was the silence itself, a discovery held back because of where the atoms had been born.

trivia.title: Einstein on the Table
trivia.summary: When the silence finally lifted, element 99 carried the name of a physicist the whole world already knew.
trivia.story: Albert Einstein did not make element 99, and the element was named for him all the same. The 1955 announcement gave the public the word einsteinium, years after the atoms had been identified. Naming it for Einstein placed a familiar figure at a very unfamiliar end of the table. The atoms had come from test debris, the chemistry from Berkeley, and the name from a life in physics. Students meet Einstein in stories about light and gravity, and here his name sits on a synthetic element with no ordinary use.

trivia.title: No Bulk on the Shelf
trivia.summary: Element 99 has a famous name, and that fame does not mean anyone keeps a jar of it in a stockroom.
trivia.story: Einsteinium has no civilian bulk use, which is a plain way of saying there is no bottle of it in ordinary trade. The amounts made are tiny, suited to research and to serving as a target for still heavier elements. Mendelevium, the element found essentially atom by atom, was produced by beginning with a target of einsteinium. That role matters more than any imagined industry. Einsteinium remains a name with a history in 1952 debris and a future only as far as the next careful experiment.

trivia.title: From a Burst of Neutrons
trivia.summary: The nuclei of element 99 were assembled in a rush of neutrons, and the chemists met them only after the rush was over.
trivia.story: In the Ivy Mike debris, uranium had been driven upward through many neutron captures before beta decays could catch up. The result was a mix of very heavy atoms, including element 99, stuck in material that had to be collected and shipped to a laboratory. Ghiorso's group sorted that mix until einsteinium stood out. The test stayed undescribed in public, and the element could still be named. What the classroom keeps is the sequence: a secret test, a quiet analysis, and a name published in 1955.

applications.title: Research only
applications.body: Einsteinium is produced in microgram amounts for chemical studies. There is no device in a home or a car that contains it.

applications.title: Found in bomb debris
applications.body: The element was first identified in the fallout of a thermonuclear test. Modern samples are made in reactors instead.

applications.title: A limit on experiments
applications.body: The sample heats itself and decays while it is being studied. Measurements are planned around that, which is part of why so little chemistry is published.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.title: A sample that glows
sample.body: Einsteinium is so radioactive that a visible sample glows by itself. The blue-white light in the tube is the sample. It is not a lamp, and it is not a large ingot.
sample.credit: R. G. Haire, U.S. Department of Energy, public domain

elements.name: Fermium

summary.beginner:
Fermium is element 100, a radioactive metal found alongside einsteinium. It has no everyday use, and chemists study it only in very small amounts.

Its symbol is Fm. At room temperature fermium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

The name honors Enrico Fermi. Fermium was also in the debris of that first large thermonuclear test. Making more of it is still a specialized project.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral fermium atom has 100 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Fermium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Fermium is studied a few atoms or a few picograms at a time, and there is no stable isotope.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f12 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 30, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The longest-lived isotope lasts about 100 days, which is long for this part of the table and still short for building a supply. Chemistry is tracer-scale.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Fermium (Z = 100) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f12 7s2. Fermium is the heaviest element that can be made by neutron capture in a high-flux reactor in amounts a chemist can track.

Heavier elements need a particle accelerator and are identified one atom at a time.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Fermium: say the name, write Fm, find Z=100 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — research only.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Fermium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f12 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. named for Fermi; atom-at-a-time chemistry.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Fermium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; no stable isotopes If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Found with einsteinium in thermonuclear-test debris.

elements.history:
Fermium was in the same Ivy Mike filter papers as einsteinium. The Berkeley group identified element 100 in 1952 and named it for Enrico Fermi, who had built the first reactor and had died in 1954. The name was published with einsteinium in 1955.

From fermium onward, the amounts are atoms, not weighable samples. Chemistry is done by seeing where a handful of atoms elute from an ion-exchange column.
elements.howDiscovered:
The same Mike debris held one more band. On the ion-exchange column, past the einsteinium, Ghiorso’s group found a weaker activity with a shorter half-life, in the position calculated for element 100. It was identified in 1952 and kept secret with the rest of the thermonuclear results until 1955.

Fermium was discovered by going one elution further on the same papers. The neutron burst had climbed one element higher than einsteinium. A reactor could not yet do that. The bomb debris could, and the column could tell the two apart.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Fermium is the next step of that same neutron burst. It was found with einsteinium in the debris of Ivy Mike, which showed that a dense neutron flux can climb this far before the nuclei decay. The astrophysical rapid process is believed to climb through this region and then to fission.

The longest-lived fermium isotope lasts about a hundred days. There is no cosmic reservoir to inherit. Atoms that have been studied were made in reactors and accelerators, by the same idea of adding many neutrons before beta decay can catch up.

trivia.title: The Same Filter Papers
trivia.summary: Element 100 was hiding in the same test debris as element 99, waiting for the Berkeley group to notice a second newcomer.
trivia.story: Fermium was in the same Ivy Mike filter papers that carried einsteinium. The Berkeley group identified element 100 in 1952, one atomic number beyond the neighbor they had just found. Two new elements from one secret test was an extraordinary yield of names and a tiny yield of atoms. The papers were not a mine, and the elements were not nuggets. They were signals in debris, strong enough for Ghiorso and his coworkers to say that element 100 was real.

trivia.title: A Name for Fermi
trivia.summary: Element 100 needed a name while the world was still absorbing the loss of the physicist who built the first reactor.
trivia.story: The Berkeley group named element 100 for Enrico Fermi, who had led the first controlled chain reaction and who died in 1954. The name fermium was published with einsteinium in 1955, so the tribute appeared after his death. Fermi's pile in Chicago had shown that a chain reaction could be controlled, and his name now labeled an element found in test debris. The two facts belong to different stories, a reactor on one side and a secret test on the other. What they share is Fermi himself, honored at the far end of the table he had helped open.

trivia.title: Atoms and Not a Sample
trivia.summary: With element 100, the old hope of a visible pinch of a new metal finally stopped making sense.
trivia.story: From fermium onward, the amounts in these discoveries are atoms, not samples anyone can weigh on a balance. A new element might be a handful of nuclei whose decays are recorded and then gone. Later, reactors also made fermium, still only in tiny amounts that did not become a weighable stock. The word sample starts to mislead if it suggests a jar. Fermium marks the turn where chemistry means tracking atoms, and the tense fact is how little there ever is.

trivia.title: A Column and a Handful
trivia.summary: Chemists still asked where element 100 would go in a separation, even when they had only a handful of atoms to follow.
trivia.story: With so few atoms, fermium's chemistry is done by watching where they emerge from an ion-exchange column. A solution washes down the column, and the atoms of each element come off at a characteristic place. There is no crystal to turn in the light and no powder to scrape into a vial. The result is still chemistry, because the atoms choose a path the way a larger sample would. A handful of fermium atoms, eluting in their turn, was enough to say how the element behaves among its neighbors.

trivia.title: Published Side by Side
trivia.summary: Elements 99 and 100 had been found together, and the public learned their names in the same delayed breath.
trivia.story: Einsteinium and fermium shared a birthplace in the 1952 debris and a publication date in 1955. Keeping both quiet protected the secret of the test that had made them. When the names appeared, Einstein and Fermi entered the table together, a theorist and a builder of the first pile. The pairing was an accident of history, two elements in one set of papers. Classrooms can remember them as neighbors in atomic number and as partners in a long silence. The shared delay did not change the atoms, and it did change when the world was allowed to learn their names.

applications.title: Research only
applications.body: Fermium is studied in very small amounts, and there is no fermium product to buy or to hold.

applications.title: The end of reactor synthesis
applications.body: Fermium is about as far as neutron capture in a reactor can go and still leave a chemist something to track. Heavier elements need an accelerator.

applications.title: Found with einsteinium
applications.body: Fermium was in the same test debris as einsteinium. The name honors Enrico Fermi.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.title: An alloy, not a pure lump
sample.body: Pure fermium metal has not been isolated as a piece you can photograph. The visible sample that has been made is an alloy of fermium with ytterbium. This disk is that alloy.
sample.credit: Ben E. Lewis., public domain

elements.name: Mendelevium

summary.beginner:
Mendelevium is element 101, named for the scientist who built the periodic table. It was identified one atom at a time, and that is still how it is studied.

Its symbol is Md. At room temperature mendelevium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

There will never be a jar of mendelevium in a classroom. The achievement was detecting a few atoms and showing they were a new element. That is a real result, and it is not a material.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral mendelevium atom has 101 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Mendelevium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Mendelevium was the first element identified essentially one atom at a time.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f13 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 31, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The chemistry that has been done uses ion-exchange elution, watching where those atoms come off a column. The oxidation states seen are +3 and +2.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Mendelevium (Z = 101) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f13 7s2. Elution position is the evidence, because there is no weighable sample.

Md2+ is more stable than a simple lanthanide analogy would suggest, a hint of the late-actinide trend toward +2.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Mendelevium: say the name, write Md, find Z=101 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — research; first identified one atom at a time.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Mendelevium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f13 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +3. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. named for Mendeleev.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Mendelevium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; chemistry tracked by ion-exchange elution If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.people: Ghiorso, Harvey, Choppin, Thompson, and Seaborg
discovery.text: Produced by alpha bombardment of einsteinium; identified atom by atom.

elements.history:
In 1955 Ghiorso, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin, Stanley Thompson, and Seaborg bombarded a tiny target of einsteinium with alpha particles and identified element 101. They used seventeen atoms. The name mendelevium honors Dmitri Mendeleev, whose table had predicted the method of looking for a gap and then finding it.

The recoil technique used for mendelevium, catching the product atom on a second foil, became the standard way to separate a new element from a much larger target.
elements.howDiscovered:
A target of a few billion atoms of einsteinium was plated on a gold foil and struck with helium ions in the Berkeley cyclotron in 1955. The product atoms recoiled out of the target onto a second, clean gold foil. That foil was dissolved, and the solution was run through an ion-exchange column. Seventeen atoms eluted in the position of element 101 and were counted by their decays.

The recoil foil is what made the experiment possible. It left the huge target behind and carried only the atoms that had been knocked forward. Mendelevium was discovered by counting those atoms, one decay at a time.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Mendelevium is past the point where even a reactor’s neutron flux is the practical route. The known isotopes are made by helium or heavier ions on einsteinium and neighboring targets, and they live for minutes to a couple of months. A rapid-process blast might assemble such a nucleus. Fission and decay would remove it inside the event.

No mendelevium survives to be part of a planet. The original cosmic question has a narrow answer: only a neutron-rich blast could build it, and that blast would not leave it behind.

trivia.title: Seventeen Atoms in All
trivia.summary: The first hunt for element 101 produced so little that the discoverers could count the evidence on their fingers and toes.
trivia.story: In 1955 Albert Ghiorso, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin, Stanley Thompson, and Glenn Seaborg went looking for element 101. They bombarded a tiny target of einsteinium with helium nuclei and watched for the new element one atom at a time. Seventeen atoms were identified, a yield so small it still startles people who think of chemistry in grams. Each atom announced itself and was gone, and the team added it to a very short list. Mendelevium began as that list, a new element whose entire first sample could be counted aloud.

trivia.title: Honoring the Table Maker
trivia.summary: Element 101 was named for the chemist whose gaps had taught everyone how to look for a missing square.
trivia.story: The name mendelevium honors Dmitri Mendeleev, who built the periodic table by leaving gaps where unknown elements had to be. His method was to trust the pattern, predict a place, and then go find what belonged there. Element 101 was found in exactly that spirit, a blank square pursued until a few atoms filled it. Ghiorso and his colleagues chose the name because the table itself had been the tool. Mendeleev did not live to see the actinides, and his way of searching is written on element 101.

trivia.title: Helium Nuclei on Einsteinium
trivia.summary: The path to element 101 started with a scarce target and a beam of helium nuclei, and the product was almost nothing.
trivia.story: Einsteinium was already rare, and the 1955 team used a tiny amount of it as the target. They sent in helium nuclei, also called alpha particles, and looked for nuclei that had become element 101. The sentence is the whole method a classroom needs: a helium beam, an einsteinium target, and a search for new atoms. No energies or machine settings belong in the story. What belongs is the outcome, seventeen atoms of mendelevium, and the names of the people who counted them.

trivia.title: Caught on a Second Foil
trivia.summary: The new atoms flew out of the target, and the team had to catch them somewhere the original material could not follow.
trivia.story: A new nucleus made in the einsteinium target can recoil, kicking itself free of the material that produced it. Ghiorso's team caught that flying atom on a second foil, away from the much larger target. The separation was physical as well as chemical: the product left home, and the target stayed behind. That recoil trick became a standard way to pull a new element out of a crowded experiment. Mendelevium was not only seventeen atoms; it was also the demonstration that those atoms could be caught in flight.

trivia.title: One Atom Then Another
trivia.summary: Earlier elements had been scarce, and element 101 asked its discoverers to believe a result that arrived singly.
trivia.story: Before mendelevium, even a few thousand atoms had seemed like a small sample. In 1955 the evidence arrived as single decays, atom after atom, until seventeen had been recorded. There was no moment when a vial turned color or a powder settled in a filter. The tense part was trust: whether a handful of events, carefully checked, deserved a permanent name. The name held, and one-atom-at-a-time discovery became the normal life of every element beyond. After those seventeen careful counts, mendelevium had earned a permanent square.

applications.title: One atom at a time
applications.body: Mendelevium was identified from a handful of atoms. That method, not a material use, is why it matters in the history of the table.

applications.title: Named for Mendeleev
applications.body: The name honors the chemist who arranged the elements by their properties. Element 101 is a late confirmation of that idea.

applications.title: No weighable sample
applications.body: Chemistry is done by watching where single atoms come off an ion-exchange column. There is nothing to machine or to sell.

isotopes.note: Representative isotope for teaching. Not a full natural-abundance table.

sample.title: No sample to photograph
sample.body: Mendelevium is made a few atoms at a time, and those atoms disappear before anyone can collect a visible piece. There is no photograph of the pure element, and this pack does not draw a pretend lump of metal.
sample.credit: Original illustration

elements.name: Nobelium

summary.beginner:
Nobelium is element 102, a radioactive metal named for Alfred Nobel. It is made in accelerators, and its chemistry is done on invisible amounts.

Its symbol is No. At room temperature nobelium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

Naming this element took years of argument, which is a reminder that a few atoms are hard to prove. There is still no piece to hold up.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral nobelium atom has 102 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Nobelium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Nobelium is unusual among actinides because the +2 oxidation state is more stable than +3 in solution.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 8, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

That preference resembles ytterbium more than the earlier actinides. The atoms are made by heavy-ion fusion and do not last long.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Nobelium (Z = 102) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 7s2. The filled 5f14 shell stabilizes No2+, the actinide echo of Yb2+.

Aqueous chemistry is done on atoms that decay while the experiment runs, so every result is a tracer result.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Nobelium: say the name, write No, find Z=102 on the table, note the family (Actinide), and connect it to one real use — research; named for Nobel.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Nobelium: electron configuration [Rn] 5f14 7s2, Typical oxidation states: +2. It is placed in the f-block rows rather than a main group column. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. late actinide; +2 is unusually important.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Nobelium: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; divalent chemistry like ytterbium in places If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Produced by heavy-ion fusion; naming was settled later.

elements.history:
Element 102 was claimed more than once. A 1957 Stockholm group proposed the name nobelium, for Alfred Nobel, on evidence that did not hold. Groups at Dubna and at Berkeley made the element in the 1960s, and the Dubna work of 1966 is the claim IUPAC later accepted. The Stockholm name was kept anyway.

Nobelium is chemically interesting because the +2 oxidation state is more stable than +3, a late-actinide echo of ytterbium. The experiments that showed this used atoms that lived for minutes.
elements.howDiscovered:
A Stockholm group claimed element 102 in 1957, and the claim did not hold. Groups at Berkeley and at Dubna then made isotopes of the element through the 1960s by heavy-ion bombardment of actinide targets. The Dubna work of 1966 is the claim later accepted. Two experiments that year, uranium bombarded with neon and americium bombarded with nitrogen, made nobelium-254. It was identified by the alpha decay of its known fermium daughter.

The method that settled it was a genetic chain: the new activity decayed into a nucleus whose chemistry and whose radiation were already familiar. A spontaneous-fission signal alone had been too easy to misassign. Nobelium was discovered when a daughter could be named.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
The rapid process may pass a few trajectories through nobelium’s proton number while a blast is neutron-rich. Fission cycling is expected to break most of those nuclei before they can decay back to a long-lived ash.

Every nobelium isotope that has been made lives minutes, or less. There is no primordial nobelium and no plausible hidden ore. The atoms in experiments were fused in accelerators.

trivia.title: A Claim That Did Not Hold
trivia.summary: In Stockholm a group announced element 102 and offered a name, and other laboratories could not make the claim stand.
trivia.story: In 1957 a group at the Nobel Institute in Stockholm announced that they had made element 102. They proposed the name nobelium, for Alfred Nobel, whose prizes are tied to that city. The evidence did not hold, and the claim failed when other scientists tried to rely on it. A failed announcement is a sharp kind of disappointment, because a name had already started to travel. Element 102 was still unconfirmed, and the word nobelium was already loose in the conversation.

trivia.title: The Name That Stayed
trivia.summary: The Stockholm evidence fell apart, and yet the name from that announcement refused to leave the table.
trivia.story: Once nobelium had been spoken, it proved hard to erase, even after the 1957 claim collapsed. Later workers made element 102 for real, and the international namers kept the Stockholm word anyway. The element was not awarded to the group whose evidence failed. The name was a survivor of a mistake, which is an unusual way for a square of the table to be labeled. Nobelium therefore remembers Alfred Nobel and also remembers a claim that did not survive its own announcement.

trivia.title: Berkeley and Dubna Both Worked
trivia.summary: After Stockholm, two famous laboratories each went after element 102, and their early accounts did not agree.
trivia.story: Through the 1960s, groups at Berkeley and at Dubna both worked on element 102. Albert Ghiorso and his Berkeley colleagues reported results, and the Dubna laboratory reported results of its own. Early claims conflicted, which is the polite word for a priority fight conducted in journals and conferences. Each side had cyclotrons, chemists, and a strong wish to be the laboratory that settled element 102. Students inheriting the story meet a mess first, and a decision only later. When the decision came, it would point to Dubna's 1966 work and still keep the word nobelium.

trivia.title: Credit to the 1966 Work
trivia.summary: Years of conflicting papers ended when the naming body pointed to one later set of experiments from Dubna.
trivia.story: The claim that the international body later accepted was Dubna's work of 1966. That decision did not pretend the earlier years had been simple, and it did not revive the failed Stockholm experiment. Berkeley's effort remained part of the history of the chase. IUPAC, the body that settles names and, in hard cases, credit, treated the 1966 Dubna work as the successful claim. Nobelium thus has a Swedish name, a confused youth, and a discovery credit that rests with Dubna.

trivia.title: An Ion That Favored Two
trivia.summary: When chemists finally followed element 102 atom by atom, its favorite electric charge was not the one they expected.
trivia.story: Nobelium surprised chemists because the plus-two oxidation state is more stable for it than plus three. Along the actinides, plus three had been the familiar habit, and nobelium preferred to stop at two. That is a late echo of ytterbium, higher in the table, which also likes the plus-two state. The experiments that showed this used atoms living for minutes, long enough to track and not long enough to store. A priority fight gave nobelium its tangled history, and a handful of short-lived atoms gave it a chemical personality.

applications.title: Accelerator-made
applications.body: Nobelium is made by crashing lighter nuclei together. The atoms are studied and are gone. There is no nobelium part.

applications.title: A chemical surprise
applications.body: In solution, nobelium prefers a +2 ion, more like ytterbium than like the actinides before it. That is a research result, not a product.

applications.title: A long argument about the name
applications.body: Proving a few atoms exist is hard, and the name took years to settle. The element is still known only at that scale.
