sample.body: Nobelium is made a few atoms at a time, and those atoms disappear before anyone can collect a visible piece. There is no photograph of the pure element, and this pack does not draw a pretend lump of metal.
sample.credit: Original illustration

elements.name: Lawrencium

summary.beginner:
Lawrencium is element 103, the last of the actinides. It is made a few atoms at a time, and there is no sample you can see.

Its symbol is Lr. At room temperature lawrencium is a solid. It is an actinide, from the heavy row under the main table, and it is radioactive. On the periodic table it is in row 7, in the strip under the main table. That row is period 7.

It is named for Ernest Lawrence, the inventor of the cyclotron, which is fitting because accelerators are the only way to make it. On the table it closes the bottom row.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral lawrencium atom has 103 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Lawrencium is a solid actinide in period 7, in the row under the main table. Lawrencium closes the actinide series, and the atoms that have been studied point to a +3 ion.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 7s2 7p1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 8, 3. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

The configuration is a research question of its own, because the 7s and 7p orbitals are close in energy. There is no bulk property to list with confidence.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Lawrencium (Z = 103) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 7s2 7p1. A 7s2 7p1 ground configuration has been argued from experiment, which would make lawrencium a p-block curiosity as well as the last actinide.

Chemistry still looks like a +3 ion. Both statements can be true at this precision.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Every isotope is radioactive, so this is a real element you will not find as a jar on a shelf.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced by boron ions on californium.

elements.history:
Albert Ghiorso and coworkers at Berkeley produced element 103 in 1961 by bombarding californium with boron ions. They named it lawrencium, for Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron. Dubna reported isotopes soon after. IUPAC confirmed the name in 1997.

Lawrencium closes the actinide series. Its ground configuration is expected to put the last electron in a 7p orbital rather than a 6d orbital, a small relativistic twist at the end of the row.
elements.howDiscovered:
Albert Ghiorso and coworkers bombarded a californium target with boron ions in 1961. The fused atoms recoiled onto a catcher, and their alpha particles were recorded. The energies and the half-life fit element 103, and a later chemical separation showed the atoms eluting at the end of the actinide series. Dubna reported isotopes of the element soon after.

Lawrencium was discovered as a recoil and an alpha energy, from a boron beam on a target that itself had been manufactured. The chemistry confirmed the place in the actinide row. The amount was atoms.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Lawrencium closes the actinide row. A cosmic rapid process that reaches the actinides is climbing, on the neutron-rich side, toward fission, not toward a stable lawrencium that a later solar system could inherit. The known isotopes live minutes at most.

The element’s formation in the laboratory is a heavy-ion fusion, boron on californium. That is a different reaction from the neutron captures of a merger. Nature’s neutron-rich blasts are not known to stock this nucleus.

trivia.title: Named for the Cyclotron
trivia.summary: Element 103 was made at the laboratory that grew up around a famous machine, and the name remembered the machine's inventor.
trivia.story: Albert Ghiorso and his coworkers at Berkeley produced element 103 in 1961. They named it lawrencium, for Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron that made this kind of hunt possible. The name points at a person and at a style of laboratory, the big-machine end of chemistry. Without Lawrence's accelerator, bombing heavy targets with lighter nuclei would have stayed a wish. Lawrencium closed a chapter by honoring the tool-builder whose machines had filled so many of the boxes above it.

trivia.title: Boron Ions on Californium
trivia.summary: The Berkeley team aimed boron ions at californium and waited for a nucleus heavy enough to be element 103.
trivia.story: The 1961 experiment bombarded californium with boron ions. Californium was itself a Berkeley element, only a decade old, and now it was a target. Boron is light beside californium, and a direct hit can fuse them into something new if the product survives even briefly. Ghiorso's group identified element 103 in the products of those collisions. The atoms were very short-lived, gone almost as soon as the detectors had reason to believe in them. Lawrencium announced itself and vanished, which is why the discovery is told with detectors rather than with photographs.

trivia.title: Dubna Studied It Too
trivia.summary: Berkeley published element 103 first, and another laboratory was soon reporting isotopes of the same element.
trivia.story: Dubna reported isotopes of element 103 soon after the Berkeley work. The element was no longer a single laboratory's private result, even though the name came from California. Both sides were learning how these very heavy nuclei decay, often in seconds or less. A short life makes every repeat experiment precious, because there is no sample to pass around in a vial. Lawrencium's early history is that double attention, Berkeley's 1961 discovery and Dubna's isotopes close behind. Neither group ever held a piece of metal, because these nuclei would not wait.

trivia.title: Closing the Actinide Row
trivia.summary: Element 103 sits at the end of a long family, and even its electron arrangement is a small surprise on paper.
trivia.story: Lawrencium closes the actinide series, the row that began back at actinium. After it, the next elements are expected to behave more like a new set of transition metals. Even the last electron is a small twist: the ground arrangement is expected to place it in a 7p orbital rather than a 6d orbital. That expectation comes from calculation and theory, a relativistic detail at the end of the row. Nobody has a bottle of lawrencium to show a class, only a short-lived atom and a square that ends the family.

trivia.title: A Name Settled in 1997
trivia.summary: Lawrencium had worn its name for decades before the international namers put an official seal on the word.
trivia.story: The name lawrencium was in use long before the last arguments over the heavy elements were finished. In 1997 IUPAC confirmed it, along with a set of other names that had been fought over. Ernest Lawrence's element therefore spent its youth in papers and its adulthood on the official table. The confirmation did not make the atoms live longer. It only agreed that element 103, discovered at Berkeley in 1961 and studied at Dubna as well, would keep the name it already had.

applications.title: The end of the actinides
applications.body: Lawrencium closes the bottom row of the table. It is made a few atoms at a time and has no material use.

applications.title: Named for a machine
applications.body: The name honors Ernest Lawrence, whose cyclotron is the ancestor of the accelerators that make these elements.

applications.title: A configuration question
applications.body: Researchers still discuss exactly which orbitals the last electrons occupy. That is a spectroscopy problem, not an application.

elements.name: Rutherfordium

summary.beginner:
Rutherfordium is element 104, the first element past the actinides. It exists only as short-lived atoms made in a laboratory.

Its symbol is Rf. At room temperature rutherfordium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 4. In class those are called period 7 and group 4.

It is named for Ernest Rutherford. Chemists expect it to behave a bit like hafnium, the metal above it, but only a few atoms are available, and they disappear quickly.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral rutherfordium atom has 104 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Rutherfordium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 4. Rutherfordium is the first transactinide, expected to resemble hafnium, and only atom-at-a-time experiments exist.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d2 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 10, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4.

A naming dispute with the Soviet discovery claim lasted for years. The chemistry that has been done is gas-phase and solution work on single atoms.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Rutherfordium (Z = 104) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d2 7s2. Relativistic effects on the 6d and 7s electrons are large enough that a simple hafnium analogy can fail in detail.

Measured volatility and complexation are compared with hafnium and with calculations, not with a weighed sample.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +4. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: First transactinide; naming dispute resolved as rutherfordium.

elements.history:
Element 104 was the first transactinide, and the first of the transfermium disputes. A Dubna group reported it in 1964, and a Berkeley group reported a clearer identification in 1969. Each side had a name. IUPAC adopted rutherfordium in 1997, for Ernest Rutherford.

Chemistry on a few short-lived atoms shows that rutherfordium behaves as a group-4 metal, the heavy analog of hafnium, which confirmed that the actinide series really does end at lawrencium.
elements.howDiscovered:
A Dubna group reported element 104 in 1964 from neon ions on plutonium, identifying it by spontaneous fission. A Berkeley group in 1969 bombarded californium with carbon ions and reported a chain of alpha decays leading to a known nobelium isotope. Fission by itself could not say which nucleus had split. A chain that ended on a known nucleus could.

The method that became standard is the second one. A heavy-ion beam fuses with a target, the recoil is caught, and detectors record the energies and the times of the alpha particles until the chain reaches an isotope already in the books. Rutherfordium’s discovery was argued until that kind of chain was clear. Chemistry on a few atoms, later, showed group-4 behavior and supported the identification.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Rutherfordium is a transactinide. The astrophysical rapid process is not expected to leave it. As the blast builds neutron-rich nuclei near mass 250 and above, fission recycles them into lighter fragments, and the survivors that later decay toward stability settle around the lead-to-uranium region, not at proton number 104.

The known isotopes live seconds. Every atom that has been identified was made by fusing heavy ions in an accelerator. A predicted island of longer-lived superheavy nuclei remains a nuclear-structure idea. It is not a place where rutherfordium has been found waiting in nature.

trivia.title: Two Reports One Number
trivia.summary: Element 104 opened a long argument, because two laboratories reported it and each believed the clearer story was its own.
trivia.story: Element 104 was the first transactinide, the first element past the actinide row, and the first of the great naming disputes. A Dubna group reported it in 1964. A Berkeley group, with Albert Ghiorso among the leaders, reported a clearer identification in 1969. Each side had detectors, decay data, and a strong sense that the other side's claim was not enough. Only a few atoms were ever in play, and they decayed, so the argument was about traces rather than about a metal anyone could hold.

trivia.title: Kurchatovium or Rutherfordium
trivia.summary: While the experiments were still disputed, each laboratory offered a name, and the two names could not both win.
trivia.story: Dubna's proposed name was kurchatovium, and Berkeley's was rutherfordium, for Ernest Rutherford. A naming fight sounds like a ceremony, and in this case it was also a Cold War argument about credit. Textbooks in different countries printed different words for the same atomic number. Students could not be sure which label would still be there when they grew up. The atoms themselves, few and short-lived, did not care what they were called while the committees argued. Only in 1997 did rutherfordium become the single official word.

trivia.title: The Name Chosen in 1997
trivia.summary: After decades of rival names, an international decision finally picked one word for element 104.
trivia.story: IUPAC settled the name in 1997, choosing rutherfordium for Ernest Rutherford. Kurchatovium did not become the official word, though it remains part of the story of the dispute. The decision ended a textbook quarrel that had lasted a generation. It did not declare that only one laboratory had ever done an experiment, and history still records both the 1964 report and the clearer 1969 identification. Rutherfordium is the name on the table, earned by a vote after a very long argument.

trivia.title: Gone before a Weighing
trivia.summary: Whatever the name, element 104 never accumulated into a speck anyone could put on a balance.
trivia.story: Rutherfordium is known from a few atoms that appear in a detector and then decay. There is no ingot, no powder, and no sample passed from one chemist to another in a bottle. Identification rests on the nuclear events, the energies and timings of the decays. A student who wants to see the element will see a symbol on a chart and a story about laboratories. Berkeley and Dubna were arguing over flashes of evidence, and those flashes were the entire substance of element 104.

trivia.title: A Handful like Hafnium
trivia.summary: A few short-lived atoms were put through chemical tests to see whether element 104 behaved like the metal above it.
trivia.story: Chemistry on a few short-lived atoms of rutherfordium showed that it behaves as a group-4 metal. That makes it the heavy analog of hafnium, the metal sitting above it in the table. The result mattered because it supported the idea that the actinide series really ends at lawrencium. These were atom-at-a-time experiments, not a weighed sample and not a commercial product. The element was seen, sorted, and gone, and the sorting agreed with the place the table had saved for it.

applications.title: Atom-at-a-time chemistry
applications.body: Rutherfordium is used only to test whether a transactinide really behaves like the metal above it, hafnium. The experiment uses single atoms.

applications.title: No material
applications.body: There is no rutherfordium alloy, crucible, or sample jar. The atoms decay in seconds or less.

applications.title: The first past the actinides
applications.body: Element 104 is the start of a new row of the middle block. Its existence is the use, in the sense that it extends the table.

elements.name: Dubnium

summary.beginner:
Dubnium is element 105, a short-lived element named for Dubna in Russia. What we know comes from a handful of atoms, not from a piece of metal.

Its symbol is Db. At room temperature dubnium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 5. In class those are called period 7 and group 5.

It sits under tantalum, so chemists look for tantalum-like behavior. The atoms decay before any ordinary measurement, like melting point, can be made.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral dubnium atom has 105 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Dubnium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 5. Dubnium is expected to resemble tantalum, and its properties are inferred from a few atoms.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d3 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 11, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5.

Discovery involved both Dubna and Berkeley, and the name honors the Russian laboratory. Solution chemistry has been compared with niobium and tantalum.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Dubnium (Z = 105) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d3 7s2. Group-5 behavior, a +5 state, is the prediction.

Early experiments disagreed about whether dubnium followed tantalum or behaved more like a heavier niobium, which is exactly the kind of question single-atom chemistry can still surprise you with.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +5. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced by heavy-ion fusion; named dubnium.

elements.history:
Dubna and Berkeley both reported element 105 around 1970, from different heavy-ion reactions. The proposed names hahnium and nielsbohrium competed through the transfermium wars. IUPAC settled on dubnium in 1997, for the town of Dubna, where the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research works.

Dubnium is the heavy analog of tantalum. The isotopes last seconds, long enough for a handful of chemical separations and not for a visible sample.
elements.howDiscovered:
Around 1970 both Dubna and Berkeley produced element 105, by different heavy-ion reactions, and both relied on decay chains rather than on a visible product. The atoms lived seconds. In the experiments that included chemistry, the atoms were swept as a gas or in solution through a separation that compared them with niobium and tantalum.

The discovery evidence is nuclear: alpha energies, half-lives, and a connection to known daughters. The chemical separations, done on a handful of atoms in the time the atoms allowed, were the supporting argument that the proton number was 105 and not a mistake in the chain.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Neutron-star mergers, and any supernovae that run the rapid process, are asked to make gold, uranium, and the rare earths. They are not asked to stockpile dubnium. Fission interrupts the climb before proton number 105 can accumulate.

The isotopes last seconds. The atoms used for the few chemical separations were fusion products, caught one at a time. If a cosmic blast ever made a dubnium nucleus, it did not last long enough to become part of a rock.

trivia.title: Reports from Both Sides
trivia.summary: Around 1970, Dubna and Berkeley each said they had made element 105, using different heavy-ion reactions.
trivia.story: Dubna and Berkeley both reported element 105 around 1970, and they did not use the same heavy-ion reaction. Each laboratory believed its decay data showed a new atomic number. The amounts were atoms, produced in collisions and gone in seconds. A second laboratory's confirmation would have settled the mood, and instead the decade opened with two claims. Element 105 entered history as a dispute before it entered history as a settled name. Seconds-long isotopes left both laboratories with decay records and with almost nothing else to show.

trivia.title: Hahnium against Nielsbohrium
trivia.summary: Two proposed names for element 105 carried famous physicists, and neither name was guaranteed a permanent home.
trivia.story: During the transfermium arguments, hahnium and nielsbohrium were the rival names for element 105. One recalled Otto Hahn, and the other recalled Niels Bohr, so both sides were offering a giant of physics. Countries printed the name that matched their claim. A student reading two books could meet two words and one atomic number. The fight was about credit as much as about language, and it lasted until an outside body chose a third word. That third word was dubnium, chosen in 1997 for the town of Dubna.

trivia.title: A Town Name Wins
trivia.summary: When the naming body finally spoke, element 105 received neither of the famous personal names that had been shouted for years.
trivia.story: In 1997 IUPAC chose dubnium, for the town of Dubna, home of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Hahnium and nielsbohrium lost the official table, though both words survive in the history of the argument. A town name was a kind of peace, pointing at a place where the work was done. The choice did not erase Berkeley's reports, and it did put Dubna in the name itself. Dubnium is therefore a Cold War ending written as a place, after years in which two personal names competed.

trivia.title: Seconds and Then Silence
trivia.summary: Element 105 lasts long enough for a hurried experiment and not long enough for anyone to see a material.
trivia.story: Dubnium isotopes last seconds, which is a long life among the heaviest elements and a blink anywhere else. That window is enough for a handful of chemical separations and not enough for a visible sample. The chemistry that was done treats dubnium as the heavy analog of tantalum. No factory, no alloy, and no jar followed from those separations. The element is a few atoms, a decay chain, and a name that remembers a Russian science town. Students say dubnium now, and the atoms remain something no one has seen.

trivia.title: A Cold War Naming Fight
trivia.summary: Element 105 became one of the sharpest examples of how a scientific credit dispute can last longer than the atoms.
trivia.story: The atoms of element 105 vanished in seconds, and the argument about them lasted until 1997. Berkeley and Dubna each carried national pride as well as data. Conferences and papers revisited the same decays for years. When dubnium became the official name, the relief was for textbooks more than for the nuclei, which had never been stored. The tense episode is that mismatch: a fleeting atom, and a human quarrel that filled a generation. Dubnium is the word that remained when the quarrel finally stopped in 1997.

applications.title: Compared with tantalum
applications.body: Dubnium chemistry, what little has been done, asks whether the atoms follow tantalum. That comparison is the work.

applications.title: Made in a fusion reaction
applications.body: Dubnium is produced by crashing a lighter nucleus into a heavier one. A few atoms are the whole product.

applications.title: No object you can hold
applications.body: Half-lives are too short for a melting point, a density, or a machine part. The element is a decay chain with a name.

elements.name: Seaborgium

summary.beginner:
Seaborgium is element 106, named for Glenn Seaborg. It is made by crashing lighter nuclei together, and the atoms vanish almost at once.

Its symbol is Sg. At room temperature seaborgium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 6. In class those are called period 7 and group 6.

Seaborgium sits under tungsten. Chemists expect it to form the same sorts of compounds tungsten does, including ones where the atom is highly charged. No one has a powder or a crystal.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral seaborgium atom has 106 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Seaborgium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 6. Seaborgium is the group-6 transactinide, expected to reach high oxidation states as tungsten does.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d4 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 12, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +6.

It was made from californium plus oxygen, and from lead plus chromium, in different experiments. The name honors the chemist who proposed the actinide row.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Seaborgium (Z = 106) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d4 7s2. Sg(VI) in oxychlorides has been studied in the gas phase, one molecule at a time.

That is evidence for the group analogy. It is not a bulk melting point or a density.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +6. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from californium and oxygen, or lead and chromium.

elements.history:
Element 106 was reported in 1974, within months, by a Berkeley group led by Ghiorso and a Dubna group led by Yuri Oganessian, using different reactions. The Berkeley evidence was the one affirmed. The discoverers asked to name it seaborgium, for Glenn Seaborg, while he was still alive. IUPAC accepted that name in 1997 after first resisting an eponym for a living person.

Seaborgium is expected to resemble tungsten, including high oxidation states. The chemistry is inferred from atom-at-a-time experiments.
elements.howDiscovered:
In 1974 a Berkeley group led by Albert Ghiorso fused oxygen with californium, and a Dubna group led by Yuri Oganessian fused chromium with lead. The Berkeley chain, alpha decays stepping down to a known isotope, was the evidence later affirmed. The atoms were identified in flight and on a detector, not in a bottle.

Seaborgium was discovered by that chain. The cross section was tiny. Hours of beam produced a few events, and each event was a sequence of recorded energies. A sequence that matches a predicted path is the discovery. A single flash is not.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Seaborgium would require a nucleus with 106 protons to survive the blast that assembled it. In the rapid process, fission is expected to cut the chain off before that proton number can accumulate and then decay into a long-lived seaborgium.

Laboratory atoms are made by fusing oxygen with californium, or chromium with lead, and they are identified by their decay chains. Those half-lives are seconds. There is no original cosmic reservoir of the element.

trivia.title: Two Papers Months Apart
trivia.summary: In 1974 two laboratories reported element 106 within months of each other, and they had not run the same experiment.
trivia.story: During 1974, Albert Ghiorso's group at Berkeley and Yuri Oganessian's group at Dubna each published a report on element 106, only months apart. The reactions were different, so the papers were not copies of one another. Both teams were hunting the same atomic number with heavy-ion beams and very few product atoms. A near-tie in the journals is its own kind of tension, because each group can see the other in print. The atoms decayed either way, and the question left behind was whose evidence would be affirmed.

trivia.title: Berkeley's Evidence Affirmed
trivia.summary: Both laboratories had published, and the later judgment of the evidence pointed to the Berkeley experiment.
trivia.story: When the claims were weighed, the Berkeley evidence was the one affirmed. That did not make the Dubna effort vanish from the history, and Oganessian's group had been in the race. Affirming one paper is a formal way of saying which decay chains were convincing. Ghiorso and his colleagues became the discoverers in that judgment. Element 106, like its neighbors, was still only a few atoms seen in detectors and then lost to decay. Ghiorso's group carried the affirmed claim, and the element still could not be passed from hand to hand.

trivia.title: A Name for Someone Living
trivia.summary: The discoverers asked to name element 106 for a chemist who was still alive, and that request broke an old habit.
trivia.story: The Berkeley discoverers asked to call element 106 seaborgium, for Glenn Seaborg. Seaborg was still alive, and naming an element for a living person was controversial. Tradition had favored the dead, or places, or ancient words, so a living colleague on the table felt too close. Seaborg had spent a career discovering elements, which made the proposal both fitting and awkward. The name sat in dispute while committees decided whether a living scientist could be honored that way. Seaborg waited, still at work, while the argument about his own name continued.

trivia.title: Accepted after Resistance
trivia.summary: The naming body first resisted seaborgium, and the word still had to survive until the official list was rewritten.
trivia.story: IUPAC at first resisted an element named for a living person. The resistance was about a rule of taste and history, not about whether Seaborg had done the work. In 1997 the union accepted seaborgium. Seaborg lived to see his name on the table, which is a rare sentence in chemistry. The tense episode ended with a yes, after years in which the answer had looked like a no. Seaborgium became official in 1997, and Glenn Seaborg could point to a square that carried his name while he lived.

trivia.title: Expected to Resemble Tungsten
trivia.summary: With only atoms to study, chemists could infer a family resemblance for element 106 and could not bottle it.
trivia.story: Seaborgium is expected to resemble tungsten, including a tendency toward high oxidation states. That expectation is inferred from atom-at-a-time experiments, not from a piece of metal on a bench. The atoms are made, observed, and gone. No commercial use followed, because there is nothing to sell and nothing to machine. The public story of element 106 is the people, the 1974 race, the living name, and a chemistry known only a few atoms at a time. High oxidation states belong to that inference, drawn from atoms that never formed a visible lump.

applications.title: A group-6 test
applications.body: Seaborgium experiments look for the high oxidation states tungsten is known for. Finding them supports the place of element 106 on the table.

applications.title: Named for Seaborg
applications.body: The name honors Glenn Seaborg, who proposed that the actinides form their own row. The element itself is not a material.

applications.title: Seconds, not samples
applications.body: The atoms are gone almost as soon as they are made. Gas-phase molecules are detected. Nothing is bottled.

elements.name: Bohrium

summary.beginner:
Bohrium is element 107, named for Niels Bohr. Only a few atoms have been made, so its properties are measured in flight, before it decays.

Its symbol is Bh. At room temperature bohrium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 7. In class those are called period 7 and group 7.

It sits under rhenium. Researchers have looked for a volatile oxide, the sort of compound rhenium forms. The result is a few detections, not a bottle.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral bohrium atom has 107 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Bohrium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 7. Bohrium is expected to resemble rhenium, and the experiments are single-atom detections.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d5 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 13, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +7.

It was produced at Darmstadt from bismuth and chromium. The half-lives of the known isotopes are seconds or less.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Bohrium (Z = 107) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d5 7s2. A volatile Bh oxide, by analogy with Re2O7, is the gas-phase experiment.

Agreement with that prediction supports placing bohrium in group 7. It does not yield a thermodynamic table.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +7. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced at GSI Darmstadt from bismuth and chromium.

elements.history:
Gottfried Münzenberg, Peter Armbruster, and coworkers at the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt produced element 107 in 1981. They fused chromium-54 with bismuth-209 and identified the product by its chain of alpha decays. The cold-fusion method they used, a gentle heavy-ion collision, became the GSI route to the next several elements.

The name bohrium, for Niels Bohr, was adopted in 1997. Bohrium is the group-7 analog of rhenium, known from a few atoms at a time.
elements.howDiscovered:
At the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt, Gottfried Münzenberg, Peter Armbruster, and coworkers fired chromium-54 at bismuth-209 in 1981. The fused nucleus recoils slowly. A velocity filter swept the fast beam aside and let the slow recoil through, and the atom stopped in a silicon detector that recorded where it landed and when it decayed.

The detector then saw a chain of alpha particles from that same position, with energies and intervals that ended on known nuclei. Bohrium was discovered as one correlated chain. The filter was the part that made a single atom observable in a flood of beam.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Bohrium is in the same class. The rapid process builds neutron-rich matter and then fission and beta decay rearrange it. The rearrangement is not thought to deposit a surviving population at proton number 107.

The atoms made at Darmstadt came from chromium ions on bismuth, and they vanished in milliseconds to seconds. Their formation was a cold fusion of two heavy nuclei, a reaction stars do not run. The universe’s neutron captures do not leave bohrium behind.

trivia.title: A Quiet Collision at GSI
trivia.summary: In Darmstadt a team fused two nuclei gently enough to hope the product would survive, and they were hunting element 107.
trivia.story: Münzenberg and Armbruster, together with their coworkers at Darmstadt's GSI laboratory, brought element 107 into view in 1981. The nuclei they joined were chromium-54 and bismuth-209, in a collision kept as gentle as such a merger can be. The method was called cold fusion in this nuclear sense, meaning a quieter merge rather than any household device. They recognized the new nucleus from the alpha particles it emitted, a trail that stepped down toward nuclei already understood. Only a few atoms were seen, and each one decayed, which was the entire discovery.

trivia.title: The Chain Was the Proof
trivia.summary: Nobody weighed element 107, so the Darmstadt team had to recognize it by the sequence of decays it left behind.
trivia.story: A single new atom is a claim only if its descendants are unmistakable. The GSI group followed alpha particles from element 107 down a chain that landed on nuclei already understood. Each energy and each timing was a fingerprint. If the chain had been muddled, the atomic number would have stayed a guess. Bohrium, as it was later named, entered science as a path through a detector, not as a substance in a crucible. M?nzenberg, Armbruster, and the GSI team had their element because the daughter nuclei were already known.

trivia.title: Earlier Reports Left Open
trivia.summary: Darmstadt's 1981 result was not the first time anyone had spoken of element 107, and earlier talk had not settled it.
trivia.story: Dubna had reported work aimed at element 107 before the GSI experiment, and those earlier claims stayed disputed. An unsuccessful or unconfirmed report can still shape a field, because other laboratories know the ground has been tried. Armbruster, Münzenberg, and the Darmstadt team are the group whose 1981 decay chains carried the discovery. The story is careful on purpose: earlier attempts were not simply ignored, and they were not the result that held. Element 107's tense episode is that sequence, a disputed start and a later experiment that convinced people.

trivia.title: Named for Niels Bohr
trivia.summary: Element 107 waited for an official name, and the name that won remembered a physicist who had changed the atom.
trivia.story: Officials settled on bohrium in 1997, a tribute to Niels Bohr. Bohr had shaped the modern picture of the atom, and a superheavy element is a distant echo of that picture. During the naming disputes, his name had also been proposed for element 105, so the honor moved before it settled. GSI's atom-at-a-time discovery and Bohr's name met in the official table sixteen years after 1981. The laboratory in Darmstadt had made the atoms, and the name pointed back to Copenhagen's most famous physicist.

trivia.title: Known a Few Atoms at a Time
trivia.summary: Element 107 is described as a heavy relative of rhenium, and that description rests on very little material indeed.
trivia.story: Bohrium is the group-7 analog of rhenium, a place in the table more than a material in a cabinet. What is known comes from a few atoms at a time. They are made in a heavy-ion collision, identified by decay, and lost. No chemical industry followed, and no accident of a bulk sample exists to tell, because there is no bulk sample. The classroom story stays with Darmstadt, with Bohr's name, and with atoms that never became a powder. Group 7 is the predicted neighborhood, and rhenium is the familiar metal sitting above it.

applications.title: A volatile oxide
applications.body: Researchers have looked for a bohrium oxide that behaves like the volatile oxide of rhenium. A few molecules are the evidence.

applications.title: Named for Bohr
applications.body: The name honors Niels Bohr, whose model of the atom started with hydrogen. Element 107 is studied one atom at a time.

applications.title: No bulk property
applications.body: There is no measured density or melting point. The periodic table predicts a heavier rhenium, and the experiments are beginning to check that.

elements.name: Hassium

summary.beginner:
Hassium is element 108, named for the German state of Hesse, where it was made. The atoms last a short time, and chemists infer their behavior from the column the element sits in.

Its symbol is Hs. At room temperature hassium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 8. In class those are called period 7 and group 8.

Hassium is under osmium. A famous osmium compound is a volatile oxide, so researchers looked for the same kind of molecule from hassium. They detected a few molecules.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral hassium atom has 108 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Hassium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 8. Hassium is the group-8 transactinide, and HsO4 has been detected as a volatile oxide.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d6 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 14, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +8.

The experiment copies the osmium tetroxide chemistry on a single-atom scale. The name comes from Hassia, the Latin name of Hesse.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Hassium (Z = 108) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d6 7s2. Detection of HsO4 is one of the clearer chemical placements in the transactinides: the molecule behaves as the group trend predicts.

Relativistic calculations still matter for the details of the bond.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +8. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from lead and iron; named for the German state of Hesse.

elements.history:
The same GSI group made element 108 in 1984 by fusing iron-58 with lead-208. Again the proof was an alpha-decay chain that landed on known nuclei. The name hassium, adopted in 1997, is from Hassia, the Latin name of the German state of Hesse, where Darmstadt sits.

Hassium is the heavy analog of osmium. In 2001 a chemical experiment on a few hassium atoms showed that they form a volatile tetroxide, as osmium does.
elements.howDiscovered:
The same Darmstadt group, in 1984, fused iron-58 with lead-208. The velocity filter again separated the recoil, and the position-sensitive detector recorded a chain of alpha decays whose times and energies connected to nuclei already identified.

Hassium was discovered by that correlation. Chemistry came much later: in 2001 a few atoms were oxidized and shown to form a volatile oxide, as osmium does. The discovery itself did not wait for the chemistry. The chain was the evidence.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Hassium is the group-8 superheavy. Fission recycling in a neutron-rich blast returns matter to lighter nuclei. It does not fill an island of hassium that the solar system could inherit.

A few hassium atoms have lived long enough, seconds, for a chemical experiment on a tetroxide. They were made by iron on lead. That laboratory fusion is the only formation channel that has actually produced the element.

trivia.title: Iron on Lead at Darmstadt
trivia.summary: The same German laboratory that had made element 107 loaded a new pair of nuclei and aimed at element 108.
trivia.story: At GSI in Darmstadt, the group made element 108 during 1984 by driving iron-58 into lead-208. It was the same style of experiment as before, a cold-fusion collision and a search for a decay chain. Lead and iron are ordinary words, and the product was anything but ordinary. A handful of atoms, after a long stretch of beam time, were the whole yield. They decayed, and the decays were the proof that element 108 had existed for a moment in the detector.

trivia.title: A Chain into Known Nuclei
trivia.summary: The Darmstadt team trusted element 108 only after its decays walked downhill into nuclei that were already on the books.
trivia.story: An alpha-decay chain is a story told backward, from a new nucleus toward older ones. For element 108, the chain landed on known nuclei, which is how a few events become a discovery. If the trail had stopped in confusion, the claim would have stayed a hope. GSI published a result built from those connected decays. Students can picture a line of flashes, each one a daughter, until the line reaches a nucleus with a familiar name. Iron-58 on lead-208 was the collision that started the line in 1984.

trivia.title: Named for the State of Hesse
trivia.summary: Element 108 took its name from a Latin word for the German state where the laboratory stands.
trivia.story: The name hassium, adopted in 1997, comes from Hassia, the Latin name of Hesse. Darmstadt sits in that German state, so the element honors the place rather than a single person. Place names had become a way through the old quarrels, a label both sides could read. Hassium does not commemorate a battle or a ruler. It commemorates a region whose laboratory, GSI, had just added several of the heaviest boxes on the table. Hassia is the old Latin name, and Hesse is the modern state a visitor would find on a map.

trivia.title: A Few Atoms and an Oxide
trivia.summary: Long after the discovery, experimenters asked whether a few atoms of element 108 would form the same kind of oxide as osmium.
trivia.story: Hassium is the heavy analog of osmium, which is a prediction from its place in the table and also a tested hint. During 2001, chemists followed a few hassium atoms and saw them form a volatile tetroxide, the oxide osmium is already known to form. That was not a bulk sample weighed on a balance, and it was not a jar of compound stored on a shelf. A few atoms, in flight through an experiment, behaved in the way the table suggested. The result belongs in the story only as that small experiment, a handful of atoms and then decay.

trivia.title: Too Brief to See
trivia.summary: Element 108 has a state named for it, and it still offers visitors nothing they can look at.
trivia.story: No one has seen a piece of hassium, because the atoms do not last long enough to gather. The discovery in 1984 and the oxide experiment in 2001 both worked with individuals, not with a material. Darmstadt's detectors recorded decays, and the chemists who followed recorded a fleeting compound-like behavior. There is no commercial use and no stockpile. Hassium is a name, a laboratory, a decay chain, and a few atoms that agreed to resemble osmium for a moment. The 2001 tetroxide test used a few atoms and still left no sample behind.

applications.title: A detected oxide
applications.body: Hassium tetroxide has been detected, one molecule at a time, by analogy with osmium tetroxide. That is the chemical result.

applications.title: Made in Hesse
applications.body: The element was produced at Darmstadt and named for the state of Hesse. The atoms last seconds.

applications.title: Not a metal sample
applications.body: No one has a speck of hassium metal. The oxide experiment is done on atoms flying through a chromatography column.

elements.name: Meitnerium

summary.beginner:
Meitnerium is element 109, named for Lise Meitner. It is known from only a few atoms, and there is no bottle of it anywhere.

Its symbol is Mt. At room temperature meitnerium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 9. In class those are called period 7 and group 9.

It sits under iridium. Almost nothing chemical has been measured, because the atoms do not last long enough for the usual experiments. The element is real, and the sample is not.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral meitnerium atom has 109 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Meitnerium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 9. Meitnerium is the group-9 transactinide, and no ordinary chemistry has been done beyond nuclear identification.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d7 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 15, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

It was made at Darmstadt from bismuth and iron. The name recognizes Meitner's role in the discovery of nuclear fission.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Meitnerium (Z = 109) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d7 7s2. Half-lives of the known isotopes are short enough that a chemical separation is barely conceivable.

Placement in group 9 is from the production chain and the periodic table, not from a measured compound.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from bismuth and iron; named for Lise Meitner.

elements.history:
GSI produced a single atom of element 109 on 29 August 1982, from iron-58 on bismuth-209. The decay chain was followed for that one atom. The name meitnerium, for Lise Meitner, was adopted in 1997. She had explained fission and had never been awarded the Nobel prize for it.

Meitnerium is the analog of iridium. No chemical experiment has been done on it. The history of the element is the history of one decay chain and a naming.
elements.howDiscovered:
On 29 August 1982 the Darmstadt group fused iron-58 with bismuth-209 and observed a single atom of element 109. The recoil stopped in the detector, and the alphas that followed came from that spot, in a sequence that reached known nuclei. One atom was the entire evidence of the first report.

Later runs produced a few more chains of the same kind. Meitnerium was discovered by the spatial correlation inside the detector: decays at one point, in the right order, after a recoil of the right velocity had arrived there. No chemical test has been added since. The chain is still the whole identification.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Meitnerium has no isotope known to live more than seconds. Nothing in the rapid-process yields of gold, lead, or uranium requires a stop at 109 protons, and fission makes such a stop unlikely.

The first atom was one decay chain from iron on bismuth. Later atoms were made the same way. If the universe forms meitnerium at all, it is as a fleeting nucleus inside a blast, not as a material that ever gathers.

trivia.title: One Atom in August
trivia.summary: On a late summer day in Darmstadt, the detectors recorded a single atom that would have to carry a whole element.
trivia.story: On 29 August 1982, Darmstadt's GSI laboratory recorded one atom of element 109, made when iron-58 struck bismuth-209. One atom is a lonely kind of evidence, and the team followed its decay chain with great care. If that chain had been ambiguous, there would have been nothing else to average with it. The atom decayed, as every atom of this element does, and the record of the decays remained. Meitnerium's experimental history opens with that one event, not with a sample anyone could divide or share.

trivia.title: A Name Long Delayed
trivia.summary: Element 109 was made in 1982, and the woman it would honor had already waited decades for credit of another kind.
trivia.story: The name meitnerium, for Lise Meitner, was adopted only in 1997, fifteen years after the single atom. Meitner had explained nuclear fission with Otto Frisch in 1939, and the 1944 Nobel Prize for that discovery went to Hahn alone. Her absence from that prize was a long injustice, and it belongs to the fission story. Putting her name on an element was a late correction of a different kind, a place in the table rather than a medal. The delay before meitnerium was official is part of the same pattern: the work acknowledged after the waiting.

trivia.title: No Chemistry Was Attempted
trivia.summary: Some heavy elements have been tested a few atoms at a time, and element 109 has not had even that experiment.
trivia.story: No chemical experiment has been carried out on meitnerium. Meitnerium's record, so far, is that chain of decays together with the name chosen later. It sits under iridium in the table, and that is a prediction about relatives, not a measured bottle of compound. The atoms do not last, and a chemical separation needs at least a little time. Classroom honesty here is simple: physicists saw a nucleus decay, and chemists have not yet had a turn. Meitnerium remains a decay chain from 29 August 1982 and a name adopted in 1997.

trivia.title: The Whole Story in One Chain
trivia.summary: With a single atom on the record, the Darmstadt group had to let one sequence of decays stand for the discovery.
trivia.story: Most discoveries allow a second event, a repeat that calms the nerves. Element 109's first announcement rested on one atom, made on 29 August 1982 and followed until the chain was clear. The iron beam on bismuth was the tool, and the alpha decays were the language. Later work would add more evidence, but the origin story remains that solitary nucleus. A whole element, named for a great physicist, began as one set of flashes in a German detector. Iron-58 striking bismuth-209 was the collision that produced that solitary atom.

trivia.title: Iridium's Unseen Neighbor
trivia.summary: Charts place element 109 beneath iridium, and the chart is ahead of any experiment a chemist has been able to finish.
trivia.story: Meitnerium is expected to be the heavy analog of iridium because of where it sits. Expectation is not a measurement, and no chemical study has been possible on the atoms that have been made. They appear and decay. GSI's 1982 atom, and the name adopted in 1997, are the solid parts of the public story. Anything about color, melting, or a compound would be an invention, so the story refuses to go there. The solid facts are the GSI atom, Meitner's missing Nobel in the fission story, and the name adopted in 1997.

applications.title: Identification only
applications.body: Meitnerium is known from its nuclear decay. Chemical experiments have not been practical, because the atoms do not last.

applications.title: Named for Meitner
applications.body: The name honors Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission. The element is not a fission fuel and has no application.

applications.title: Under iridium
applications.body: On the table, meitnerium sits under iridium. That is a prediction of its chemistry, not a measurement.

elements.name: Darmstadtium

summary.beginner:
Darmstadtium is element 110, named for Darmstadt, the city of the laboratory that made it. Its atoms last milliseconds.

Its symbol is Ds. At room temperature darmstadtium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 10. In class those are called period 7 and group 10.

It sits under platinum. Any sentence about it being a noble metal is a prediction from the table, not a test someone has run on a piece of metal.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral darmstadtium atom has 110 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Darmstadtium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 10. Darmstadtium is the group-10 transactinide, known from nuclear decay chains rather than from chemistry.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d9 7s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 17, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +6.

It was produced from lead and nickel. The name follows the city, as hassium follows the state.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Darmstadtium (Z = 110) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d9 7s1. Millisecond lifetimes stop solution chemistry.

The isotope is identified by the alpha particles it emits and by the known daughters in the chain. Chemical analogy to platinum remains a prediction.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +6. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from lead and nickel; named for Darmstadt.

elements.history:
On 9 November 1994, GSI fused nickel-62 with lead-208 and observed element 110. A second isotope followed days later. The laboratory waited, then proposed the name darmstadtium, for Darmstadt, which IUPAC adopted in 2003.

Darmstadtium is the heavy analog of platinum. The isotopes live for milliseconds to seconds. Identification rests on the decay chain, not on a weighable product.
elements.howDiscovered:
In November 1994 the Darmstadt group fused nickel-62 with lead-208. The velocity filter delivered the recoils to a silicon detector, and chains of alpha particles were recorded at the implantation sites. A second isotope followed within days, from nickel-64 on the same lead.

Two isotopes, with chains that agreed with each other and with the known region they decayed into, were the discovery. Darmstadtium was not seen as a product that accumulated. It was seen as correlated events. Milliseconds to seconds later, each atom was gone.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Darmstadtium lies beyond the region where the rapid process is known to leave survivors. Calculations that follow a merger’s ejecta produce the familiar heavy elements and a fission cycle. They do not produce a reservoir of element 110.

The isotopes live from milliseconds to about a second. Each one was fused from nickel and lead. That is the formation history the atoms actually have. A cosmic original, in the sense of a stock older than the Earth, is not expected.

trivia.title: November at the GSI
trivia.summary: A Darmstadt team fused nickel with lead and watched the detectors for an element that would live only briefly.
trivia.story: On 9 November 1994, the GSI team fused nickel-62 with lead-208 and observed element 110. Sigurd Hofmann and Gottfried Münzenberg are the names usually attached to that Darmstadt work. The proof was a decay chain, the same kind of fingerprint that had carried the previous GSI elements. A few atoms appeared in the data and then decayed. There was nothing to photograph and nothing to store, only a nuclear event and a laboratory ready to try again. Hofmann and M?nzenberg could order another beam, and they could not keep the atom.

trivia.title: A Second Isotope Days Later
trivia.summary: The first sighting of element 110 was followed, within days, by another isotope that strengthened the claim.
trivia.story: A single chain can be a discovery, and a second isotope is a gift to the people who have to defend it. Days after 9 November 1994, GSI observed another isotope of element 110. The quick repeat mattered because these atoms live only milliseconds to seconds. Nobody could set the first atom aside and study it at leisure. The laboratory's tense week was that pair of observations, close together, and then the long wait to give the element a name.

trivia.title: Named for Darmstadt
trivia.summary: Element 110 took the name of the city where the atoms were made, after the laboratory chose to wait before proposing it.
trivia.story: The laboratory waited, then proposed darmstadtium, for the city of Darmstadt. IUPAC adopted the name in 2003. A city name continued the pattern of hassium and of other place-names that had calmed earlier fights. Hofmann, Münzenberg, and their colleagues had made the atoms, and the city received the public word. Darmstadtium remembers a place and a November experiment, not a commercial metal. IUPAC's 2003 decision fixed the city name, years after nickel-62 struck lead-208 and those first short chains appeared.

trivia.title: Milliseconds to Seconds
trivia.summary: Element 110 is described as a heavy relative of platinum, and the atoms disappear before that description can be weighed.
trivia.story: Darmstadtium is the heavy analog of platinum by its place in the table. The isotopes live for milliseconds to seconds, which ends any dream of a visible piece. Identification rests on the decay chain, not on a product that can be weighed. No chemical industry and no household use exists, because the atoms are gone before a use could be tried. The story is the GSI team, the nickel-on-lead collisions, and the brief lives recorded in 1994. Platinum is the map above it, and that map was never checked against a lump of darmstadtium.

trivia.title: A Chain and Not a Metal
trivia.summary: Visitors sometimes expect a new element to look like a lump of metal, and element 110 offers only a line of decays.
trivia.story: If a museum asked for darmstadtium, the honest exhibit would be a plot of detector signals. Hofmann's group and the rest of the GSI team produced those signals by fusion, then read the alpha decays. Each atom was a visitor that left immediately. Platinum sits above it as a real metal people have held for centuries, and the comparison is only a map. Element 110's entire material history is a few decays in Darmstadt and a name adopted nine years later.

applications.title: Milliseconds
applications.body: Darmstadtium atoms last milliseconds. They are identified by the particles they emit as they decay.

applications.title: Named for the city
applications.body: The laboratory that made the element is in Darmstadt, and the element carries the city's name.

applications.title: A platinum analog, on paper
applications.body: Group 10 suggests a heavier platinum. No chemical test has confirmed or denied that. There is no use as a metal.

elements.name: Roentgenium

summary.beginner:
Roentgenium is element 111, named for Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays. It is produced a few atoms at a time.

Its symbol is Rg. At room temperature roentgenium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 11. In class those are called period 7 and group 11.

It sits under gold. Calculations suggest its electrons are strongly affected by relativity, so it may not simply be a heavier gold. Nobody has a sample to compare.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral roentgenium atom has 111 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Roentgenium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 11. Roentgenium is the group-11 transactinide, and relativistic effects on the 7s electron are predicted to be large.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 18, 1. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3.

It was made from bismuth and nickel at Darmstadt. Identification is by the decay chain.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Roentgenium (Z = 111) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s1. A relativistic contraction of the 7s orbital is predicted to be even stronger than the effect that makes gold yellow.

That could change the chemistry relative to gold. The prediction is not yet a measurement.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +3. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from bismuth and nickel; named for Röntgen.

elements.history:
GSI made element 111 in December 1994, days after darmstadtium, by fusing nickel-64 with bismuth-209. The name roentgenium, for Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays, was adopted in 2004.

Roentgenium is the analog of gold. Relativistic calculations suggest its chemistry will not be a simple copy of gold’s, but no chemical study has been possible. The atoms do not last.
elements.howDiscovered:
Days after the darmstadtium run, the same group switched the target from lead to bismuth and the beam to nickel-64. In December 1994 the detector recorded chains assigned to element 111. The odd proton number changed the pattern of the decays, and the chains still ended in known territory.

Roentgenium was discovered by that change of target and beam, on an apparatus already tuned, and by chains that matched the new arithmetic. The method was unchanged: filter, implant, and read the alphas from one pixel.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Roentgenium is in the same predicted gap. The island of stability, if it is inhabited anywhere, is usually drawn toward more neutrons than the isotopes accelerators have reached, and even that island is a calculation. No natural roentgenium has been observed.

The known atoms last milliseconds and were made from nickel on bismuth. Neutron capture in a merger is the only cosmic process energetic enough to be discussed, and fission is expected to win before element 111 can accumulate.

trivia.title: Days after Element 110
trivia.summary: Darmstadt had just announced one new element when the same style of experiment produced the next number.
trivia.story: December 1994 had barely registered element 110 when GSI joined nickel-64 to bismuth-209 and recorded element 111. Hofmann's group was again at the center of the work. The two discoveries so close together felt like a rush at the end of a long technique. Cold-fusion collisions, careful separators, and decay chains had become the Darmstadt method. Element 111 arrived as a few atoms, identified and then gone, in the same season as element 110. Nickel-64 on bismuth-209 was the collision, and Hofmann's group read the chain before the atoms vanished.

trivia.title: Named for the X-ray Pioneer
trivia.summary: Element 111 received the name of the physicist who discovered X-rays, a tribute chosen years after the atoms.
trivia.story: The name roentgenium, for Wilhelm Röntgen, was adopted in 2004. Röntgen's X-rays had let physicians see inside the body, and his name now labels an element no one can see. The gap between 1994 and 2004 was the time needed to confirm the chains and to agree on a word. Hofmann's Darmstadt group had made the atoms, and the name pointed to a German discovery of a different century. Roentgenium honors a person, a laboratory, and a handful of decays.

trivia.title: Calculations and Not a Bottle
trivia.summary: Element 111 sits under gold on the chart, and theorists warn that the resemblance may not be simple.
trivia.story: Roentgenium is the analog of gold by position, under gold in the table. Calculations that fold in relativity imply the chemistry may pull away from gold's familiar pattern. Those are calculations, not measurements, because no chemical study has been possible. Those nuclei vanish before anyone can start the ordinary chemical tests. A classroom can say where the element sits, and it should not pretend that anyone has watched a roentgenium compound form. Relativistic calculations are the only chemical guide, and they warn against treating roentgenium as ordinary gold.

trivia.title: Atoms That Would Not Stay
trivia.summary: The discovery of element 111 was real, and it left the discoverers with nothing they could keep until morning.
trivia.story: Each atom of element 111 decayed, leaving a chain of alpha particles and a record in a computer. Hofmann's group could repeat the class of experiment, and they could not store the product. That is the ordinary life of a superheavy element, and it still feels extreme. There is no accident story of a spilled sample, because there was never a sample to spill. The tense fact is the brevity itself, a discovery that exists as evidence and not as matter in a tray.

trivia.title: Gold's Heavy Placeholder
trivia.summary: Charts draw element 111 beneath gold, and the drawing is a prediction waiting on atoms that disappear.
trivia.story: People understand gold, so the table invites a comparison the moment roentgenium is mentioned. The comparison is a seat in group 11, not a measured nugget. Calculations that include relativity suggest the chemistry may diverge from gold in important ways. Until atoms live longer, that suggestion stays on paper. GSI in 1994, the name in 2004, and a few decay chains are the parts of the story that have actually happened. Hofmann's group made the atoms in December 1994, days after element 110, and none of those atoms could be saved.

applications.title: A few atoms
applications.body: Roentgenium is produced a few atoms at a time and identified by its decay chain. There is no sample to machine or to plate onto a contact.

applications.title: Named for Röntgen
applications.body: The name honors Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays. The element is not an X-ray source.

applications.title: A prediction about gold
applications.body: Calculations say relativity may change roentgenium's chemistry relative to gold. The prediction is waiting on an experiment that the lifetime barely allows.

elements.name: Copernicium

summary.beginner:
Copernicium is element 112, named for Copernicus. Some experiments hint that single atoms behave a little like a heavy, volatile metal, but no one has a sample to hold.

Its symbol is Cn. At room temperature copernicium is a solid. It is a transition metal, from the wide middle block of the table. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 12. In class those are called period 7 and group 12.

It sits under mercury, the metal that is already a liquid. Copernicium might be even more weakly bound. The evidence is the behavior of individual atoms on a detector, not a drop of liquid.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral copernicium atom has 112 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Copernicium is a solid transition metal in period 7 and group 12. Copernicium is the group-12 transactinide, and experiments suggest it is more volatile than a normal metal.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 18, 2. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

It was made from lead and zinc. Adsorption experiments compare single atoms with mercury and with noble gases.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Copernicium (Z = 112) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2. A closed 6d10 7s2 shell, strongly stabilized by relativity, is predicted to make copernicium unusually noble and volatile.

The adsorption data point that way. They are not a measured boiling point.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from lead and zinc; named for Copernicus.

elements.history:
GSI produced element 112 in 1996 from zinc-70 on lead-208. The decay chain was confirmed in later experiments, including work at RIKEN. The name copernicium, for Nicolaus Copernicus, was adopted in 2010. It is the last element made by the cold-fusion route at GSI.

Copernicium is the heavy analog of mercury and may be unusually volatile. Adsorption experiments on a few atoms hint that it behaves more like a noble metal vapor than like a typical group-12 metal.
elements.howDiscovered:
In 1996 the Darmstadt group fused zinc-70 with lead-208. The recoil separator and the silicon detector recorded a decay chain for element 112. Independent confirmations followed, including an experiment at RIKEN that saw the same kind of chain.

Copernicium was discovered when a chain from that fusion was confirmed by a second laboratory. A single unconfirmed sequence is a candidate. A repeated sequence, with the same energies, is an element. This was the last element found by the cold-fusion route of nickel and zinc on lead and bismuth.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Copernicium would be a survivor only if a very neutron-rich nucleus with 112 protons could finish its decays without fissioning. Current rapid-process models do not leave such a survivor in the mix that later becomes stars and planets.

The atoms that have been made came from zinc on lead, lived for seconds at most, and were identified by alpha-decay chains. Their formation is an accelerator result. It is not a chapter of the history of the solar cloud.

trivia.title: Zinc on a Lead Target
trivia.summary: Darmstadt tried one more cold-fusion pair, zinc against lead, in a hunt for element 112.
trivia.story: A zinc-70 beam struck lead-208 at GSI in 1996, and element 112 showed up in the products. Hofmann's group identified it by the decay chain, the long fingerprint of alpha particles. Copernicium was the final new element Darmstadt reached by that cold-fusion approach. The technique that had carried the laboratory from element 107 through the early 110s reached its end at copernicium. Only a few atoms were observed, and they decayed, leaving the claim to be confirmed by later work. Zinc-70 on lead-208 was the last cold-fusion pair GSI used to open a new box on the table.

trivia.title: A Chain Checked in Japan
trivia.summary: The first decay chain needed company, and a laboratory in Japan was among the places that supplied it.
trivia.story: A discovery built on a few chains invites a second laboratory to try. The decay chain of element 112 was confirmed in later experiments, including work at RIKEN in Japan. Confirmation did not create a stock of the element. It meant another group saw the same kind of nuclear story. Darmstadt had made the first atoms in 1996, and RIKEN's later chains helped the result stand. RIKEN did not replace Darmstadt as the maker of the first atoms, and its confirmation still involved only a few decays.

trivia.title: Named for Copernicus
trivia.summary: Element 112 took the name of the astronomer who moved the Earth, a choice made years after the first atoms.
trivia.story: Officials agreed on copernicium in 2010, honoring the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus. Copernicus had rearranged the heavens, and a superheavy element is a rearrangement at the other end of nature. Fourteen years separated the 1996 atoms from the official name. Hofmann's group and GSI had done the making, and the name looked back to a Polish astronomer. Copernicium closed GSI's cold-fusion series with a word from the history of the sky. The 2010 name arrived long after the 1996 atoms had decayed, which is the usual delay at this end of the table.

trivia.title: A Hint from a Few Atoms
trivia.summary: Much later, a few-atom experiment asked whether element 112 might drift through an apparatus the way a volatile metal would.
trivia.story: Copernicium is the heavy analog of mercury, and mercury is famous for being a volatile metal. Adsorption experiments on a few atoms, carried out in the two-thousands, hinted that copernicium behaves more like a noble-metal vapor than like a typical group-12 metal. The hint is not a weighed ingot and not a bulk property measured in grams. A few atoms stuck or failed to stick, and then they decayed. Any classroom sentence about this chemistry has to stay at that size: a small experiment, a suggestion, and no sample left behind.

trivia.title: The End of a Darmstadt Route
trivia.summary: After element 112, the gentle fusion method that had served Darmstadt so well was no longer the way forward.
trivia.story: Cold fusion at GSI had been a triumphant method, and copernicium was its last new element. Heavier elements would be pursued with a different projectile, calcium-48, mainly at Dubna. The handoff is a change of laboratories and of technique, not a failure of the 1996 result. Hofmann's chains, RIKEN's confirmations, and the 2010 name remain the story of element 112. What no one has is a piece of copernicium, only the record of atoms that vanished on schedule. Calcium-48, used later at Dubna, would carry the table past this point.

applications.title: A volatile atom
applications.body: Single copernicium atoms have been studied to see whether they stick to a gold surface or fly on like a gas. They behave more like a volatile metal.

applications.title: Under mercury
applications.body: Copernicium sits under mercury, the metal that is already a liquid. The experiments ask whether element 112 is even less metallic.

applications.title: Named for Copernicus
applications.body: The name honors Copernicus. There is no copernicium device. The result is a place on the table plus a hint about the atom.
