elements.name: Nihonium

summary.beginner:
Nihonium is element 113, the first superheavy element of the right-hand block, and it was named in Japan, where one discovery team worked. Only a few atoms have been made.

Its symbol is Nh. At room temperature nihonium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 13. In class those are called period 7 and group 13.

It sits under thallium. Chemists expect a +1 chemistry, the same inert-pair idea that makes thallium poisonous and unusual. That is a prediction. The atoms decay in less than a second.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral nihonium atom has 113 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Nihonium is a solid post-transition in period 7 and group 13. Nihonium opens the superheavy p-block, and a +1 oxidation state is the inert-pair prediction.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p1. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 18, 3. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

One production route is zinc on bismuth. Another is calcium on americium, followed by decay. The name comes from Nihon, a Japanese name for Japan.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Nihonium (Z = 113) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p1. The 7p electron is predicted to be relatively easy to remove while the 7s pair stays inert, echoing thallium.

No aqueous chemistry has been done. The placement rests on decay chains.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced by zinc on bismuth, or americium on calcium.

elements.history:
A RIKEN team led by Kosuke Morita produced element 113 in 2004 by fusing zinc-70 with bismuth-209, and confirmed the decay chain in later runs. A Dubna–Livermore collaboration also observed it as a decay product of element 115. IUPAC credited RIKEN. The name nihonium, from Nihon, a Japanese name for Japan, was adopted in 2016.

Nihonium opens the superheavy p-block. It is expected to behave like a heavy thallium, with the +1 state favored, but that is a prediction rather than a measured bottle of compound.
elements.howDiscovered:
A team at RIKEN, led by Kosuke Morita, fused zinc-70 with bismuth-209 starting in 2004. Their gas-filled recoil separator sent the products into a detector, and they recorded a chain that passed through element 111 and onward into known nuclei. Further chains over the next several years reproduced it. A Dubna collaboration saw the same element as a daughter of element 115.

Nihonium was discovered by a cold-fusion chain that was patient. The cross section was so small that the beam ran for months per event. The confirmation was a second chain, and a third, with the same steps. The daughter seen in the element-115 work tied the two laboratories’ nuclei together.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Nihonium is heavier still, and the same fission limit applies. The rapid process is the only astrophysical channel anyone seriously considers for nuclei this heavy, and it is expected to recycle them.

The atoms made at RIKEN came from zinc on bismuth, a cold-fusion reaction with a tiny yield, and decayed in milliseconds. A second route, the decay of element 115, is also a laboratory chain. No original natural stock is known or expected.

trivia.title: A Chain Seen at RIKEN
trivia.summary: In Japan a team fused zinc with bismuth and watched a decay chain that pointed to element 113.
trivia.story: Kosuke Morita's team at RIKEN in Japan made element 113 in 2004, using a zinc-70 beam on bismuth-209. They saw a decay chain, then worked for years to confirm it in later runs. A chain seen once is a start, and a chain seen again is how a superheavy claim grows up. Only a few atoms were involved, and every one of them decayed. The experiment lived in Japan, at RIKEN, and the element was still waiting for an official judgment about credit.

trivia.title: Also Seen on the Way Down
trivia.summary: While RIKEN hunted element 113 directly, another collaboration kept meeting it as the daughter of a heavier atom.
trivia.story: A Dubna and Livermore collaboration also observed element 113, not as their main target but as a decay product of element 115. A daughter nucleus can confirm a parent, and it can also start an argument about who discovered the daughter. Two routes to the same atomic number made the priority question sharper. Both routes still dealt in single atoms and decay chains. Element 113 was seen in Japan by fusion and seen again in the decays that followed heavier Dubna experiments.

trivia.title: Credit Given to RIKEN
trivia.summary: Two routes existed, and the naming body had to say which laboratory would be credited with the discovery.
trivia.story: IUPAC assigned priority for element 113 to RIKEN in 2015. The decision recognized Morita's team and the chains they had built and confirmed. Dubna's observation of element 113 as a decay product remained scientifically real and did not receive the discovery credit. It was the first element whose discovery IUPAC credited to an Asian laboratory. That sentence is more careful than a boast about an entire continent, and it is the sentence the record supports. Morita's confirmed chains were what the 2015 decision had in front of it, not a bulk sample.

trivia.title: A Word from Nihon
trivia.summary: Once credit was settled, element 113 needed a name, and the discoverers offered a Japanese name for Japan.
trivia.story: Officials adopted nihonium in 2016, taking it from Nihon, a Japanese name for the country itself. Morita and the RIKEN team had made the case for the element, and the name placed the country on the table. A year had passed between the 2015 credit decision and the official word. Nihonium does not describe a use, because there is no use, only a few atoms. The name is the public ending of a long experimental patience. Japan's laboratory had the credit, and the atoms that earned it were already gone.

trivia.title: A Prediction under Thallium
trivia.summary: Charts put element 113 under thallium, and chemists are careful to call that family resemblance a prediction.
trivia.story: Nihonium opens the superheavy p-block, the part of the seventh row where p orbitals are expected to matter. Theory treats it as a heavy cousin of thallium and expects the plus-one charge to be favored. That is a prediction, not a measured bottle of compound. No commercial use and no bulk reaction belong in the story. What happened in the laboratory is the RIKEN chain, the Dubna daughter atoms, the 2015 credit, and a name from Nihon. The plus-one state is a forecast from theory, and no one has weighed a nihonium compound.

applications.title: Made in Japan
applications.body: One of the teams that made nihonium worked in Japan, and the element is named for that. The product was a few atoms.

applications.title: The start of a new block
applications.body: Nihonium is the first superheavy element of the p-block, under thallium. A +1 chemistry is the prediction.

applications.title: No chemistry yet in a beaker
applications.body: The atoms decay in less than a second. No compound has been isolated. The use of the element is the knowledge that it exists.

elements.name: Flerovium

summary.beginner:
Flerovium is element 114, named for the Flerov laboratory. Among the superheavy elements it is predicted to live a little longer, but longer still means a fraction of a second.

Its symbol is Fl. At room temperature flerovium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 14. In class those are called period 7 and group 14.

It sits under lead. Some calculations say it might be strangely unreactive for a metal in that column. Experiments on single atoms are the only tests, and they are subtle.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral flerovium atom has 114 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Flerovium is a solid post-transition in period 7 and group 14. Flerovium is the group-14 transactinide, predicted to be relatively long-lived and possibly more noble than lead.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p2. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 18, 4. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

It is made from plutonium and calcium. Gas-adsorption experiments have been used to ask whether the atoms stick to gold surfaces like a metal.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Flerovium (Z = 114) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p2. A relativistically stabilized 7p1/2 pair is the reason some theories call flerovium a noble metal or even a volatile one.

The island-of-stability idea is about nuclear lifetimes, a separate question from that chemistry.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from plutonium and calcium; named for Flerov’s laboratory.

elements.history:
A Dubna–Livermore collaboration produced element 114 in 1998 by bombarding plutonium with calcium-48, a rare doubly magic projectile. The name flerovium, for Georgy Flerov and the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions, was adopted in 2012. Calcium-48 fusion became the route to every element past copernicium.

Flerovium is the analog of lead. Some of its isotopes live for seconds, long enough that it was once discussed as a shore of the predicted island of stability. The half-lives are longer than those of its neighbors, and still far too short to see.
elements.howDiscovered:
In 1998 a Dubna–Livermore collaboration fired calcium-48, a rare neutron-rich projectile, at a plutonium target. A gas-filled separator carried the recoils to a detector, and the decays that followed were assigned to element 114. Later experiments mapped several isotopes and connected their chains to nuclei Dubna and Darmstadt had both seen.

Flerovium was discovered by that calcium beam. Calcium-48 fuses more willingly with actinide targets than the nickel and zinc beams do, which is why the cross sections were large enough to work with. The evidence was still a chain of alphas and a spontaneous fission at the end, correlated in one detector pixel.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Flerovium is sometimes mentioned in guesses about a shore of longer half-lives, because some of its isotopes last seconds rather than milliseconds. Seconds are not a cosmic stock. The rapid process would still have to produce a more neutron-rich parent and have it survive fission.

The atoms in hand were made with calcium-48 on plutonium. Calcium-48 is a rare nucleus on Earth and is used as a beam. Stars do not fire it at a plutonium target. The element’s real formation channel is that experiment.

trivia.title: Calcium on Plutonium
trivia.summary: A Dubna and Livermore team chose a rare projectile and a plutonium target in a search for element 114.
trivia.story: During 1998, partners from Dubna and Livermore sent a calcium-48 beam into plutonium and produced element 114. Calcium-48 is a rare, doubly magic projectile, a nucleus theorists regard as especially sturdy. The experiment belonged to the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions and to its American partner at Livermore. Yuri Oganessian is the scientist to picture at the head of Dubna's superheavy program. The yield was a few atoms, identified by decay and then gone. Oganessian's Dubna program and the Livermore partners shared that small, decisive yield.

trivia.title: Named for Georgy Flerov
trivia.summary: Element 114's name remembered both a physicist and the laboratory in Dubna that already carried his name.
trivia.story: The name flerovium, adopted in 2012, honors Georgy Flerov and the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions. Flerov had pushed heavy-element work in Dubna for decades. Naming the element for him also named the place where calcium-48 beams were doing their famous work. Livermore shared the experiments, and the official word pointed to the Russian laboratory and its founder. Flerovium is a person's name and a laboratory's name at the same time. The 2012 decision put both the man and the Flerov Laboratory into the official word.

trivia.title: The Route past Copernicium
trivia.summary: After element 112, a particular calcium beam became the way laboratories tried to climb any higher.
trivia.story: After copernicium, laboratories reached each new element by fusing calcium-48 into a heavy target. The 1998 plutonium experiment was an early step on that road, not a one-time trick. Dubna, with Livermore and later other partners, used the same projectile against heavier and heavier targets. Each success was still only atoms. Element 114 matters in this story as the doorway through which 115, 116, 117, and 118 were later approached. Every later element through oganesson relied on that same rare projectile, still producing only atoms that decayed.

trivia.title: Seconds on a Distant Shore
trivia.summary: Some atoms of element 114 lasted longer than their neighbors, and people wondered whether a fabled island was nearby.
trivia.story: Flerovium is the analog of lead, a statement about the table rather than about a metal anyone has held. A few of its isotopes hang on for seconds, which tempted physicists to talk about the near edge of a predicted island of stability. Those lifetimes beat the neighboring elements, and they still end long before a person could ever see a speck. An island, in this metaphor, means nuclei that might last longer, and flerovium only gestured toward it. The atoms decayed, the seconds ended, and no sample remained for a photograph.

trivia.title: Oganessian and the Beams
trivia.summary: Behind the calcium experiments at Dubna stood a long program and a scientist whose name would later label another element.
trivia.story: Yuri Oganessian led the Dubna heavy-element program that made calcium-48 its signature tool. Element 114 was one of the early prizes of that program, shared with Livermore. The work asked for rare isotope material, long beam times, and patience with null weeks. When atoms finally appeared, they decayed before a second shift could look at them as matter. Flerovium's story is that patience, the 1998 production, and a name that remembers Flerov. Livermore shared the work, and the atoms still vanished before anyone could point to a speck.

applications.title: A longer-lived superheavy
applications.body: Flerovium is predicted to live longer than its neighbors, and some isotopes last a fraction of a second. That is long enough for a cautious chemical test.

applications.title: Does it behave like lead
applications.body: Adsorption experiments ask whether a flerovium atom sticks to gold the way a metal would. The answer is subtle and still being argued.

applications.title: Named for a laboratory
applications.body: The name honors the Flerov laboratory, where the element was made from plutonium and calcium. There is no flerovium material.

elements.name: Moscovium

summary.beginner:
Moscovium is element 115, named for the Moscow region. It is identified by the chain of particles it emits as it decays, not by a lump of metal.

Its symbol is Mc. At room temperature moscovium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 15. In class those are called period 7 and group 15.

It sits under bismuth. A few atoms are made by crashing calcium into americium. They are gone almost immediately. The element is a place on the table with a measured decay chain behind it.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral moscovium atom has 115 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Moscovium is a solid post-transition in period 7 and group 15. Moscovium is the group-15 transactinide, identified by alpha-decay chains.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p3. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 18, 5. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1.

No chemical experiment has been reported on a moscovium atom. The group trend would suggest a heavier bismuth, increasingly dominated by a lower oxidation state.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Moscovium (Z = 115) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p3. The discovery claim rests on chains that end at known nuclei.

Chemistry, if it is ever done, will be a single-atom adsorption or a gas-phase molecule, not a titration.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +1. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from americium and calcium; named for Moscow.

elements.history:
Dubna and Livermore made element 115 in 2003 by fusing calcium-48 with americium-243. The decay chain passed through element 113, which linked this work to the RIKEN result. The name moscovium, for Moscow, was adopted in 2016.

Moscovium is the analog of bismuth. Like the other superheavies, it is identified by the energies and timings of alpha particles and by the known nuclei the chain eventually reaches.
elements.howDiscovered:
In 2003 the Dubna–Livermore group fused calcium-48 with americium-243. The chains decayed through element 113 on the way down, which linked them to the RIKEN nihonium chains, and the timings and energies repeated across several atoms.

Moscovium was discovered as those repeated chains. The americium target supplied 95 protons, the calcium supplied 20, and the compound nucleus lost a few neutrons. The arithmetic was simple. The proof was the sequence of decays, seen more than once, ending where the chart was already known.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Moscovium has no path into a planet. Fission in the rapid process is expected to fragment nuclei before 115 protons can be a decay product that lingers. The known isotopes live for tenths of a second.

They were made by calcium-48 on americium. That fusion is a human arrangement of two heavy nuclei. The universe’s way of building heavy nuclei, neutron capture, is not known to leave moscovium behind.

trivia.title: Americium Meets Calcium
trivia.summary: Dubna and Livermore aimed calcium-48 at americium and looked for a decay chain heavy enough to be element 115.
trivia.story: The 2003 experiment, run by Dubna and Livermore, joined calcium-48 with americium-243 and produced element 115. The method continued the calcium-beam route that had opened element 114. A few atoms were the yield, and they announced themselves by decaying. There was no weighable product and no second chance to hold the same atom. The collaboration's claim rested on the energies and timings of those decays. Americium-243 caught the calcium-48 beam, a few atoms of element 115 appeared, and their decays were the only proof on record.

trivia.title: A Path through 113
trivia.summary: The decay chain of element 115 passed through element 113, tying a Dubna experiment to work underway in Japan.
trivia.story: The decay chain of element 115 passed through element 113. That link connected the Dubna and Livermore result to the chains Kosuke Morita's RIKEN team was studying. A parent and a daughter in different laboratories can support each other if the energies match. They can also complicate credit, which is what happened when IUPAC later credited RIKEN with element 113. Element 115 kept its own story: a 2003 fusion, a chain, and atoms that did not survive it. The timings had to match, or the link between the two laboratories would have failed.

trivia.title: Named for Moscow
trivia.summary: Element 115 received a city name, chosen long after the first decay chains and pointed at the capital near Dubna.
trivia.story: The name moscovium, for Moscow, was adopted in 2016. Dubna lies in the Moscow region, so the name honors the place that hosted the calcium beams. Livermore was the American partner in the 2003 work, and the official word named the Russian side's city. Place names had become the calm ending of superheavy stories. Moscovium remembers a capital, a collaboration, and a few atoms from 2003. By 2016 those atoms were long gone, and the capital's name was what the table could still display.

trivia.title: Proof in Times and Energies
trivia.summary: With no material to show, the discoverers of element 115 had to let particle energies and clocks make the argument.
trivia.story: Moscovium is the analog of bismuth, which tells you the column and not the contents of a bottle. Like the other superheavy elements, it is identified by alpha-particle energies and by the times between decays. The chain eventually reaches known nuclei, and that landing is what makes the start of the chain believable. No chemical use was found, and none should be invented, because the atoms are gone. The experiment is nuclear from beginning to end. Bismuth is the familiar element above it, and that kinship has not been tested in a bottle.

trivia.title: Nothing to Put in a Jar
trivia.summary: Element 115 has a place, a name, and a discovery year, and it still has no sample a museum could display.
trivia.story: A visitor asking to see moscovium can be shown the chart and the story of Dubna and Livermore. The 2003 atoms decayed. Later experiments confirmed chains of the same kind, still without producing a visible speck. There is no commercial use and no household object. Moscovium remains a collaboration, a calcium beam on americium, and a name adopted in 2016 for Moscow. Dubna and Livermore's 2003 fusion remains the discovery in this account, told through a decay chain rather than a collected material.

applications.title: Identified by its decays
applications.body: Moscovium is known because the atoms emit a characteristic chain of alpha particles ending at known nuclei. That chain is the evidence.

applications.title: Under bismuth
applications.body: The table places moscovium under bismuth. No chemical experiment has been reported.

applications.title: Named for Moscow
applications.body: The discovery collaboration named the element for the Moscow region. A few atoms were the whole discovery.

elements.name: Livermorium

summary.beginner:
Livermorium is element 116, named for Livermore, California. It is made by crashing calcium into a heavier target, one atom at a time.

Its symbol is Lv. At room temperature livermorium is a solid. It is a metal from the block just to the right of the transition metals. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 16. In class those are called period 7 and group 16.

It sits under polonium. Polonium is already highly radioactive. Livermorium is far more so, and far rarer. There is no use and no sample.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral livermorium atom has 116 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Livermorium is a solid post-transition in period 7 and group 16. Livermorium is the group-16 transactinide, still known only from atom-at-a-time nuclear experiments.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p4. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 18, 6. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2.

The production reaction is curium plus calcium. Identification is the decay chain. Chemical analogy to polonium is a prediction.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Livermorium (Z = 116) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p4. Even-Z superheavy nuclei in this region can be slightly longer-lived than their odd neighbors, and livermorium's discovery used that.

The lifetime is still far too short for a compound you could weigh.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is +2. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from curium and calcium; named for Livermore.

elements.history:
The Dubna–Livermore team reported element 116 in 2000 from calcium-48 on curium. The name livermorium, for Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, was adopted in 2012, pairing the Russian laboratory in the flerovium name with its American partner.

Livermorium is the analog of polonium. The atoms are gone in milliseconds. What is known is nuclear, not chemical: decay energies, and the fact that the even proton number makes some isotopes slightly longer-lived.
elements.howDiscovered:
The Dubna–Livermore collaboration reported element 116 in 2000 from calcium-48 on curium. The separator and detector were the ones used for flerovium. The chains were shorter-lived, and they stepped through element 114, which gave the new nucleus a daughter already on the board.

Livermorium was discovered by that connection. A chain that passes through an element just established is easier to trust than a chain that ends in fission with no named daughter. Curium plus calcium-48 was the reaction. The pixel and the clock were the method.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Livermorium is subject to the same limit. Even proton number can make some isotopes slightly longer-lived than their odd neighbors, and the longer life is still milliseconds. Nothing accumulates.

The atoms were produced from calcium-48 on curium and identified by their decay chains. A neutron-star merger is the cosmic event that builds the heaviest surviving elements, uranium and thorium among them. Livermorium is beyond that surviving set.

trivia.title: Calcium on Curium
trivia.summary: Dubna and Livermore changed the target to curium, kept the calcium beam, and reported element 116.
trivia.story: In the year 2000, Dubna and Livermore sent calcium-48 into curium and reported element 116. Curium, named for the Curies, had become a target for a nucleus far beyond anything the Curies could have weighed. The product lived and died in the detector. A few atoms, a decay chain, and a partnership between a Russian laboratory and a California one were the whole event. Element 116 was real as a nuclear observation and absent as a material. The year was 2000, and the calcium-48 beam was already the favored way upward.

trivia.title: A Laboratory and Not a Surname
trivia.summary: The name proposed for element 116 sounds like a person, and it actually points at a laboratory and its city.
trivia.story: The name livermorium, adopted in 2012, honors Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. It also recalls the city of Livermore, where that laboratory stands. It is not the name of a person called Livermore. The word pairs the American partner with flerovium, which had honored the Russian laboratory and Georgy Flerov. Two element names thus share the credit of a collaboration, one for each home of the work. Students who hear a person's surname in livermorium should look again, because the honor belongs to the laboratory and the city.

trivia.title: Pairing the Two Laboratories
trivia.summary: When the names for elements 114 and 116 were chosen, each partner in the collaboration received a public word.
trivia.story: Flerovium pointed to Dubna, and livermorium pointed to Livermore. The pairing was a neat ending to years of joint papers. Oganessian's program and the American team had shared targets, beams, and authorship. The names made that sharing visible to students who will never read the original articles. Element 116's title is a laboratory, a city, and a reminder that the atoms were made by a partnership. The 2000 curium experiment and the 2012 name belong together, a joint discovery labeled for the American home of the work.

trivia.title: Gone in Milliseconds
trivia.summary: Element 116 disappears so quickly that the only facts on record are nuclear, written in the decays.
trivia.story: The atoms of livermorium disappear within milliseconds. The recorded facts are nuclear: the energies of the decays, and a small extra lifetime for some isotopes that have an even number of protons. Slightly longer, in this country of the table, still means far too short to see. Livermorium is the analog of polonium by its column, and that is a map rather than a measured metal. No reaction was bottled, and no use was found. Even the slightly longer isotopes are still gone before a chemist could trap them in a flask.

trivia.title: Polonium's Empty Seat
trivia.summary: The table seats element 116 under polonium, and the seat has never held a sample anyone could study at leisure.
trivia.story: Polonium is already a rare and radioactive element, and livermorium is only a predicted heavy relative. The 2000 experiment did not produce a flake of metal or a solution in a tube. Dubna and Livermore produced decays. The 2012 name gave those decays a public word tied to the American laboratory. Students should leave the story with the partnership, the milliseconds, and the certainty that chemistry here has not been done in bulk. The 2000 chains and the 2012 name are the record, and a stored sample is not part of it.

applications.body: Livermorium is made by firing calcium at curium. The method is the same family of reactions that built this part of the table.

applications.body: Livermorium sits under polonium, which is already highly radioactive. Element 116 is rarer and shorter-lived. It has no use as a substance.

applications.body: The name honors Livermore, California, a partner in the discovery. The result is a decay chain, not a sample.

elements.name: Tennessine

summary.beginner:
Tennessine is element 117, named for Tennessee. It was made from berkelium and calcium, and the atoms disappear almost immediately.

Its symbol is Ts. At room temperature tennessine is a solid. It is a halogen, a reactive nonmetal in the column next to the noble gases. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 17. In class those are called period 7 and group 17.

It sits under the halogens, in the column of fluorine, chlorine, and iodine. Whether it still behaves as a halogen is an open question. There is no crystal and no vapor to look at.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral tennessine atom has 117 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Tennessine is a solid halogen in period 7 and group 17. Tennessine is the group-17 transactinide, produced from berkelium-249 and calcium-48.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p5. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 18, 7. In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1.

The berkelium target had to be made and used quickly because it decays. Only a few decay chains have been observed. Halogen character is predicted to be weaker than iodine's.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Tennessine (Z = 117) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p5. Relativistic effects are expected to make the +1 and +3 states more important than a simple At- analogy.

That is a calculation. The experimental fact is the decay chain, not a measured electron affinity.

In compounds the oxidation state to learn is --1. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

discovery.text: Produced from berkelium and calcium; named for Tennessee.

elements.history:
Element 117 required a target of berkelium-249, which had to be made in a reactor at Oak Ridge and shipped to Dubna before it decayed. The Dubna–Livermore–Oak Ridge collaboration reported the element in 2010. The name tennessine, for Tennessee, was adopted in 2016, in the halogen pattern of names ending in -ine.

Tennessine is the analog of astatine. Only a handful of atoms have been made. Its chemistry is a prediction: a halogen in name, probably more metallic than iodine, and impossible to bottle.
elements.howDiscovered:
Element 117 required a target of berkelium-249, which Oak Ridge made in a reactor and shipped to Dubna before it decayed. In 2010 the Dubna–Livermore–Oak Ridge collaboration bombarded that target with calcium-48. The separator delivered recoils whose decay chains included a new step, element 117, and then passed through element 115 and downward.

Tennessine was discovered by those chains, and by a second campaign that produced more of them. The target’s own half-life was part of the experiment: wait too long, and the berkelium is gone. The evidence was the same kind of correlated decays used for the neighboring superheavies, on a target that had to be manufactured first.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Tennessine would have to be assembled and then survive both fission and a very short lifetime. No isotope known lives long enough to be a mineral, and the rapid process is not expected to populate proton number 117 in the ejecta that mixes into the Galaxy.

The atoms that have been counted were made from calcium-48 on berkelium-249, a target that itself had to be manufactured in a reactor before it decayed. Both the target and the product are laboratory nuclei. There is no original cosmic tennessine.

trivia.title: Waiting on Berkelium
trivia.summary: Element 117 could not be attempted until a special target existed, and that target was already running out of time.
trivia.story: Tennessine had to wait for a berkelium-249 target, and only a reactor at Oak Ridge could prepare that target in time. Berkelium-249 decays, so the target was in a race against its own half-life from the moment it was created. Oak Ridge could not make it and then wait for a convenient season. The collaboration needed the material at Dubna while it was still the right isotope. The tense episode of tennessine begins before the beam, in the wait for a target that would not keep.

trivia.title: Shipped before It Faded
trivia.summary: A berkelium target left Tennessee for Russia, and everyone involved knew the isotope was ticking downward.
trivia.story: The berkelium target was shipped from Oak Ridge to Dubna before it decayed away. Yuri Oganessian and the Dubna team, with Livermore and with Hamilton and colleagues at Vanderbilt, were ready for that arrival. The 2010 experiment used calcium-48 on the berkelium. A handful of atoms of element 117 appeared in the decay data. Then they were gone, which is the only ending these experiments have. Oak Ridge's timing, Dubna's beam, and a handful of decays in 2010 are what made tennessine real.

trivia.title: Tennessee on the Table
trivia.summary: Element 117 took its name from the state that had produced the essential target, following an old halogen pattern.
trivia.story: The name tennessine, for Tennessee, was adopted in 2016. The ending -ine follows the halogen pattern, the same pattern as chlorine, bromine, and iodine. Oak Ridge had made the berkelium, so the state name recognized that role as well as the American partners. Dubna had run the beam, and the name pointed to Tennessee. Tennessine is a place name with a chemical ending, and it is not a substance anyone has bottled. The -ine ending marks the halogen column, and the atoms never lasted long enough to test that kinship in a flask.

trivia.title: A Handful and a Prediction
trivia.summary: Only a few atoms of element 117 have been made, and any sentence about its chemistry is a forecast.
trivia.story: Only a handful of tennessine atoms have been made. It is the analog of astatine, a halogen in the naming pattern. Its chemistry is a prediction: probably more metallic than iodine, and impossible to bottle. No measurement of a compound sits behind that sentence. The real story is the berkelium target, the 2010 collaboration, and atoms that decayed before a chemist could keep them. Astatine is the element above it on the chart, and a more metallic character than iodine is only a forecast.

trivia.title: Four Partners One Element
trivia.summary: Element 117 carried the names of several laboratories because no single campus could have supplied every piece.
trivia.story: The discovery is credited to a Dubna, Livermore, and Oak Ridge collaboration, with Vanderbilt among the partners. Oganessian led the heavy-element tradition at Dubna, and Hamilton was among the American scientists on the effort. Oak Ridge supplied the target that nobody else could readily provide in time. Livermore shared the long partnership on calcium-48 experiments. Tennessine is what those partners saw in 2010: a few atoms, a decay chain, and a name that remembers Tennessee. No single campus owned every piece of that experiment.

applications.title: Made from berkelium
applications.body: Tennessine was produced by crashing calcium into a berkelium target. The target itself was a campaign, because berkelium decays.

applications.title: A halogen, maybe
applications.body: Tennessine sits in the halogen column. Whether it still behaves as a halogen is a prediction. There is no vapor and no crystal.

applications.title: Named for Tennessee
applications.body: The name honors the state of Tennessee, home of the laboratory that made the berkelium. Only a few atoms were detected.

elements.name: Oganesson

summary.beginner:
Oganesson is element 118, the last element on the table today, named for Yuri Oganessian. It sits under the noble gases, but only a few atoms have ever been made, and they do not last.

Its symbol is Og. At room temperature oganesson is a gas, so a sample fills its container. It is a noble gas. Left alone, it almost never joins other elements to make compounds. On the periodic table it is in row 7, column 18. In class those are called period 7 and group 18.

A noble gas at the end of a row would normally be unreactive. Oganesson is so heavy that the usual rules may bend, and it might not be a calm gas at all. That is a prediction. The atoms decay in less than a second.

The picture shows the electrons around the nucleus. Each ring is a shell, a layer of electrons. A neutral oganesson atom has 118 electrons, the same number as its protons.
summary.intermediate:
Oganesson is a noble gas in period 7 and group 18. Oganesson is the group-18 transactinide, and relativistic calculations suggest it may be more reactive than a classic noble gas.

The electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p6. As shell counts, from the nucleus outward, that is 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 18, 8. Oxidation states are not listed for this entry.

It was made from californium and calcium. There is no measured melting point, density, or spectrum from a bulk sample. Teaching treats it as the end of period 7, not as a cylinder of gas.

The rings in the picture are subshells, the smaller groups of electrons inside a shell. A line joins the two electrons that share one orbital.
summary.advanced:
Oganesson (Z = 118) has the ground-state configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p6. The 7p shell is predicted to be split and destabilized enough that oganesson may be a semiconductor-like solid rather than a noble gas, if a solid could ever be assembled.

The experimental knowledge is a handful of decay chains.

Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. Only a few atoms are made at a time, so the chemistry is inferred from the column above it and from calculations that include relativity. There is no piece you can hold.

The picture estimates how tightly each subshell is held, using Slater's rules. Ring radius follows 1/sqrt(E), so a tightly held inner shell sits closer to the nucleus. These are compiled teaching values, not a measurement this device just made.

curriculum.beginner: Learn Oganesson: say the name, write Og, find Z=118 on the table, note the family (Noble gas), and connect it to one real use — research; noble-gas analog.
curriculum.intermediate: Course pass on Oganesson: electron configuration [Rn] 5f14 6d10 7s2 7p6, Oxidation states are not listed for this entry. It sits in group 18. Compare one physical number (melting point, ionization energy, or radius) with a neighbor. eka-radon; may be more reactive than radon.
curriculum.advanced: Go further on Oganesson: justify periodic trends with Z_eff and shells; read isotopes and any spectral lines as catalogued data; predicted condensed phase is uncertain; teaching, not a sample If a reaction illustration exists, treat it as a known equation, not a simulation of your lab.

discovery.text: Produced from californium and calcium; named for Yuri Oganessian.

elements.history:
Dubna and Livermore reported element 118 in 2006, from calcium-48 on californium-249, after an earlier 1999 claim from Berkeley had been withdrawn. A single atom’s decay chain was the first evidence. Further atoms confirmed it. The name oganesson, for Yuri Oganessian, who led the Dubna heavy-element program, was adopted in 2016. It was only the second time an element was named for a living person.

Oganesson closes period 7, in the noble-gas seat. Relativistic calculations suggest it may be a reactive solid rather than a gas like radon. No one has a sample. The history of the element is the history of a few decay chains and of the end of the table as it now stands.
elements.howDiscovered:
A 1999 claim of element 118 from Berkeley was withdrawn. In 2006 the Dubna–Livermore group fused calcium-48 with californium-249 and reported a decay chain of a single atom, ending in a spontaneous fission after a sequence of alphas. Further atoms, in later runs, gave chains with the same structure.

Oganesson was discovered by the repetition of that chain. One atom opened the case. The later atoms closed it. The half-lives are under a millisecond, so there is no chemistry and no second method. A recoil separator, a pixelated detector, and a beam of calcium-48 on a californium target are the whole of the discovery.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Oganesson is the heaviest element yet made, and it has no cosmic reservoir. The rapid process, the only astrophysical candidate for nuclei this large, is expected to end in fission recycling well before a nucleus with 118 protons can decay into something a solar system inherits.

The atoms reported from Dubna came from calcium-48 on californium and existed as single decay chains. Their half-lives are under a millisecond. The element was formed in an accelerator. The Universe’s ordinary channels, Big Bang fusion, stellar burning, and neutron capture, do not leave it.

trivia.title: A Claim Later Withdrawn
trivia.summary: Before the real element 118 was made, a 1999 announcement from Berkeley collapsed, and the data behind it did not survive.
trivia.story: In 1999 a Berkeley group claimed element 118. The claim was withdrawn after the data were shown to be false. Those data were Victor Ninov's, and they did not hold up when others looked closely. The episode is a serious one, and it does not need extra drama: a published result was retracted because the evidence was not real. Element 118 was still undiscovered, and the next claim would have to come from a different experiment. The false start made every later chain face a stricter kind of doubt.

trivia.title: Calcium on Californium
trivia.summary: Dubna and Livermore aimed calcium-48 at californium, and this time the decay chains belonged to element 118.
trivia.story: The report that held, published in 2006 by Dubna and Livermore, described element 118 from calcium-48 striking californium-249. A single atom's decay chain was the first evidence, a lonely proof of the kind meitnerium had once required. Further atoms confirmed the result. The retracted Berkeley claim was left behind as a warning, and these new chains were checked because of that memory. Only a few atoms were seen, and each decayed. Californium-249 received the calcium-48 beam at Dubna, with Livermore as partner, and further atoms eventually agreed with the first chain.

trivia.title: Named for a Living Leader
trivia.summary: Element 118 was named for the Dubna physicist who led the superheavy program, while he was still alive to hear it.
trivia.story: The name oganesson, for Yuri Oganessian, was adopted in 2016. He had led the Dubna heavy-element program through the calcium-48 years. Before oganesson, the only element named for a scientist who was still living was seaborgium. A living name had once been controversial, and by 2016 the community accepted it again for this leader. Oganesson remembers a scientist, a laboratory partnership with Livermore, and a handful of atoms. Seaborg had been the first living namesake, and Oganessian became the second when the 2016 name was adopted.

trivia.title: A Solid in the Calculations
trivia.summary: Element 118 sits in the noble-gas column, and relativistic calculations suggest it may not behave like the gases above it.
trivia.story: Oganesson closes period 7 and sits in the noble-gas seat, directly under radon. Calculations that include relativity point toward a reactive solid, even though radon, just above it, is a gas. The suggestion is a calculation, not a measurement, because no one has a sample. Nothing was weighed, melted, or bottled. What the record actually contains is a few decay chains, and then the table, as it stands, comes to an end. Under radon on the chart, oganesson keeps a noble-gas seat while the calculations talk about a reactive solid.

trivia.title: A Few Chains and a Closed Row
trivia.summary: With element 118 confirmed, the seventh row of the table had a last square, filled by atoms that no one kept.
trivia.story: The seventh period ends at oganesson, a noble-gas position occupied by a nucleus seen only a few times. Dubna and Livermore's 2006 report, coming after the withdrawn 1999 claim, is the discovery the record keeps. The atoms decayed. Calculations may argue about a solid, and experiments have not produced one. What remains is a name for Oganessian, a partnership, and the last square of the table we have. The withdrawn 1999 claim remains the cautionary chapter, and the 2006 chains are the chapter the table keeps.

applications.title: The end of the table
applications.body: Oganesson is the last element known today. It completes period 7, under the noble gases.

applications.title: A few atoms
applications.body: It was made from californium and calcium, a few atoms at a time. They decay in less than a second. There is no cylinder of oganesson.

applications.title: Maybe not a noble gas
applications.body: Calculations suggest oganesson may be more reactive than radon, and perhaps not a gas at all, if anyone could ever gather it. The measured fact is the decay chain. The chemistry is still a prediction.
